Immediately remove and destroy all infected plants showing little leaf symptoms to prevent spread. Control the brown leafhopper vector to stop disease transmission. Do not keep infected plants as they serve as disease reservoirs.

Dipping seedling roots in Carbofuran 0.2% solution for 15-20 minutes before transplanting provides systemic protection for 3-4 weeks. This kills brown leafhoppers that feed on young plants, preventing early transmission of little leaf phytoplasma. This critical early protection helps plants establish without infection.

This is Bacterial Wilt (Pseudomonas solanacearum). Use resistant varieties. Practice crop rotation with cruciferous crops. Remove and destroy infected plants. Apply copper fungicides. Control nematodes which increase infection risk.
Cercospora Leaf Spot. Use resistant variety Pant Samrat. Spray Bordeaux mixture 1% or Copper oxychloride/Zineb. Remove infected leaves. Improve air circulation.
Alternaria Leaf Spot. Spray Bordeaux mixture 1% or Copper oxychloride/Zineb. Remove infected plant parts. Avoid overhead watering.
Little Leaf disease (phytoplasma). Destroy affected plants. Spray insecticides like Methyldemeton, Dimethoate, or Malathion to control leafhopper vectors. Use healthy planting material.
Damping Off disease. Treat seeds with Agrosan/Ceresin @ 2g/kg seed before sowing. Ensure good drainage. Avoid overwatering. Use sterilized soil for seedlings.
Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV). Destroy infected plants. Control weeds. Avoid planting near cucumber, pepper, tobacco, or tomato. Wash hands and tools. Spray insecticides for aphid control.
Collar Rot (Sclerotium rolfsii). Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride @ 4g/kg. Spray Mancozeb @ 2g/L. Remove diseased parts. Improve drainage to avoid water accumulation.
Fruit Rot (Phomopsis vexans). Treat seeds with hot water (50°C for 30 minutes). Spray Difolatan/Captan 0.2% or Zineb/Bordeaux mixture. Practice crop rotation. Collect and destroy infected debris.
Yes, Verticillium Wilt. Use resistant varieties. Practice 4-5 year crop rotation with non-host crops. Solarize soil. Remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid overwatering.
Begomovirus infection. Use virus-free planting material. Control whitefly vectors with insecticides. Remove infected plants early. Use yellow sticky traps. Grow resistant varieties if available.
Test soil for bacterial presence. Use resistant varieties. Practice 3-4 year rotation with cereals/crucifers. Solarize soil for 6-8 weeks. Apply lime to raise pH. Ensure good drainage.
Start spraying at first symptom appearance. Spray Copper oxychloride 0.3% or Mancozeb 0.25% at 10-15 day intervals. Continue for 3-4 sprays. Add sticker/spreader for better coverage.
Effective fungicides: Azoxystrobin 23SC @ 1ml/L, Difenoconazole 25EC @ 0.5ml/L, or Mancozeb 75WP @ 2g/L. Alternate between different fungicide groups to prevent resistance.
Hot water treatment: 50°C for 30 minutes for fungal diseases. Chemical treatment: Thiram/Captan @ 2g/kg seed. Biological: Trichoderma viride @ 4g/kg seed. Dry seeds properly after treatment.
Wash hands with soap before handling plants. Disinfect tools with 10% bleach. Prohibit smoking near fields. Control weeds. Isolate from tobacco, tomato, pepper crops. Use virus-free seeds.
Seed treatment with Trichoderma. Avoid deep planting. Ensure good drainage. Apply neem cake @ 250kg/ha. Drench soil with Carbendazim 0.1% if infection occurs. Remove infected plants.
Harvest during dry weather. Handle fruits carefully to avoid injuries. Don't harvest diseased fruits. Store in cool, dry place. Pre-harvest spray with Captan 0.2% 10 days before harvest.
Spray neem oil 5% or garlic-chili extract. Apply Trichoderma viride as soil amendment. Use copper-based fungicides (allowed in organic). Improve air circulation. Remove infected leaves.
Remove plants at first symptoms. Uproot completely including roots. Burn or bury deep (at least 1m). Disinfect tools after each plant. Don't compost infected material.
Cut stem near base, suspend in water. Milky bacterial ooze confirms. Laboratory isolation needed for definitive diagnosis. Vascular browning is key symptom.
Warm (25-30°C), humid conditions with leaf wetness. Rainy seasons increase severity. Dense planting and poor air circulation exacerbate disease.
Survives in infected plant debris, seeds, and soil. Can persist for 1-2 years. Deep ploughing and debris removal reduce inoculum.
Many weeds serve as reservoirs: Datura, Solanum nigrum, other solanaceous weeds. Control weeds in and around fields to reduce disease pressure.
Harvest healthy plants first. Disinfect tools between plants if TMV suspected. Don't touch healthy plants after infected ones without washing hands.
Combine: Resistant varieties + seed treatment + crop rotation + sanitation + balanced nutrition + timely spraying + biological control. Monitor regularly and take early action.
Use resistant varieties. Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops. Improve drainage. Remove infected plants. Solarize soil.
Spray Mancozeb 0.25% or Carbendazim 0.1%. Remove infected fruits and leaves. Avoid overhead irrigation. Practice crop rotation.
Rogue infected plants immediately. Control leafhopper vectors with insecticides. Use disease-free planting material. Remove weed hosts.
Control whitefly vectors using yellow traps. Remove infected plants. Use resistant varieties recommended by agricultural universities.
Practice crop rotation (avoid Malvaceae crops), use Trichoderma-treated FYM, and ensure proper field drainage.
Spray fungicides like Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil at recommended doses at first symptom. Remove infected leaves.
Avoid fruit injury, ensure good air circulation, and spray Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl during fruit development.
Small circular brown to grey spots appear on leaves with yellow halo. Severe infection causes leaf drying and premature defoliation.
Spray Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or Carbendazim 1 g/L at 10–15 day intervals. Start spraying at first appearance of spots.
Sunken brown spots appear on fruits which enlarge and cause fruit rot. Fruits may dry and become mummified under severe infection.
Use disease-free seeds, remove infected fruits, follow crop rotation, and avoid overhead irrigation to reduce moisture on fruits.
Spray Carbendazim 1 g/L or Tebuconazole 1 ml/L at 10–15 day intervals. Start sprays at early fruit development stage.
Leaves show yellowing, curling, stunting and mosaic patterns. Plants become bushy with reduced flowering and fruiting.
Control whitefly vectors using yellow sticky traps, neem oil sprays, and systemic insecticides like Imidacloprid at early crop stage. Remove infected plants immediately.
Plants show gradual yellowing and wilting of lower leaves, brown discoloration in vascular tissues, and stunted growth.
Use resistant varieties, follow crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops, and solarize soil before planting to reduce fungal load.
Dip seedlings in 0.2% Carbosulfan 25 DS solution before transplanting to control leafhopper vectors.
Spray Methyl Parathion 750 ml, Dimethoate 500 ml, Monocrotophos 500 ml, Endosulfan 1.0 L, or Imidacloprid 125 ml per ha at 10-day intervals.
Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately. Keep field free of weeds that host leafhoppers.

Consult State Agricultural Universities for resistant/tolerant brinjal varieties suitable for your region.
Raise seedlings under insect-proof net, control whiteflies using yellow sticky traps, and avoid planting near infected crops.
Yes, rogue and destroy infected plants early to prevent virus spread by whiteflies to healthy plants.

Crop rotation alone does not control the virus, but rotating with non-host crops reduces whitefly buildup and lowers infection risk.
Use well-drained soil, avoid overwatering, treat seeds with Trichoderma, and ensure good air circulation.
Remove infected plant parts, spray Carbendazim or Mancozeb, and avoid overhead irrigation.

Spray Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil at first sign of spots. Remove infected leaves.
Use Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl. Ensure proper spacing for air movement.

This is damping off caused by Pythium, Phytophthora, Fusarium and Rhizoctonia solani. Pre-emergence damping off causes failure of seedling emergence resulting in patchy stands. Post-emergence damping off causes toppling of seedlings after emergence, resulting in mortality. This is common in nurseries.

Change nursery site every year. Solarize soil with transparent polyethylene (25µm) sheet for 45 days during summer, or treat with formalin (5%) at least 21 days before sowing. You can also apply bioagents like Trichoderma harzianum or T. viride at 40 grams per square meter.

Treat seeds with Captan or Thiram (0.3%). After seedling emergence, drench the bed with a mixture of mancozeb (0.25%) and carbendazim (0.1%) and repeat at 10-day intervals. Give light but frequent irrigation for best results.

This is Phomopsis blight and fruit rot caused by Phomopsis vexans. Pale sunken spots with black pycnidia develop on fruits and may cover the entire surface. On leaves, circular grey spots with light centers appear, leading to yellowing and premature leaf fall. On stems, elongated blackish brown lesions form. The pathogen is seed-borne and survives in plant debris.
Collect and burn old plants as soon as the crop is over. This removes the source of inoculum as the pathogen survives in infected plant debris. Use disease-free seeds for next planting.

Treat seeds with carbendazim (0.2%). For foliar spray, use mancozeb (0.25%) or carbendazim (0.1%) or a combination of mancozeb (0.2%) and carbendazim (0.05%) or copper oxychloride (0.3%). Repeat sprays at 10-14 day intervals. Warm (25°C) and wet weather favors the disease.

This could be wilt complex. Verticillium wilt shows wilting and yellowing of foliage followed by collapse of entire plants. The pathogen is soil-borne. Infected plants become stunted, don't flower or set fruit properly. If infection occurs after flowering, flowers and fruits are deformed and drop off.
Practice soil solarization before planting and follow proper crop rotation. Use resistant varieties like Pusa Purple Long (PPL), Black Beauty and K 2282 for effective disease management.

Bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum) shows yellowing, curling and wilting of leaves, followed by plant death. The bacterium has wide host range and survives in moist soil. Disease develops when temperature is above 20°C and is more severe at 30°C or more with high soil moisture. Disease is worse if root knot nematodes are present.

Follow at least three-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops. Avoid growing tomato, potato, pepper and other solanaceous crops as they are hosts for the same bacterium. Solarize field soil for at least 45 days before planting.

Apply bleaching powder at 15 kg per hectare before transplanting. Also apply carbofuran at 1.25 kg per canal at the time of field preparation and immediately irrigate the field. Use resistant varieties or hybrids if available.

This is little leaf disease caused by Phytoplasma. The disease is characterized by smallening of leaves and shortening of nodes and internodes, giving the plant a bushy appearance. Fruiting is very rare. The phytoplasma survives on weed hosts like Datura and Vinca rosea, and is transmitted by leafhopper vector Hishimonas phycitis.

Destroy weeds like Datura and Vinca rosea from in and around the field as they harbor the disease. Dip seedlings in tetracycline (0.05%) before transplanting followed by soil application of carbofuran at 1.25 kg per canal to control the leafhopper vector.

This is cucumber mosaic virus. Whiteflies and jassids are important vectors for mosaic disease in brinjal. Infected leaves are deformed, small and leathery. Plants infected early show stunted growth. Another important viral disease is caused by Potato Virus Y transmitted by aphids.

Properly manage vectors like whiteflies, jassids and aphids. Rogue and destroy infected plants immediately. Eradicate weed hosts around fields. Use resistant varieties. Spray imidacloprid 0.5 ml per liter of water twice at 15-day intervals starting 20 days after transplanting to control vectors.

Warm weather (around 25°C) and wet conditions favor infection and subsequent disease development. The disease spreads more rapidly during monsoon or when there is frequent rain or high humidity. Proper drainage and avoiding overhead irrigation can help reduce disease severity.

Yes, in nursery bed Phomopsis vexans causes damping off of seedlings. Use disease-free seeds treated with carbendazim (0.2%) and maintain proper nursery sanitation. The pathogen is seed-borne, so seed treatment is crucial.

Wilt complex in brinjal includes Verticillium species, Fusarium solani, Sclerotium rolfsii and Macrophomina phaseolina. This disease is becoming a limiting factor in successful brinjal cultivation. Characteristic symptoms are wilting and yellowing of foliage followed by collapse of entire plants.

Disease is further aggravated if soil is infested with root knot nematodes. Nematode feeding creates wounds on roots that provide entry points for the bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum. Combined infection leads to more severe wilting and greater plant losses. Nematode management is important for wilt control.

Jassids transmit mycoplasma disease like little leaf and virus diseases like mosaic in brinjal. Apart from direct damage by sap sucking, their role as disease vectors makes them even more important to control. Vector management is crucial for disease prevention.

While whiteflies directly suck sap and lower plant vigor, more importantly they cause damage by transmitting leaf curl diseases. Infested plants show vein and leaf yellowing, mosaic of leaves, leaf curling and plant stunting. The virus transmission is the major economic threat from whiteflies.

Give light but frequent irrigation to nursery beds. Heavy watering creates waterlogged conditions that favor damping off pathogens. Light, frequent watering maintains adequate moisture without creating conditions favorable for disease development.

Yes, apply bioagents like Trichoderma harzianum or T. viride at 40 grams per square meter of nursery bed. These beneficial fungi colonize the soil and compete with or parasitize the damping off pathogens, providing effective biological control.

Treat the soil with transparent polyethylene sheet (25 micrometers thick) for 45 days during summer months. This uses solar heat to kill soil-borne pathogens including those causing damping off. Alternatively, treat soil with formalin (5%) at least 21 days before sowing.

The pathogen is soil-borne and the primary inoculum usually comes from the soil where it can survive for many years. This is why crop rotation and soil solarization are recommended as control measures. The fungus persists in soil and infected plant debris.

Infected plants become stunted in growth and do not flower and set fruit if infection is early. If infection takes place after flowering or fruit setting, the flowers and fruits are deformed and finally drop off. Early infection causes more severe yield loss.

The bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum has a wide host range including tomato, potato, pepper, tobacco and many other plants. It can also survive in moist soil for longer periods in the absence of plant debris. This is why 3-year rotation with non-solanaceous crops is essential.

Perform an ooze test: Cut the stem of a wilted plant and dip it in clean water. If bacterial wilt is present, you'll see milky white bacterial streaming (ooze) coming out from the cut stem into the water. This is a simple field diagnostic test.

The phytoplasma causing little leaf disease survives on weed hosts like Datura species and Vinca rosea. These weeds act as reservoir hosts maintaining the pathogen between crop seasons. Destruction of these weeds from in and around the field is essential for disease management.

The disease is transmitted through leafhopper vector Hishimonas phycitis. The leafhopper acquires the phytoplasma from infected weeds or plants and transmits it to healthy brinjal plants while feeding. Controlling the vector with carbofuran helps reduce disease spread.

Immediately rogue (remove) and destroy infected plants showing mosaic symptoms. This prevents virus spread to healthy plants through insect vectors. Remove infected plants along with roots and destroy them away from the field to eliminate virus sources.

Plants infected by virus in early stages show severely stunted growth and rarely produce marketable fruits. Early infection affects the entire growth cycle of the plant. Late infections may only affect upper portions while some fruit production is still possible from earlier-formed flowers.

While not detailed in this document, Cercospora leaf spot typically causes circular brown spots with grey centers on leaves. For specific management, use the same fungicides recommended for other leaf diseases - mancozeb (0.25%) or combination sprays at 10-14 day intervals. Maintain field sanitation.

Many weeds act as hosts for whiteflies and viruses transmitted by them. Removal of weed hosts around the field reduces whitefly population sources and virus reservoirs. Keep field surroundings clean to minimize whitefly migration into brinjal crop.

Use disease-free seeds and treat them with carbendazim (0.2%) before sowing. Since Phomopsis is seed-borne, seed treatment is crucial. Carbendazim protects seedlings from infection during germination and early growth stages.

Disease usually develops when average temperature is above 20°C. More severe wilting is seen at higher temperatures of 30°C or more, especially with high soil moisture. Hot, wet conditions create ideal environment for rapid bacterial multiplication and disease spread.

Pre-emergence damping off causes failure of seedling emergence from soil, resulting in patchy appearance in nursery. Post-emergence damping off causes toppling over of seedlings after emergence at any time, resulting in mortality. Both types require different management timings.

Fruiting is very rare in plants affected by little leaf disease. The disease causes smalling of leaves and shortening of nodes and internodes giving a bushy appearance. The physiological disturbance is so severe that flower and fruit development is almost completely suppressed.

Spray imidacloprid 0.5 ml per liter of water twice at 15-day intervals starting 20 days after transplanting plants. Early control of vectors (whiteflies, jassids, aphids) before virus spread is critical. Protect young plants when they are most vulnerable.

Use resistant varieties like Pusa Purple Cluster, Arka Anand, Pant Samrat, etc. Rotate with non-solanaceous crops such as maize, soybean, wheat, rice, or sesame. Avoid continuous cropping of brinjal or other solanaceous plants in the same field.
Spray Zineb 75% WP @ 600–800 g/acre in 300–400 L water, or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 120 g in 240 L water/acre. Apply at early disease onset and repeat as needed.
Spray Carbendazim 50% WP @ 120 g in 240 L water per acre at the first sign of infection. Repeat after 10–15 days if needed.
Use tolerant varieties like JC-1 and JC-2. Remove and destroy infected plants early. Control leafhopper vectors using insecticides. Avoid solanaceous weed hosts.
Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride 1% WP @ 5 g/kg seed. For soil treatment, mix 1 kg Trichoderma with 25 kg FYM and broadcast per acre. Use raised beds and avoid overwatering.

Little leaf disease shows these symptoms: small, narrow, soft yellow leaves; shortened petioles making leaves stick to stem; shortened internodes giving bushy appearance; enlarged axillary buds but shortened petioles and leaves; mostly no flowering, if present flowers remain green; rare fruiting with hard, tough fruits that fail to mature and become mummified.

For vector control: grow okra as trap crop, remove affected parts, apply phorate 10% CG @ 6000 g/acre, or spray phosphamidon 40% SL @ 250-300 ml in 200 l water/acre, quinalphos 25% EC @ 400 ml in 200-400 l water/acre, or betacyfluthrin 8.49% + imidacloprid 19.81% OD @ 70-80 ml in 200 l water/acre.

Is saal ye upay karein: 1) Bimar paudhon ko jaldi ukhad kar jala dein, 2) Datura, Catheranthus roseus, Argemone mexicana jaise kharpatawar ko nikalein, 3) JC-1, JC-2 jaise pratirodhi kismen lagayein, 4) Jassid control ke liye okra trap crop lagayein, 5) Nursery se hi healthy paudhe lagayein.

Little leaf virus tolerant varieties include JC-1 and JC-2. These varieties show good field tolerance against little leaf disease caused by phytoplasma. Contact your nearest KVK or SAU for latest variety recommendations.

Bacterial wilt symptoms include: sudden wilting and death of plants; petioles of older leaves droop down; leaves show epinasty with yellowing; stunting of whole plant; typical browning of vascular tissues in roots and stems; whitish bacterial ooze from cross sections of infected plants.

Grow resistant varieties like Pusa Purple Cluster, Pusa Anupama, Arka Anand, Arka Keshav. Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous hosts like maize, soybean, wheat, rice, gingelly. Use green manuring with Brassica sp (biofumigation). Apply soil solarization with transparent polyethylene sheet (125 µm) for 8-10 weeks during March-June in nurseries.

Biological control ke liye: 1) Neem cake ka istemal karein, 2) 1 kg Trichoderma viride 1% WP ko 25 kg FYM mein milayein aur ek acre mein uniformly failayein, 3) Turant baad pani dein. Ye soil-borne bacteria ko control karne mein madad karta hai.

Bacterial wilt resistant/tolerant varieties: Pusa Purple Cluster, Pusa Anupama, Arka Anand, Arka Keshav, Arka Nidhi, Arka Neelkanths, JC-1, JC-2, Pant Samrat, Pant Brinjal Hybrid1. These varieties show good field resistance against Ralstonia solanecearum.

Phomopsis blight symptoms: damping-off in nurseries and collar rot on young plants; circular to irregular grayish brown spots with light centers on leaves, leaves become yellowish; dark brown oval lesions on stem with grayish centers having pycnidia; constrictions at stem base leading to canker; small pale sunken spots with concentric rings on fruits that enlarge and become watery (soft rot); black pycnidia on spots; dry rot through calyx making fruits black and mummified.

Cultural control: Procure seeds from healthy fruits followed by hot water treatment at 50°C for 30 minutes. Avoid continuous brinjal cultivation. Rotate with non-solanaceous crops like paddy-gingelly. Do summer deep ploughing to reduce inoculum. Remove and destroy diseased crop debris. Use resistant varieties like JC-1, JC-2, Pant Samrat, Pant Brinjal Hybrid1, Azad B-2.

Spray zineb 75% WP @ 600-800 g in 300-400 l of water/acre or carbendazim 50% WP @ 120 g in 240 l of water/acre. Apply when disease appears and repeat at 10-15 day intervals. Ensure good coverage of foliage and developing fruits.

Pre-emergence: Seedlings killed just before reaching soil surface; young radical and plumule killed with complete rotting. Post-emergence: Infection of young collar tissues at ground level; infected tissues become soft and water-soaked; seedlings topple over or collapse.

Raised nursery bed (15 cm height) banayein for better drainage. Zyada pani dene se bachein aur poorly drained areas avoid karein. Plug tray method aur sterilized potting mixture ka use karein. Nursery treatment: 250 gm Trichoderma viride 1.0% WP ko 50 litre pani mein milayein aur 400 sq. mt. area mein drench karein.

Seed treatment: Mix 5 g Trichoderma viride 1% WP per kg seed with minimum water, coat uniformly, shade dry before sowing. Seedling root dip: Mix 10 g Trichoderma viride 1% WP in 1 liter water, dip seedling roots for 15 minutes. Soil treatment (main field): Mix 1.0 kg Trichoderma viride 1% WP with 25 kg FYM, broadcast over acre, irrigate immediately.

Soil drench with captan 75% WP @ 1000 g in 400 l of water/acre in nursery. Apply as drench to soil before or at time of sowing. Can also be applied after disease appearance to check further spread. Ensure even distribution over entire nursery area.

Spray carbendazim 50% WP @ 120 g in 240 l of water/acre. Apply at first appearance of leaf spots and repeat at 10-15 day intervals. Also effective against Alternaria leaf spot. Ensure good coverage of both leaf surfaces.

Seed treatment very important hai kyunki pathogen seed borne hai. Seeds healthy fruits se procure karein. Hot water treatment at 50°C for 30 minutes karein. Ye seed surface par pathogen ko kill karta hai. Seeds ko shade dry karein before sowing. Ye treatment damping-off aur seedling infection reduce karta hai.

Rotate with non-solanaceous hosts. Good rotation crops: maize, soybean, wheat, rice, gingelly (sesame), and green manuring crops. For Phomopsis blight: paddy-gingelly rotation effective. Avoid continuous brinjal, potato, tomato, chilli cultivation. Rotation reduces soil-borne pathogens (bacterial wilt, Phomopsis, nematodes) and breaks pest cycles.

Summer months (March-June) mein karein. Soil ko well-moistened rakhein. Transparent polyethylene sheet (125 µm thick) se beds ko cover karein. 8-10 weeks ke liye in nurseries, 3 weeks main field mein. Edges ko soil mein bury karein for proper sealing. High temperature (45-55°C) soil pathogens, nematodes, weed seeds ko kill karta hai. After solarization, sheet carefully remove karein.

Biofumigation is growing and incorporating Brassica species (mustard, cabbage family) as green manure. Brassica plants contain glucosinolates which break down into toxic compounds when incorporated into soil. These compounds suppress soil-borne pathogens including bacterial wilt bacteria. Grow Brassica crop, at flowering chop and incorporate into soil 2-3 weeks before brinjal planting.

First spray 7-10 days after transplanting for damping-off, wilt protection. Second spray at 30 days with carbendazim or zineb. Third spray at 45 days. During flowering and fruiting, spray every 10-15 days if weather favorable for disease (high humidity, rainfall). Use combination of fungicides - don't repeat same fungicide. Stop sprays 7 days before harvest. Spray after rain.
Spray carbendazim 50% WP @ 120 g in 240 L water per acre at first disease appearance.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops like maize, soybean, wheat, rice, sesame, or green manure crops to break pest and disease cycles.
Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride 1% WP @ 5 g/kg seed, or hot water treat at 50°C for 30 minutes for Phomopsis control.
Removing and burning crop residues reduces overwintering pests and diseases like Phomopsis, mites, and bacterial wilt for the next season.
Small, narrow, yellow leaves; shortened internodes; bushy appearance; reduced flowering; and hard, immature fruits.
Sudden wilting, drooping petioles, yellowing, browning of vascular tissues, and white bacterial ooze from cut stems.
Small, pale, sunken spots with concentric rings on fruits, turning watery or dry with black pycnidia dots.
Pre-emergence rotting or post-emergence water-soaked collar lesions, leading to seedling collapse and toppling.
Circular to irregular grayish-brown spots with light centers on leaves, leading to yellowing and defoliation.
Pusa Purple Cluster, Pusa Anupama, Arka Anand, Arka Keshav, Pant Samrat, and Pant Brinjal Hybrid-1.
JC-1, JC-2, Pant Samrat, Pant Brinjal Hybrid-1, and Azad B-2 are resistant to Phomopsis blight.
JC-1 and JC-2 are tolerant varieties against little leaf disease.
Monitor weather (high humidity, rain), previous disease history, pest vector populations, and use early warning systems if available.

Powdery mildew appears as white powdery growth on tender leaves and inflorescence. The lesions turn brown after 2-3 weeks, then shrink and become dry before shedding. You'll notice drying and dropping of flowers and tender fruits. Infected apples turn dull with coarser skin, and when heavily infected show deep cracks and gradually shrivel. Tender nuts become deformed on the shell, and lesions turn grey on infected apples and nuts.

Powdery mildew thrives in cold nights followed by warm daytimes that create mist and fog in early mornings. The optimum temperature is 26°C (range 25-28°C) and relative humidity of 95% (range 80-100%). The disease spores are dispersed by wind, and rainfall actually inhibits its development. Overlapping branches without sunlight penetration and lack of rain create ideal conditions for survival.

Practice sanitation by removing water shoots underneath tree canopies, pruning branches to allow proper aeration, and clearing dropped branches and leaves to eliminate the inoculum source. These practices can reduce and delay disease occurrence for weeks. Focus on preventing overlapping branches and ensuring sunlight penetration into the crown.

Several fungicides have been recommended including sulphur dusts, wettable powders, and water-based organic fungicides. Chemical control is currently the main method for controlling powdery mildew disease in cashew plantations in Tanzania.

Infected nuts deteriorate in quality during storage, decay easily, and produce poor quality kernels when processed. The disease causes deformation on the shell of tender nuts, and infected apples show deep cracks and gradually shrivel and dry up.

Powdery mildew is caused by Oidium anacardii Noack, a fungus of the genus Odium belonging to Deuteromycotina (Fungi Imperfecti). The disease is not dormant and can occur on the tree canopy year-round through wind dispersal.

Perennation and survival of the pathogen from one season to another occurs in fallen infested leaves, water shoots, and off-season flowers. The disease is not dormant and can persist on the tree canopy throughout the year.

Yes, cashew varieties partially resistant to powdery mildew have been developed in Tanzania. These improved varieties have a certain level of resistance or tolerance compared to unimproved varieties. They are commercialized and available to farmers as grafted seedlings through Cashew Development Centres (CDCs) and Polyclonal Seed Orchards.

Anthracnose shows early symptoms of reddish-brown shiny water-soaked lesions and resin exudation on affected parts. Infected shoots appear as 'hanging nuts' which may act as disease sources for the next season. The disease attacks all young and tender vegetative organs including nuts and pseudo fruits/apples.

Anthracnose is caused by the fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporoides Penz. This fungal disease not only affects cashew but also infects other tropical fruit trees including mango, citrus, avocado, and papaya.

Anthracnose is favored by high relative humidity of 95-100% and temperatures ranging between 22°C and 28°C during the flowering and fruiting period. These conditions create an ideal environment for disease development.

Yes, cashew varieties resistant or partially resistant to anthracnose have been developed in Tanzania. These varieties have been commercialized and are available to farmers as grafted seedlings from Cashew Development Centres.

Dieback symptoms include withering of panicles followed by progressive dieback of small flower stalks starting from the tips and advancing downward to the main floral shoots. The normal greenish color of healthy shoots progressively turns brown, resulting in flower loss. Infected young nuts and apples become black and fluffy, remaining attached to floral stalks. Heavy infection appears similar to fire damage.

Cashew dieback is caused by the fungus Phomopsis anacardii Early and Punithalingam. The disease is believed to be facilitated by damage caused by mirid (Helopeltis spp) or coconut bug (Pseudotheraptus wayii) on cashew plants.

Damage caused by insect attacks from Helopeltis spp or Pseudotheraptus wayii are considered predisposing factors to dieback infection. The fungus attacks young and tender shoots and flowers following insect damage, with dieback infection starting at tips and spreading downwards.

Pestalotia leaf spot forms angular to irregular lesions on mature leaves. The lesions are reddish-brown on the upper surface and pale gray to whitish on the underside. Over time, lesions become thinner, papery, and necrotic. They mostly appear on leaf tips and enlarge gradually, expanding downward to cover more than half the leaf. Severe infection may cause defoliation.
Pestalotia leaf spot is caused by the fungus Pestalotia heterocornis Guba. The pathogen develops optimally at temperatures between 26-28°C and relative humidity of 80-100%.
The dispersal mechanism of the Pestalotia pathogen is mainly through wind and free-running water. Masses of conidia appear on both lower and upper sides of infected leaves.
The disease can be best controlled by application of copper-based fungicides such as Kocide at the rate of 3-5 grams per liter of water at two-week intervals.

Infected plantlets cease to grow and wither gradually, showing circular water-soaked stripes on the root collar. The roots may rot, leading to lodging (falling over) of the plants. This disease mainly affects young cashew seedlings in nurseries with poor drainage or container-raised young plants.

Damping off is caused by multiple fungal organisms including Fusarium spp, Pythium spp, Phytophthora palmivora Butler, Cylindrocladium scoparium Morgan, Sclerotium rolfsii Sacc, and Pythium ultimum Trow. Most occur mainly at the nursery stage.

Ensure the nursery or land for container-raised plants is well-drained to prevent waterlogging. Seed beds can be treated by spraying with carbendazim 50% WP, Chlorothalonil 75% WP, carbendazim thiram zineb 80% WP, or cymoxanil manacozeb 72% WP.

Infected cashew leaves develop silver/grey lesions with dark reddish-brown margins that enlarge and coalesce, causing defoliation. Infected young nuts blacken, while older nuts develop characteristic dark lesions. Under favorable conditions, white spore masses of the fungus form within the nut lesions.
The disease is more active during wet weather, especially during off-season rains when severe infections affect young flushing material. Wet conditions favor disease development and spread.

Remove, gather, burn, and bury all diseased fruits, branches, and twigs left in the cashew plantation to reduce pathogen sources in the field. This sanitation practice is crucial for disease management.

Spray fungicides such as Trifloxystrobin 10% SC, Difenoconazole WG, Picoxystrobin, and Trifloxystrobin + tebuconazole. Disease control should commence when first symptoms occur, particularly during the fruiting season.
Two varieties that are tolerant or resistant to cashew leaf and nut blight have been developed: AZA 2 and AZA 17. These varieties are commercialized and available to farmers as grafted seedlings.

Infected plants show gradual loss of natural green color, with leaves turning yellow (chlorosis) on some branches. From a distance, affected trees appear yellow and green. Within three to four weeks, the entire tree wilts. The disease can spread to nearby trees until all trees in the field are wilted.

Fusarium wilt is caused by the fungus Fusarium oxysporum. The disease can cause an entire cashew plant to wilt within three to four weeks after first symptoms appear and can spread progressively through a field.

Current management includes field sanitation and destruction of infected plant parts. Some fungicides have shown positive responses in laboratory tests, and field trials are in progress. No other management options have been finalized yet, as this is a relatively new and devastating disease.

Powdery mildew infests all tender tissues of cashew trees, mainly tender leaves and inflorescence including parts not well unfolded. The disease seldom attacks old and mature leaves, preferring young, actively growing tissues.

Tanzania has developed improved cashew varieties with resistance or tolerance to major diseases including powdery mildew, anthracnose, and leaf and nut blight (AZA 2 and AZA 17). These varieties are available as grafted seedlings through Cashew Development Centres (CDCs) and Polyclonal Seed Orchards. Improved varieties generally have better disease resistance than unimproved local varieties.

Anthracnose attacks all young and tender vegetative organs including shoots, nuts, and pseudo fruits (apples). It does not typically affect mature, hardened tissues, focusing instead on actively growing plant parts.

Hanging nuts (infected shoots that remain attached) act as a source of disease infection during the next season. These infected plant materials harbor the pathogen and provide inoculum for subsequent infections.

Integrated disease management includes: using resistant or tolerant varieties, practicing proper sanitation (removing diseased materials, water shoots, and debris), ensuring good tree spacing and pruning for air circulation, applying appropriate fungicides when needed, and managing insect pests that can predispose trees to diseases like dieback.

Pestalotia lesions mostly appear on the leaf tip and enlarge gradually, coalescing and expanding from the leaf tip downward to cover more than half of the leaf. Masses of conidia appear on both lower and upper sides of the leaves.

Seed beds can be treated by spraying with carbendazim 50% WP, Chlorothalonil 75% WP, carbendazim thiram zineb 80% WP, or cymoxanil manacozeb 72% WP. This preventive treatment helps protect young seedlings from damping off pathogens.

Powdery mildew causes drying out and dropping of numerous flowers and tender fruits, directly reducing nut production. It also deforms tender nuts, causes apples to shrivel and crack, and results in poor kernel quality during processing, all contributing to significant yield and quality losses.

Disease control timing varies by disease. For leaf and nut blight, control should commence when first symptoms occur, particularly during the fruiting season. For anthracnose, focus on flowering and fruiting periods when conditions are favorable (95-100% humidity, 22-28°C). Preventive measures like sanitation and pruning should be done before the flowering season.

Powdery mildew spores are mainly dispersed by wind. Rainfall actually inhibits disease development. The disease can occur on the tree canopy year-round through wind dispersal and is not dormant at any time.

Proper spacing prevents overlapping branches and twigs that create conditions without sunlight penetration and poor air circulation. These shaded, poorly ventilated conditions are optimal for powdery mildew and other fungal diseases. Good spacing allows sunlight penetration and air movement, creating unfavorable conditions for disease development.

Yes, the anthracnose pathogen Colletotrichum gloeosporoides affects multiple tropical fruit trees. It can infect mango, citrus, avocado, and papaya in addition to cashew. This broad host range means the disease can spread between different fruit crops.

Fusarium wilt is described as a devastating disease. It can cause an entire cashew plant to wilt within three to four weeks after first symptoms appear. The disease can spread to nearby trees until all trees in an entire field are wilted, making it extremely severe.

Maintain good drainage to prevent waterlogging and damping off. Treat seed beds with appropriate fungicides. Use disease-free planting material. Ensure proper spacing for air circulation. Source grafted seedlings from certified Cashew Development Centres that provide improved, disease-resistant varieties.

Monitor tender leaves and young shoots for white powdery growth (powdery mildew), reddish-brown water-soaked lesions (anthracnose), withering of flower panicles (dieback), irregular leaf spots with different colored surfaces (Pestalotia), and yellowing of branches (Fusarium wilt). Check during favorable disease conditions: high humidity periods, flowering and fruiting seasons, and after wet weather.

Include sanitation by removing suckers, clearing dropped branches and leaves. Also practice thinning and pruning unwanted branches to improve air circulation and sunlight penetration, which creates unfavorable conditions for the disease.

Apply Sulphur dusts and Wettable powder at 250gm per tree at 14 days intervals. Water-based organic fungicides like Triadimenol, Hexaconazole, and Penconazole can be used at 10-15ml per litre per tree at 21-day intervals. Commercial products include Intini, Sijaona 1884, Topper et al., and others.
Water-based organic fungicides such as Triadimenol, Hexaconazole, and Penconazole should be applied at the rate of 10-15ml per litre per tree at an interval of 21 days.
Clear off and burn diseased and dead shoots, leaves, fruits on trees and fallen dry twigs. Remove fruits and leaves after harvest to eliminate sources of infection for the next season.

Use Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 1ml per 0.6-0.8 litre, or Prochloraz 25% EC at 1ml per 0.8-1.5 litres. Other options include copper oxyachloride, copper hydroxide, captafol, benomyl, Anilazine, Triadimenol, and Dithianon.
Apply Chlorothalonil 75% WP at the rate of 1ml per 0.6-0.8 litre of water. This provides effective control when applied at the right concentration.
Apply Prochloraz 25% EC at the rate of 1ml per 0.8-1.5 litres of water for effective anthracnose control.
Remove all infected leaves on the entire trees as soon as symptoms are observed. This helps prevent the spread of the disease and reduces inoculum sources.

Yes, use weaver ants to control sucking pests like Helopeltis and Pseudotheraptus, which cause damage that predisposes trees to dieback infection. Biological control targets the insect vectors rather than the disease directly.

Use Lambda cyhalothrin EC 5 mls per litre, or Beta-cypermethrin 4.5% EC 1ml per 2.5-3 litres, or Dimethoate 40% EC 1ml per 1-1.5 litre, or Triallofos 90% crystal 1g per 1 litre. These target the insect pests that facilitate dieback infection.
Apply Lambda cyhalothrin EC at 5 mls per litre of water to control sucking pests that predispose cashew to dieback disease.
Apply Metalaxl Mancozeb 58% WP at 1g per 0.8-1litre, or Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 1g per 0.8-1litre. Both are effective copper-based fungicides for this disease.
Apply Metalaxl Mancozeb 58% WP at the rate of 1 gram per 0.8-1 litre of water for effective Pestalotia leaf spot control.
The nursery and the land for container-raised young plants should be well drained to stop waterlogging. Proper drainage is the most important cultural practice to prevent damping off diseases.

Apply Carbendazim 50% WP at 1g/0.5-1 litre, or chlorothalonil 75% WP at 1g/0.8-1 litre, or cymoxanil manacozeb 72% WP at 1g per 0.8-1litre. These fungicides protect young seedlings from damping off pathogens.
Apply Carbendazim 50% WP at the rate of 1 gram per 0.5-1 litre of water as a protective treatment for cashew seedlings against damping off.
Clear off, gather, burn and bury all diseased fruits and leaves infected in the field. This removes inoculum sources and prevents disease spread to the next season.

Use difenoconazole at 14g/litre, or Pecoxystrobin at 10 mls per litre, or Chlorothalonil at 14 g/l, or Trifloxistrobin+Tebuconazole at 14mls per litre. These are effective fungicides for this disease.
Apply difenoconazole at 14 grams per litre of water for effective control of leaf and nut blight disease.
Resistant varieties include AZA2 and AZA 17. These varieties have been specifically developed for tolerance or resistance to leaf and nut blight disease.
Clean the equipment after use and plant sanitized materials from authorized institutes. This prevents the spread of the pathogen through contaminated tools and infected planting material.
Source plant sanitized materials only from authorized institutes. Using certified, disease-free planting material from reputable sources is crucial for preventing Fusarium wilt introduction.
Apply sulphur dust at 250gm per tree at 14-day intervals for effective powdery mildew control. Regular application maintains protective coverage.
Copper oxyachloride and copper hydroxide are effective copper-based fungicides for anthracnose control. These can be used along with other fungicides like captafol and benomyl.

Combine cultural methods (removing infected leaves), biological control (using weaver ants against sucking pests), and chemical control (applying insecticides like Lambda cyhalothrin) to manage both the insect vectors and the disease.
Apply Dimethoate 40% EC at 1ml per 1-1.5 litres of water to control sucking pests that predispose cashew trees to dieback infection.
Apply Pecoxystrobin at 10 mls per litre of water for effective control of leaf and nut blight disease.
Yes, Trifloxistrobin+Tebuconazole is a combination fungicide that can be applied at 14mls per litre for leaf and nut blight control. Combination products provide broader spectrum protection.
Apply cymoxanil manacozeb 72% WP at 1 gram per 0.8-1 litre of water to protect seedlings from damping off pathogens.
Both traditional sulphur-based products (dusts and wettable powders) and modern water-based organic fungicides are available. Water-based options include Triadimenol, Hexaconazole, and Penconazole.
Remove and burn diseased shoots, leaves, and fruits during the growing season. After harvest, clear all fallen dry twigs, fruits, and leaves to eliminate overwintering inoculum for the next season.
Apply Beta-cypermethrin 4.5% EC at 1ml per 2.5-3 litres of water to control sucking pests that facilitate dieback infection.
Apply Triallofos 90% crystal at 1 gram per 1 litre of water to effectively control insect pests associated with dieback disease.

Pruning unwanted branches improves air circulation and sunlight penetration, creating unfavorable conditions for fungal diseases. It also removes potential disease harboring sites and improves spray coverage.
Apply water-based organic fungicides like Triadimenol, Hexaconazole, and Penconazole at 21-day intervals at the rate of 10-15ml per litre per tree.

Yes, you can rotate among Chlorothalonil, Prochloraz, copper-based fungicides, benomyl, Anilazine, Triadimenol, and Dithianon. Rotation helps prevent resistance development and provides different modes of action.
Apply Chlorothalonil at 14 grams per litre of water for effective leaf and nut blight control during the fruiting season.

Damping off is caused by multiple fungal pathogens including Fusarium, Pythium, and Phytophthora. Using broad-spectrum fungicides like Carbendazim, chlorothalonil, or cymoxanil manacozeb provides protection against this complex of pathogens.

Field sanitation removes inoculum sources by eliminating diseased plant material, fallen leaves, and debris. This reduces pathogen populations and prevents disease carry-over between seasons, making it a fundamental disease management practice.

Dieback is facilitated by damage from sucking pests like Helopeltis and Pseudotheraptus. Controlling these insects through biological methods (weaver ants) or insecticides prevents the wounds that allow the Phomopsis fungus to enter and infect the plant.

Cleaning equipment after use prevents mechanical transmission of Fusarium oxysporum from infected to healthy fields. The pathogen can survive on contaminated tools and spread during pruning or other cultural operations.
Gather all diseased fruits, branches, and twigs, then burn and bury them. This ensures complete destruction of the pathogen and prevents reinfestation from decomposing infected material.

Suckers (water shoots) create dense vegetation under the canopy that reduces air circulation and sunlight, creating humid conditions favorable for powdery mildew. Removing them is a key sanitation practice.

Multiple fungicide groups work: chlorinated fungicides (Chlorothalonil), imidazoles (Prochloraz), copper-based products, benzimidazoles (benomyl), and triazoles (Triadimenol). Using different groups helps resistance management.
Apply Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 1 gram per 0.8-1 litre of water for effective Pestalotia leaf spot control.

Combine resistant varieties (AZA 2, AZA 17), cultural practices (sanitation, pruning, thinning), biological control (weaver ants), appropriate fungicide applications at correct rates and intervals, and proper nursery management with good drainage. Use certified planting material from authorized sources.

Treat seedbeds preventively with fungicides like Carbendazim, chlorothalonil, or cymoxanil manacozeb before disease appears. Prevention is more effective than treatment once damping off establishes, as infected seedlings often cannot be saved.

Remove all infected leaves on the entire tree immediately upon observation. Prompt action prevents the disease from progressing downward from tips to main shoots and reduces inoculum for spread to other trees.

After harvest, remove and burn all fallen dry twigs, remaining fruits, and diseased leaves. This eliminates the 'hanging nuts' and other infected materials that serve as inoculum sources for the next growing season.

Record fungicide applications (product, rate, date, interval), sanitation activities (pruning dates, material removal), disease observations (symptoms, severity, location), pest control measures, and variety performance. This helps optimize management strategies and track treatment effectiveness.

Calculate based on 250 grams of sulphur dust per tree. For example, if you have 100 trees, you'll need 25 kg (100 trees × 250g) for each application. Apply at 14-day intervals throughout the growing season.

Sulphur dust (250gm per tree at 14-day intervals) is traditional and effective. Water-based organic fungicides like Triadimenol, Hexaconazole, and Penconazole (10-15ml per litre at 21-day intervals) offer longer protection intervals and may be easier to apply with spray equipment.
Mix 10-15ml of Triadimenol, Hexaconazole, or Penconazole per litre of water. For example, for a 20-litre spray tank, add 200-300ml of fungicide. Apply this mixture per tree at 21-day intervals.

Chlorothalonil 75% WP is used at 1ml per 0.6-0.8 litre of water. This concentrated rate means you'll need 0.6-0.8 litres of prepared spray per application. Adjust total volume based on tree size and canopy coverage needed.

Rotate between different chemical groups: use Chlorothalonil (chlorinated), then Prochloraz (imidazole), followed by copper-based products, then benomyl (benzimidazole), and Triadimenol (triazole). This prevents pathogens from developing resistance to any single mode of action.

Burn diseased shoots, leaves, fruits, and dry twigs away from the orchard in a designated area. After burning, bury the ash to ensure complete pathogen destruction. Never leave infected material in or near the plantation.

Lambda cyhalothrin EC at 5ml per litre or Dimethoate 40% EC at 1ml per 1-1.5 litres are cost-effective options. Compare local prices and availability. Beta-cypermethrin (1ml per 2.5-3 litres) requires less product per litre, potentially reducing costs.

Weaver ants control sucking pests (Helopeltis and Pseudotheraptus) that predispose trees to dieback. Establish colonies by transferring nests from existing populations or purchasing from suppliers. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that harm beneficial ants.

Apply insecticides (Lambda cyhalothrin, Beta-cypermethrin, Dimethoate, or Triallofos) when monitoring shows presence of Helopeltis or Pseudotheraptus bugs. Early intervention before significant plant damage prevents conditions that favor Phomopsis infection.
Remove all infected leaves immediately and burn them away from the orchard. Do not leave them on the ground or compost them, as this allows the Phomopsis pathogen to persist and reinfect trees.

Both Metalaxl Mancozeb 58% WP and Chlorothalonil 75% WP are effective at 1g per 0.8-1 litre. Metalaxl Mancozeb offers systemic and contact activity, while Chlorothalonil is purely contact. Rotate between them for comprehensive protection.

Focus on mature leaves, especially leaf tips where lesions typically start. Ensure thorough coverage of both upper (reddish-brown) and lower (pale gray) leaf surfaces since conidia appear on both sides.

Choose well-drained soils that prevent waterlogging. Avoid low-lying areas or heavy clay soils. If using containers, ensure adequate drainage holes. Sandy loam soils with good drainage are ideal for cashew nurseries.

Cymoxanil manacozeb 72% WP (1g per 0.8-1 litre) offers broad-spectrum control against multiple pathogens including Fusarium, Pythium, and Phytophthora. Carbendazim and chlorothalonil are also effective alternatives.

Ensure excellent drainage, apply fungicides (Carbendazim 50% WP at 1g/0.5-1 litre, chlorothalonil 75% WP at 1g/0.8-1 litre, or cymoxanil manacozeb 72% WP at 1g/0.8-1 litre) before sowing. Avoid overwatering and maintain proper spacing.

Use containers with adequate drainage holes. Fill with well-draining potting mix. Avoid overwatering. Apply protective fungicides (Carbendazim, chlorothalonil, or cymoxanil manacozeb) preventively. Elevate containers to ensure water doesn't accumulate underneath.

Apply difenoconazole (14g/litre), Pecoxystrobin (10ml/litre), Chlorothalonil (14g/l), or Trifloxistrobin+Tebuconazole (14ml/litre) at first symptom appearance, particularly during the fruiting season when disease is most active.

Both AZA 2 and AZA 17 are resistant or tolerant to leaf and nut blight. Choose based on local adaptation, yield potential, and availability from Cashew Development Centres. Both perform better than unimproved varieties.

The disease is most active during wet weather and off-season rains. Intensify sanitation (clear, burn, and bury diseased material), apply fungicides preventively before wet periods, and ensure good drainage to reduce favorable conditions.

The combination (14ml/litre) provides two modes of action: Trifloxistrobin (strobilurin) and Tebuconazole (triazole), offering broader spectrum control, resistance management, and potentially better efficacy than single-ingredient products.

Clean all pruning tools, cultivation equipment, and harvesting tools after each use, especially when moving between fields. Use disinfectants or flame sterilization. Plant only sanitized materials from authorized institutes to prevent pathogen introduction.

Sanitized materials from authorized institutes are disease-tested, grown in pathogen-free conditions, and certified disease-free. This prevents introducing Fusarium oxysporum into new plantings. Always request certification documentation.

Immediately remove and destroy infected plants (clean equipment after). Avoid working in infected areas when equipment will be used in healthy areas. Source replacement plants only from authorized institutes with sanitized materials.

Thinning removes excess branches, improving air circulation and sunlight penetration. This reduces humidity within the canopy, creating unfavorable conditions for powdery mildew and other fungal diseases. It also improves spray penetration.

Prune during dry periods to remove unwanted branches, improve air circulation, and eliminate disease-harboring sites. Clean equipment between trees if diseases are present. Remove suckers and water shoots regularly throughout the year.

Dropped branches and leaves harbor powdery mildew inoculum that can reinfect trees. The pathogen survives in fallen infected material and off-season flowers. Regular clearing removes these inoculum sources, delaying disease occurrence.

Apply 250gm of sulphur dust per tree at 14-day intervals using a duster or hand application. Ensure even coverage on tender leaves and inflorescence where disease attacks. Apply during calm conditions to prevent drift.

Use copper oxyachloride or copper hydroxide during wet conditions when anthracnose is most active. Copper fungicides are effective but can be phytotoxic in some conditions, so rotate with other fungicides like Chlorothalonil and Prochloraz.

Hanging nuts are infected shoots that remain attached after anthracnose infection. They serve as inoculum sources for the next season. Remove and burn them during sanitation to break the disease cycle.

Watch for withering panicles and progressive dieback of flower stalks starting from tips. When shoots turn from green to brown, immediately remove infected leaves and apply insecticides (Lambda cyhalothrin, Beta-cypermethrin, Dimethoate, or Triallofos) to control pest vectors.

Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill weaver ants. If chemical control is necessary, use selective products or spot-treat only heavily infested areas. Weaver ants provide ongoing biological control of Helopeltis and Pseudotheraptus.

Apply Metalaxl Mancozeb 58% WP or Chlorothalonil 75% WP (1g per 0.8-1 litre) at regular intervals based on disease pressure. During favorable conditions (26-28°C, 80-100% humidity), spray every 10-14 days for effective control.

Water seedlings carefully to avoid waterlogging. Use well-drained nursery beds or containers with drainage holes. Water in the morning so foliage dries during the day. Apply fungicides (Carbendazim, chlorothalonil, or cymoxanil manacozeb) preventively.

Yes, proper spacing improves air circulation, reduces humidity, and allows faster foliage drying. This creates less favorable conditions for Fusarium, Pythium, and Phytophthora. Combine with good drainage and preventive fungicides.
Obtain AZA 2 and AZA 17 as grafted seedlings from Cashew Development Centres (CDCs) or authorized institutes. These are the official sources for certified, disease-resistant planting material.

Ensure thorough coverage of both leaves (to control leaf blight) and developing nuts. Apply difenoconazole (14g/l), Pecoxystrobin (10ml/l), Chlorothalonil (14g/l), or Trifloxistrobin+Tebuconazole (14ml/l) when first symptoms appear.

Use resistant varieties (AZA 2, AZA 17) from authorized sources, ensure proper spacing for air circulation, establish on well-drained soil, implement regular sanitation (pruning, thinning, clearing debris), and plan for integrated pest management including weaver ants.

Start control when you observe: white powdery growth (powdery mildew), reddish-brown water-soaked lesions (anthracnose), withering panicles (dieback), angular leaf spots (Pestalotia), water-soaked stripes on seedlings (damping off), or silver-grey leaf lesions (leaf blight).

Begin sanitation (removing suckers, clearing debris, pruning) before the flowering season. Start fungicide applications (sulphur dust at 250gm per tree every 14 days or water-based fungicides at 10-15ml per litre every 21 days) at first sign of disease or preventively during favorable conditions.

Use equipment that provides thorough coverage of all plant parts - young shoots, leaves, fruits, and nuts. Knapsack sprayers, motorized sprayers, or mist blowers work well. Ensure proper calibration for rates like Chlorothalonil (1ml per 0.6-0.8 litre) or Prochloraz (1ml per 0.8-1.5 litres).

Regularly inspect shoots and flowers for feeding damage, wilting, or presence of bugs. Early detection allows timely application of insecticides (Lambda cyhalothrin, Beta-cypermethrin, Dimethoate, or Triallofos) or establishment of weaver ant colonies before significant damage occurs.

During off-season: clear all diseased fruits, leaves, and branches; burn and bury them; prune to improve canopy structure; and remove water shoots. This reduces inoculum for the next season when off-season rains could trigger leaf and nut blight.

Record: date and products for each fungicide/insecticide application, rates used, disease symptoms observed with severity and location, sanitation activities (pruning, clearing dates), weather conditions, pest observations, and treatment effectiveness. This optimizes future management decisions.

Mix wettable sulphur powder (250gm per tree) thoroughly with water to create a sprayable suspension. Apply at 14-day intervals with equipment ensuring good coverage of tender leaves and inflorescence. Keep mixture agitated to prevent settling.

Focus on young, tender vegetative growth, flowering, and fruiting stages. Anthracnose attacks all young tender organs including shoots, nuts, and apples. Apply fungicides (Chlorothalonil, Prochloraz, copper products) during these critical periods, especially under humid conditions (95-100% RH).

First, remove all infected leaves to reduce pathogen load. Then apply insecticides (Lambda cyhalothrin 5ml/l, Beta-cypermethrin 1ml per 2.5-3l, Dimethoate 1ml per 1-1.5l, or Triallofos 1g/l) to control pests. Continue monitoring and repeat as needed.

Early intervention may save some seedlings. Apply fungicides immediately (Carbendazim 1g/0.5-1l, chlorothalonil 1g/0.8-1l, or cymoxanil manacozeb 1g/0.8-1l), improve drainage, reduce watering. However, prevention through proper drainage and preventive treatment is more reliable.

Prioritize: (1) resistant varieties (AZA 2, AZA 17), (2) sanitation (low-cost, high-impact), (3) biological control (weaver ants), (4) targeted fungicide/insecticide applications based on monitoring, (5) proper timing to prevent rather than cure diseases. Comprehensive records help identify cost-effective practices.

Trifloxistrobin+Tebuconazole (14ml/l) provides both preventive and curative action with dual modes. For purely preventive, Chlorothalonil (14g/l) is effective. Difenoconazole (14g/l) and Pecoxystrobin (10ml/l) offer good systemic activity for existing infections.

Monitor for: reduced disease incidence and severity, healthy canopy with good leaf retention, normal flowering and fruiting, minimal need for curative treatments, good nut quality, and consistent yields. Compare records year-over-year to track improvement.

Deep plough in summer to destroy the fungus. Prepare raised seed beds 15 cm high with drainage channels. Rub the seed bed before sowing with slow-burn farm waste like paddy husk, tobacco stubbles, waste grass, or palmyrah leaves. Regulate watering to avoid excessive dampness and provide light, frequent irrigation.

Select scion wood for propagation that is free from infection. Take care to prevent disease introduction in newly planted plantations. Immediately prune any infected portions, followed by spraying or pasting copper oxychloride or cow dung at cut ends. Prune 3 inches below the infection site to ensure complete pathogen eradication.
Collect and burn diseased leaves, twigs, and gall midge-infected leaves. Regular sanitation helps reduce disease pressure and prevent spread to healthy tissues.
Collect and burn infected leaves promptly. Follow common cultural, mechanical, and biological practices including sanitation, debris removal, and monitoring.
It is often claimed that the primary cause of inflorescence blight is the tea mosquito bug, and fungi are only secondary organisms. Managing the tea mosquito bug helps control this disease.
Collect and burn diseased twigs and gall midge-infected fruits. Cover fruits on trees 15 days prior to harvest with newspaper or brown paper bags to protect from infection.

Rub the seed bed before sowing with slow-burn farm waste materials like paddy husk, tobacco stubbles, waste grass, and palmyrah leaves. This sterilizes the soil surface and reduces damping off pathogens.

Prune infected portions immediately, ensuring some healthy portion is also removed (3 inches below the infection site) to ensure complete pathogen eradication. Follow by spraying or pasting copper oxychloride or cow dung at cut ends.
Select scion wood for propagation that is free from infection. Take every care to prevent disease introduction in newly planted plantations by using clean, disease-free propagation material.
The primary cause of inflorescence blight is the tea mosquito bug, and fungi are only secondary organisms. Control the tea mosquito to prevent blight development.
Cover fruits on the tree 15 days prior to harvest with newspaper or brown paper bags. This physical barrier prevents anthracnose infection during the final maturation period.

Whitish or pinkish growth of fungus appears on affected branches. After heavy rains, a film of silky threads can be seen on branches. In advanced stages, bark splits and peels off. Affected branches turn yellow and shed leaves, giving a barren appearance to portions of the tree.

The fungus penetrates into deeper tissues and causes death of shoots from the tip downwards - hence the name dieback. Sometimes only one branch is affected, but often many branches are infected, causing extensive damage.
Pathogens survive in plant debris which serves as the source of primary inoculum. The disease spreads from this debris to healthy plants during favorable conditions.
High humidity and moist conditions favor disease development. The disease is most common during October-November and is very important during the south-west monsoon period.
It is a very common disease of cashew, often assuming great importance during the south-west monsoon period. It can cause extensive branch death and give trees a barren appearance.
Disease occurs in nurseries where drainage conditions are poor. The organisms attack the roots or collar region of seedlings or both regions and cause their death.
When seedlings are infected by Phytophthora palmivora, they become pale. Water-soaked lesions appear at the collar region which turn dark and girdle the stem. Seedlings droop and ultimately die.
On leaves, water-soaked lesions can be observed in severe cases. These lesions enlarge and coalesce, often covering the entire leaf lamina.
Disease is soil-borne and the pathogen survives in soils of plantations. Primary infection occurs through soil and secondary infection occurs by conidia through rain or wind.
High humidity, high soil moisture, cloudiness, and low temperatures below 24°C for a few days are ideal for infection and disease development.

The fungus infests tender leaves, twigs, and inflorescences. It forms reddish-brown, water-soaked lesions on affected regions. Tender leaves become crinkled and fruits shriveled. Infected inflorescences turn black.
On the affected region, exudation of resin can be seen. The lesions enlarge and kill the shoots. Repeated infection of terminal shoots can lead to death of the tree over time.
The disease has been reported in epidemic form from Tamil Nadu. It is known to cause severe loss in Brazil. Repeated infections can eventually cause tree death.
Fungus survives in dead twigs and other host material for a long time, which serves as the source of primary infection for the next season.
High humidity, frequent rains, and a temperature range of 24-32°C favor the development of anthracnose disease.

The characteristic symptom is drying of floral branches. Symptoms appear as minute water-soaked lesions on the main rachis and secondary rachis. The lesions are pinkish-brown, enlarge, and soon turn scabby. Gummy exudates can be seen at affected regions.
The lesions develop into bigger patches and result in drying up of the inflorescences. The incidence is very severe when cloudy weather prevails.
Fungus survives in crop debris and survived conidia act as source of primary infection. The disease then spreads during favorable conditions.
High humidity, frequent rains, and a temperature range of 24-32°C favor the development of inflorescence blight disease.
During the south-west monsoon months of June-August, extensive leaf fall and shoot rot symptoms are observed.
Black elongate lesions first develop on the stem with exudation of gum. Later, infection spreads up and down, causing tender stems to collapse and tender leaves to shrivel up.
Lower mature leaves are infected with black elongated lesions on the midrib, which later spread to the main lateral veins and the leaf blade. The infected leaves are soon shed.
Pathogen survives in the soil. Primary infection occurs through soil and secondary infection spreads by conidia through rain or wind.
High humidity and low temperatures below 24°C favor the development of this disease. These conditions are common during the south-west monsoon months.
Bacterial blight on cassava shows blight, wilting, dieback, and vascular necrosis.
Typical symptoms of Bacterial blight on cassava leaves: blight, wilting, dieback, and vascular necrosis.
Brown spot on cassava shows circular to angular brown spots, dark borders, yellow margins, and grey centers with black necrotic lines on the underside.
Typical symptoms of Brown spot on cassava leaves: circular to angular brown spots, dark borders, yellow margins, and grey centers with black necrotic lines on the underside.
Green mite on cassava shows yellowing, mottling, death and leaf fall. Stems show a 'candle stick' effect with the loss of terminal shoots.
Typical symptoms of Green mite on cassava leaves: yellowing, mottling, death and leaf fall. Stems show a 'candle stick' effect with the loss of terminal shoots.
Mosaic virus on cassava shows chlorotic mosaic of the leaves, leaf distortion, and stunted growth.
Typical symptoms of Mosaic virus on cassava leaves: chlorotic mosaic of the leaves, leaf distortion, and stunted growth.
Healthy cassava leaves appear normal and healthy, with even colour and no spots, lesions, pustules or discoloration.

This is Cherry Leaf Scorch, a fungal disease. Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves in autumn. Ensure good air circulation by pruning. Fungicide sprays in early spring, as leaves emerge, can help protect new growth.

For Powdery Mildew, use sulfur-based fungicides, potassium bicarbonate, or horticultural oils. Fungicides containing myclobutanil or trifloxystrobin are also effective. Apply at first sign of disease and repeat as per label instructions, ensuring good coverage.

Prevent Brown Spot by cleaning up all fallen leaves and fruit debris in autumn, as the fungus overwinters there. Prune the canopy to improve sunlight penetration and air flow, which reduces leaf wetness. Avoid overhead irrigation.

Cherry Purple Spot is a fungal disease that mainly affects the appearance of the fruit. While it may not severely impact yield, it lowers market quality. Management involves fungicide sprays during the fruiting period and maintaining orchard hygiene.

This is the classic symptom of Cherry Shot Hole disease. It starts as small spots which then dry up and fall out, leaving holes. It can be caused by fungi like *Stigmina carpophila* or bacteria. Wet spring weather favors its spread.

This is Bacterial Gummosis, often caused by *Pseudomonas* species. It enters through wounds. Avoid mechanical injury to the tree. Prune infected branches well below the canker, disinfecting tools between cuts. There is no direct chemical cure; focus on tree health and wound prevention.

A silvery sheen on leaves is the key symptom of Silver Leaf disease, caused by the fungus *Chondrostereum purpureum*. It produces a toxin and eventually causes branch dieback. The fungal brackets appear on dead wood. Remove and destroy infected branches promptly, making cuts well into healthy wood.

To reduce Powdery Mildew naturally: 1) Plant in sunny, well-ventilated areas. 2) Prune to open the canopy. 3) Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which promotes succulent, susceptible growth. 4) Spray a dilute solution of baking soda (1 tablespoon per gallon of water) with a little horticultural oil as a preventative.

This is White Root Rot caused by *Dematophora necatrix*. It is a severe soil-borne disease. There is no effective cure. Remove and destroy the infected tree along with as many roots as possible. Do not replant a susceptible tree in the same spot. Solarize the soil if possible.

These are Crown Galls caused by the bacterium *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*. It enters through wounds. The galls disrupt nutrient flow. There is no cure. Prevent by buying certified disease-free plants and avoiding injury to roots and crown during planting and cultivation. Remove severely affected young trees.

Yes, these symptoms match Prunus Necrotic Ringspot Virus (PNRSV). It is spread through infected grafting material and pollen. There is no treatment. Remove and destroy infected trees to prevent spread. Always use certified virus-free planting stock.

Control Coryneum Blight with fungicide sprays. Apply a fixed-copper fungicide during late dormancy (before buds swell). Follow up with a second spray at petal fall. Fungicides containing chlorothalonil or myclobutanil can also be used during the growing season if weather is wet, at 10-14 day intervals.

Prevent Phytophthora root and collar rot by: 1) Planting on well-drained soil or raised beds. 2) Avoiding water accumulation around the trunk. 3) Using resistant rootstocks if available. 4) Applying phosphonate-based fungicides (e.g., potassium phosphite) as a soil drench or trunk injection as a preventative measure in high-risk areas.

For Cherry Leaf Scorch, the most important cleanup is in AUTUMN. Rake and destroy (burn or bury) all fallen leaves. This removes the fungus which overwinters on this debris, significantly reducing the source of infection for the following spring.

This is Whiskers Rot or soft rot, caused by *Rhizopus stolonifer*. It's a common post-harvest disease that enters through wounds. Prevent by handling fruit carefully to avoid bruising, rapid cooling after harvest, and storing fruit at low temperatures. Fungicide dips before storage can help but focus on gentle handling and cool chain management.

To control Brown Spot on fruit, apply fungicides starting at shuck split (when the old flower parts fall off) and repeat at 10-14 day intervals until harvest, especially if weather is wet. Effective fungicides include captan, chlorothalonil, or newer systemic ones like boscalid or fluopyram.

The key spray timings for Purple Spot are during the pre-harvest period. Begin applications when fruit starts to color and repeat at 10-14 day intervals until harvest, following the pre-harvest interval (PHI) of the chosen fungicide. Fungicides like pyraclostrobin + boscalid or fluopyram + tebuconazole are effective.

This is Cercospora Leaf Spot, a fungal disease. It appears when trees are stressed by poor air movement, waterlogged soil, or imbalanced nutrition (lack of nitrogen/potassium). The fungus survives in soil and plant debris, spreading under wet, humid conditions with too much sun or shade.

The Cercospora fungus survives in infected soil and old plant debris. It spreads through wind, rain splash, or contaminated tools. Conditions like crowded planting (poor air flow), excessive moisture, and nutritional deficiencies (especially nitrogen and potassium) favor its development.

1) Improve air circulation through proper pruning. 2) Ensure well-drained soil and avoid overwatering. 3) Apply balanced fertilizer (including nitrogen and potassium). 4) Remove and burn fallen leaves/debris in autumn. 5) Avoid planting in low, sandy, or waterlogged spots.

This is Bacterial Gummosis caused by Pseudomonas syringae. It creates sunken cankers that ooze gum, often at pruning wounds or bud bases. Infected buds may open then collapse in early summer. Young trees (2-8 years) in low, sandy, or wet areas are most susceptible.

Bacterial gummosis thrives in spring with high moisture, low temperatures, and splashing rain. Trees in low/sandy spots are especially vulnerable. Vigorous trees are less susceptible, while young trees (2-8 years old) are most affected. It rarely occurs in the first year.

1) Prune infected branches well below cankers, disinfecting tools between cuts. 2) Avoid pruning during wet weather. 3) Improve drainage in low areas. 4) Maintain tree vigor with balanced nutrition. 5) Copper-based sprays in autumn/early spring may offer some protection but aren't curative.

Silver Leaf disease shows twig/branch dieback with silver leaves that may develop brown edges. To confirm: cut through a thick branch (≥2.5cm), wet the cut surface - a brown stain in the wood indicates infection. The fungus Chondrostereum purpureum produces toxins that kill branches.

The fungus survives in soil and twig cankers. It spreads through spores, especially under high soil moisture and warm temperatures. Infected wood left in the orchard or poor pruning practices during wet periods increase risk.

1) Remove and burn infected branches immediately, cutting at least 15cm below visible staining. 2) Avoid major pruning in wet weather. 3) Remove dead trees/stumps. 4) Paint large wounds with pruning sealant. 5) Maintain tree health to improve resistance.

This is White Root Rot caused by Dematophora necatrix. Symptoms include yellow foliage, shriveled fruit, stunted growth. White mycelium covers small roots, then spreads upward causing bark decay with gray/black patches. Trees usually die within 1-3 years of infection.

The fungus survives in soil and spreads through water, contaminated tools, or movement of infected soil. It thrives in wet, waterlogged soil with heavy rain and temperatures of 14-17°C. Conidia spores spread via rain splash or wind to new trees.

No effective cure exists. Remove infected trees with as many roots as possible. Solarize soil before replanting. Improve drainage and avoid overwatering. Consider using resistant rootstocks if available. Isolate infected areas to prevent spread through soil movement.

This is Collar Rot caused by Phytophthora fungus. It destroys root/crown tissues rapidly. Trees may collapse suddenly or show chronic stunting for years before dying. Young trees are especially vulnerable due to smaller root systems. The fungus overwinters in infected debris.

Collar rot favors cool, wet soil (10-16°C). Poor drainage, waterlogging, and planting in low spots increase risk. Overwatering in heavy soils creates ideal conditions. The fungus spreads through water movement and infected planting material.

1) Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds. 2) Avoid water accumulation around trunks. 3) Use resistant rootstocks. 4) Apply phosphonate fungicides (potassium phosphite) as soil drench or trunk injection preventively. 5) Remove infected trees with surrounding soil.

This is Coryneum Blight or Shot Hole caused by Stigmina carpophila. Leaves show red/purple spots that drop out creating 'shotholes.' Fruit develops purple-red spots from shuck-split to harvest. Severe infections make leaves look tattered.

The fungus overwinters in infected dormant buds and small twig cankers. In spring, spores spread through splashing rain and wind during wet weather. Temperatures of 70-80°F with moisture create ideal conditions for infection.

1) Apply copper fungicide during late dormancy (before bud swell). 2) Second spray at petal fall. 3) Continue with chlorothalonil or myclobutanil at 10-14 day intervals if wet weather persists. Ensure good coverage, especially during warm (70-80°F), rainy periods.

Powdery mildew starts as circular powdery lesions on inner canopy leaves. Severe infections cause leaves to blister, shoots to distort/stunt, and fruits to develop slightly depressed areas. The fungus overwinters in buds and bark structures, spreading to new growth in spring.

Powdery mildew becomes severe during years of low rainfall but high humidity, with warm temperatures (70-80°F). Dense canopies with poor air circulation create ideal microclimates. Unlike many fungi, it doesn't require leaf wetness, thriving in humid but dry foliage conditions.

1) Prune for open canopy and good air flow. 2) Apply sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, or horticultural oils. 3) Use fungicides like myclobutanil or trifloxystrobin. 4) Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization. 5) Remove severely infected shoots. Spray at first sign and repeat as needed.

These are Crown Galls caused by Agrobacterium tumefaciens bacteria. The galls are soft/spongy (not hard), with older centers decaying. Young trees become stunted; older trees develop secondary wood rots. The bacteria survive in soil and enter through wounds.
