1) Purchase certified disease-free plants. 2) Avoid wounding roots/trunk during planting and cultivation. 3) Disinfect pruning tools. 4) Don't plant in previously infected soil without solarization. 5) Use biological control agents (Agrobacterium radiobacter K84) as root dip for susceptible varieties.

This is Prunus Necrotic Ringspot Virus (PNRSV). Symptoms vary widely: chlorotic rings, necrotic spotting, shotholes, leaf deformity, and stunting. Often only scattered leaves or single branches show symptoms. Yield reduces about 5% with normal strains.

PNRSV spreads through grafting with infected material, pollen transmission, and possibly pruning tools. Weed hosts serve as virus reservoirs. Long dry spells increase disease incidence by stressing trees. There's no chemical cure - prevention through clean planting stock is essential.

1) Remove and destroy symptomatic trees to prevent spread. 2) Always use certified virus-free planting material. 3) Control weeds that may host the virus. 4) Disinfect pruning tools between trees. 5) Avoid planting new trees near infected orchards. No treatment exists for infected trees.

Cercospora shot hole: Brown spots with reddish margins, looks 'burnt,' favors stressed plants. Coryneum shot hole: Purple spots with tan centers that cleanly drop out, affects buds/twigs. Both create holes but have different fungal causes (Cercospora spp. vs. Stigmina carpophila) and management approaches.

White Root Rot: White cottony mycelium on roots, spreads upward causing purple cankers, trees die in 1-3 years. Phytophthora Collar Rot: Attacks root crown, sudden collapse with leaves attached, favors cool wet soil. White rot has distinctive fungal mats; Phytophthora causes rapid decline in spring.

Bacterial Gummosis: Amber gum oozing from cankers at wounds/bud bases, sunken areas, worse in spring wetness. Silver Leaf Canker: No gum, shows silver leaves then dieback, wood shows brown stain when cut. Bacterial (Pseudomonas) vs fungal (Chondrostereum) causes require different management.

1) Use disease-free planting material. 2) Maintain tree vigor with balanced nutrition. 3) Ensure good drainage and avoid water stress. 4) Prune for air circulation and sunlight penetration. 5) Practice strict sanitation (remove infected debris). 6) Monitor regularly and apply targeted controls when needed.

1) Test drainage and improve if needed (add organic matter, create raised beds). 2) Solarize soil if previous disease history exists. 3) Ensure proper pH (6.0-6.5). 4) Allow fallow period or grow cover crops. 5) Avoid planting where old stone fruit trees were removed without soil treatment.

1) Rotate fungicides with different modes of action (FRAC groups). 2) Mix contact and systemic fungicides. 3) Apply at recommended rates and timings. 4) Use cultural controls to reduce spray frequency. 5) Never apply sub-lethal doses. 6) Keep records of products used each season.

Excess nitrogen promotes succulent growth vulnerable to powdery mildew, aphids, and fungal diseases. Potassium deficiency increases susceptibility to leaf spots and winter injury. Balanced nutrition with adequate micronutrients (zinc, boron) improves disease resistance. Soil testing guides proper fertilization.

1) Prune during dormant season to minimize infection risk. 2) Create open vase shape for air/sun penetration. 3) Remove dead/diseased wood first, cutting well below infection. 4) Disinfect tools between cuts when disease present. 5) Avoid leaving stubs. 6) Remove water sprouts and crossing branches.

Winter: Remove/destroy mummies, fallen leaves, pruned wood. Spring: Rake debris, monitor bud stages. Summer: Remove diseased fruit/leaves promptly. Autumn: Comprehensive cleanup of all debris before winter. Year-round: Keep weed-free, maintain clean equipment, remove suspicious trees immediately.

Cherry leaf spot appears as small circular purple to brown spots on leaves. Cream-colored fungal growth may appear on the lower surface. Infected leaves turn yellow and fall early, weakening the tree and reducing yield.

Spray protective fungicides like Mancozeb or Captan at 7–10 day intervals during rainy periods. For curative control, use Difenoconazole or Tebuconazole. Start sprays at petal fall and continue during wet weather.
Powdery mildew shows white cottony patches on leaf undersides, later covering the leaf surface. Leaves may curl or blister, and infected fruits become unmarketable and collapse during storage.

Prune to improve air circulation and avoid excess nitrogen. Spray wettable sulfur or potassium bicarbonate early. For severe infection, use fungicides like Hexaconazole or Myclobutanil at 10–14 day intervals.
Brown rot starts as light brown blossom blight and small dark spots on fruit that enlarge rapidly. Infected fruits rot, become covered with tan fungal spores, and may dry into mummies on the tree.
Remove mummified fruits and infected twigs. Spray Propiconazole, Tebuconazole, or Captan during bloom and pre-harvest. Maintain orchard sanitation to reduce disease carryover.
Fungal shothole appears as small round purple-brown spots on leaves. The center dries and falls out, leaving holes. Fruits may show sunken necrotic spots with red halos.
Prune infected twigs, avoid overhead irrigation, and improve air flow. Apply copper fungicide during dormant stage and protective fungicides during wet spring periods.
Bacterial canker causes gum oozing from branches and trunk, dead buds, leaf spots, and dieback of twigs. Severely infected branches may girdle and die.
Avoid pruning during wet or frost-prone periods. Remove infected branches and burn them. Apply copper sprays during leaf fall and before bud break to reduce bacterial load.
Crown gall appears as rough, tumor-like swellings on roots or trunk near soil line. Young galls are soft, later becoming hard and woody.
Use disease-free nursery plants. Avoid wounding roots and trunk during planting. Do not plant cherries in previously infected soil.
Fruits remain small, pale, and tasteless. Symptoms appear one year after infection. Some branches may show symptoms while others look normal.
Remove infected trees completely. Control mealybugs which spread the virus. Plant only certified virus-free nursery stock.
X-disease causes small, pale, misshapen fruits and early bronzing of terminal leaves. Symptoms often appear on only part of the tree at first.
Remove infected trees to prevent spread. Control leafhopper vectors. Use certified disease-free planting material and avoid grafting from unknown sources.
Young trees grow poorly after planting in old orchard sites. Trees leaf out but stop growing early, with weak roots and stunted shoots.
Avoid replanting cherry in old orchard soil without treatment. Use soil solarization, organic amendments, and nematode management. Plant resistant rootstocks if available.
Cherry leaf scorch shows small purple to brown circular spots on leaves. The infected area later dries and may fall out, causing early leaf drop and weakening the tree.
Collect and destroy fallen leaves, prune to improve air circulation, avoid overhead irrigation, and keep orchard clean to reduce fungal spread.
Powdery mildew appears as white powdery growth on leaf surfaces and young shoots. Infected leaves curl, become brittle, and may fall early.
Start sprays from pink bud stage and continue at 7–14 day intervals until mid-summer. Prune infected shoots in winter to reduce initial infection.
Brown rot starts as small light-brown spots on fruits that expand rapidly. Under humid conditions, tan fungal growth appears, and fruits rot or dry into mummies.
Remove mummified fruits, infected twigs, and fallen fruits from the orchard. This reduces the source of spores that cause infection in the next season.
Bacterial canker causes gum oozing from trunk and branches, sunken dark brown lesions, dead buds, and shoot dieback.
Apply full-dose copper sprays during dormant to early bud swell stage. Avoid spraying copper after bud burst to prevent leaf burn and phytotoxicity.
Small purple spots appear on leaves, which later turn brown and fall out, leaving shot holes. Young shoots may develop raised reddish specks that crack and ooze gum.
Follow orchard hygiene, remove infected twigs, and spray protectant fungicides from bud break through the growing season during wet weather.
Healthy cherry leaves are uniformly green, without spots, holes, white powder, or yellowing. Leaf surface is smooth and free from lesions.
Regular scouting, orchard sanitation, proper pruning for airflow, and timely fungicide sprays during wet periods help keep cherry leaf spot under control.
High humidity and temperatures between 10–25°C favor powdery mildew. It spreads even without free water and is worse in dense, shaded canopies.
Warm, wet, and humid weather during bloom and near harvest increases brown rot infection and spread.
The bacteria spread through rain splash, infected planting material, pruning wounds, and natural openings in buds and leaves.
Spores spread by rain splash and wind from infected twigs and buds, especially during wet spring weather.
Begin preventive sprays at bud break and continue during rainy periods through summer to protect new leaves.
Pruning improves air circulation and light penetration, reducing humidity in the canopy and slowing powdery mildew spread.
Handle fruits gently to avoid skin injuries, remove rotten fruits daily from packing areas, and disinfect grading equipment regularly.
Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock, avoid wounding trees, and select well-drained sites with good airflow.
Infected twigs carry spores over winter. Removing and destroying them reduces the infection source for the next season.
Early defoliation weakens trees, reduces fruit size and yield, and lowers flower bud formation for the next season.
Powdery mildew reduces leaf area, weakens shoots, causes premature leaf drop, and reduces overall tree vigor.
Ripe fruits are highly susceptible. Warm and humid conditions allow rapid fungal growth, causing fruits to rot just before or after harvest.
Begin preventive fungicide sprays at bud break. Repeat every 10–14 days during frequent rains. Maintain orchard sanitation and remove infected leaves after harvest.
Scout weekly during wet spring and early summer. Check lower canopy leaves first, as early symptoms usually start there after rain.
Opening the canopy by pruning improves airflow and light penetration, reducing humidity where powdery mildew thrives.
Spray at 7-day intervals during rapid shoot growth and high disease pressure. Extend to 14 days when conditions are dry and canopy growth slows.
Primary infection starts from overwintered fungal structures on fallen leaves and bark. Secondary infection spreads by wind-blown spores from infected leaves during the season.
Maintain clean orchards, avoid fruit injuries, ensure good spray coverage before harvest during wet weather, and remove infected fruits immediately.
Brown rot survives on mummified fruits on trees and orchard floor and on infected twigs, which release spores in the next season.
Avoid pruning during wet or frost periods. Disinfect tools between cuts and remove infected wood well below visible cankers.
The bacteria enter through natural openings in buds and leaves and through wounds caused by pruning, frost injury, or mechanical damage.
Start preventive sprays at bud break and continue during wet spring periods. Focus on early protection of young leaves and shoots.
Cool, wet conditions in late winter and spring favor spore production and infection of young leaves and shoots.
Comparing with healthy leaves helps farmers and vision models avoid false positives and correctly identify disease symptoms early.
Remove infected twigs, collect fallen leaves, and plan early preventive sprays for the next spring to reduce carryover inoculum.

Apply Chlorothalonil (Bravo) at petal fall for early season control - it's the standard despite being expensive. Tank mix Captan with SI fungicides (like Indar, Nova, Elite) for improved control and resistance management. Spray at 7-10 day intervals from petal fall to harvest, plus 1-2 post-harvest applications. Copper fungicides provide excellent control but can be phytotoxic - add hydrated lime as a safener. Strobilurin fungicides like Gem and Pristine also provide excellent control. Alternate-row-middle spraying reduces fungicide use by 20%.

Without control, cherry leaf spot causes severe leaf loss in mid-summer, leading to significant loss of fruit quality and yield. Fruit becomes unmarketable when severe defoliation occurs early in the season. Tree death can result when leaf spot causes early defoliation before a cold winter - trees fail to develop necessary winter hardiness. Defoliation also reduces next year's fruit production and weakens trees, making them susceptible to other diseases and environmental stresses. This disease requires control every season.

Use a wetness/temperature disease forecasting system to time fungicide sprays more effectively. This system monitors leaf wetness duration and temperature to predict infection periods. When conditions favor infection, apply fungicides preventively. The forecasting system has helped growers reduce unnecessary applications while maintaining good control. Monitor weather conditions closely - leaf spot develops rapidly during wet, humid periods with temperatures between 60-70°F. Apply protectant fungicides before infection periods begin.

SI fungicides (Sterol Inhibitors) provide excellent control: Indar, Elite, Orbit, and Rubigan work well for fruit brown rot; all except fenarimol control blossom blight. Tank mix with Captan for resistance management. Strobilurin fungicides Gem and Pristine (trifloxystrobin-boscalid) have good efficacy. Apply Iprodione (Rovral) during bloom for excellent blossom blight control, though it's expensive and now limited to bloom use only. Close to harvest, highly effective fungicides are essential as truck loads can be rejected due to brown rot.

Brown rot on unharvested fruit, particularly on un-harvested blocks left due to set-aside requirements, maintains disease at very high levels. These mummified fruits serve as inoculum sources for future infections. Harvest as much fruit as possible to reduce disease pressure. Use ethephon as a fruit loosener to help harvest a high percentage of fruit. Infested fruit is more susceptible to brown rot and other diseases, requiring increased fungicide applications. Remove and destroy any mummified fruit remaining after harvest.

SI fungicides work well: myclobutanil (Nova), fenbuconazole (Indar), tebuconazole (Elite), propiconazole (Orbit), and fenarimol (Rubigan). Strobilurin fungicides trifloxystrobin (Gem) and pyraclostrobin-boscalid (Pristine) also provide control. Sulfur can be effective and is often added at reduced rates when spraying for other diseases. Copper compounds are another option. Powdery mildew becomes more problematic in dry years, unlike brown rot and leaf spot. Monitor SI fungicide use to prevent resistance development.

Powdery mildew disrupts mechanical harvesting operations and reduces growth of young trees. The disease causes distorted leaves and reduced shoot growth, which can interfere with shaker efficiency. Unlike brown rot and leaf spot which are worse in wet conditions, powdery mildew is primarily a problem in dry years. The disease will likely increase as SI fungicide usage is reduced for leaf spot control due to resistance concerns. Establish economic thresholds, particularly for young trees where growth reduction is most critical.

Various copper formulations can be used but are not very effective due to widespread copper-resistant strains of Pseudomonas syringae. Copper can damage foliage after a few applications - use lime as a safener. Hydrated lime added with copper causes problems with alkaline hydrolysis of tank-mixed insecticides. Chemical control alone is insufficient. Focus on cultural practices: plant windbreaks around orchards to reduce wind-driven rain that spreads bacteria, maintain orchard health and tree vigor through proper nutrition and water management. Avoid planting susceptible varieties. Moderate to severe problem in sweet cherries.

Bacterial canker causes blighting of blossoms and spurs, leaf and fruit spotting, bud failure (dead-bud), and cankering of limbs and trunk. Look for sunken, dark areas on bark that may ooze gum. Leaves show brown spots with yellow halos. Fruit develops small dark spots. Infected spurs die back. Most damage occurs during wet, windy weather in spring. The disease is moderate to severe in sweet cherries, less so in tart cherries. Winter injury and mechanical damage increase susceptibility. Check new varieties for susceptibility before planting.

Armillaria root rot is a serious disease destroying some of Michigan's best orchard sites. It's an extremely long-lived soilborne pathogen with no known chemical control. Once established, leave land out of stone fruit production for at least 15-20 years. Finding management tools is critical to the cherry industry's future. Remove infected trees immediately including as much root system as possible. Do not replant cherries in same location. Screen new planting sites carefully for presence of Armillaria before establishing orchards. Research is needed on resistant rootstocks and biological control organisms.

Site selection is very important - avoid soils with poor drainage. Phytophthora is probably present in most soils and may be on nursery trees. Plant on well-drained sites or use tiling on marginal soils. Plant on berms in poorly drained areas. Use mazzard rootstock rather than mahaleb rootstock on marginal soils - mazzard is more tolerant. Chemical control with mefenoxam (Ridomil Gold) is available, fosetyl-Al (Aliette) for non-bearing trees only. Prevention through site selection is much more effective than chemical treatment. Kills root system causing tree dieback and loss in heavy soils.

X-disease is caused by a leafhopper-borne phytoplasma. Infected trees on mazzard rootstock are the source for disease spread. No chemical control is available (injectable oxytetracycline registration was dropped). Focus on eradication of alternate hosts and infected trees. Remove infected trees immediately when detected. Control chokecherry and wild plums near orchards which serve as reservoirs. PCR diagnostic methods are available but not widely implemented. Monitor for symptoms: small leaves, poor fruit set, early ripening of sour-tasting fruit. Use certified disease-free nursery stock.

Virus diseases cause high yield losses when virus-free trees are initially infected from pollen-borne inoculum, then gradual decline in yields for the remaining life of orchards. Trees propagated on virus-sensitive rootstocks can be killed when infected. Plant only virus-free certified nursery stock. Control dandelions and manage ground cover to reduce tomato ringspot virus spread by nematodes. Apply gibberellic acid (Pro-Gibb) to maintain competitive yields in infected orchards - widely used to counteract tart cherry yellows disease. Yields decline progressively without intervention.

Use Galltrol-A (Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84) as a pre-plant root inoculation. This biological control agent provides excellent control when applied properly. Dip roots or spray root systems before planting. Plant only symptom-free nursery stock - inspect carefully before purchasing. Crown gall is serious in nurseries where affected plants are unmarketable. Bacteria enter through wounds, so handle trees carefully during planting. Avoid wounding roots. Do not plant in fields with history of crown gall. No chemical fungicides are effective.

Tank mix protectant fungicides like Captan with SI fungicides to delay resistance. Loss of Iprodione (Rovral) for pre-harvest use will result in more rapid resistance development to SI fungicides. Use strobilurin fungicides (Gem, Pristine) in rotation with SI products. Establish effectiveness of full rate strobilurin and SI product mixtures. Rotate between different fungicide groups - don't rely on single mode of action. Monitor for control failures which may indicate resistance. Some control failures in well-sprayed orchards may be due to SI-resistant strains already present.

Widespread resistance to SI fungicides is currently prevalent in Michigan. Limited control can still be achieved using tank mix of SI plus Captan. Dodine (Syllit) resistance developed so it's usually not used more than once or twice per season - tank mix dodine plus Captan recommended. Impending fungicide resistance to SI fungicides could jeopardize reductions in fungicide use already made. Loss of Captan and Chlorothalonil would increase reliance on single-site fungicides, increasing resistance problems. Rotate fungicide groups and always use protectant partners. Test for resistance if control is poor.

Copper fungicides provide excellent leaf spot control but can be phytotoxic to tart cherry trees causing foliage damage and defoliation. Add hydrated lime as a safener to reduce phytotoxicity. However, lime causes problems with alkaline hydrolysis of tank-mixed insecticides. Develop field guidelines for copper use to eliminate phytotoxicity risks and increase grower adoption. Use during cooler periods, avoid high temperatures. Don't exceed label rates. Limit number of applications. Check for adverse effects on soil microbe activity. Test on small area first if unfamiliar with product or variety response.

European brown rot is rare in the Great Lakes region; however, severe outbreaks occur if susceptible variety like Meteor is planted. This disease is endemic but usually not problematic except on highly susceptible varieties. Avoid planting Meteor in regions where European brown rot occurs. On Meteor, chlorothalonil (Bravo), fenarimol (Rubigan), myclobutanil (Nova), and sulfur were not efficacious when applied on same schedule as other materials. Fenbuconazole (Indar) is highly effective. Iprodione (Rovral) provides fair control. Identify susceptibility of promising new varieties before widespread planting.

Cyprodinil (Vangard) provides control. SI fungicides, Captan, benomyl, and thiophanate methyl are not effective and may actually increase the problem. Iprodione (Rovral) is no longer effective due to recent label changes prohibiting use later than bloom. Loss of broad spectrum fungicides could lead to increased problems with Alternaria and other fruit rots. Control strategies for Alternaria fruit rot including new fungicides need development. Focus on maintaining tree health, good air circulation, and harvest timing. Remove overripe or damaged fruit promptly.

Black knot is not currently a problem in Michigan cherry orchards but is significant in New York and Ontario tart cherries. Scout for knots regularly. Remove and destroy infected limbs on trees in orchard and in adjacent fence rows or neighboring plum orchards immediately. Emphasize exclusion efforts. Chlorothalonil (Bravo) is the most effective fungicide - maintain current registration. Loss of Bravo could result in black knot becoming significant problem in Michigan. SI fungicides are not effective. Watch for disease on wild plums and remove infected material. Promote immediate eradication of any black knot infections found.

Screen powdery mildew isolates for development of SI resistance. As SI usage is reduced for leaf spot control due to resistance concerns, powdery mildew will likely increase as a problem. Rotate between different fungicide groups. Use strobilurins (Gem, Pristine) which provide excellent control. Sulfur is still effective and can be tank-mixed at reduced rates. Establish economic thresholds for mildew control, particularly for young trees where growth reduction is most critical. Monitor regularly during dry conditions when powdery mildew is most active unlike other cherry diseases.

Apply 1-2 post-harvest applications to protect leaves and maintain tree health. Early defoliation from leaf spot reduces carbohydrate reserves, weakens trees, and reduces winter hardiness. Trees can die when leaf spot causes early defoliation prior to cold winter - they fail to develop necessary winter hardiness to survive. Post-harvest sprays protect leaves through late summer and fall, allowing trees to build reserves for next year's crop and winter survival. Chlorothalonil (Bravo) is standard for post-harvest despite expense. Copper can be used with lime safener. Critical for long-term orchard health.

Establish the importance of bloom sprays to overall brown rot control. Some fungicides are only labeled for bloom use to control blossom blight. Iprodione (Rovral) provides excellent blossom blight control but is very expensive and now limited to bloom applications. SI fungicides except fenarimol control blossom blight. Chlorothalonil (Bravo) controls brown rot blossom blight but can't be used past shuck split. Bloom applications may be less critical than near-harvest sprays, but blossom blight infections can reduce fruit set. Weather conditions at bloom determine necessity - wet weather increases infection risk.

Identify sources of primary and secondary inoculum and assess their relative importance. Primary inoculum comes from mummified fruit from previous season - on trees, ground, or unharvested blocks. Blossom infections produce spores that spread to fruit. Establish the effect of wounding, inoculum density, and fruit-to-fruit contact on brown rot severity. Infected fruit becomes more susceptible to further rot. Evaluate if latent or quiescent infections of young fruits are important. Previous work shows importance in semi-arid regions. Sanitation may effectively reduce disease but cost-effectiveness needs establishment. Remove mummies during dormant pruning.

Alternate-row-middle spraying for leaf spot has resulted in 20% reduction in fungicide use. Continue to evaluate spray application strategies designed to reduce pesticide use. Use wetness/temperature disease forecasting system to time sprays based on infection periods rather than calendar. Apply only when conditions favor infection. Some growers reduced applications significantly through monitoring programs. Ensure good spray coverage - use appropriate gallonage and pressure. Adjust sprayer speed and nozzle selection. Consider canopy density and growth stage. Establish effectiveness of reduced rates with newer chemistries. IPM approach allows targeted applications.

Most damage occurs during wet, windy weather in spring. Wind-driven rain spreads bacteria. Plant windbreaks around orchards to reduce wind and rain splash. Maintain orchard health and tree vigor - stressed trees more susceptible. Winter injury increases susceptibility. Mechanical damage creates infection sites. Frost damage and hail wounds allow entry. Wet springs with temperatures 60-70°F ideal for bacterial growth. Avoid sites with poor air drainage or frost pockets. Don't plant susceptible varieties in areas with history of disease. Proper nutrition and water management reduce stress and improve resistance.

Unlike brown rot and leaf spot, powdery mildew is a problem in dry years. Doesn't require leaf wetness for infection like other diseases. Warm days (70-80°F) with cool nights favor development. High humidity helps but rain actually reduces spores. Most active during dry, warm periods with moderate humidity. Young, succulent growth most susceptible. As SI usage reduced for leaf spot control, powdery mildew will likely increase. Monitor during dry weather when other diseases are less active. Inspect new growth regularly. Sulfur works well during dry periods. Establish economic thresholds particularly for young trees.

Fruit rot control critical because truck load quantities, even entire blocks, can be rejected due to brown rot. Highly effective brown rot fungicides essential particularly close to harvest. Some fungicides only labeled for bloom blossom blight control. Recent loss of Rovral pre-harvest label will result in more rapid resistance development to SI fungicides. Must use materials with short PHI. Pristine and SI fungicides with 0-1 day PHI allow applications very close to harvest. Wet weather before harvest increases infection risk. One infected fruit can spread to many others in contact during transport. Processors have zero tolerance for rot.

Screen cherry germplasm for sources of resistance and breed for leaf spot resistance. Host resistance not currently a significant factor in commercial varieties. Variety selection important but resistance breeding needed. Some varieties may be slightly less susceptible but none highly resistant. Research priority to develop resistant varieties which would dramatically reduce fungicide use. Until resistant varieties available, must rely on chemical and cultural controls. Breeding programs working on this but commercial varieties years away. Choose varieties with good overall disease package. Don't select based solely on one disease. Consider total pest and disease pressure for your area.

Screen cherry germplasm for sources of resistance and breed for mildew resistance. Currently no highly resistant commercial varieties. Host resistance not significant factor yet. Variety selection based on mildew resistance not currently possible. Breeding programs needed to develop resistant varieties. Until available, rely on fungicides and cultural practices. Some varieties may show slight differences in susceptibility but not enough to rely on for control. Choose varieties based on overall performance package including disease, pest, and production characteristics. Consider total disease pressure for your region when selecting varieties.

Look for white mycelial fans under bark at crown and major roots. Mushroom-like fruiting bodies (honey mushrooms) may appear at tree base in fall. Trees show general decline - poor growth, small leaves, early fall color, dieback. Affected trees often in groups or expanding circles. Pull back soil from crown to check for mycelial fans - distinctive white tissue between bark and wood with mushroom odor. Black rhizomorphs (root-like structures) in soil. Trees decline over several years then die. Once symptoms appear, tree cannot be saved. Extremely long-lived pathogen - infects trees through root contact with infected stumps or roots. No chemical control available.

Trees show general decline with poor growth, wilting, small leaves, branch dieback. Kills root system causing tree dieback and loss when orchards planted on heavy soils. Crown may show dark discoloration and gummosis. Roots have dark, water-soaked appearance with rotted cortex that sloughs off easily. Feeder roots destroyed. Trees may suddenly collapse during hot weather. Most damage in low spots with poor drainage. Young trees most susceptible especially first few years after planting. Pull up affected tree to examine roots - healthy roots white and firm, infected roots dark and mushy. Minor problem if good site selection practiced.

Infected trees show small, narrow, cupped leaves with reddening. Poor fruit set with fruits ripening prematurely - 2-3 weeks early. Fruit is small, pointed, sour-tasting, and lacks flavor. Shoots show stunted growth with rosetting of leaves. Trees on mazzard rootstock are source for disease spread - survive and spread disease. Trees on mahaleb rootstock decline and die within 2-3 years after symptoms appear. Leafhoppers spread the phytoplasma pathogen. No cure once infected - remove trees immediately. Early detection important. PCR diagnostic methods available for confirmation. Monitor chokecherry and wild plums near orchards as reservoir hosts.

Gibberellic acid (Pro-Gibb or Pro-Gibb plus 2X) widely used in tart cherry production to maintain competitive yields. Application counteracts adverse effects of 'tart cherry yellows disease' caused by viruses. Yields decline progressively in infected orchards without GA treatment. Apply during bloom according to label. Improves fruit set and size in virus-infected trees. Does not cure virus but masks symptoms and maintains production. Cost-effective treatment allowing continued production from infected orchards. Eventually all orchards become infected due to pollen-borne inoculum. Start with virus-free stock but plan for GA applications as trees age and become infected.

Galls are rough, tumor-like growths on crown, trunk, or roots. Usually at or near soil line. Start small and soft, become large and woody. Young galls cream to greenish-white, turn brown and corky with age. Can reach several inches in diameter. Galls disrupt water and nutrient flow causing stunted growth above. Serious in nurseries where affected plants unmarketable. Bacteria enter through wounds during planting or cultivation. Check roots carefully before planting. Galls may not appear until second or third year. Small galls can be pruned out on mature trees but remove entire tree if severe. Prevention through use of Galltrol-A and careful handling critical.

Need to develop temperature/leaf wetness/humidity based model for predicting infection of blossoms and second model for fruit. Develop inoculum-based model for timing fungicide sprays. Closer monitoring of weather data if models were developed. Evaluate if latent or quiescent infections of young fruits important - previous work shows importance in semi-arid regions. Currently no reliable prediction models for Michigan conditions. Weather-based forecasting could reduce unnecessary applications while maintaining control. Research needed to establish infection thresholds and critical weather parameters. Temperature, wetness duration, and humidity all important but specific relationships not defined for cherries.

Research priorities: Need reduced risk fungicides to replace carbamate and B2 fungicides and for rotation with copper, strobilurin, and boscalid fungicides. Develop programs to reduce reliance on single-site fungicides and delay resistance development. Develop field guidelines for copper use to eliminate phytotoxicity risks and increase adoption. Check adverse effects of copper on orchard environment (decreased soil microbe activity). Screen cherry germplasm for sources of resistance and breed for leaf spot resistance. Loss of Captan and Chlorothalonil would dramatically impact control options, making resistance management much more difficult.

Research priorities: Test new fungicides to find alternatives to carbamate and B2 fungicides and for delaying resistance to SI fungicides. Establish effectiveness of full rate strobilurin and SI product mixtures. Identify sources of primary and secondary inoculum and assess their relative importance. Closer monitoring of weather data if models were developed. Establish importance of bloom sprays to overall control. Establish if control failures in well-sprayed orchards due to SI-resistant strains. Establish effect of wounding, inoculum density, and fruit-to-fruit contact on severity. Establish if sanitation effectively reduces disease and is cost effective. Develop temperature/wetness/humidity based models for blossoms and fruit.

Research on fundamental ways to manage this disease critical to long-term sustainability. Screen Prunus germplasm for sources of resistance since current commercial germplasm with resistance not available. Investigate use of biological control organisms for suppressing disease. Finding management tools to control this disease is critical to future of cherry industry. Extremely long-lived soilborne pathogen with no known chemical control currently. Serious disease destroying some of Michigan's best orchard sites. Once infected, land must be left out of stone fruit production 15-20 years. Research highest priority for long-term viability of cherry production in affected areas.

Research priorities: Establish susceptibility of new varieties - do not introduce susceptible varieties. Evaluate new bactericides and plant inducers. Basic studies to identify genes in cherry that control host-pathogen interactions. Improve understanding of cultural practices that influence outbreaks. Copper resistance widespread making chemical control difficult. Need alternative materials effective against resistant strains. Plant inducers that activate tree defense systems show promise. Understanding genetic resistance mechanisms could lead to resistant varieties. Cultural practices (windbreaks, vigor management) important but need better guidelines on effectiveness and implementation.

Support current efforts to sequence X-disease phytoplasma genome. New knowledge should be gained that could lead to possible control approaches. No chemical control currently available (injectable oxytetracycline registration dropped). Understanding pathogen genetics may identify vulnerable points for intervention. Could lead to development of resistant varieties through genetic engineering or traditional breeding. May identify ways to disrupt pathogen in vector or plant. PCR diagnostic methods available but not widely implemented - need to promote use for early detection. Eradication of alternate hosts and infected trees currently only management. Genomic research offers best hope for future control strategies.

Research priorities: Determine if plant inducers can prevent infection. Screen promising rootstock selections for virus sensitivity. Adapt new methods for virus resistance based on coat protein and related resistance strategies. High yield losses when virus-free trees initially infected from pollen-borne inoculum, then gradual decline for remaining life of orchards. Trees on virus-sensitive rootstocks can be killed. Plant inducers that boost tree immunity might prevent or reduce infection. Resistant rootstocks would prevent tree death on sensitive stocks. Coat protein-mediated resistance successfully used in other crops - adaptation to cherry could be breakthrough. Increase enforcement for virus-free stock from nurseries.

Screen Prunus germplasm for Phytophthora-resistant rootstocks as is done for apple rootstocks. Mazzard rootstock more tolerant than mahaleb on marginal soils but more resistant options needed. Pathogens probably present in most soils and may be on nursery trees, making site selection very important. Resistant rootstocks would allow production on sites currently too risky. Could expand suitable acreage for cherry production. Research similar to successful apple rootstock programs. Test existing rootstocks under controlled inoculation. Screen wild Prunus species for resistance genes. Develop and evaluate new resistant rootstock selections.

For shot hole disease control, apply Lime sulphur 22% SC at 0.8-2.0 liters per acre, or Captan 50% WP at 1 kg in 300-400 liters of water per acre, or Captan 75% WP at 0.67 kg in 6-8 liters of water per acre. Apply during vegetative stage for effective control.

Shot hole disease appears as brown spots on leaves that gradually expand with a reddish-brown margin. The spots occur on both sides of the leaf. As the disease progresses, the centers of spots drop out leaving holes, making leaves appear to have been shot through. Many spots make leaves look burnt and tattered.

Practice diligent sanitation and water management. Avoid overhead sprinklers or use low angle sprinklers to prevent wetting foliage. Remove and dispose of infected tissue as soon as it appears. After leaf drop, inspect plants carefully and prune infected buds and twigs with lesions. Destroy all pruned material.

Powdery mildew appears as light-colored circular lesions on leaves inside the tree canopy which develop a powdery white appearance. Lesions may coalesce to cover entire leaves. Severe infections cause leaf blistering, distorted and stunted shoots. Infected fruits may have slightly depressed areas containing fungal growth.

Powdery mildew infections become severe during years of low rainfall combined with high humidity and warm temperatures between 70-80°F (21-27°C). The disease is more problematic inside the tree canopy where humidity is higher and air circulation is reduced.

Maintain proper spacing during planting to promote good air circulation around tree canopies and lower humidity. Prune trees to open up the canopy and improve air movement. These practices create less favorable conditions for powdery mildew development.

Bacterial gummosis shows as cankers on twigs at the base of flower and leaf buds, in pruning wounds, or at the base of spurs. These cankers exude amber-colored gum. Cankers spread upward forming sunken areas in winter. Infected buds may be killed or open normally in spring before collapsing in early summer.

Ensure a suitable cherry variety and rootstock is chosen based on geographic location and environmental conditions. This prevents stress to trees which predisposes them to canker disease. Avoid planting in low or sandy spots where the disease is worse. Select vigorous, healthy planting material.

Bacterial gummosis caused by Pseudomonas syringae is favored by high moisture and low temperatures in spring. The disease spreads through splashing rain. It is worse in low or sandy spots in the orchard. Young trees 2-8 years old are most affected, while vigorous trees are less susceptible.

The first sign is twig and branch die-back. Affected leaves develop a silver luster. Later, leaves may show brown areas in the middle and edges. To confirm, cut through a branch at least 2.5cm diameter, wet the cut surface and check for a brown stain in the wood. The fungus produces toxins affecting leaves and may kill branches or entire trees.

Prune at the first sign of silvering, making cuts below the diseased area into healthy wood. Cover pruning wounds larger than 1.5cm with pruning sealer. Remove and bury or burn all infected branches, leaves and twigs immediately. This reduces disease inoculum for the following year.

Symptoms depend on tissue damage extent and speed. Crown rots advance rapidly - trees collapse and die after first warm spring weather. Leaves wilt, dry and remain attached. Chronic root infections cause reduced growth, early senescence and leaf fall. Trees may be unthrifty for several years before dying. Young trees are most vulnerable due to smaller root systems.

Plant cherry in well-draining soil to minimize water saturation. Use resistant rootstock - susceptibility varies by Phytophthora species. Plant on berms to improve crown drainage. Design irrigation to keep trunk and crown dry from sprinklers. Avoid sites with Phytophthora history when planting susceptible rootstocks. Use more frequent but shorter irrigations.

Symptoms include yellow foliage, shriveled fruit, and little or no new growth. Cottony white mycelia cover small feeder roots which decay. Mycelia grow into soil and upward in the tree, forming small pale patches under or in bark of major roots, root crown and lower trunk. Older mycelium becomes gray or black. Diseased trees defoliate and die within 1-3 years.

Establish a dry zone and prevent soil movement or water runoff from infected sites. Uproot and dispose of infected trees immediately. Remove adjacent trees that may also be infected. Remove as many root pieces from soil as possible. Trench around the infected site to break root grafts and contain the disease.

Crown gall appears as rough, abnormal galls developing on roots or trunk. Unlike hard wood galls, crown galls are soft and spongy. The centers of older galls decay. Young trees become stunted, while older trees often develop secondary wood rots as a result of the infection.

Symptoms include chlorosis, necrosis, leaf deformity and stunting. Normal PNRSV symptoms are a few rings or chlorotic areas developing into severe necrotic spotting with a shothole appearance. In late spring, scattered older leaves or entire spurs show necrotic spotting or etched rings. Sometimes one branch shows tattered leaves. Yield is reduced about 5% on infected trees.

Use nursery stock tested and found free of all known viruses. If propagating your own trees, use both virus-indexed bud wood and virus-certified rootstock. Don't introduce infected pollen into healthy orchards during pollination. Establish new plantings in large blocks, preferably distant from older orchards. Consider thermotherapy or apical meristem culture to eliminate viruses.

Rogue infected trees in new virus-indexed orchards. However, it's not economical to rogue or replant mature infected orchards unless trees are infected with the rugose strain. In severe cases with rugose strain, complete orchard removal should be considered. Monitor new plantings regularly and remove infected trees promptly.

Coryneum blight/shot hole is favored by temperatures of 70-80°F (21-27°C) and wet weather. Splashing and wind-blown rain spread the disease. The fungus overwinters on infected dormant buds and in small twig cankers. Cool, wet spring conditions are particularly favorable for disease development and spread.

Brown spots on cherry leaves can be caused by Cercospora leaf spot or shot hole disease. Spots gradually expand with reddish-brown margins. In shot hole, centers eventually drop out leaving holes. Spots occur on both leaf surfaces. When severe, many spots make leaves look burnt. Proper diagnosis is important for correct treatment.

Purple spots with tan-white centers are characteristic of Coryneum blight (shot hole disease). First symptoms appear as small red spots on young leaves which enlarge and become purple. The centers then turn tan-white before dropping out to create characteristic 'shotholes'. This fungal disease requires wet conditions to spread.
Early symptoms appear as tiny purple to reddish pinhead spots on young leaves, often starting on the lower canopy after rainfall.
Infected young shoots become stunted and deformed, with curled leaves covered in white powder. Severely infected tips may die back.
Yes. Brown rot can infect fruits earlier in the orchard and remain latent, showing symptoms only during storage or transport when fruits ripen.
Fruits remain small, pale, and tasteless. Symptoms often appear one year after infection and may affect only parts of the tree initially.
Remove infected trees, control mealybug vectors, avoid grafting from unknown sources, and plant certified virus-free nursery stock.
Affected fruits are small, pale, misshapen, and often occur on only part of the tree while the rest may look normal.
Remove infected trees promptly and manage leafhopper vectors. Use certified disease-free planting material to prevent introduction.
