Apply 1% Bordeaux mixture before monsoon starts and again 35-40 days after monsoon. This prophylactic spraying protects against Phytophthora palmivora infection which thrives in high humidity (>98%) and temperatures of 20-24°C during monsoon rains.

Yes, place Trichoderma harzianum-enriched coir pith cakes in the leaf axils of coconut palms. This biological control agent helps suppress Phytophthora palmivora and is an effective organic method, especially during monsoon season.

Look for withering of the spindle with pale color, brown and bent spear leaf, foul smell from the affected area, rotting of the bud, and eventually the palm may die. The disease is caused by Phytophthora palmivora and spreads through rain splash.

Remove all rotten tissue immediately, apply Bordeaux paste to the affected area, and cover it with polythene sheet. Also destroy all infected debris away from the field to prevent spread through rain splash and contaminated tools.

Bud Rot is most severe during monsoon season when humidity is very high (above 98%) and temperatures are between 20-24°C. The pathogen Phytophthora palmivora thrives in these wet, humid conditions and spreads rapidly through rain splash.

Look for yellowing and wilting of older leaves, internal stem discoloration when you cut the trunk, reddish-brown ooze or bleeding from the stem, and trunk rot. This is caused by Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi that enter through wounds.

Avoid any mechanical injury to the trunk as fungi enter through wounds. Improve soil drainage, apply lime or dolomite in acidic soils to maintain soil health. These practices prevent soil-borne Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi from infecting palms.

Yes, use Trichoderma harzianum for bio-suppression of Stem Bleeding. It helps control the soil-borne Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi. However, severely infected palms should be uprooted and burned to prevent spread.

Uproot and burn severely infected palms completely. This prevents the soil-borne Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi from spreading to healthy palms through root contact, soil movement, and contaminated tools.

High soil moisture, poor drainage, and wounded trunks favor Stem Bleeding. The soil-borne Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi thrive in waterlogged conditions and enter through injuries. Improve drainage and avoid trunk wounds to prevent this disease.

Bud Rot spreads through rain splash from infected palms, contaminated pruning tools, and infected debris left in the field. The oomycete pathogen Phytophthora palmivora survives in soil and plant debris.

Use integrated approach: Apply 1% Bordeaux mixture prophylactically before monsoon, place Trichoderma-enriched coir pith in leaf axils, remove and paste rotten tissue with Bordeaux paste, and destroy all infected debris away from field.

Stem Bleeding is caused by soil-borne fungi Ganoderma species and Thielaviopsis paradoxa. These fungi enter through wounds and cause internal stem discoloration, trunk rot, and reddish-brown ooze from the stem.

Applying lime or dolomite in acidic soils improves soil health and pH, making conditions less favorable for Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi. Also improve drainage to reduce high soil moisture that favors these pathogens.

Mix copper sulphate and lime in equal proportions to make thick paste. After removing rotten tissue from bud, apply this Bordeaux paste generously to the affected area and cover with polythene to prevent rain wash.

If detected early and treated properly with removal of rotten tissue, Bordeaux paste application, and sanitation, some palms may survive. However, severe infection with complete bud rotting leads to death of the palm.

Make a small cut in the trunk to check for internal discoloration. In Stem Bleeding, you'll see brownish-black discoloration of internal tissues along with reddish-brown ooze. External symptoms include yellowing of older leaves.

Early symptoms include withering of the spindle with pale yellowish color and slight drooping of the spear leaf. At this stage, immediate treatment with Bordeaux mixture and removal of affected tissue can save the palm.

Dig drainage channels to remove excess water, avoid waterlogging, and raise planting beds in low-lying areas. Good drainage prevents high soil moisture that favors Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi causing Stem Bleeding.
Timely fungicidal treatment for bud rot and leaf rot reduces rotting smells that attract weevils. Infected palms are more susceptible to weevil infestation.

For Bud Rot control, remove and destroy infected buds. Then, drench the crown and surrounding soil with a protective fungicide like Bordeaux mixture (1%) or copper oxychloride (0.25%). As a systemic treatment, apply fosetyl-Al or potassium phosphonate (20-30 ml/tree) via trunk injection or soil drench. Repeat applications pre-monsoon and during heavy rains.

Cultural management includes: 1) Avoid mechanical injury to the trunk during intercultural operations. 2) Ensure proper drainage to avoid waterlogging. 3) Remove infected bark and tissue from the bleeding patch until healthy wood is seen. 4) Solarize the wound by exposing it to sun for 2-3 days. 5) Apply a paste of Bordeaux mixture or Chaubattia paste (copper carbonate + red lead) after wound cleaning.

Effective fungicides include broad-spectrum protectants like mancozeb (0.2%) or chlorothalonil (0.1%). For curative action, use systemic fungicides like hexaconazole (0.05%), carbendazim (0.1%), or tebuconazole (0.075%). Begin sprays at disease onset and repeat at 15-day intervals, ensuring thorough coverage of both leaf surfaces.

Prevention is key as the viroid is incurable: 1) **Use Certified Material:** Plant only viroid-indexed, disease-free seedlings. 2) **Sanitation:** Sterilize pruning and harvesting tools with 2% sodium hypochlorite or 5% formalin between trees/plots. 3) **Roguing:** Immediately remove and destroy symptomatic trees (stunted growth, small, rounded nuts). 4) **Quarantine:** Restrict movement of planting material from infected areas. 5) **Avoid intercropping** with potential viroid hosts.

Initiate sprays at the beginning of the monsoon season. Use protective fungicides like mancozeb 75% WP (0.25%) or chlorothalonil 75% WP (0.2%) at 15-day intervals. If disease pressure is high, rotate with systemic fungicides like hexaconazole 5% SC (0.05%) or propiconazole 25% EC (0.1%) at 21-day intervals. Ensure thorough spray coverage. Cease applications at least 30 days before harvest.

Prevention is critical as Ganoderma is a soil-borne root rot pathogen: 1) **Avoid Injury:** Prevent mechanical damage to roots and lower trunk. 2) **Improve Drainage:** Ensure no water stagnation around the tree base. 3) **Soil Drench:** Periodically drench soil around the tree with carbendazim (0.1%) or propiconazole (0.1%) as a preventive measure in known problem areas. 4) **Biological:** Incorporate Trichoderma viride/harzianum (2.5 kg/ha mixed with 100 kg FYM) into the soil annually. 5) **Remove Inoculum:** Uproot and burn severely infected trees, including all roots, and treat the pit with formalin.

For curative control after symptoms appear, use systemic fungicides with good penetrative action. Apply carbendazim 50% WP (0.1%), thiophanate-methyl 70% WP (0.1%), or propiconazole 25% EC (0.1%). Adding a sticker-spreader improves efficacy. For best results, combine with a protectant like mancozeb (0.2%) in a tank mix. Apply twice at 15-day intervals, and remove severely blighted leaves before spraying.

Phytoplasma is spread by leafhoppers and planthoppers. Management focuses on vector control: 1) **Insecticides:** Apply systemic insecticides like imidacloprid 17.8 SL (0.005%) or thiamethoxam 25 WG (0.005%) as a soil drench or foliar spray during peak vector activity (often post-monsoon). 2) **Oil Sprays:** Neem oil (1%) sprays can act as a repellent. 3) **Roguing:** Remove and destroy symptomatic plants (showing leaf rolling, yellowing, and decline) to reduce inoculum. 4) **Weed Control:** Eliminate alternative host weeds from the orchard vicinity.

Bud rot in cashew is identified by softening and rotting of terminal buds, foul smell, black or brown discoloration of young shoots, and drying of emerging leaves. In severe cases, the growing point collapses and plant growth stops.
Spray Copper oxychloride 50% WP @ 3 g/l or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/l at 10–15 day intervals during wet conditions. Ensure proper drainage and avoid water stagnation around seedlings.

Leaf rot starts as water-soaked brown lesions on young leaves which enlarge and merge, causing rotting of leaf tissue. The affected leaves dry, tear, and may develop a fan-like appearance in severe infection.
Ensure proper spacing for aeration, prune and destroy infected leaves, avoid overhead irrigation, improve drainage, and maintain field sanitation to reduce fungal inoculum load.
Gray leaf spot appears as circular to irregular grayish spots with dark brown margins on leaves. Severe infection causes leaf yellowing and premature leaf drop, reducing photosynthesis.
Spray Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 g/l or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/l at 15-day intervals. Rotate fungicides to avoid resistance and ensure full leaf coverage.
Stem bleeding is identified by reddish-brown gum oozing from cracks on the trunk. The bark softens, internal tissues decay, leaves yellow and drop, and nut yield declines over time.

Chisel and remove diseased bark, apply Bordeaux paste (1%), improve drainage, avoid trunk injuries, and apply Trichoderma-enriched FYM around the basin. Maintain balanced nutrition to improve tree resistance.

Yellowing of leaflets in WCLWD indicates systemic infection causing vascular blockage, nutrient transport disruption, and progressive decline of tree vigor. Yellowing starts from older leaves and spreads upward.

Remove severely affected trees, control vector insects, maintain orchard hygiene, apply balanced nutrition, and avoid using infected planting material. Preventive management is more effective than curative control.
Drying of leaflets occurs due to blockage of vascular tissues, reduced water movement, and chronic stress caused by WCLWD infection. Leaflets turn brown from tips and dry completely over time.
Flaccidity indicates loss of turgor pressure due to impaired water transport in vascular tissues. It is commonly associated with systemic wilt-like diseases such as WCLWD.

Use raised nursery beds for good drainage, avoid water stagnation, provide adequate spacing for air circulation, remove and destroy infected seedlings immediately, and apply prophylactic fungicide sprays before the monsoon season.

Integrated management combines sanitation, removal of infected parts, improved drainage, balanced fertilization, and need-based fungicide sprays like copper oxychloride to reduce disease pressure and improve plant resistance.
Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/l or Copper oxychloride 50% WP @ 3 g/l at 10–15 day intervals during humid and rainy periods. Ensure thorough coverage of young leaves.
High humidity, frequent rainfall, poor air circulation, dense canopy, and water stagnation favor leaf rot development by promoting fungal growth and spore spread.
Gray leaf spot reduces leaf area through spotting and premature defoliation, lowering photosynthesis and weakening trees, which ultimately leads to reduced flowering, poor nut set, and yield loss.
Prune overcrowded branches to improve airflow, remove and destroy infected leaves, maintain proper spacing, avoid overhead irrigation, and keep the orchard clean to reduce disease spread.

If untreated, lesions expand upward and downward, internal tissues rot, the trunk becomes hollow, leaves turn yellow and shed, crown size reduces, nut production declines, and the tree may eventually die.

Trichoderma acts as an antagonistic fungus that suppresses the pathogen in soil and on wounds. Applying Trichoderma-enriched FYM or paste around affected areas helps reduce disease severity and improves recovery.
WCLWD yellowing is usually progressive, uneven, and associated with wilting and decline symptoms, while nutrient deficiency shows more uniform patterns and responds quickly to fertilizer correction.
As the disease progresses, more leaves dry and fall, canopy becomes sparse, photosynthesis declines, flowering and fruiting reduce, and the tree gradually weakens and may die.
Gently press or bend the leaves; flaccid leaves feel soft and limp, do not recover quickly, and are often accompanied by yellowing or drying, indicating impaired water transport in the plant.
Early detection allows timely intervention, reduces disease spread, lowers control costs, prevents severe yield loss, and helps maintain overall orchard health and productivity.
High humidity, continuous rainfall, poor drainage, overcrowded planting, wounds on young shoots, and prolonged leaf wetness are major risk factors that favor bud rot infection in cashew.
Raise seedlings on well-drained beds, maintain proper spacing, avoid over-irrigation, provide partial shade, remove diseased seedlings promptly, and apply preventive fungicide sprays before monsoon.
Frequent rainfall, high relative humidity, dense canopy, poor ventilation, prolonged leaf wetness, and infected plant debris in the orchard increase the risk of leaf rot in cashew.
Integrated management includes pruning to improve airflow, removing infected leaves, improving drainage, applying balanced fertilizers, and using fungicides only when disease pressure is high.
Gray leaf spot spreads through fungal spores carried by rain splash and wind from infected leaves and debris. Warm and humid conditions accelerate spore germination and infection.
Remove fallen infected leaves, maintain proper spacing and pruning for aeration, avoid overhead irrigation, and apply preventive fungicide sprays during early disease-favorable periods.
Mechanical injuries to the trunk, poor drainage, waterlogging, nutrient imbalance, and prolonged soil moisture favor pathogen entry and increase susceptibility to stem bleeding in cashew.
Removing and destroying infected bark, avoiding accumulation of infected debris, and keeping the basin clean reduce pathogen sources and slow disease spread within the orchard.
Yellowing starts in older leaves, gradually spreads to younger leaves, followed by wilting, drying, canopy thinning, reduced flowering, and eventual decline of the tree.
WCLWD is systemic and causes irreversible vascular damage; once leaflet drying is visible, the infection is advanced, making curative treatments ineffective and management mainly preventive.
Drought and heat stress worsen flaccidity by further reducing water availability in already impaired vascular tissues, accelerating wilting and drying symptoms.
Training improves early disease recognition, correct identification, proper timing of interventions, safe pesticide use, and adoption of IPM practices, leading to better control and higher yields.

Early signs include slight softening of terminal buds, water-soaked lesions at the growing tip, pale yellowing of young leaves, and a mild foul smell from the affected area before complete rotting occurs.
During monsoon, improve drainage, avoid overhead irrigation, increase field sanitation, monitor plants more frequently, and apply preventive fungicide sprays before prolonged rainy spells.
Small water-soaked brown spots on young leaves that enlarge gradually, slight rotting at leaf tips or margins, and mild yellowing around lesions indicate early leaf rot infection.
Proper pruning opens the canopy, improves sunlight penetration and airflow, reduces leaf wetness duration, and creates unfavorable conditions for fungal growth responsible for leaf rot.
Small grayish specks with faint brown margins appear on older leaves first. These spots slowly enlarge and may merge if conditions remain humid.
Begin spraying at the first appearance of spots or when humid weather is forecast. Repeat sprays at 10–15 day intervals during disease-favorable periods for effective control.
Early symptoms include small dark patches on the bark, mild oozing of reddish-brown gum from cracks, and localized softening of bark tissues before extensive bleeding occurs.
Avoid mechanical injuries, disinfect tools, chisel and clean existing wounds, apply Bordeaux paste or copper fungicide to wounds, and maintain dry conditions around the trunk base.
Regular surveillance helps detect early yellowing symptoms, identify affected trees, enable timely removal of severely infected plants, and reduce disease spread within the orchard.
Orchard hygiene reduces secondary infections, limits vector breeding sites, and prevents further stress on already weakened trees, slowing disease progression.
Provide supplemental irrigation during dry periods, apply balanced nutrients, mulch to conserve moisture, and reduce additional stresses to prolong productivity of mildly affected trees.
Use tolerant varieties, maintain soil health, adopt IPM, ensure good canopy management, improve drainage, and follow regular monitoring and timely interventions to build long-term disease resilience.

After fungicide application, maintain good drainage, avoid water stagnation, monitor for recurrence, remove newly infected tissues promptly, and apply organic amendments to improve plant recovery and resistance.
Monitor emergence of healthy new shoots, absence of foul smell or fresh rotting at the bud, gradual greening of new leaves, and no spread of lesions over 2–3 weeks after treatment.
Prune and destroy affected leaves, improve canopy aeration, avoid overhead irrigation, apply balanced nutrition to promote new healthy foliage, and continue monitoring during humid periods.
Leaf rot damages leaf tissues and creates entry points for secondary pathogens. Prolonged humidity and weakened plant defenses increase susceptibility to additional fungal and bacterial infections.
Check leaves 7–10 days after spraying for reduction in new spot formation, drying of existing lesions, no further spread to new flush, and improved leaf color and retention.
Rotate fungicides with different modes of action, avoid repeated use of the same active ingredient, use recommended doses, and integrate cultural practices to reduce disease pressure.
Look for reduced or stopped gum exudation, drying and healing of treated wounds, absence of new lesions, and gradual improvement in leaf color and canopy density over time.
Proper spacing improves airflow and soil drying, reduces humidity around trunks, minimizes waterlogging, and lowers chances of trunk injury during farm operations, reducing stem bleeding risk.
Progressive yellowing reduces photosynthetic capacity, weakens trees, lowers flowering and nut set, and leads to gradual yield decline over successive seasons.
Remove trees when more than 50–60% of the canopy is dried, productivity has dropped sharply, and the tree becomes a source of infection or vector attraction to protect nearby healthy trees.

When most leaves remain limp throughout the day, fail to recover overnight, and are accompanied by extensive yellowing and drying, flaccidity is considered severe and indicates advanced disease stage.

A RAG-based system combines vision-based diagnosis with curated agronomic knowledge to provide timely, localized, and actionable recommendations, helping farmers take correct management steps quickly and safely.
Young cashew trees are most susceptible to Bud Rot, particularly during the monsoon season when temperatures are low and humidity is very high.
The earliest symptom is the yellowing of one or two of the youngest leaves. Black spots may also appear on the spindle (spear) leaves.
The spots have irregular, water-soaked margins. When the infected leaf unfolds, these conspicuous, irregular spots become visible on the leaf blade. The basal tissues of the leaf rot quickly.
The spindle withers and drops. The tender leaf base and soft crown tissues rot into a slimy, foul-smelling mass of decayed material. Ultimately, the entire crown falls off, leading to tree death.
In seedlings, the spear leaf turns pale and can be easily pulled off with a gentle tug.
The defining symptom is the exudation of a dark reddish-brown liquid from longitudinal cracks or wounds on the trunk. This liquid trickles down for several inches to several feet.
Lesions spread upwards. The oozing liquid dries and turns black. Tissues beneath the lesions rot, turning yellow first, then black. The interior of the trunk may become hollow due to tissue decay.

Disease: Stem Bleeding Impact on Canopy and Yield
Information: The outer whorl of leaves turns yellow, dries, and sheds prematurely. Bunch production is adversely affected, and nut fall is common. In chronic cases, the trunk tapers at the apex and the crown size reduces.
The first symptom is the appearance of water-soaked brown lesions on the spear leaves (the youngest, unopened central leaves).

As the infected spear leaf unfurls, the rotten portions of the leaf blade dry out and get blown off by the wind. This leaves behind a leaf with missing sections, giving it a characteristic 'fan' shape.
In acute cases, the spear leaf fails to unfurl altogether, remaining as a rotted, closed spindle at the center of the crown.
The initial symptom is the withering, yellowing, and drooping of the outermost whorl of leaves.
A reddish-brown liquid exudes through cracks at the base of the trunk, and this oozing spreads upward over time. The tissues at these bleeding spots feel soft to the touch.

Disease: Tanjavur Wilt Basal Decay and Bracket
Information: The basal stem tissues decay and rot. The bark becomes brittle and peels off in flakes. The definitive sign is the formation of shelf-like fungal fruiting bodies called 'brackets' (Ganoderma) at the base of the trunk. The internal wood is discolored and emits a bad smell.

Disease: Root Wilt (Phytoplasma) Association with Other Problems
Information: Root Wilt weakens the tree's overall health and defense mechanisms. This makes affected trees highly susceptible to secondary diseases like Leaf Rot and severe attacks by pests like the Rhinoceros beetle and Red Palm Weevil.

There is a high chance of confusing the symptoms of Root Wilt with those caused by other pests and diseases. Accurate diagnosis requires careful observation and often laboratory testing to confirm the presence of phytoplasma.

While both may cause wilting, Bud Rot presents with specific rotting signs: black spots on the spindle, water-soaked irregular leaf spots, a foul smell from the crown, and a slimy decay of the bud tissue. Simple drought stress does not cause localized rot or a foul odor.

Disease: Stem Bleeding vs. Mechanical Injury Ooze
Information: Stem Bleeding ooze is a dark reddish-brown, often viscous liquid that continues to exude from cracks over a long period and dries to a black crust. Sap from a fresh mechanical injury is usually clearer, less colored, and stops flowing once the wound calluses.
The initial water-soaked brown lesions on the spear leaf enlarge and coalesce (merge together), resulting in extensive areas of rotting tissue.
The internal tissues become discolored (brownish) and disintegrated, losing their structural integrity. They emit a characteristic bad smell due to decay.

Disease: Environmental Condition for Bud Rot Spread
Information: Prolonged periods of high humidity combined with low temperatures, typically experienced during persistent monsoon rains, are most conducive for Bud Rot spread and severe infection.

By damaging the vascular tissues of the trunk, Stem Bleeding disrupts the flow of water and nutrients. This directly leads to poor bunch development, reduced nut size and quality, and increased nut drop.

Disease: Leaf Rot as a Secondary Problem
Information: Trees already weakened by other stresses, particularly those affected by Root Wilt (Phytoplasma) disease, are much more susceptible to severe Leaf Rot infection.
The tree eventually dies. The progression involves crown collapse, complete rotting of the basal stem, and often the presence of fungal brackets before death.

Its symptoms—like general decline, yellowing, and poor growth—are non-specific and common to many other problems, including nutrient deficiencies, water stress, and other root diseases. This ambiguity makes visual diagnosis unreliable.
A foul, decaying odor from the crown is a strong diagnostic clue for advanced Bud Rot infection, indicating bacterial decay of the soft tissues.
Longitudinal cracks in the bark are the sites from which the reddish-brown liquid oozes. The disease activity internally leads to the cracking and exudation.
The pathogen typically infects through the tender, unopened spear leaf, which is most vulnerable during wet conditions.
It appears as a hard, shelf-like, woody structure growing out from the base of the trunk. It often has a shiny, varnished upper surface and a porous white underside.
The basal tissues of an infected leaf rot so quickly and thoroughly that they can be easily separated from the crown with little to no force.
In chronic cases, the trunk gradually tapers (becomes narrower) towards the apex (top), giving it an unhealthy, unbalanced appearance.

Leaf Rot starts as distinct water-soaked brown lesions on the spear leaf, leading to rotting and 'fan' shaped leaves after unfolding. Nutrient deficiencies typically cause chlorosis (yellowing) or necrosis (browning) in specific patterns (tips, margins) on older leaves first, not rotting on the spear.
The bark becomes brittle and often peels off in flakes when touched, unlike the firm, adherent bark of a healthy tree.

Disease: Root Wilt as a Predisposing Factor
Information: A tree with Root Wilt should be flagged as a high-risk plant. It acts as a focal point for secondary pests and diseases, requiring more intensive monitoring and potentially removal to protect the rest of the orchard.

Preventive measures, such as prophylactic fungicide sprays (e.g., copper oxychloride), should be applied just before the onset of the monsoon season, as this is when conditions become highly favorable for the disease.
Rust on coffee shows irregular yellow to orange powdery lesions on the lower surfaces, with spots merging into larger brown lesions, leading to drying, defoliation, and bare branches.

Typical symptoms of Rust on coffee leaves: irregular yellow to orange powdery lesions on the lower surfaces, with spots merging into larger brown lesions, leading to drying, defoliation, and bare branches.
Leaf miner on coffee shows Transparent areas in the leaf and larvae maybe present on the underside of the coffee leaf.
Typical symptoms of Leaf miner on coffee leaves: Transparent areas in the leaf and larvae maybe present on the underside of the coffee leaf.
Cercospora brown eye spot on coffee shows brown eye-spots surrounded by yellow halos and cherries with brown, sunken, oval blotches with purplish halos.
Typical symptoms of Cercospora brown eye spot on coffee leaves: brown eye-spots surrounded by yellow halos and cherries with brown, sunken, oval blotches with purplish halos.
Phoma on coffee shows dark-colored, zoned patches starting at the edges, with small black pycnidia on the lesions.
Typical symptoms of Phoma on coffee leaves: dark-colored, zoned patches starting at the edges, with small black pycnidia on the lesions.
Red spider mite is one of the coffee leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Berry blotch is one of the coffee leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Healthy coffee leaves have even colour and no spots, lesions, pustules or discoloration.
Anthracnose on cucumber shows yellow halos and watermelon spots being smaller and dark brown to black.
Typical symptoms of Anthracnose on cucumber leaves: yellow halos and watermelon spots being smaller and dark brown to black.
Bacterial wilt on cucumber shows dull green leaves, or yellow and brown at the margins.
Typical symptoms of Bacterial wilt on cucumber leaves: dull green leaves, or yellow and brown at the margins.
Downy mildew on cucumber shows yellow to pale green spots and velvety grey fuzz.
Typical symptoms of Downy mildew on cucumber leaves: yellow to pale green spots and velvety grey fuzz.
Gummy stem blight on cucumber shows dark brown circular spots starting at the margins and rapidly spreading across the entire leaf, with lesions varying in color from light brown to nearly black.

Typical symptoms of Gummy stem blight on cucumber leaves: dark brown circular spots starting at the margins and rapidly spreading across the entire leaf, with lesions varying in color from light brown to nearly black.
Angular leaf spot is one of the cucumber leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Powdery mildew is one of the cucumber leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Nutrient deficiency is one of the cucumber leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Healthy cucumber leaves have even colour and no spots, lesions, pustules or discoloration.
Downy mildew is one of the cucurbit leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Leaf curl is one of the cucurbit leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Mosaic virus is one of the cucurbit leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Healthy cucurbit leaves have even colour and no spots, lesions, pustules or discoloration.
Use carbendazim or mancozeb sprays at 15-day intervals. Remove infected fruits. Pre-harvest sprays of thiophanate-methyl give good control. Maintain orchard sanitation.
Remove and destroy infected fruits. Avoid injuries during harvesting. Post-harvest dip in carbendazim solution. Maintain proper tree vigor through balanced fertilization.

Multiple pathogens including Alternaria spp. and Cylindrocladium spp. can cause leaf spots. Apply copper-based fungicides or mancozeb. Improve air circulation through pruning. Remove fallen infected leaves.
Prune infected branches 6 inches below canker. Apply Bordeaux paste on cut surfaces. Avoid water stress. Use resistant varieties if available.
Apply thiophanate-methyl or carbendazim at 15-day intervals. Copper oxychloride also provides good protection. Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness.
Use mancozeb or chlorothalonil as protective sprays. Difenoconazole or azoxystrobin for curative action. Remove severely infected leaves. Maintain proper plant spacing.

Spray protective fungicides like Mancozeb or Carbendazim at 2 g per liter of water. For curative control, use systemic fungicides such as Tebuconazole or Difenoconazole. Begin spraying at flowering and repeat at 10–15 day intervals during humid weather to prevent fruit and leaf infection.

Leaf spot appears as small brown to dark circular spots on leaves, often with yellow halos. In severe cases, spots merge, causing leaf drying and premature defoliation. Disease is more common during rainy and humid periods.

Remove and destroy infected fruits and twigs to reduce inoculum. Avoid fruit injuries during handling. Maintain proper orchard sanitation and prune dead branches. Apply Carbendazim or Copper oxychloride sprays during fruit development to prevent spread.
Removing infected leaves, fallen fruits, and diseased twigs reduces the source of infection. This lowers disease pressure in the next season and improves overall orchard health.
Avoid overhead irrigation, maintain proper spacing for air circulation, and spray protective fungicides like Copper oxychloride or Mancozeb during early fruit development to prevent infection.

Infection begins at blossom-end of the fruit and spreads on entire fruit surface. Necrotic spots of 2-10 mm diameter appear on unripe fruits turning into dark brown to black spots. These spots coalesce and cover entire fruit. Affected fruits shrivel and may cling to tree or fall down. Dark sunken spots appear on fruits, leaves, and stems, causing fruits to rot quickly after harvest.

Spray copper oxychloride or carbendazim at regular intervals. Alternative fungicides include chlorothalonil. Apply fungicides preventively and maintain proper intervals between applications for effective control of anthracnose disease.

Collect and destroy infected plant debris. Remove older fruits left on trees as they provide inoculum for disease spread. Maintain proper orchard sanitation. Prune overcrowded branches to improve airflow and reduce humidity. Avoid overhead irrigation to minimize leaf wetness.

Wet and windy conditions favor the disease development. Fungal infection is promoted by humid conditions. High relative humidity combined with rainfall creates ideal conditions for anthracnose spread in custard apple orchards.

Black canker appears as irregularly shaped spots ranging from small specks to large blotches. Spots have an indistinct 'feathered' edge. The lesions are purple-black in color and usually superficial. Tissue damage under the spots is no more than 10 mm deep.

The disease is favored by extremely wet weather and cool-to-moderate temperatures (15°C to 20°C). Prolonged rainy periods in spring that provide at least six hours of continuous wetness create ideal conditions for black canker development.

The pathogen persists in infected plant parts which serve as source of inoculum. Disease spreads from these infected debris to healthy plants during favorable wet conditions. Proper removal and destruction of infected plant material is essential to reduce disease spread.

Diseased fruits show purplish to black spots or blotches confined to fruit surface, eventually covered with white mycelia and black pycnidia. Diplodia rot is distinguished by dark internal discoloration and extensive corky rotting. The penetrated flesh eventually softens or hardens and cracks depending on secondary microbes presence. Hardened fruit lesions with deep browning are characteristic.

Optimum temperature for Diplodia rot is 25.9°C to 31.5°C and relative humidity is 80%. The pathogen persists in infected plant parts which serve as source of inoculum. Warm humid conditions promote rapid disease development.

Remove and destroy infected fruits and plant parts to reduce inoculum source. Maintain proper orchard sanitation and hygiene. Improve airflow through canopy thinning and pruning. Avoid fruit injuries during handling and harvest to prevent pathogen entry.

Small yellowish spots first appear along leaf margins, which gradually enlarge and turn into brownish patches with concentric rings. Severe infection leads to drying and defoliation. Brown or black circular spots appear on leaves, and severe infection causes defoliation.

Apply fungicides like mancozeb or chlorothalonil for effective control. Spray at regular intervals to prevent disease spread. Maintain proper application timing and coverage for best results against various leaf spot pathogens.

Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness. Prune overcrowded branches to improve airflow. Remove and destroy infected plant debris. Maintain field hygiene by removing weeds and alternate hosts. The pathogen survives through spores or mycelium in diseased plant debris.

Dark brown-purplish patches appear on infected fruits and rachis just below its attachment with shoots. For Cylindrocladium leaf spot, dark purple spots about 1-2 mm diameter develop first on fruit shoulders and spread down the sides. Spots enlarge, dry out and crack.

Relative humidity above 70% coupled with warm weather (12-25°C temperature) and intermittent rains favor the disease. The pathogen survives through spores (conidia) or mycelium in diseased plant debris or other hosts, which serve as inoculum sources.

White powdery growth appears on leaf surfaces, young shoots, and sometimes fruits. This fungal disease reduces photosynthesis and weakens plants. Affected leaves may become distorted and drop prematurely.

Spray wettable sulfur or potassium bicarbonate for effective control. Apply at first sign of disease and repeat at recommended intervals. Sulfur-based products are particularly effective against powdery mildew fungi.

Ensure good ventilation in orchards through proper spacing and pruning. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizers which promote succulent growth susceptible to infection. Maintain proper plant spacing for air circulation.
Yellowing leaves, wilting, stunted growth, and root decay are characteristic symptoms. Affected plants show sudden decline and may die. Root system becomes brown, soft and decayed.

Poorly drained soils and waterlogging create conditions favorable for Phytophthora spp. and Fusarium spp. These fungal pathogens attack roots in saturated soil conditions, causing decay and plant death.

Improve drainage and avoid water stagnation. Plant on raised beds in areas with poor drainage. Ensure proper soil structure and avoid overwatering. Select well-drained sites for orchard establishment.
Apply Trichoderma viride in soil as a bio-control agent. Trichoderma colonizes root zone and suppresses pathogenic fungi. Apply as soil drench or incorporate into planting mix.

Drench soil with fungicides like metalaxyl if severe. Apply as soil drench around affected plants. Repeat applications may be needed for established infections. Follow label recommendations for rates and timing.
Purple blotch (Phytophthora capsici) creates purple fruit lesions and internal rot. Dark purple spots develop on fruit shoulders and spread. The disease causes significant internal decay.
Improve drainage to reduce water splash. Remove infected fruit promptly. Reduce water splash through proper irrigation management. Maintain good orchard sanitation.
Apply metalaxyl or phosphonate fungicides for control. These systemic fungicides provide both protective and curative action against Phytophthora. Apply preventively during wet periods.
Pseudocercospora spot causes indented purple-grey fruit spots. These spots are distinctive in their coloration and slightly sunken appearance on fruit surface.
Prune for ventilation and improve airflow. Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness. These cultural practices reduce humidity and disease development.
Apply copper fungicides or mancozeb for effective control. Spray at regular intervals during periods favorable for disease development. Copper-based products provide good protective action.
Pink disease is a fungus causing bark death and gum exudation. Pink to orange fungal growth appears on bark surface. Affected branches show dieback and may be girdled.
Managed by pruning infected branches and copper sprays. Remove affected bark and apply copper-based fungicides to wounds. Prune during dry weather to prevent spread.
Armillaria root rot causes root decay in old orchard sites. White mycelial fans appear under bark at soil line. Honey mushrooms may appear at tree base. Affected trees decline and die.
Requires removal of infected stumps and soil solarization. Remove all woody debris before replanting. Fumigation or solarization of soil may be necessary in severely infested sites.
Sudden wilting and decline, often linked to planting after solanaceous crops. Decay occurs at soil line causing tree collapse. Bacterial wilt causes rapid plant death.
Avoid planting after solanaceous crops. Ensure proper drainage at planting site. Don't plant too deep - keep graft union above soil line. Use disease-free planting material.

Irregular lesions with fungal growth or ooze indicate biotic diseases, while uniform yellowing or scorching often indicates abiotic stress. Pattern recognition helps narrow down possible causes before lab confirmation.

Early symptoms appear as small diffuse spots or shallow indentations on the fruit surface. These spots are dark purple to grey in color and usually measure up to 15 mm in diameter. They are often mild at first but can expand and merge under favorable conditions.

As the disease progresses, spots coalesce into large disfigured areas with necrotic tissue. In advanced cases, superficial cracks appear on the fruit skin, and the hardened skin restricts normal fruit expansion, leading to deformed and unmarketable fruits.

Yes. In some cases, symptoms appear as scattered superficial lesions without deep necrosis. These are less common and may be confused with minor skin injuries, so close inspection is needed for accurate diagnosis.
The causal organism is the fungus Pseudocercospora annonicola. It is a distinct species from the Pseudocercospora that causes husk spot in macadamia, even though the symptoms may appear similar.

The disease was first recognized in 1987 on the Atherton Tableland in Queensland, Australia. It was initially called 'Masasso spot' after the grower who reported it. The disease caused up to 35% loss of marketable fruit.

Pseudocercospora spot occurs in all major custard apple production regions, particularly during wet seasons. The disease is prevalent in Queensland and northern New South Wales and can cause severe losses under prolonged humid conditions.
Yes. African Pride is more susceptible to Pseudocercospora spot compared to KJ Pinks and Pinks Mammoth. Choosing less susceptible cultivars reduces disease pressure and management costs.
Pseudocercospora spot can cause up to 35% loss of marketable fruit in severe outbreaks, mainly due to fruit disfigurement, cracking, and reduced size that makes fruit unfit for market.

Two main symptoms: 1) Dark brown to black spots on unripened fruit (similar to black canker). 2) Pepper spots - small, discrete specks with well-defined margins that can coalesce on severely affected fruit. These are caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides.
Leaf symptoms are occasionally seen but are less common than fruit symptoms. They are more frequently observed on related species like cherimoya. The same fungus causes both leaf and fruit symptoms.
Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. This fungus has a wide host range including avocado, mango, banana, passionfruit, fig, and papaw. It attacks custard apple fruit primarily.

Spores from dead twigs, leaves, and fruit spread through overhead irrigation, heavy dews, or warm showery weather. The fungus penetrates fruit peel at fruit set and remains dormant until ripening. Injury can trigger earlier symptom development.

Wet conditions increase disease severity. Wet and windy weather particularly favors disease spread and development. There's a direct correlation between higher annual rainfall and increased anthracnose incidence.

1) 20-25 year old orchards have inoculum buildup in large trees. 2) Older trees have more dead/dying tissue for fungus proliferation. 3) Larger trees are harder to spray effectively, especially inner top third. 4) Lightly pruned older trees retain moisture longer, favoring infection.

Unharvested fruit left hanging on trees become spore sources. In NSW, continuous fruit presence for months allows spore buildup and movement to uninfected fruit. Queensland's winter leaf drop creates a disease cycle break after harvest.
Yes. Higher infection occurs when custard apple orchards are near neglected avocado orchards. Avocados host the same Colletotrichum gloeosporioides pathogen, creating cross-infection risks.

Avoid placing prunings under trees or keeping tree skirts low. Low branches touching the ground inhibit drying air movement and can become inoculum sources. Proper pruning disposal reduces disease spread.
Spray dormant trees twice with copper oxychloride fungicide combined with Biopest oil®. Use high volume sprays for thorough coverage. Important: Do not apply copper after buds have broken.

Spray every 2-3 weeks with mancozeb, Cabrio®, or Biopest®. Rotate these fungicides to prevent resistance buildup. Control depends on spray coverage quality. These also control Pseudocercospora spot in African Pride varieties.
Yes. Octave (prochloraz) has minor use permit PER11944 for anthracnose control. Apply during flowering and early fruit set at 21-28 day intervals. Reduce to 14 days during prolonged wet weather.

Same strategies as for Pseudocercospora spot: 1) Regular pruning for air circulation. 2) Proper irrigation management. 3) Sanitation of fallen debris. 4) Timely harvesting. 5) Monitoring nearby alternative hosts.

NSW: Continuous fruit hanging for months allows spore buildup within trees. Queensland: Winter leaf drop after harvest creates distinct disease cycle break. This geographical difference affects disease management approaches.

Stress factors can limit disease to pepper spots rather than larger rotted areas. This has been demonstrated in avocados and likely applies to custard apples. Plant stress management may reduce severe symptom development.

Anthracnose pepper spots have discrete, well-defined margins compared to diffuse spots of Pseudocercospora. Accurate identification is crucial as management strategies differ between these fungal diseases.

Rotating mancozeb, Cabrio®, and Biopest® prevents resistance buildup in Colletotrichum gloeosporioides populations. Consistent use of single fungicides selects for resistant strains, reducing long-term control effectiveness.

Some growers suggest birds or bats may spread the disease, but this needs verification. While possible given animal movement patterns, scientific confirmation is lacking for custard apple anthracnose specifically.

Protectant fungicides like mancozeb depend on thorough coverage for effectiveness. The inner top third of large trees is particularly challenging to spray properly. High volume applications during dormant season are essential for coverage.
On small fruits, tiny purple spots appear first and rapidly expand to cover most or all of the fruit surface. These early spots may be subtle initially but spread quickly under moist conditions.

On larger fruits, purple blotch starts as distinct spots or blotches about 2 cm in diameter, which then rapidly expand to around 5 cm. The lesions have clear margins and sometimes a halo around the initial infection point.
Yes. Under moist conditions, affected fruits may become covered with white fungal growth on the surface. This visible mycelial growth indicates active infection and high disease pressure.
Yes. Infected fruits drop readily from the tree due to tissue damage and weakening of fruit attachment. This leads to significant yield loss, especially during wet seasons.

Internally, extensive discoloration of the flesh occurs and may affect most or all of the pulp. This internal rotting makes fruits unfit for consumption even if surface symptoms appear mild initially.

Unlike black canker or Diplodia rot, mature fruits affected by purple blotch do not become hard. Instead, they remain soft with extensive internal discoloration, helping differentiate the diseases in the field.
Purple blotch is caused by the soil-borne oomycete Phytophthora capsicii. This pathogen survives in soil and organic matter and infects fruits under favorable moisture and temperature conditions.
Purple blotch was earlier thought to be caused by Phytophthora palmivora. Molecular diagnostic techniques later confirmed that the actual causal organism is Phytophthora capsicii.

During dry conditions, Phytophthora capsicii survives as thick-walled oospores and chlamydospores protected within organic matter. These structures are highly resilient and can persist in soil for five years or more.

Under wet conditions, oospores germinate to produce zoosporangia that release motile zoospores. These swim in water films and splash from soil onto leaves, branches, and fruits up to about one metre, and can be carried higher by wind-blown rain droplets.
Zoospores germinate within about 24 hours after reaching a suitable host surface and quickly produce infective propagules, leading to rapid disease development under wet and warm conditions.

Purple blotch is more severe on farms with heavy, wet soils where waterlogging occurs. Continuous wet weather increases disease incidence and severity by favoring Phytophthora activity and spore movement.
A small infected spot on harvested fruit can rapidly spread to cover the entire fruit. When packed, infected fruits can contaminate whole trays, leading to significant post-harvest losses.
Very dark, irregular-shaped spots with distinct edges that become hard and cracked. External symptoms resemble Black Canker, but internal symptoms differ significantly.

Internal discoloration extends deep into fruit, producing brown, dry, corky tissue. Affected fruit shrivel, dry out (mummify), and remain on tree. This distinguishes it from Black Canker where damage is superficial (≤10mm deep).

Sometimes confused with calcium deficiency which tends to occur at basal end of fruit. However, Diplodia spots are irregular with distinct edges, while calcium deficiency shows different symptom patterns.
Lasiodiplodia theobromae (also referred to as Botryodiplodia theobromae in some literature). This fungal pathogen causes dry rot and mummification of fruits.
Humid warm conditions favor disease development. The fungus produces sticky spores on dead twigs and mummified fruit, spread by rain splash and wind to infect new fruit.
Chemical control rarely needed in well-managed orchards. During outbreaks, spray with mancozeb under permit number PER11943. Preventive management is more effective than chemical intervention.
Diplodia typically affects crowded, unpruned trees. Remove mummified fruit and dead twigs before fruiting commences. Proper pruning improves air circulation and reduces inoculum sources.
Purple to black, irregularly shaped spots ranging from small specks to large blotches with indistinct 'feathered' edges. Spots start isolated but develop into large, dry blotches with cracks.
Tissue damage under spots is shallow, no more than 10mm deep. This distinguishes it from Diplodia rot where damage extends deep into fruit with corky internal tissue.
Phomopsis annonacearum fungus causes Black Canker. This pathogen creates characteristic purple-black blotches with feathered edges on fruit surfaces.
Mainly a problem in crowded orchards with poor air circulation and light penetration. Overgrown, densely planted orchards create ideal conditions for disease development.
Chemical control rarely required in well-managed orchards. During outbreaks, spray with copper and mancozeb under permit number PER11943. Focus on cultural prevention first.
Same strategies as for Pseudocercospora spot: proper pruning, sanitation, irrigation management, and maintaining orchard hygiene to reduce disease pressure.
Dark purple spots (1-2mm diameter) first develop on fruit shoulders, then spread down sides. Spots don't become sunken but enlarge, dry out, and crack. Symptoms can resemble spotting bug damage.
Cylindrocladium spots are irregularly shaped, while spotting bug lesions are perfectly round. Also, Cylindrocladium damage doesn't extend far into fruit, unlike some insect damage.
Primarily infects fruit but also attacks leaves (causing spots and leaf drop) and to lesser extent, roots. The fungi have broad tissue colonization ability.
Cylindrocladium colhounii and Cylindrocladium scoparium fungi cause this fruit rot disease. Both species can infect custard apple under favorable conditions.
Serious only after prolonged autumn wet weather. During severe outbreaks, regular fungicide sprays used for other diseases should provide adequate control without needing specific treatments.
Same strategies as Pseudocercospora spot plus specific ant control. Prevent ants from carrying infested soil into tree canopy where they can spread the fungus.
Superficial black fungal growth on leaves, twigs, and fruit resembling a layer of soot. The mould grows on honeydew secretions from sap-sucking insects, not directly infecting plant tissues.

Sooty moulds grow on honeydew excreted by sap-sucking insects (aphids, mealybugs, scales, whiteflies). Insects excrete sweet, sticky honeydew after processing large volumes of plant sap, providing growth substrate for fungi.
Common genera: Capnodium, Fumago, Scorias. Less common: Antennariella, Aureobasidium, Limacinula. Species present depend on environment, host plant, and insect species producing honeydew.
1) Coats leaves reducing sunlight penetration and photosynthesis. 2) Can stunt plant growth. 3) Causes premature leaf senescence and drop. 4) Affected fruits remain edible but require cleaning.
Homoptera order insects: aphids, mealybugs, soft scales, whiteflies, leafhoppers, psyllids. Both immature and adult stages produce honeydew while feeding on plant sap.

Control the underlying sap-sucking insect infestation (scale or mealybugs). Once insects are managed, honeydew production stops and sooty mould naturally declines. Also control ants that protect honeydew-producing insects.

Clean fruit with water containing detergent and light brushing. Some growers use semi-automated systems with pressurized water sprays. Various cleaning methods have been developed for commercial operations.
Use sticky bands placed around tree trunks in spring to restrict ant movement into canopy. Ants protect honeydew-producing insects and can spread sooty mould spores.
Mummified fruit harbor Lasiodiplodia theobromae fungi that produce sticky spores. These serve as primary inoculum sources for new infections each season, spread by rain and wind.
Black Canker: irregular purple-black spots with feathered edges, damage ≤10mm deep. Diplodia: very dark spots with distinct edges, hard/cracked surface, deep corky internal damage, fruit mummifies.
Main infection period March to June (autumn months). Disease becomes serious only after prolonged wet weather during this season, with rare occurrence in other periods.
Tripartite relationship: 1) Sap-sucking insects feed on plant sap. 2) Insects excrete honeydew as waste. 3) Sooty mould fungi grow on honeydew substrate without directly parasitizing the plant.
1) Regular pruning to prevent crowding. 2) Remove dead twigs and mummified fruit pre-season. 3) Improve air circulation. 4) Use mancozeb only during outbreaks (PER11943). 5) Maintain tree vigor.

Young trees may wilt rapidly and decline, often showing severe defoliation. Leaves that remain on the tree appear dull green and hang almost vertically, indicating disruption of water transport in the plant.

Older trees show a slow decline over about two years with little yellowing. Mature leaves drop on affected limbs, new flush is weak and pale green, branches become sparsely foliated and sunburn-prone, and fruit remain small and unmarketable despite normal flowering and fruit set.

Affected trees show dark discoloration of the water-conducting tissues in the basal trunk and large roots. Cross-sections at ground level reveal black staining of outer growth rings, and roots may be severely diseased.
Wilting is most common in late summer or early autumn when fruits are approaching maturity. Heavy fruit load can reduce root growth, making susceptible rootstocks unable to escape infection quickly.
The disease is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas solanacearum, a soil-borne pathogen that infects roots and vascular tissues, leading to wilting and tree decline.

Bacterial wilt has been present since custard apples were grown in Australia. Early plantings in the 1960s–70s on sugar apple rootstock suffered severe losses, with over 70% tree mortality within 10 years.
Pink disease appears as patches of pale pink or white fungal growth on branches. The bark and outer sapwood are killed, leading to bark cracking and gum exudation from infected limbs.
Pink disease is caused by the fungus Corticium salmonicolor, which infects branches and kills bark and sapwood tissues under favorable moist conditions.
Pink disease has occurred sporadically since the 1950s. It is usually confined to a few trees in an orchard rather than causing widespread epidemics.
Pink disease is more common in very old or stressed trees, especially after prolonged wet weather, in high-density orchards and shaded canopy areas where humidity remains high.

No. Pink disease typically affects only a few trees in an orchard, especially older or stressed trees in shaded areas. However, without pruning and sanitation, affected limbs can decline and die back over time.
Armillaria root rot causes a slow decline of trees with dieback of twigs and leaves. Affected trees show reduced vigor over time, and canopy thinning becomes noticeable before severe decline occurs.

Diagnosis is based on white plaques of fungal growth under the bark of the trunk and the presence of black 'shoestring' rhizomorphs on major roots. After wet weather, honey-colored mushrooms may appear at the base of infected trees and have a distinct mushroom smell.
Armillaria root rot is caused by the fungus Armillaria luteobubalina, a soil-borne pathogen that survives on old roots and stumps for many years.

Armillaria fungi survive for many years on old stumps and roots of susceptible trees. When custard apples are planted into recently cleared land, the pathogen can infect new plantings from these residual infected roots.
Yellow box (Eucalyptus melliodora) is a common host of Armillaria and increases the risk when custard apples are planted after land clearing of such tree species.
Trees show pale yellow foliage and weak vegetative flushes. Roots appear black with rotting of fine root tips, leading to reduced water and nutrient uptake and gradual decline.

Poor drainage (waterlogging) and inadequate irrigation or mulching (root dehydration) predispose roots to infection. Fungi such as Cylindrocladium spp., Pythium spp., and Phytophthora cinnamomi are often associated with root damage, although Phytophthora is rarely isolated from custard apple.

Anthracnose appears as small necrotic spots of 2-10 mm diameter on unripe fruits. These spots turn dark brown to black and gradually coalesce to cover the entire fruit surface. Infection typically begins at the blossom-end of the fruit and spreads. Affected fruits may shrivel and either cling to the tree or fall down prematurely.

Prune dead twigs before flowering and regularly remove infected fruits and dead leaves. Maintain adequate nutrient concentration in plants, particularly calcium and nitrogen through leaf and soil analysis. Avoid planting susceptible varieties. Older fruits left on trees provide inoculum for disease spread, so remove them promptly.

Wet and windy conditions strongly favor anthracnose development. The disease thrives in humid environments with frequent rain splashes. Proper orchard spacing and air circulation help reduce these favorable conditions.

Black canker appears as irregularly shaped spots ranging from small specks to large blotches. The spots have an indistinct 'feathered' edge. Tissue damage under the spots extends no more than 10 mm deep into the fruit.

Use mulching under trees to reduce soil splash. Regularly monitor for disease and remove dead twigs and mummified fruits. Maintain proper plant canopy through appropriate pruning and training. Prune trees to at least 50 cm above the ground to prevent soil-borne infection.

Black canker is favored by extremely wet weather and cool-to-moderate temperatures (15 to 20°C). When prolonged rainy periods occur in spring with at least six hours of continuous leaf wetness, the disease risk is highest.

Diplodia rot shows purplish to black spots or blotches confined to the fruit surface, eventually covered with white mycelia and black pycnidia. It's distinguished by dark internal discoloration and extensive corky rotting. The penetrated flesh eventually softens or hardens and cracks depending on secondary microbe presence.

Use mulching under trees to reduce soil splash. Remove dead twigs and mummified fruits regularly. Maintain proper plant canopy to reduce high humidity through appropriate pruning and training. Prune trees to 50 cm above the ground to minimize soil contact.
Diplodia rot thrives at optimum temperatures of 25.9 to 31.5°C with relative humidity around 80%. The pathogen persists in infected plant parts which serve as sources of inoculum.

Small yellowish spots first appear along leaf margins, which gradually enlarge into brownish patches with concentric rings. Severe infection leads to drying and defoliation. Dark brown-purplish patches may also appear on infected fruits and rachis just below the shoot attachment.

Dark purple spots about 1 to 2 mm in diameter develop first on the fruit shoulders and spread down the sides. Spots enlarge, then dry out and crack. They appear irregular in shape, distinguishing them from spotting bug damage which appears round, and the damage doesn't extend deep into the fruit.

Collect and burn infected plant parts to minimize disease spread. Increase air circulation by proper training and pruning. Follow common cultural, mechanical, and biological practices recommended for the crop.

Leaf spot disease is favored by relative humidity above 70% coupled with warm weather (12-25°C) and intermittent rains. The pathogen survives through spores or mycelium in diseased plant debris or other hosts.

Mulch under trees to reduce soil splash. Remove dead twigs and mummified fruits each season. Prune tree skirts to 50 cm above the ground. Regularly monitor fruit for infection during the season so spraying can start before fruit diseases become severe.

Combine cultural practices (pruning dead twigs, removing infected fruits and leaves, maintaining proper nutrition especially calcium and nitrogen), avoid susceptible varieties, remove older fruits serving as inoculum sources, and monitor for resistant/tolerant varieties through ICAR Institutes/KVKs/SAUs. Wet and windy conditions favor the disease, so improve air circulation.

Primary infection occurs by conidia present in infected plant debris. The fungus survives in plant debris and other hosts. Secondary spread happens through rain splashes and wind carrying conidia to flowers and fruits. Infection begins at blossom-end and spreads over entire fruit. Older fruits left on trees provide continuing inoculum source.

Primary infection through infected seed and soil. Fungus survives in plant debris. Secondary infection by airborne conidia spreading during favorable weather (70%+ humidity, 12-25°C, intermittent rains). Spores spread by wind and rain splash. For Cylindrocladium, the fungus survives in soil and plant debris, spreading to leaves and fruits during wet periods.

Primary infection occurs by conidia present in infected plant debris. The fungus (Botryodiplodia theobromae, Patouillard) survives in plant debris and other hosts. Secondary spread through rain splashes and wind at optimum temperature 25.9-31.5°C and 80% humidity. Penetrates fruit through wounds or natural openings, causing characteristic purplish-black spots with white mycelia.

Primary infection occurs by conidia present in infected plant debris. Phomopsis anonacearum (Borel) Maas survives in plant debris and other hosts. Secondary spread through rain splashes and wind. Disease favored by extremely wet weather, cool-to-moderate temperatures (15-20°C), and prolonged rainy periods with at least 6 hours continuous wetness.
Blight is one of the fig leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Brown spot is one of the fig leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Rust is one of the fig leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Healthy fig leaves have even colour and no spots, lesions, pustules or discoloration.
