Anthracnose causes sunken dark lesions on mature fruit with pink spore masses. Necrotic patches appear on the fruit surface. It is primarily a postharvest disease but also affects leaves and developing fruits.

Anthracnose thrives in warm wet weather with high humidity. The fungal pathogen spreads through water splash, infected plant debris, and wind, making rainy seasons particularly conducive for disease spread.
Use resistant cultivars when available. Maintain orchard sanitation by removing infected plant debris, fallen fruits, and diseased plant parts to reduce inoculum sources.
Apply copper-based fungicides before flowering and during fruit development. Use both systemic and non-systemic fungicides for comprehensive protection against anthracnose.

Combine resistant cultivars, orchard sanitation, proper irrigation management to reduce leaf wetness, and timely fungicide applications. This integrated approach provides better disease control than single methods.

Algal leaf spot shows orange to rust-colored tufts on leaves. As the disease matures, lesions become reddish-purple. On twigs, the bark may crack. The causal organism is Cephaleuros virescens, a green alga.
Algal leaf spot develops in wet humid conditions with poor air circulation. The pathogen is a green alga that spreads through zoospores in splashing water, making dense plantings more susceptible.
Ensure proper fertilization, irrigation management, and regular pruning. Improve air circulation by proper spacing and removing dense foliage to reduce humidity around leaves.
Apply copper-based fungicide sprays to control algal leaf spot. Copper compounds are effective against the algal pathogen and also provide protection against other fungal diseases.
Guava rust shows orange to red pustules on leaves, shoots, and fruits. It causes leaf distortion, defoliation, and circular lesions with halos. The disease primarily affects young tissues.
Guava rust develops in warm temperatures with high humidity. The fungal rust pathogen spreads through wind-borne spores and infected plant material, with young flush being most susceptible.
Maintain good sanitation by removing infected leaves and shoots. Ensure adequate fertilization to keep plants healthy and vigorous. Regular pruning improves air circulation and reduces humidity.

Apply appropriate fungicides specifically labeled for rust diseases. Fungicide applications should be timed during flush emergence and repeated at recommended intervals during favorable disease conditions.
Root knot nematode causes galls on roots, reduced plant vigor, yellowing of foliage, and wilting in hot weather. The soil-borne nematode Meloidogyne spp. creates characteristic root galls.
Root knot nematodes thrive in sandy soils under warm conditions. They spread through soil movement, infected planting material, and irrigation water, making proper sanitation crucial.
Use resistant varieties when available. Solarize soil before planting by covering with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks in summer. Check roots at mid-season for early detection of galls.
Yes, apply entomopathogenic nematodes like Heterorhabditis and Steinernema species. These beneficial nematodes parasitize and kill root knot nematodes, providing biological control.
Anthracnose is primarily a postharvest disease. Handle fruits carefully to avoid wounds, maintain proper storage temperature and humidity, and ensure fruits are free from field infections at harvest.
No, algal leaf spot is caused by Cephaleuros virescens, which is a green alga, not a true fungus. However, it is managed similarly to fungal diseases with copper-based sprays and cultural practices.
Guava rust primarily affects young tissues including new leaves, tender shoots, and young fruits. Mature tissues are more resistant. Time fungicide applications to protect new flush growth.

During summer months, moisten the soil, cover with clear plastic sheets, and seal edges. Leave for 4-6 weeks. High soil temperatures kill nematodes. This is most effective before planting new orchards.

Orchard sanitation removes disease inoculum sources like fallen leaves, fruits, and infected plant debris. This reduces pathogen populations and prevents disease spread to healthy plants, forming the foundation of integrated disease management.
Anthracnose spreads through water splash during rain or irrigation, wind-blown infected plant debris, and contact between infected and healthy fruits. Warm wet weather greatly accelerates spread.

Algal leaf spot spreads through zoospores that are dispersed by splashing water from rain or overhead irrigation. Dense canopies with poor air circulation and prolonged leaf wetness favor disease spread.

Guava rust spreads through wind-borne spores that can travel long distances. Infected plant material and contaminated equipment can also spread the disease. Warm humid conditions favor spore germination and infection.

Root knot nematodes spread through movement of infested soil on equipment, infected planting material, and irrigation water. They are particularly problematic in sandy soils and cannot move far on their own.

Anthracnose causes fruit rots, algal and rust spots create blemishes, and fruit borer creates holes and frass. These reduce market value and shelf life. Postharvest losses from anthracnose can be severe without proper management.

Copper-based fungicides are effective against multiple pathogens including anthracnose fungus, algal leaf spot, and rust. They provide both protective and limited curative action, are relatively safe, and can be used in organic systems.

Manage Anthracnose by applying fungicides like Carbendazim or Mancozeb. Prune and destroy infected plant parts to reduce spread. Ensure good orchard sanitation and avoid overhead irrigation to minimize leaf wetness, which favors the disease.

For Guava Rust and Leaf Spot, effective fungicides include systemic products like Hexaconazole or Tebuconazole, and protectants like Mancozeb. Apply at first symptom onset and repeat as per label instructions, ensuring thorough coverage of leaves.

Manage Fusarium wilt caused by Fusarium oxysporum through integrated approaches: 1) Plant resistant varieties, 2) Ensure proper field drainage to avoid waterlogging, 3) Use soil amendments to improve soil health, and 4) Avoid using infected planting material. The pathogen survives in soil and spreads through contaminated equipment.

Spray Mancozeb to control Anthracnose caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. The pathogen spreads through rain splash from infected plant parts and survives in diseased twigs. Favourable conditions are warm, humid weather during rainy seasons.

Differentiate by symptoms: Wilt shows systemic yellowing, wilting, and vascular browning. Anthracnose shows localized dark spots on fruits and die-back of twigs. Your vision model can identify anthracnose but not wilt, so for wilt-like symptoms, check for vascular discoloration in cross-sections.

Fusarium wilt, caused by Fusarium oxysporum, is favoured by warm temperatures and waterlogged soils. The pathogen produces white to pink mycelium and chlamydospores that survive in soil. Avoid waterlogging and ensure proper drainage to prevent disease development.

Anthracnose spreads via rain splash from infected plant parts. Limit spread by: 1) Pruning and destroying infected twigs showing die-back, 2) Maintaining proper spacing for air circulation, 3) Avoiding overhead irrigation, and 4) Cleaning tools between plants to prevent mechanical spread.

For suspected wilt when vision returns null: 1) Cut stem cross-sections to check for vascular browning, 2) Send samples to a plant pathology lab for Fusarium isolation, 3) Observe pattern - wilt often starts on one side of tree, 4) Check soil conditions for waterlogging history. Lab confirmation is needed for definitive diagnosis.

For Powdery Mildew caused by Oidium caricae, spray Wettable Sulphur 0.25%, Dinocap 0.05%, Chinomethionate 0.1%, or Tridemorph 0.1%. The disease shows white mycelial growth on leaves, flower stalks, and fruits, leading to yellowing and defoliation. Fungicides should be applied when symptoms first appear.

Anthracnose on mature guava fruits shows sunken dark necrotic lesions with pinkish spore masses under humid conditions. The flesh is affected, reducing marketability. Spray Mancozeb 0.25% preventively. The fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporioides produces hyaline, aseptate, oval-elliptical conidia in dark brown-black acervuli.

Apply fungicides for Guava Rust (Puccinia psidii) based on regular scouting. Time applications when dark bordered circular brown lesions with yellow halos appear on leaves, shoots, inflorescences, or fruits. Early application prevents distortion, defoliation, and reduced growth. Follow a schedule based on disease pressure and weather conditions.

Anthracnose spreads primarily through wind and rain dispersal of conidia from infected plant parts. Under humid conditions, the pinkish spore masses facilitate rapid spread. Cultural practices like proper spacing, pruning for air circulation, and avoiding overhead irrigation can reduce spread alongside fungicide sprays.

Distinguish by symptoms: 1) Powdery Mildew - White mycelial growth on surfaces (vision: null), 2) Anthracnose - Sunken dark lesions with pink spores on fruits (vision: anthracnose), 3) Rust - Circular brown lesions with yellow halos on multiple parts (vision: Guava_Rust_leaf_spot). Each requires different fungicide strategies.

Prevent Powdery Mildew with cultural practices: maintain proper plant spacing for air circulation, avoid dense canopy through pruning, remove infected plant debris, and monitor regularly since the vision model cannot detect this disease (null). These practices reduce humidity and spore survival.

For early Rust detection (vision label: Guava_Rust_leaf_spot), check leaves, young shoots, inflorescences, and developing fruits for dark bordered circular brown lesions with yellow halos. Early detection allows timely fungicide application to prevent distortion, defoliation, and growth reduction.

For both Anthracnose (vision: anthracnose) and Rust (vision: Guava_Rust_leaf_spot), broad-spectrum fungicides like Mancozeb may provide some control. However, optimal strategy: 1) Time applications before expected humid periods, 2) Use fungicide rotations to prevent resistance, 3) Combine with cultural practices like pruning infected parts.

The first external symptom is the appearance of yellow coloration with slight curling of leaves on terminal branches. Plants later show unthriftiness with yellow to reddish discoloration of leaves, followed by premature shedding. Some twigs become bare and fail to produce new leaves or flowers, eventually drying up.
Wilt is caused by several pathogens including Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. psidii, F. solani, Macrophomina phaeseoli, Rhizoctonia bataticola, Cephalosporium sp. and Gliocladium roseum.
Wilt spreads through movement of plants containing sick soil to virgin areas, short distance spread by water, and root injury which predisposes the disease.

Aspergillus niger strain AN-17 is effective. Apply Aspergillus niger multiplied in FYM at 5 kg/pit for new plants while planting. For older plants, apply Aspergillus niger enriched FYM at 10 kg per plant.

Wilted trees should be uprooted and burnt. Dig a trench around the tree trunk. While transplanting, avoid severe root damage. Pits may be treated with formalin and kept covered for 3 days, then transplant after two weeks.
Yes, the cross of Psidium malle x P. guajava has been found free from wilt and can be used as resistant rootstock for effective disease control.
High rainfall during August/September, water stagnation in fields for long duration, and temperature ranges of 23-32°C with 76% relative humidity are conducive for wilt disease development.

The plant dies backward from the top of branches. Young shoots, leaves and fruits are readily attacked while tender. The growing tip changes from greenish to dark brown and later to black necrotic areas, extending backwards causing die-back. The disease appears in epidemic form during August to September.

Pin-head spots are first seen on unripe fruits, which gradually enlarge. Spots are dark brown, sunken, circular with minute black stromata in the center producing creamy spore masses in moist weather. Several spots coalesce to form bigger lesions. The infected area becomes corky and hard, often developing cracks in severe infection.
Spray Bordeaux mixture (3:3:50) or Copper oxychloride (0.3%) just after initiation of disease. For post-harvest treatment, dip fruits for 20 minutes in 500 ppm tetracycline.
Application of bio-agent Streptosporangium pseudovulgare on fruits before emergence of symptoms is effective for controlling anthracnose.

Anthracnose spreads by wind-borne spores from dead leaves, twigs and mummified fruits. Dense canopy is congenial for spore germination due to suitable moisture. Movement of infected planting material and transportation of fruits from high disease pressure areas without treatment also spread the disease.

Closer planting without canopy management, lack of timely harvesting, availability of free water in the form of dew or rain which encourages spore production and dispersal, and lack of timely control measures increase disease severity.

Minute brown or rust-colored circular necrotic areas appear on green fruits. In advanced stages, the epidermis tears open in a circinate manner. The margin is elevated with a depressed area inside, creating a crater-like appearance. White mycelium with numerous spores is noticeable in older cankers.
Control canker with 3 to 4 sprays of 1% Bordeaux mixture or lime sulphur at 15-day intervals in the early stage of infection.
Spore germination is maximum at 30°C and does not germinate below 15°C or above 40°C. Relative humidity of 98% favors disease development. The pathogen is primarily a wound parasite.

Minute shallow brown velvety lesions appear on leaves during early spring flush, enlarging to 2-3 mm diameter. Spots may vary from specks to big patches, crowded or scattered. Leaf tips, margins or areas near the mid vein are most often infected.

On immature fruits, lesions are nearly black. As fruits enlarge, lesions get sunken. Cracks frequently develop on older blemishes due to fruit enlargement. Lesions are usually smaller than leaf spots and are darkish green to brown or black in color.
Control can be achieved by spraying Copper oxychloride (0.3%) 3-4 times at 15-day intervals when initial symptoms are noticed.

Disease begins from April and is more serious during May to August. The pathogen sporulates readily during high rainfall period (July-September) with greatest incidence in September. In winter, symptoms are not available.

The disease appears as water-soaked brown irregular patches on the lower surface and yellowish color on the upper surface of leaves. Older leaves are mostly affected and severely affected leaves curl and subsequently drop off.
Spray mancozeb or Dithane-M-45 (0.2%) at monthly intervals to manage Cercospora leaf spot.

Sooty mould develops on honeydew secreted by scale insects, aphids, white flies and mealy bugs. Symptoms consist of blackish brown velvety thin membranous covering on leaves. In severe cases, foliage appears black. Affected leaves curl and shrivel under dry conditions.

Control honeydew-secreting insects by suitable insecticides, as the mould will die without its growth medium. Foliar spraying of wettasul + chlorpyriphos + Gum Acacia (0.2 + 0.1 + 0.3%) at 15-day intervals is very effective.

In pre-emergence phase, infected seeds and seedlings show water-soaked discoloration, becoming soft and rotting. In post-emergence phase, hypocotyl at ground level or upper leaves discolor to yellowish to brown, spreading downwards, turning soft and rotting. Affected seedlings topple down and die.
Dip guava seeds in captan/thiram (0.2%) for two minutes before sowing. Drench soil with Copper oxychloride (0.3%) to reduce disease intensity in nursery.

Remove and burn diseased seedlings and weeds. Avoid excessive water use and close planting as the organism is moisture-loving. Prepare seedbeds with proper drainage. Avoid planting susceptible hosts as the fungus survives on several hosts.

Symptoms start at calyx disc during rainy season. Affected area is covered with whitish cotton-like growth that develops rapidly, covering almost entire surface in 3-4 days during humid weather. Skin below the growth becomes soft, turns light to dark brown and emits an unpleasant smell. Fruits either remain intact or drop off.
Spray Dithane Z-78 (0.2%) or Ridomil or Aliette (0.2%) or Copper oxychloride (0.3%) for foliar infection. Soil drenching with Copper oxychloride (0.3%) or Ridomil or Aliette (0.2%) is also effective.

Cool wet conditions with high soil moisture favor disease development. High humidity, temperature from 28-32°C, poorly drained soils and injuries are important for disease initiation. Infection ceases when temperature is less than 15°C or more than 35°C.

Rain and wind are important for spread. The pathogen produces numerous sporangia on diseased tissues when temperature is near 25°C, which is an important inoculum source. Rain drops are necessary for liberation of sporangia from infected plant material or soil.

Discoloration appears in the region below and adjoining the persistent calyx, gradually increasing in size and turning dark brown. The affected area becomes soft. The mesocarp tissue also shows discoloration, becoming pulpy and light brown. At advanced stage, fruit shrinks with concentric wrinkles on skin, finally covered with dark pycnidia.

Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) or carbendazim or Thiophonate methyl (0.1%) before onset of winter fruiting. Care should be taken that no spraying is done 15 days prior to harvesting. Avoid fruit injury.

Infection starts as brownish discoloration mostly at stem end, gradually proceeding downwards in an irregular wavy manner. The whole fruit may get involved. Decay takes the form of soft watery breakdown from infection via wound or stem end. In advanced cases, numerous small pycnidia are produced over entire fruit surface.

Ensure careful handling to reduce wounding. Captan and homeopathic drug arsenic oxide are effective against the fungus. Applications of Bacillus subtilis and Streptosporangium pseudovulgare on guava fruits have been found effective.

Infection occurs at or near the distal end in the region of persistent calyx. Rot begins with a translucent zone around distal end that becomes brown. With disease evolution, lesion becomes dark black and wrinkled with dry skin while maintaining translucent margins. Spots are slightly sunken and tend to increase in size with pycnidia formation.
Apply orchard sprays with Copper oxychloride (0.3%) or Dithane M-45 (0.2%) at 15-day intervals.

The fungus infects mature leaves during wet weather. In advanced stage under favorable conditions, severe spots appear around middle lamina. Under humid conditions, brick red color spots are common on lower surface. Abundant spotting causes defoliation. Lesions can coalesce forming large irregular to semi-circular areas up to 4-5 mm diameter.
The disease could be managed with Copper oxychloride (0.3%) spray during rainy season.

Parasites like Loranthus sp. are commonly present on trunk or branches, making the tree weak. Infected host plant foliage is sparse and reduced in size. Bearing capacity and fruit quality are considerably lowered. The point of penetration is characterized by swollen growths called 'burrs'.

Cut affected branches sufficiently below to eradicate haustoria. In early stages, it can be removed easily. Treat cut surface with wound dresser like Copper oxychloride (0.3%) paste/spray to prevent secondary infections. Spraying emulsion of diesel (30-40%) in soap water is recommended and found effective.

Fruits of all affected branches remain underdeveloped, hard and stony. The entire plant eventually gets defoliated and dies. Roots show rotting at basal region and bark is easily detachable from cortex. Light brown discoloration is noticed in vascular tissues.
Organic manures, oil cakes and lime help check the disease. Maintenance of proper tree vigor by timely and adequate manuring, interculture and irrigation enables trees to withstand infection.
Eco-friendly approach includes biological control using Aspergillus niger, soil amendment with organic matter, and intercropping. These integrated methods have been found effective for wilt control.
Yes, partially wilted plants recovered fully after rejuvenation or heavy pruning of the tree.
Unopened buds and flowers are affected by the disease, which causes their shedding. This occurs during the epidemic form that appears during August to September.
On leaves, the fungus causes necrotic lesions at the tip or on the margin. These lesions are usually ashy grey and bear fruiting bodies.
Anthracnose is caused by Gloeosporium psidii (Delacroix Sacc.) which is also known as Glomerella psidii (Del.) Sheld. or Colletotrichum psidii Curzi.
Canker is caused by Pestalotia psidii Pat., which is primarily a wound parasite.

In severe cases, raised cankerous spots develop in great numbers and fruits break open to expose seeds. Infected fruits remain underdeveloped, become hard, malformed and mummified, and drop. In cv. Sardar (Lucknow-49), canker pustules are large, more elevated and numerous.
In winter, cankerous spots are common. In rainy season, minute red specks are formed on affected areas.
Algal spot is caused by Cephaleuros virescens Kuntze (also known as C. mycoidae Karst.) and C. parasiticus.
Alga infects immature guava leaves during early spring flush. Leaf tips, margins or areas near the mid vein are most often infected. Immature fruits also show lesions that are nearly black.

Sooty mould is caused by multiple fungi including Phragmocapnias betle, Scorias philippensis, Tichomerium grandisporum, Limacinula musicola, Aithaloderma clavatisporum, Tripospermum sp., Polychaeton sp., Leptoxyphium sp. and Conidiocarpus sp.
Damping off is caused by Rhizoctonia solani Kuhn. The pathogen is also responsible for causing fruit rot if fruits are kept on soil after harvest or touching the ground.

Fruit rot occurs during rainy season when fruits are kept on soil after harvest or touching ground. Initially, lesions appear firm, brownish and water-soaked, enlarging into irregular-shaped sunken cankers. Rotting is rapid and infected fruits become covered with dense grayish brown mould. Sclerotial bodies are seen in due course on fruits.
Fruit rot is caused by Phytophthora parasitica Dastur (also known as P. nicotianae var. parasitica) and P. citricola.
Plant spacing and fertilizer regimes should be managed to avoid unnecessarily dense plant canopy. This helps reduce the high humidity and dense foliage conditions that favor disease development.
When disease appears on young and half-grown fruits, they shrink, turn dirty brown to dark brown, become hard in texture and either remain intact as mummified fruit or drop off.
Disease incidence varies from 8-30%, depending upon weather and foliage conditions.
Stylar end rot is caused by Phomopsis psidii De camara and P. destructim.
Serious losses up to 10% occur in the orchard if disease is not properly controlled.
Soft watery rot is caused by Botryodiplodia theobromae Pat. The infection results from infection via wound or through the stem end.
Botryosphaeria rot is caused by Botryosphaeria ribis Gross. & Duggar, which causes serious losses during December. The fungus produces asexual stage responsible for infection in orchards.
Hyaloderma leaf spot is caused by Hyaloderma sp. It is a relatively new disease that requires more research on epidemiology, biology and control.

Initial infections on the underside of the leaf may cause chlorotic patches or spots to occur on the upper side of leaf. The lesions spread easily to healthy leaves and can coalesce, forming large irregular to semi-circular lesion areas on leaf surface.

Several leaf spot diseases affect guava including Cercospora leaf spot, algal leaf spot, and Hyaloderma leaf spot. These appear as various colored spots (brown, rust-colored, brick red, or yellowish) on leaves, particularly during wet weather conditions.

Wilt is a pernicious disease and a curse to guava industry because the exact cause is still not fully understood, it affects young as well as old fruit-bearing trees (with older trees more prone), and eventually leads to complete defoliation and death of the entire plant.

Diseases and pests severely impact guava yield and quality through: premature fruit drop, underdeveloped and hard fruits, fruit rot and decay, secondary infections through wounds, reduction in photosynthetic activity due to leaf damage and sooty mould, tree weakness from parasites, and up to 10% yield losses from diseases like stylar end rot. Fruit fly and borers cause direct fruit damage while diseases like wilt can kill entire trees.

Wilt (caused by Fusarium spp., Rhizoctonia spp.) is most destructive as it leads to tree mortality. Management includes: 1) Avoiding waterlogging in orchards, 2) Applying Trichoderma and Pseudomonas bio-agents to soil, 3) Using resistant varieties, 4) Maintaining orchard sanitation, 5) Recognizing symptoms like yellowing/drooping leaves, branch drying, and root rot.

Anthracnose identification: Visual symptoms include dark sunken spots on fruits, flower blight, and premature fruit drop. Your vision model can detect this with 'anthracnose' label. The disease affects fruits, flowers, and leaves, reducing quality and yield. Regular monitoring during flowering/fruiting is crucial.

Anthracnose management includes: 1) Pruning and destroying diseased twigs and infected plant parts, 2) Spraying protective fungicides during flowering and fruiting stages, 3) Using your vision model's 'anthracnose' detection for timely intervention, 4) Maintaining orchard hygiene to reduce disease pressure.

Algal leaf spot symptoms: Circular, reddish-brown, velvety spots on leaves and fruits. Management: 1) Improve air circulation through proper pruning, 2) Spray copper-based fungicides, 3) Reduce canopy density to minimize humidity, 4) Remove severely infected leaves to prevent spread.

Guava decline symptoms: Drying of twigs from tip backwards, fruit drop, and gradual tree decline. Management: 1) Regular pruning of affected branches, 2) Soil application of bio-fungicides, 3) Balanced fertilizer use, 4) Proper irrigation management, 5) Addressing underlying stress factors contributing to decline.

Anthracnose symptoms include: 1) Small, dark, sunken lesions on fruits with pinkish spore masses, 2) Brown or black spots with irregular margins on leaves, 3) Severe infections lead to fruit drops and yield loss. Your vision model can detect this with 'anthracnose' label for early intervention.

Recommended fungicides for Anthracnose: 1) Syngenta Cuman - 750-1000L per hectare, 2) Biostadt Roko - 100-200 gm per ha (0.5 g/l water), 3) Multiplex Tecozo - 1-2 ml per liter spray. Apply before flowering season and during fruit development for effective prevention.

Advanced Guava Wilt symptoms: 1) Wilting starting from lower branches progressing upward, 2) Yellowing and necrosis of leaves, 3) Browning of vascular tissue in stems (visible when cut), 4) Stunted growth and reduced fruit production. This is not detectable by your vision model (null label).

Recommended products for Guava Wilt: 1) Multiplex Bio Jodi - 2 ml/liter water, 2) T Stanes Bio Cure-F - 1.2 lit/acre or 3 lit/ha spray. Combine with resistant varieties, soil sterilization, and proper irrigation management. Fungicidal drenches may help severely affected trees.

Powdery Mildew symptoms: 1) White, powdery spots on leaves, young shoots, and fruits, 2) Affected leaves curl, wither, and drop prematurely, 3) Reduced fruit quality and yield. Your vision model cannot detect this disease (null label), requiring manual inspection.

Recommended fungicides for Powdery Mildew: 1) Tata Contaf Plus - 2 ml/liter water (spray leaf undersides), 2) Multiplex Multiclear Bio Pesticide - 4-5 ml/liter water (spray inflorescence/affected areas), 3) Syngenta Ampect Xtra - 0.3 liters/hectare. Also consider sulfur-based fungicides and neem oil.

Bacterial Wilt distinguishing features: 1) Wilting of leaves and entire branches, 2) Yellowing and drooping leaves, 3) Sticky, oozy exudates from infected areas, 4) Dark, necrotic streaks in stems. Unlike fungal wilt, bacterial wilt shows bacterial ooze and spreads rapidly. Not detectable by vision (null).

Bacterial Wilt control: 1) Multiplex Bactinash-200 - 0.3-0.5 g/liter water for spray/drenching, 2) Tata Blitox Fungicide - 2-3 g/liter water spray or 1-2 kg/ha soil application, 3) Copper-based bactericides as preventive, 4) Prompt removal of infected plants, 5) Drip irrigation to prevent bacterial splash.

Rust identification: 1) Small, raised pustules on leaves turning orange/reddish-brown, 2) Premature leaf drop, 3) Reduced fruit quality. Your vision model detects this as 'Guava_Rust_leaf_spot'. Manual inspection confirms pustule presence and color development stages.

Guava Rust fungicides: 1) Syngenta Tilt Propiconazole - 150-200ml/acre, 2) Multiplex Treat Fungicide - 1 ml/liter water (spray both leaf sides), 3) Multiplex Multiclear Bio Pesticide - 4-5 ml/liter water. Apply copper-based fungicides during rainy season, prune infected parts, ensure proper spacing.

Root-Knot Nematode symptoms: Above-ground - stunted growth, reduced vigor, yellowing/wilting leaves. Below-ground - swollen, galled roots with knotty growths. Diagnosis requires soil/root sampling since vision cannot detect this (null label). Symptoms often appear in patches within orchard.

Nematode control products: 1) T Stanes Bio-Nematon - 1.2 kg/acre or 3.0 kg/ha, 2) Bayer Velum Prime Nematicide - 2-2.5 ml/liter water. Combine with soil solarization before planting, resistant varieties, and nematode-resistant cover crops in orchard management.

Anthracnose cultural control: 1) Prune infected branches and remove fallen fruit to reduce inoculum, 2) Maintain proper spacing between trees for air circulation, 3) Use vision model's 'anthracnose' detection for early intervention, 4) Time fungicide applications before flowering and during fruit development.

Wilt prevention: 1) Choose resistant varieties, 2) Solarize or steam-sterilize soil before planting, 3) Ensure adequate but not excessive soil moisture, 4) Apply biological products like Multiplex Bio Jodi or T Stanes Bio Cure-F, 5) Monitor for early symptoms since vision cannot detect wilt (null).

Reduce Powdery Mildew by: 1) Pruning affected branches to improve air circulation and sunlight, 2) Applying sulfur-based fungicides preventively, 3) Using neem oil as alternative control, 4) Regular monitoring since vision cannot detect (null), 5) Maintaining balanced nutrition to improve plant resistance.

Critical sanitation for bacterial diseases: 1) Prompt removal and destruction of infected plants, 2) Avoid overhead irrigation (use drip irrigation), 3) Disinfect tools between trees, 4) Apply copper-based bactericides preventively, 5) Consider resistant varieties for Bacterial Wilt management.

Most critical Rust prevention period is during rainy season when humidity favors disease development. Apply copper-based fungicides preventively during this time. Use vision model's 'Guava_Rust_leaf_spot' detection for early intervention. Remove severely infected leaves/branches and ensure adequate tree spacing.

Nematode soil management: 1) Solarize soil before planting to reduce populations, 2) Incorporate nematode-resistant cover crops, 3) Use products like Bio-Nematon or Velum Prime, 4) Select less susceptible guava varieties, 5) Maintain soil health with organic matter to support natural nematode predators.

Beneficial sanitation practices: 1) Regularly remove fallen leaves and fruit to reduce disease reservoirs, 2) Prune trees to improve air circulation and sunlight, 3) Maintain clean orchard floor, 4) Use vision detection for identifiable diseases, 5) Implement integrated approaches combining sanitation with other controls.

Product selection factors: 1) Specific disease being targeted, 2) Growth stage of crop, 3) Weather conditions (rainy season needs different products), 4) Previous chemical use and resistance concerns, 5) Integration with vision detection capabilities, 6) Safety intervals for harvest, 7) Cost-effectiveness and availability.

Monitoring schedule should include: 1) Weekly visual inspections for all diseases, 2) Regular vision system scans for detectable diseases, 3) Seasonal emphasis (rust in rainy season, anthracnose during flowering/fruiting), 4) Soil/root checks for wilt/nematodes, 5) Record keeping of observations and interventions, 6) Weather-based adjustment of monitoring frequency.

Proper application techniques: 1) Thorough coverage of all plant parts (both leaf surfaces for Tata Contaf Plus), 2) Correct timing (preventive applications before disease development), 3) Appropriate dilution rates as per product labels, 4) Equipment calibration for accurate application, 5) Weather-appropriate timing (avoid rain, high wind), 6) Safety precautions during application.

Cost-effective management: 1) Prioritize prevention over cure, 2) Use vision detection for early intervention reducing treatment costs, 3) Focus on cultural controls (pruning, sanitation) with low costs, 4) Time chemical applications based on monitoring rather than calendar, 5) Use biological products where effective, 6) Calculate economic thresholds for treatment decisions.

Weather-based adjustments: 1) Increase monitoring during rainy/humid periods favoring fungal diseases, 2) Apply preventive fungicides before expected wet periods, 3) Adjust irrigation to avoid excess moisture promoting wilt, 4) Use vision system more frequently during high-risk periods, 5) Time pruning during dry periods to minimize infection risk.

Important records: 1) Disease incidence observations (including vision detection logs), 2) Weather conditions during disease development, 3) Control measures applied (products, rates, dates), 4) Treatment effectiveness evaluations, 5) Costs of disease management, 6) Yield impacts of diseases, 7) Resistance development monitoring if applicable.
Leaf spot is one of the loquat leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
Healthy loquat leaves have even colour and no spots, lesions, pustules or discoloration.

Common rust on maize shows rust-colored to dark brown elongated pustules on both leaf surfaces, containing cinnamon brown urediniospores, with leaves potentially showing chlorosis and death under severe infection.

Typical symptoms of Common rust on maize leaves: rust-colored to dark brown elongated pustules on both leaf surfaces, containing cinnamon brown urediniospores, with leaves potentially showing chlorosis and death under severe infection.

Gray leaf spot on maize shows small necrotic spots with halos expanding into rectangular gray to brown lesions, typically 1/8 inch wide and 2 to 3 inches long, with distinct parallel edges limited by veins.

Typical symptoms of Gray leaf spot on maize leaves: small necrotic spots with halos expanding into rectangular gray to brown lesions, typically 1/8 inch wide and 2 to 3 inches long, with distinct parallel edges limited by veins.
Northern leaf blight on maize shows canoe-shaped lesions with gray-green margins that turn tan with dark fungal sporulation, starting on lower leaves and spreading upwards.
Typical symptoms of Northern leaf blight on maize leaves: canoe-shaped lesions with gray-green margins that turn tan with dark fungal sporulation, starting on lower leaves and spreading upwards.

Maize streak virus on maize shows pale circular spots progressing to narrow, broken chlorotic stripes along secondary and tertiary veins, with severely affected leaves displaying white to yellow lesions.

Typical symptoms of Maize streak virus on maize leaves: pale circular spots progressing to narrow, broken chlorotic stripes along secondary and tertiary veins, with severely affected leaves displaying white to yellow lesions.

Maize lethal necrosis on maize shows long yellow stripes, yellowing and drying from the edges toward the midrib, and eventual leaf death. The disease leads to dwarfing, premature aging, and scattered dead plants in the field.

Typical symptoms of Maize lethal necrosis on maize leaves: long yellow stripes, yellowing and drying from the edges toward the midrib, and eventual leaf death. The disease leads to dwarfing, premature aging, and scattered dead plants in the field.

Leafhopper infestation in mango appears as yellowing and curling of tender leaves, sucking damage on flowers and buds, honeydew secretion, and development of black sooty mould on leaves and panicles. Severe attack causes flower drop and poor fruit set.

Leafhopper infestation causes yellowing and curling of tender leaves, sap sucking from flowers and buds, honeydew secretion, and black sooty mould growth on leaves and panicles. Severe attack results in flower and fruit drop.
Mealybug attack appears as white cottony masses on panicles, shoots, and fruits. Honeydew secretion leads to black sooty mould growth. Infested panicles shrink and dry, causing flower and fruit drop.
Thrips damage causes silvery or bronze patches on leaves and fruits, curling of leaves, scarring on fruit surface, and flower drop. Affected leaves appear distorted and dry.
Gall midge infestation causes blister-like galls on leaves, inflorescence, and young fruits. Panicles bend at right angles, buds dry up, and heavy flower drop is seen, leading to poor fruit set.

Sooty mould appears as black powdery fungal growth on mango leaves, stems, and fruits. It grows on honeydew secreted by insects like mealybugs and leafhoppers and reduces photosynthesis by blocking sunlight.
Fruit fly infestation causes small puncture marks on mango fruits where eggs are laid. The pulp rots from inside due to larval feeding, leading to premature fruit drop and foul-smelling decay.
Stem borer attack causes holes in the trunk and branches with extrusion of sawdust-like frass. Affected branches dry up and show wilting, and tunneling inside the stem weakens the tree.

Die back is characterized by drying of twigs from top downwards, particularly in older trees, followed by drying of leaves which gives a fire scorch appearance. The disease is most conspicuous during October-November. When you slit open affected branches along the long axis, you'll observe internal browning in wood tissue. Cracks appear on branches and gum exudes before they die out. In nursery plants, when the graft union is affected, the plant usually dies, showing darkening of the pith.

To manage die back: (1) Select scion wood for propagation that is free from infection, (2) Immediately prune any infected portions, removing some healthy tissue (3 inches below infection site) to ensure complete pathogen eradication, (3) After pruning, spray or paste copper oxychloride (0.3%) or cow dung at the cut ends, (4) Collect and burn all affected branches, (5) Prevent introduction of disease in newly planted orchards by using disease-free planting material, and (6) Avoid using contaminated garden tools.

Die back spreads through multiple pathways: (1) Planting material containing diseased foliage, (2) Disease twigs bearing fruiting bodies serve as the main source for perpetuation and spread to the next season, (3) Using infected budsticks when propagating in new areas, (4) Inoculum already present in the orchard, and (5) Contaminated garden tools that transfer the pathogen between plants during pruning or grafting operations.

Sooty mould appears as a black velvety thin membranous covering on leaves, stems, and fruits. In severe cases, entire trees appear black and look unsightly. This disease is very common wherever honeydew-secreting insects like mango hoppers, scales, coccids, and mealy bugs are present. The black coating doesn't directly infect the plant tissue but grows on the honeydew secreted by these insects.

Control sooty mould by managing the honeydew-secreting insects: (1) Spray monocrotophos (0.05%) at 10-15 day intervals to control insects - once insects are controlled, the mould dies for want of growth medium, (2) Apply starch at 2% concentration, (3) Spray combination of wettable sulphur + monocrotophos + gum acacia (0.2% + 0.05% + 0.3%) or Indian oil formulation No. 1 & 2 (4%) at 15-day intervals, and (4) Ensure pesticide application covers both sides of leaves.

On mango leaves, bacterial canker initially produces water-soaked irregular satellite to angular raised lesions measuring 1-4 mm in diameter. These lesions are light yellow in color with a yellow halo initially. With age, they enlarge or coalesce to form irregular necrotic cankerous patches with dark brown color. The disease also affects leaf stalks, causing similar water-soaked lesions that turn into typical cankers.

On mango fruits, bacterial canker appears as water-soaked, dark brown to black colored lesions that gradually develop into cankerous, raised, or flat spots. These spots grow bigger, usually 1 to 5 mm in diameter, and can cover almost the whole fruit. The spots often burst, extruding gummy substances containing highly contagious bacterial cells. You may also observe black streaks on infected fruits.

Prevent bacterial canker by: (1) Regular inspection of orchards and maintaining good sanitation, (2) Using seedling certification to ensure disease-free planting material, (3) Taking mango stones for raising seedlings only from healthy fruits, (4) Establishing windbreaks to reduce brushing and wounding of leaves which reduces infection chances, (5) Removing symptomatic portions of trees to reduce inoculum, and (6) Eliminating collateral hosts (weeds) in and around the orchard area.

For bacterial canker control: (1) Apply three sprays of Streptocycline at 200 ppm at 10-day intervals to reduce fruit infection, (2) In severe infections, spray Streptocycline at 300 ppm or copper oxychloride (0.3%) for more effective control, and (3) Use the antagonistic phytoplane bacterium Bacillus coagulans, which has been found effective as a biological control agent.

Bacterial canker development is favored by: (1) High humidity levels around 90% relative humidity, (2) Moderate temperatures between 25-30°C, (3) High wind velocity which is congenial for disease severity and causes wounding, (4) Rains occurring together with wind which promote wounding of leaf surfaces and enhance infection, and (5) Growing susceptible varieties in and around the orchard. Long-distance spread occurs through infected planting material and mango stones.

Phoma blight is noticed only on matured or old leaves. Fully developed spots are characterized by a dark margin and dull grey necrotic center. In severe cases, these spots coalesce to form larger patches, which result in withering and defoliation of infected leaves. The disease does not affect young leaves, making it distinctive from other foliar diseases.

Manage phoma blight through: (1) Spraying copper oxychloride at 0.3% concentration to control fungal growth, and (2) Maintaining balanced nutrition, as proper nutrient management provides resistance to phoma blight. Adequate nutrition strengthens the plant's natural defense mechanisms against this disease.

Vegetative malformation is pronounced in young seedlings and is caused by Fusarium subglutinans. Affected seedlings develop abnormal vegetative growth that is swollen and has very short internodes. The growth appears compact and bunched together due to the reduced spacing between nodes, creating an abnormal appearance compared to healthy seedlings.

In floral malformation, flower buds are transformed into vegetative buds, producing a large number of small leaves and stems characterized by appreciably reduced internodes, giving a witches' broom appearance. The flower buds seldom open and remain dull green instead of developing into normal flowers. This prevents normal fruit set and severely affects yield.

Manage malformation by: (1) Pruning and burning floral malformed panicles and vegetative malformed shoots to reduce disease incidence, (2) Applying NAA at 200 ppm or planofix (90 ml per 20 liters) in the first week of October before bud differentiation stages, followed by deblossoming in late December or January at bud burst stage, and (3) Spraying chelated Zinc (100 ppm) and Copper (40 ppm) during flower bud differentiation and flowering stage combined with carbendazim (0.1%) spray during November-December.

Sooty mould spreads through: (1) Insects excreting honeydew or sugary substances that provide a growth medium for the fungus, and (2) The growth of fungus being associated with infestation of scale insects, mango hoppers, coccids, and mealy bugs. The fungus grows on the honeydew secreted by these insects rather than directly infecting the plant tissue. Controlling the insect population effectively stops the disease spread.

Die back disease is most conspicuous during October-November period. During this time, you'll observe the characteristic symptoms of twig drying from top downwards and leaf drying that resembles fire scorch. The timing coincides with certain environmental conditions and tree physiological stages that make the disease symptoms more pronounced and easier to identify.

Long-distance spread of bacterial canker occurs primarily through: (1) Infected planting material being transported to new areas, and (2) Infected mango stones used for raising seedlings. Within an orchard, the disease spreads through wind-splashed rains, collateral hosts like weeds, and high wind velocity that causes wounding. This is why it's critical to use only certified disease-free planting material and stones from healthy fruits when establishing new orchards.

Phoma blight specifically affects only matured or old leaves of mango trees. The disease does not appear on young leaves, making it distinct from other foliar diseases. The fungus shows preference for older foliage, where it causes spot formation with characteristic dark margins and dull grey necrotic centers.

Balanced nutrition provides resistance to phoma blight in mango trees. Proper nutrient management strengthens the plant's natural defense mechanisms, making it less susceptible to infection. Well-nourished trees with adequate macro and micronutrients show better resistance compared to nutritionally deficient trees. This makes fertilization an important component of integrated disease management.

Malformation disease in mango is caused by the fungus Fusarium subglutinans. This pathogen causes two types of malformation: vegetative malformation affecting young seedlings with abnormal swollen growth and short internodes, and floral malformation where flower buds transform into vegetative buds creating a witches' broom appearance with dull green buds that seldom open.

Chemical control of malformation involves: (1) Spraying chelated Zinc at 100 ppm and Copper at 40 ppm during flower bud differentiation and flowering stages, and (2) Spraying carbendazim at 0.1% concentration during November-December. These treatments should be combined with cultural practices like pruning malformed parts for effective disease management.

Growth regulators help manage malformation by: (1) Applying NAA (Naphthalene Acetic Acid) at 200 ppm in the first week of October before bud differentiation stages, or (2) Using planofix at 90 ml per 20 liters of water in early October. This is followed by deblossoming in late December or January at the bud burst stage. This treatment sequence reduces the incidence of both vegetative and floral malformation.

Pruning floral malformed panicles and vegetative malformed shoots is crucial because: (1) It reduces the incidence of malformation by removing the source of inoculum, (2) The pruned material must be burnt to prevent disease spread, and (3) Removing malformed parts prevents the fungus from perpetuating in the orchard. This sanitation practice should be done regularly as part of integrated disease management.

Floral malformation severely impacts mango yield because the flower buds are transformed into vegetative buds instead of developing into flowers. These malformed buds produce numerous small leaves and stems but seldom open to produce flowers. Since no flowers develop, there is no fruit set, resulting in complete yield loss from affected panicles. The witches' broom appearance indicates non-productive growth.

Vegetative malformation is most pronounced in young seedlings. At this stage, affected plants develop abnormal vegetative growth that is swollen with very short internodes, creating a bunched, compact appearance. Seedlings are particularly vulnerable to this form of malformation caused by Fusarium subglutinans, which can affect their overall development and vigor.

Treatment timing for malformation prevention: (1) First week of October - apply NAA (200 ppm) or planofix (90 ml/20 liters) before bud differentiation stages, (2) November-December - spray carbendazim (0.1%) and chelated micronutrients (Zn++ 100 ppm, Cu++ 40 ppm) during flower bud differentiation and flowering stage, and (3) Late December or January - perform deblossoming at bud burst stage. Proper timing is critical for effective disease reduction.

In severe cases of phoma blight, the individual spots coalesce to form larger patches on the leaves. This extensive spotting and patch formation results in withering of the infected leaves followed by defoliation. The loss of leaves can weaken the tree, reduce photosynthetic capacity, and impact overall tree health and productivity if left unmanaged.

Anthracnose on stored fruits appears as black spots that are initially round but later coalesce to form large irregular blotches, sometimes covering the entire fruit surface. The spots have large deep cracks where the fungus penetrates deep into the fruit, causing extensive rotting. Under moist conditions, the blackened areas become covered with minute pinkish reproductive bodies of the fungus. You may also observe staining, russetting, and tear streaking involving only the skin of the fruit.

Postharvest anthracnose infection actually starts from the field as latent infection. The fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporioides infects the fruit while it's still on the tree but remains dormant. Symptoms only become visible after harvest during storage when conditions become favorable for the pathogen to develop. This is why preharvest field management is critical for controlling postharvest disease.

Prevent postharvest anthracnose through scheduled preharvest sprays with thiophanate methyl or carbendazim (Topsin M or Bavistin at 0.1%) in the field. These sprays reduce latent infection that would otherwise develop during storage. This preharvest strategy is a major component of controlling postharvest anthracnose, as it targets the pathogen before it establishes latent infection in the fruit.

Postharvest anthracnose control involves hot water treatment to eradicate leftover latent infection: (1) Hot water treatment alone at 52°C (±1°C) for 3 minutes gives good control, or (2) Hot water treatment duration can be reduced to 15 minutes by supplementing with fungicides like carbendazim or thiophanate methyl (Bavistin or Topsin M at 0.05%). These treatments eradicate latent infections that escaped preharvest control measures.

Stem end rot caused by Diplodia natalensis starts at the base of the pedicel (stem attachment point). A circular brown area develops near the stem end, which gradually expands as a dark brown to black area towards the lower portion of the fruit and may eventually cover the entire fruit surface. The rotting is very fast - the entire fruit can rot within 2-3 days. The disease is observed only on ripe fruits. It may also start from points other than the stem end if the fruit gets bruised.

Prevent stem end rot through preharvest sprays of carbendazim or thiophanate methyl (Bavistin or Topsin M at 0.1%) applied 15 days before harvesting. These sprays control the postharvest rot by reducing pathogen load on the fruit surface and preventing infection establishment. This prophylactic treatment is essential for reducing disease incidence during storage.

Since stem end rot starts from the stem end, harvest fruits along with a 5 cm stalk to check the disease. This intact stalk acts as a barrier preventing pathogen entry. If fruits must be harvested without a stalk, the opening should be immediately closed with wax to seal the wound and prevent pathogen invasion. Proper harvesting technique is critical as the stem end is the primary infection point.

Control stem end rot by dipping fruits in hot water at 52°C (±1°C) with 0.05% carbendazim for five minutes. This combination treatment eradicates any pathogen present at the stem end and prevents disease development during storage. The hot water and fungicide combination provides effective control of Diplodia natalensis.

Black rot caused by Aspergillus niger shows characteristic yellowing with irregular dull grayish spots that develop into black necrotic areas with growth of black mould. The tissue below and around the spots disintegrates and emits a foul odor. The fruits rot very fast. Rotting may start from any point but injury is essential for the disease to begin. It may also start from the stem end as a natural opening exists there.

Prevent black rot by: (1) Harvesting fruits carefully as any injury predisposes them to Aspergillus rot - injury is essential for disease initiation, (2) Not allowing fruits to touch soil which harbors the pathogen, (3) Performing fruit harvesting and handling carefully in a clean manner to avoid wounds and contamination, and (4) Dipping fruits in hot water at 52°C (±1°C) with 0.05% carbendazim for five minutes for disease control.

Stem end rot typically starts at the base of the pedicel (stem end) where a circular brown area develops and spreads. However, the disease may also start from points other than the stem end when fruits get bruises or injuries. The stem end is the primary infection site because it provides a natural opening for the pathogen Diplodia natalensis to enter, especially when fruits are harvested without proper stalk retention.

Under moist conditions, anthracnose symptoms become more pronounced with the blackened areas becoming covered with minute pinkish reproductive bodies of the fungus. Moisture favors fungal growth and sporulation. The pathogen creates deep cracks in the spots where it penetrates deep into the fruit, causing extensive rotting. High humidity during storage accelerates disease development from latent infections.

Stem end rot progresses very rapidly. The rotting is so fast that the entire fruit can rot within just 2-3 days after symptoms first appear. The disease starts as a circular brown area at the stem end and quickly develops into a dark brown to black area that spreads toward the lower portion of the fruit, potentially covering the entire fruit surface in this short timeframe. This rapid progression makes early detection and prevention critical.

Black rot can be controlled by dipping fruits in hot water at 52°C (±1°C) with 0.05% carbendazim for five minutes. This treatment combines the sanitizing effect of hot water with the fungicidal action of carbendazim to eliminate Aspergillus niger spores and prevent disease development. However, prevention through careful handling to avoid injuries remains the most important management strategy.

The complete anthracnose control strategy involves both preharvest and postharvest measures: (1) Preharvest - scheduled sprays with thiophanate methyl or carbendazim (0.1%) in the field to reduce latent infection, and (2) Postharvest - treatment of fruits with either hot water alone at 52°C for 3 minutes, or hot water at 52°C with fungicides (0.05% carbendazim or thiophanate methyl) for 15 minutes to eradicate remaining latent infections. This integrated approach targets the pathogen at both infection and expression stages.

Black rot is distinguished by: (1) Characteristic yellowing with irregular dull grayish spots that develop into black necrotic areas, (2) Growth of distinctive black mould (Aspergillus niger), (3) Tissue disintegration below and around spots that emits a foul odor - this smell is a key diagnostic feature, (4) Requirement of injury for infection to start, and (5) Very fast rotting once established. The combination of black mould growth and foul odor is particularly characteristic of Aspergillus rot.

Stem end rot caused by Diplodia natalensis is observed only on ripe fruits. The disease does not affect immature or green fruits. This specificity for ripe fruits is important for timing control measures and understanding disease risk - fruits become susceptible as they ripen, making postharvest management and proper storage conditions critical during the ripening period.

Anthracnose causes several types of skin symptoms on mango fruits: (1) Staining - discoloration of the fruit skin, (2) Russetting - rough, brownish patches on the skin surface, and (3) Tear streaking - streak-like patterns on the skin. These symptoms involve only the skin of the fruit and are attributed to Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. These surface symptoms may appear alongside or separate from the deeper rotting symptoms with black spots and cracks.

Mango fruits should not be allowed to touch soil because soil harbors the black rot pathogen Aspergillus niger and many other decay organisms. Contact with soil can contaminate fruit surfaces with spores and inoculum. Since black rot requires an injury to infect, any subsequent wound or damage during handling allows soil-borne pathogens to enter and cause rapid rotting with the characteristic foul odor and tissue disintegration. Keeping fruits off the ground is a critical sanitation practice.

Black tip symptoms become visible when mango fruits attain some size. A small etiolated (pale) area develops near the distal end (tip) of the fruit, which gradually spreads and turns nearly black, covering the tip of the fruit completely. The black area remains hard and the growth of the fruit is checked. This disorder is also known as chimney disease and is particularly visible on cultivars like Dushehri.

Manage black tip by: (1) Spraying borax (1%) or other alkaline solutions like caustic soda and washing soda - the first spray should be done positively at pea stage followed by two more sprays at 15-day intervals, and (2) Planting mango orchards in north-south direction and at least 3 km away from brick kilns to reduce incidence. The alkaline sprays help neutralize the acidic toxic gases.

Internal necrosis caused by boron deficiency shows: (1) First, water-soaked grayish spots develop on the lower side of the fruit, (2) Later, spots enlarge and develop into dark brown necrotic areas, (3) Internal tissue starts disintegrating, (4) The pericarp and mesocarp disintegrate, exposing the flesh, (5) Yellow colored droplets come out, and (6) Affected fruits drop easily from the tree.

Correct boron deficiency through: (1) Foliar spray of borax (1%) at pea stage followed by two more sprays at 15-day intervals, and (2) Soil application of 250 grams boron per tree (for 10-15 year old trees) around the tree basin. Both foliar and soil applications ensure adequate boron availability for proper fruit development and prevent tissue necrosis.

Fruit clustering (Jhumka) is characterized by formation of several fruitlets at the tip of the panicle. The fruitlets are darker green in color and their shape is slightly curved compared to normal fruits. These fruits generally hang for more time compared to normal fruits but do not grow further and eventually drop. The fruits do not have seed formation. This disorder is particularly visible in Dushehari cultivar.

Prevent fruit clustering by: (1) Avoiding spray of insecticides and fungicides during flower opening or pollination stages, (2) Keeping pollinator population high during flowering season, (3) Planting pollinizing cultivars in the orchard, and (4) Increasing pollinator population by keeping bee hives in the orchards. Proper pollination is key to preventing this disorder.

Woody stem galls are characterized by woody growths of 10-15 inches diameter formed on limbs and branches. The cause is not known. Galls are abundant on cultivars like Chinnasuvarnarekha and Langra, and moderate in Neelam. These large galls can cause branches to break near the gall sites, potentially damaging the tree structure.

Manage woody stem galls by removing the galls using a saw and applying Bordeaux paste to the cut surface. This physical removal prevents further damage and the Bordeaux paste protects the wound from secondary infections. Regular monitoring and timely removal of galls helps maintain tree health and structural integrity.

Red nose (also called soft nose) is severe in late maturing varieties like Neelam and Mallika, particularly in delayed harvest, leading to substantial loss. Numerous red-nosed fruits are seen on trees during the end of summer with onset of showers. The red nose gradually becomes soft and rots. Fruits with red nose are unfit for export. The cause is not known.

Prevent red nose by: (1) Timely harvesting of fruit - avoiding delayed harvest is critical, especially for late maturing varieties like Neelam and Mallika, and (2) Providing proper nutrition to the plant to maintain fruit health. Harvesting at the right maturity stage before the onset of monsoon showers significantly reduces this disorder.

Fruit tumors are growths of pea to marble size that develop on the fruit and are very unsightly. The stylar end (bottom) part of the fruit is much affected while the stem end is practically free from tumors. The cause of this disorder is not known. These tumors reduce the market value and aesthetic quality of the fruit.

Manage fruit tumors by removing affected fruits from the tree and burying them in the soil. This sanitation practice prevents potential spread if the disorder has any transmissible component and reduces inoculum load in the orchard. Regular monitoring and removal of affected fruits helps maintain overall orchard health.

Jelly seed (softening of tissue) is characterized by the pulp near the stone becoming jelly-like with tissue disintegration while the outer pulp near the peel remains normal. The taste becomes repulsive and fruits lose table quality. From the outer appearance, fruits look normal - the disorder is internal. Dashehari cultivar is more susceptible compared to others like Chausa and Langra. Incidence is higher in Lucknow region, particularly in late harvested fruits.

Control jelly seed through an integrated approach: (1) Apply black plastic mulch (100 micron thick) in the tree basin during October-November, (2) Foliar spray of calcium chloride dehydrate (2%) and potassium sulphate (1%) one month before fruit harvesting, (3) Apply 250 grams borax per tree in soil during November, and (4) Harvest fruits at proper maturity (not late) and ripen in storage rather than allowing them to ripen on plants.

Spongy tissue, also called internal breakdown, is a serious malady affecting Alphonso mango, which is the main export cultivar. It occurs in ripe fruits and renders them unfit for consumption. This disorder has become a bottleneck in export and expansion of Alphonso cultivation in Maharashtra and Gujarat where it is grown commercially. Convecting heat arising from soil and intense solar radiation are reported to be the main causes.

Prevent spongy tissue by mulching with paddy straw and dry leaves, which has been found effective for its control. Mulching helps moderate soil temperature and reduces convecting heat from the soil, which is one of the main causes of this disorder. The mulch layer also protects against intense solar radiation effects on the fruit.

Potassium deficiency is characterized by scorching of leaf margins, which is the characteristic symptom. Scorching starts from the tip and progresses downwards. Fruit quality is reduced in potassium-deficient trees. Additionally, trees with potassium deficiency are easily prone to pest and disease attack due to weakened plant health.

Correct potassium deficiency by: (1) Applying 1 kg muriate of potash or sulphate of potash along with 2 kg urea and 6 kg superphosphate during July-August in the tree basin, and (2) Incorporating dropped leaves along with manures to enrich soil health and fertility. This balanced fertilization approach ensures adequate potassium availability while maintaining overall soil nutrient balance.

Zinc deficiency symptoms include: (1) Leaves become small and narrow with margins bent upward or downward, (2) Internodal length is reduced drastically, (3) Twigs with crowded leaves give a rosette appearance, (4) Pale interveinal areas and green veins are typical, (5) Trees with zinc hunger do not grow well, and (6) Yield, size, and quality of fruits are reduced. Small plants with severe zinc deficiency may die. This deficiency is conspicuously seen in alkaline, saline, and sandy soils.

Treat zinc deficiency by spraying zinc sulphate at 5 grams plus 10 grams urea per liter of water, applied twice at 15-day intervals. The addition of urea helps in better absorption of zinc through the leaves. This foliar application quickly corrects the deficiency and improves tree growth and fruit quality.

Black tip spreads through toxic gases - sulphur dioxide, ethylene, carbon monoxide, and fluoride - emitting from brick kilns operating nearby the orchard. Wind direction (particularly western winds) and velocity play an important role in spreading these toxic gases to the orchard. The closer the proximity to brick kilns and the stronger the wind carrying these gases, the more severe the black tip incidence.

Plan orchard location to minimize black tip by: (1) Planting mango orchards at least 3 km away from brick kilns to reduce exposure to toxic gases, and (2) Orienting the orchard in north-south direction which helps reduce gas exposure based on prevailing wind patterns. Proper site selection during orchard establishment is crucial for long-term prevention of this disorder.

Fruits affected by internal necrosis (boron deficiency) drop easily because: (1) The internal tissue disintegrates, weakening fruit structure, (2) The pericarp and mesocarp breakdown, compromising fruit integrity, (3) Yellow colored droplets exude from the fruit, indicating severe tissue degradation, and (4) The water-soaked spots that develop into dark brown necrotic areas weaken the attachment to the tree. This tissue breakdown causes premature fruit drop.

Clustered fruits (Jhumka) differ from normal fruits in several ways: (1) Multiple fruitlets form at the tip of the panicle instead of single fruits, (2) They are darker green in color, (3) Their shape is slightly curved compared to normal fruits, (4) They hang for more time on the tree, (5) They do not grow beyond initial size, and (6) They lack seed formation. Eventually, these abnormal fruits drop from the tree.

Woody stem galls show varying susceptibility among cultivars: (1) Chinnasuvarnarekha - galls are abundant, (2) Langra - galls are abundant, and (3) Neelam - galls are moderate. The severity of gall formation varies by cultivar, with some varieties being more prone to developing these large woody growths on limbs and branches.

Fruits with red nose are unfit for export because: (1) The red nose gradually becomes soft and rots, compromising fruit quality and shelf life, (2) The appearance is unattractive and does not meet export quality standards, and (3) The disorder leads to substantial loss, especially in late maturing varieties like Neelam and Mallika. Export markets have strict quality requirements that red-nosed fruits cannot meet.

Dashehari cultivar is most susceptible to jelly seed (softening of tissue) disorder compared to other cultivars like Chausa and Langra. The problem is particularly severe in the Lucknow region, especially in late harvested fruits. The disorder has been recorded in several mango varieties, but Dashehari shows the highest susceptibility.

No, jelly seed disorder cannot be detected from the outer appearance - affected fruits look completely normal externally. The disorder is internal, with only the pulp near the stone becoming jelly-like with tissue disintegration, while the outer pulp near the peel remains normal. This makes detection difficult without cutting the fruit open, which affects marketability.

Proper harvest timing is critical for jelly seed control. It is desirable to: (1) Harvest fruits at proper maturity - not late, and (2) Ripen fruits in storage rather than allowing them to ripen on plants. Late harvested fruits show higher incidence of jelly seed, especially in susceptible cultivars like Dashehari. Early harvest at proper maturity followed by controlled ripening reduces disorder incidence.

Black plastic mulch (100 micron thick) applied in the tree basin during October-November helps control jelly seed by: (1) Moderating soil temperature, (2) Conserving soil moisture which aids nutrient uptake, (3) Improving calcium and other nutrient movement to fruits through better water relations, and (4) Creating favorable conditions for nutrient absorption. This is part of an integrated approach combining mulch, foliar sprays, and soil amendments.

Spongy tissue is a major concern because: (1) Alphonso is the main export cultivar, (2) The disorder renders fruits completely unfit for consumption, (3) It has become a bottleneck in export, affecting international trade, (4) It limits expansion of Alphonso cultivation in commercial growing states of Maharashtra and Gujarat, and (5) Despite extensive research, no conclusive control measures have been obtained, making it a persistent problem.

Dropped leaves should be incorporated along with manures to enrich soil health and fertility. These fallen leaves contain nutrients, including potassium, that can be recycled back to the soil. By incorporating them with organic manures, you: (1) Return nutrients to the soil, (2) Improve soil organic matter content, (3) Enhance nutrient cycling, and (4) Maintain overall soil fertility. This sustainable practice complements fertilizer application.

The rosette appearance in zinc deficiency occurs because internodal length is reduced drastically, causing leaves to crowd together on twigs. This creates a bunched or rosette-like pattern where multiple small, narrow leaves cluster at the shoot tip with very short distances between them. Combined with pale interveinal areas and green veins, this distinctive rosette pattern is diagnostic of zinc deficiency.

Severe zinc deficiency causes: (1) Trees do not grow well overall, (2) Yield is significantly reduced, (3) Fruit size decreases, (4) Fruit quality deteriorates, and (5) Small plants with severe zinc deficiency may die. The deficiency affects both vegetative growth (rosette appearance, small narrow leaves) and reproductive success (poor fruit set and quality), making it critical to address promptly.

In zinc deficiency, leaf margins are bent either upward or downward. This curling or bending of margins, combined with the leaves becoming small and narrow, is a characteristic symptom. The leaves also show pale interveinal areas with green veins remaining, creating a distinctive pattern. These multiple leaf symptoms together help diagnose zinc deficiency.

In black tip disorder, the black area that develops at the tip of the fruit remains hard. Unlike soft rots or other fruit disorders where affected tissue becomes soft, the blackened tip maintains a hard texture. Additionally, the growth of the fruit is checked or stopped once black tip develops, preventing normal fruit development and size increase.

For black tip prevention, the first spray of borax (1%) or other alkaline solution should be done positively at pea stage (when fruits are pea-sized), followed by two more sprays at 15-day intervals. This timing is critical because it coincides with early fruit development when fruits are most susceptible to toxic gas damage. The spray schedule ensures protection during the vulnerable growth period.

Internal necrosis progresses in stages: (1) First, water-soaked grayish spots develop on the lower side of the fruit, (2) Later, these spots enlarge and develop into dark brown necrotic areas, (3) Internal tissue starts disintegrating, (4) The pericarp and mesocarp disintegrate, exposing the flesh, (5) Yellow colored droplets exude from the fruit, and (6) Finally, affected fruits drop easily. This progressive deterioration is due to boron deficiency.

Using both foliar spray (borax 1% at pea stage with two more sprays at 15-day intervals) and soil application (250 grams boron per tree around the basin) provides: (1) Immediate correction through foliar uptake during critical fruit development, (2) Long-term soil boron availability for sustained nutrition, (3) Multiple routes of boron entry ensuring adequate supply, and (4) Comprehensive management addressing both immediate and future needs.

Fruit clustering (Jhumka) affects yield because: (1) The clustered fruitlets do not grow beyond their initial small size, (2) They do not develop seeds, indicating incomplete fertilization, (3) Although they hang for more time than normal fruits, they eventually drop without contributing to yield, and (4) The panicle produces multiple non-viable fruitlets instead of a few normal, marketable fruits. This results in complete yield loss from affected panicles.

Woody stem galls, which can be 10-15 inches in diameter, can cause significant structural damage including breaking of tree branches near the gall sites. The large size and weight of these galls on limbs and branches can: (1) Create weak points in the tree structure, (2) Cause branch breakage, especially during fruiting or high winds, (3) Reduce tree stability, and (4) Compromise overall tree health and productivity.

Calcium chloride dehydrate spray (2%) applied one month before harvesting helps prevent jelly seed because: (1) Calcium deficiency is one of the factors causing this disorder, (2) Foliar calcium application ensures direct uptake during critical fruit maturation, (3) It compensates for slow calcium movement through transpiration stream in susceptible cultivars like Dashehari, and (4) Adequate calcium strengthens cell walls and prevents tissue breakdown near the stone.

Jelly seed severely affects quality and marketability because: (1) The taste becomes repulsive, making fruits unpalatable, (2) Fruits lose table quality completely, (3) The pulp near the stone disintegrates into jelly-like consistency, (4) Despite normal external appearance, the internal defect makes fruits unmarketable, and (5) Detection requires cutting fruit open, which affects sales since consumers cannot identify affected fruits before purchase. This hidden defect causes significant economic loss.

For powdery mildew management in January: (1) Remove weeds and infected young leaves showing powdery mildew symptoms, (2) Remove infected leaves and malformed panicles infected by mildew, and (3) This cultural control helps reduce inoculum before the main flowering season. January is critical for sanitation measures to prevent disease buildup.

In February, spray sulphur at 0.2% or tridemorph (0.1%) for powdery mildew control. These sprays should be applied along with insecticides for hopper control. February is a critical month as flowering begins and mildew can severely affect flower development and fruit set if not controlled.

At pea stage (March), apply need-based spray of insecticide + fungicide + NAA (20 ppm) for integrated control of hopper, powdery mildew, and fruit drop. This combined spray addresses multiple problems simultaneously during this critical fruit development stage. The addition of NAA helps reduce physiological fruit drop.

In April, apply third spraying of dinocap or tridemorph (0.1%) after fruit setting on a need basis. Also remove powdery mildew infected leaves and malformed panicles. This late-season spray protects developing fruits and ensures clean foliage, though application should be based on disease pressure assessment.

To prevent anthracnose in June: (1) Practice early harvesting of mature fruits to avoid fruit fly infestation and anthracnose development, (2) Timely picking reduces latent infection that develops during storage. In July, continue timely picking of fruits and spray copper oxychloride (0.3%) for red rust and anthracnose control. Early harvest is critical as the disease worsens during monsoon season.

During monsoon (July-August), spray copper oxychloride (COC) at 0.3% for anthracnose and red rust control. In August, continue spraying COC for both diseases. The rainy season favors anthracnose development, so regular copper sprays are essential. Also practice field sanitation and removal of weeds from the orchard.

In October, remove diseased foliage and twigs infected with anthracnose (twig blight stage). After pruning, spray 0.3% copper oxychloride (3g/l). This sanitation during the post-harvest period reduces inoculum for the next season. Proper removal and destruction of infected plant parts is critical for long-term disease management.

In November, spray copper oxychloride (3 g/L) for die back, phoma blight, and anthracnose control. Also practice deep ploughing of orchards to expose insect eggs and pupae, and remove weeds that harbor insects and diseases. This pre-winter treatment reduces disease pressure before the next flowering season.

In October, manage die back by: (1) Pruning infected and dried branches 10 cm below the dried portion, (2) Pasting the cut surface with copper oxychloride, and (3) Spraying 0.3% copper oxychloride (3g/l) after pruning. This pruning and protective paste application prevents further spread and protects wounds from secondary infection.

In November, spray copper oxychloride (3 g/L) for die back, phoma blight, and anthracnose control. This preventive spray during the dormant season protects trees before winter and reduces disease pressure for the upcoming growing season. Combined with sanitation measures like weed removal and deep ploughing, it provides comprehensive control.

For bacterial canker: (1) In May, spray streptocycline (200 ppm) or copper oxychloride (0.3%) at 15-day intervals, and (2) In June, apply second spray of streptocycline at 200 mg/L. The May-June period is critical as wind-splashed rains during pre-monsoon and early monsoon favor bacterial spread. Regular sprays during this period are essential.

In April, spray for sooty mould using one of these options: (1) Wettable sulphur + monocrotophos + Gum Acacia (0.2% + 0.05% + 0.3%), or (2) Indian oil formulation (3%), or (3) Starch at 2%. These treatments control both the honeydew-secreting insects and the sooty mould fungus growing on the honeydew.

Sooty mould management in April focuses on controlling honeydew-secreting insects (hoppers, scales, mealybugs) with insecticides like monocrotophos (0.05%), because the mould grows on the honeydew they excrete. By controlling the insects, you eliminate the growth medium for the fungus, effectively managing both problems simultaneously. The spray also includes sulphur for direct fungal control.

Spray borax (1%) in: (1) April - at 15-day intervals, and (2) May - continue borax (1%) spray for control of black tip and internal necrosis.
