The April-May period coincides with fruit development when fruits are most susceptible to toxic gases. Regular borax sprays provide alkaline protection against acidic pollutant gases.

Prevent internal necrosis by spraying borax (1%) in: (1) April - at 15-day intervals for black tip and internal necrosis control, and (2) May - continue borax spray. Internal necrosis is caused by boron deficiency, so regular borax (boron source) application during fruit enlargement ensures adequate boron supply for proper tissue development.

Practice deblossoming in: (1) January - deblossoming of emerging floral buds, and (2) December - deblossoming of emerging floral buds. This cultural practice removes malformed flower buds before they fully develop, reducing disease incidence and allowing the tree to produce healthy panicles in subsequent flushes. It's done during winter months when early flowering occurs.

Apply NAA (200 ppm) or planofix (90 ml/20 liters) during the first week of October for malformation control. This timing is before bud differentiation stages, which is critical for the growth regulator to be effective. The October application helps regulate flowering and reduces both vegetative and floral malformation incidence.

Spray copper oxychloride (3 g/L) for phoma blight in: (1) October - along with die back and anthracnose control after pruning, and (2) November - combined spray for die back, phoma blight, and anthracnose. The post-harvest period (October-November) is important for controlling this mature leaf disease before winter.

In October, apply 200-400 grams copper sulphate per tree near the root zone for gummosis control. This soil application provides copper that helps control the gummosis pathogen and strengthens tree defense. The treatment is done in October as part of post-harvest disease management activities.

Spray copper oxychloride (COC) at 0.3% for red rust control in: (1) July - along with anthracnose control, and (2) August - continued spraying for red rust and anthracnose. The monsoon months (July-August) favor red rust development, making copper sprays during this period essential for disease management.

In February, spray mancozeb (0.2%) for blossom blight control. This preventive fungicide application during flowering protects blossoms from infection. Blossom blight can cause significant flower drop and reduced fruit set, making February sprays critical for protecting the flowering process and ensuring good crop development.

For damping off control in nursery: (1) July - nursery soil treatment with formaldehyde or application of Trichoderma in affected nursery, stone dip treatment with thiram or captan or Trichoderma (0.3%) for 5 minutes, (2) August - proper drainage in nursery, drenching of soil with COC (0.3%) or 1.5% Bordeaux mixture. Combined soil treatment, seed treatment, and drainage management provides comprehensive control.

Trichoderma controls damping off through: (1) Application in affected nursery soil (July), and (2) Stone dip treatment with Trichoderma (0.3%) for 5 minutes (July). This beneficial fungus acts as a biocontrol agent, competing with and antagonizing damping off pathogens. It's an environmentally friendly alternative to chemical fungicides for nursery disease management.

Anthracnose appears as black spots on fruits, flowers, and leaves. These lesions often start as small, dark spots that can enlarge and coalesce, causing blossom blight, leaf spotting, and fruit rot, especially under warm, humid conditions.

Key cultural practices include: 1) Pruning to improve air circulation and reduce humidity in the canopy. 2) Removing and destroying infected plant parts (leaves, flowers, fruits) to reduce inoculum. 3) Planting resistant varieties if available.

Spray Carbendazim. It is a systemic fungicide effective against Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, the fungus causing anthracnose. Applications should be timed before or during periods of warm, humid, rainy weather which favor disease development.

The anthracnose pathogen Colletotrichum gloeosporioides produces acervuli (fruiting bodies) containing conidia (spores). Key features include the presence of dark, hair-like setae around the acervuli and curved, single-celled conidia.

Severe outbreaks are triggered by warm, humid, and rainy weather. Rain splash is the primary mode of spreading the spores from infected plant parts to healthy tissues, making the monsoon and post-monsoon periods high-risk.

The fungus survives on infected plant parts (mummified fruits, dead twigs, fallen leaves) left in the orchard. It spreads primarily through rain splash, which disperses the spores from these sources to new flowers, leaves, and fruits.

Powdery mildew appears as a distinctive white, powdery or flour-like fungal growth on the inflorescence (flower panicles) and young, tender fruits. It can cause flowers to wither and prevent fruit set, or blemish and distort young fruits.
Spray Wettable Sulfur. It is a contact fungicide highly effective against powdery mildew. Timely application at the flowering and early fruit set stages is crucial for control.

The fungus Oidium mangiferae grows as superficial mycelium on the plant surface. It produces conidia (asexual spores) in chains, which give the characteristic powdery appearance. These spores are easily dislodged and spread by wind.

Powdery mildew thrives under conditions of cool nights with high humidity, followed by warm, dry days. This diurnal fluctuation, common during the flowering season, is ideal for spore germination and disease spread.

Powdery mildew spreads primarily through wind-borne conidia. The lightweight spores produced in chains on the plant surface are easily carried by wind currents to infect new flowers and young fruits on nearby trees.
Planting resistant or tolerant mango varieties is a key long-term, preventive strategy. This reduces dependency on fungicides and provides inherent protection against the disease.

Anthracnose appears as dark, sunken lesions on leaves, flowers, and fruits. Infected fruits often rot before ripening. The disease is devastating in humid regions, spreading rapidly during warm, moist conditions, especially in the rainy season.

Powdery mildew looks like white powder on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Severe infections cause premature flower and fruit drop. Young leaves may become distorted. It thrives in dry conditions with high humidity during early morning and evening.

Sooty mould is a secondary fungal infection that grows on honeydew secreted by sap-sucking pests like aphids, mealybugs, and scale insects. The black, sooty layer on leaves blocks sunlight, reducing photosynthesis and weakening the tree, though it doesn't directly infect plant tissue.
Bacillus subtilis can be used as a microbial control agent against anthracnose (Colletotrichum gloeosporioides) on mango trees.
Tea tree oil is mentioned as a natural substance that can be applied to help control powdery mildew (Oidium mangiferae) on mango plants.
Wash affected leaves with mild soapy water to physically remove the black sooty mould layer. This helps restore photosynthesis while you address the underlying pest problem causing the honeydew.

White superficial powdery fungal growth appears on inflorescence, leaves, stalks and young fruits, causing shedding. Affected flowers fail to open and fall prematurely. Young fruits may be entirely covered; as they grow, epidermis cracks forming corky tissue. Fruits may drop at marble size.

Young leaves show infection when color changes from brown to light green. White patches appear on both sides, more conspicuous on lower surface. Patches coalesce into larger purple-brown areas, often restricted to veins. Leaves may twist, curl and distort.

High humidity, cloudy weather and high wind velocity for 3-4 days. Optimal conditions: minimum temperature 10-13°C, maximum 27-31°C, RH 82-91%. In UP plains, severity peaks third/fourth week of March. Close planting without canopy management also increases severity.
Spray wettable sulphur (0.2%) when panicles are 3-4 inches in size. This early application helps prevent initial infection during panicle development stage.
15-20 days after first spray, apply dinocap (0.1%). Maintain this interval for effective disease control during flowering period.
15-20 days after second spray, apply tridemorph (0.1%). Avoid spraying at full bloom stage to prevent flower damage.

Pathogen persists on older leaves and malformed panicles during off-season. Spread occurs through wind-borne spores released between 11:00-16:00 hours. Spores take 5-7 hours for infection after germination.
Prune diseased leaves and malformed panicles harboring the pathogen to reduce primary inoculum load before flowering season.

Oval or irregular vinaceous brown to deep brown spots of various sizes scattered over leaf surface. Later lesions become blighted, rupture and show 'shot hole' symptoms. Young leaves are more susceptible than older ones.
Produces elongated black necrotic areas on twigs. Causes wither tip where young branch tips start drying from tip downwards. Petioles turn grey or black when affected.
Small black spots appear on panicles and open flowers, gradually enlarging and coalescing to cause blossom blight. Infected flowers fall off, leaving persistent spikes on peduncles.
Fruit infection is more common during transit and storage. Symptoms appear as dark lesions that can expand during post-harvest handling and storage conditions.
Temperature 25-30°C with ≥95% Relative humidity for 12 hours is conducive. Free moisture in orchard enhances spread. Closer spacing without pruning and poor orchard hygiene increase severity.

Spread by rain splash infecting all above-ground tissues. Fungus produces spores on dead twigs, leaves, inflorescence and fruits. Pathogen remains viable for 14 months on fallen leaves and dead plant material. Movement of infected planting material/fruits also spreads disease.
Spray Bavistin (carbendazim 0.1%) at 15-day intervals during flowering to effectively control blossom infection.
Spray copper oxychloride (0.3%) to control foliar infection on leaves and twigs.
Spray hexaconazole (0.01%) or carbendazim (0.1%) at 15-day intervals, ensuring last spray falls 15 days prior to harvest.
Hot water treatment at 52°C ± 1°C for 20 minutes. Duration can be reduced to 10 minutes by adding carbendazim or prochloraz (both 0.05%) to hot water.
Cover fruits on tree 15 days prior to harvest with newspaper or brown paper bags. This physical barrier prevents infection during critical ripening period.
Use Streptosporangium pseudovulgare as a biocontrol agent against anthracnose pathogen.
Collect and burn diseased leaves, twigs, gall midge infected leaves and fruits. This removes inoculum sources and reduces disease pressure.
Avoid spraying at full bloom stage as this can damage flowers and affect pollination. Spray before and after full bloom following the recommended schedule.

Powdery mildew shows white powdery growth on all parts, especially flowers and fruits, causing shedding. Anthracnose shows brown/black spots on leaves (shot holes), blossom blight with black spots on flowers, and affects fruits mainly postharvest. Powdery mildew favors cooler temperatures (10-13°C min), while anthracnose prefers warmer (25-30°C).

Causes shedding of infected flowers and young fruits, leading to serious crop loss. Affected flowers fail to open and fall prematurely. Fruits may drop at marble size. Young leaves distort affecting photosynthesis. Sepals are more susceptible than petals.
Pathogen remains viable for 14 months on fallen leaves, dead stems and diseased twigs attached to trees. This long persistence makes sanitation critical for management.

Profuse oozing of gum on affected wood, bark of trunk and larger branches, especially on cracked areas. In severe cases, gum droplets trickle down stems, bark turns dark brown with longitudinal cracks, rots completely, and trees dry up due to cracking, rotting and girdling effects.
Remove or clean diseased bark/portion and apply one of these pastes: Bordeaux paste, copper oxychloride paste, or cow dung paste. This helps seal wounds and prevent further infection.
Apply copper sulphate 500g per tree (adjusting for tree age) in soil around the tree trunk. Regular copper oxychloride sprays for leaf spot diseases also reduce gummosis incidence.

Circular, slightly angular, elongated spots 2-4mm diameter, brown in color. During rainy season, lesions vary in size, shape and color. On young fruits, infection appears grey to grayish brown with dark irregular margins. As fruits grow, spots enlarge with cracked, fissured, corky centers.
Frequent sprays of copper oxychloride (0.3%) to protect new flushes of growth are effective for scab control in nurseries.

Black velvety raised fungal outgrowth appears on midribs/veins of leaves, twigs and branches as spots that gradually increase and encircle trunk, limbs, branches and twigs. Creates characteristic black banded appearance. Incidence is low on main branches.
Gunny rubbing on twigs/branches to physically remove the black fungal growth, followed by chemical sprays for complete control.
Spray Bordeaux mixture (5:5:50) or copper oxychloride (0.3%) after gunny rubbing for effective control.

Leaves become lusterless and sparse. Trees wilt and die gradually. Infected roots are very light, crumble easily and powder with fingers. Fungal brackets (fruiting bodies) appear at tree base during rainy season.
Collect and destroy fungal brackets. Expose roots and drench with dinocap 2 ml/l, cover with soil and incorporate green leaves in tree basin to reduce disease.

Sudden dropping of leaves after seedling emergence. During prolonged rainy/humid weather, circular to irregular water-soaked patches appear at/below ground level. Patches enlarge and girdle entire seedling base.

Avoid water stagnation near root zone. Raise nursery on elevated beds. Fumigate nursery beds before sowing. Apply Trichoderma in affected areas. Spray Bordeaux mixture (1.5%) on plants and soil weekly.

Rusty red fructification of alga appears on leaves, veins, petioles, young twigs and fruits. Initially spots are greenish-grey and velvety, turning reddish-brown. Algal growth is superficial but conspicuous.
Spray Bordeaux mixture (5:5:50) or copper oxychloride (0.3%) twice during July/August at 15-day intervals, as disease starts with onset of rains.
Disease incidence is less when plant vigor is maintained with balanced nutrients. Healthy, well-nourished trees resist algal infection better.
Found on trunks, branches and twigs of full-grown trees in high humidity, heavy rainfall areas and poorly managed orchards. Appear as whitish, pinkish superficial patches of different shapes.
Gunny rubbing followed by spraying trunk, branches and twigs with commercial caustic soda (1.0%). Field sanitation and balanced nutrition also help control lichens.
Lasiodiplodia theobromae (synonyms: Botryodiplodia theobromae) causes gummosis. The perfect stage is Physalospora rhodina (sexual stage of Botryodiplodia theobromae).

Scab symptoms are very similar to anthracnose, making visual differentiation difficult. Both cause spots on leaves and fruits, but scab produces more distinct corky, cracked tissue on fruits as they enlarge.
Named for its characteristic black velvety fungal growth that forms bands around twigs, branches and sometimes trunk, creating conspicuous black banded appearance.
Presence of fungal brackets (fruiting bodies) at tree base during rainy season, combined with light, crumbly roots and overall tree decline.
Prolonged rainy and humid weather, waterlogged conditions, poor drainage, and overcrowded seedlings create ideal conditions for disease development.
Cephaleuros virescens is an alga, not a fungus, causing superficial parasitic growth on mango surfaces. It's a photosynthetic organism that appears rusty red.
High humidity, heavy rainfall areas, poorly managed orchards with neglected trees. Lichens indicate stressed trees and poor orchard maintenance.

Gummosis: Gum oozing, bark cracking. Black Banded: Black velvety fungal bands encircling branches. Lichens: Whitish/pinkish crusty patches, not banded. Gummosis affects internal tissues, others are superficial.

It attacks leaves, flowers, panicle stalks, and fruits, causing superficial white powdery appearance. Disease spreads rapidly by wind. Infection typically starts from inflorescence and spreads downward covering floral axis, tender leaves, and soft stem. Flowers fail to open, blacken or become brown, dry, and may fall from panicles. This significantly reduces fruit set.

Disease occurs when rains or mists are accompanied by cooler nights during flowering, especially when weather is cool and dry. Minimum temperature of 13-15°C, maximum temperature of 23-25°C with moderate relative humidity (64-72%) favors disease development. Pathogen survives in affected plant debris and under favorable conditions, airborne conidia are disseminated by wind.

Prune branches to keep them short for easy orchard management, entry of sunlight, and air flow within canopy. Apply balanced dose of fertilizers. Grow resistant varieties like Neelum, Zardalu, Banglora, Torapari-khurd, and Janardhan pasand. Use need-based spray of CIB&RC approved label claim fungicides. Integrated approach combining cultural, varietal resistance, and chemical control is most effective.

On leaves: lesions start as small, angular, brown to black spots that enlarge to form extensive dead areas. On panicles: first symptoms are small black or dark-brown spots which enlarge, coalesce, and kill flowers before fruit production. Petioles, twigs, and stems are susceptible and develop typical black color. Twig dieback occurs when severe, elongated, blackened lesions form on stems and twigs die back apically. On ripe fruits: sunken, prominent, dark brown to black decay spots develop; fruits may drop prematurely.

Under favorable climatic conditions of high humidity, frequent rains, and temperature of 24-32°C coinciding with flowering, anthracnose infections occur in the field. The pathogen survives between seasons on infected and defoliated branch terminals and mature leaves. These serve as inoculum sources for new infections.

Prune trees yearly and remove fallen plant debris. Practice wider plant spacing and intercropping with non-host plants to inhibit severe epidemics. Use need-based spray of CIB&RC approved label claim fungicides. Cultural practices that reduce humidity and improve air circulation are essential components of integrated management.

Two types exist: 1) Vegetative Malformation: more common on young seedlings, characterized by disrupting apical growth resulting in several small flushes. Multi-branching of shoot apex with scaly leaves is known as 'Bunchy Top' or 'Witches' Broom'. Malformed seedlings remain stunted and die. 2) Floral Malformation: shows variation in panicle. Malformed head dries up in black mass and persists for long time.

Disease spreads through propagating materials. The fungus doesn't sporulate in situ but sporulates on dried malformed panicles. Disease is severe at temperatures between 10-15°C during December to January before flowering. Disease is mild in areas with 15-20°C, sporadic between 20-25°C. Plants at 4-8 years are susceptible. In some cases, mites have been reported to carry the fungus and cause spread.

Destroy diseased plants. Use disease-free planting material. Incidence is reduced by spraying 100-200ppm NAA during October. Prune diseased parts along with basal 15-20cm apparently healthy portions. Sanitation and use of clean propagation material are critical for preventing disease spread.

Disease is noticed on leaves, leaf stalks, stems, twigs, branches, and fruits, initially producing water-soaked lesions, later turning into typical canker. Water-soaked irregular to angular raised lesions measuring 1-4mm in diameter form. Lesions are light yellow initially with yellow halo but with age enlarge or coalesce to form irregular necrotic cankerous patches with dark brown color. Water-soaked, dark brown to black lesions are observed which gradually develop into cankerous, raised or flat spots. These spots often burst, extruding gummy substances containing highly contagious bacterial cells.

Bacteria enters through natural openings such as stomata, wax and oil glands, leaf and fruit abrasions, leaf scars, and at apex of branches in panicle. Periods of high humidity, surface wetness, and wind accompanied with rain cause most rapid and maximum dissemination. Bacteria survives in infected plant parts and spreads through rain splashes and wind. Disease is rapid during rainy days.

Sanitation and seedling certification are recommended as preventive measures. Mango stones for raising seedlings (rootstock) should always be taken from healthy fruits. Use of windbreaks helps in reducing brushing/wounding which creates entry points for bacteria. Disease-free planting material is essential.

Pathogen causes dieback, tip dieback, graft union blight, twig blight, seedling rot, wood stain, stem-end rot, black root rot, fruit rot, dry rot, and brown rot of panicle. Disease is most conspicuous during October-November. It's characterized by drying back of twigs from top downwards, particularly in older trees, followed by drying of leaves giving appearance of fire scorch. Internal browning in wood tissue is observed when slit open along long axis. Cracks appear on branches and gum exudes before they die out.

Pathogens survive in plant debris which is the source of primary inoculum. High humidity and moist conditions favor disease development. The disease is most common in October-November. Environmental stress conditions predispose trees to infection.

Scion wood selected for propagation should be free from infection. Take every care to prevent disease introduction in newly planted orchards. Any infected portion should immediately be pruned, followed by spraying/pasting of copper oxychloride or pasting with cow dung at cut ends. Pruning should be done so that some healthy portion is also removed to ensure complete pathogen eradication (3 inches below infection site).

Sudden dropping of leaves after seedling emergence. During prolonged rainy and humid weather, infection occurs at or below ground level with circular to irregular water-soaked patches. These patches enlarge and ultimately girdle entire base of seedlings. The disease affects young seedlings primarily.

Disease is soil-borne and pathogen survives in soils of orchards. Primary infection occurs by soil and secondary by conidia through rain or wind. High humidity, high soil moisture, cloudiness, and low temperatures below 24°C for few days are ideal for infection and disease development.

Epicarp darkens around base-pedicel. Circular black patch which under humid atmosphere causes soft rot aided by pectinolytic and cellulolytic enzymes. More portions of fruit turn black and soften. Fruits lose ascorbic acid and non-reducing sugars rapidly. This is a significant postharvest disease.

Fungus persists in infected plant parts which serve as source of inoculum. Relative humidity of 80% with temperature range of 25.9-31.5°C favors disease development. These warm, humid conditions are typical of postharvest storage environments.

On matured green fruits, small brown spots appear with greyish white center which later turn to bigger lesions with large number of acervuli seen as black dots. The disease also affects leaves (brown spots) and twigs (black spots). Disease is caused by Pestalotia mangiferae.

Temperature between 20-25°C enhances mycelial growth with sporulation taking place at pH 5.5-6.0. Wounding leads to more disease incidence. The pathogen is opportunistic, requiring injury to establish infection.

Symptoms noticeable only on old leaves. Initially, lesions are angular, minute, irregular, yellow to light brown, scattered over leaf lamina. As lesions enlarge, color changes from brown to cinnamon and they become almost irregular. Fully developed spots characterized by dark margins and dull grey necrotic centers. In severe infection, spots coalesce forming patches measuring 3.5-13cm in size, resulting in complete withering and defoliation of infected leaves.

Pathogen is seed-borne fungus and inoculum present in seeds is source of primary infection. Fungus also survives on glumes, fruit, and plant debris. Rainy seasons favor disease development. Seed treatment and debris management are important control measures.

Follow common cultural, mechanical, and biological practices. Collect and burn affected branches. Balanced nutrition provides resistance to phoma blight. Proper tree nutrition is a key component of disease management.

Scab fungus attacks leaves, panicles, blossoms, twigs, bark of stems, and mango fruits. Spots are circular, slightly angular, elongated, 2-4mm in diameter, brown. On young fruits, infection is grey to greyish brown with dark irregular margins. As fruit attains size, spots enlarge and center may become covered with crack fissure and corky tissues.

Pathogen survives in form of resting spores in soil debris. Suitable temperatures and moisture promote release of Elsinoe mangiferae spores. This cycle of secondary infections continues throughout summer until leaves and fruit fall from tree at onset of winter.

Red rust caused by algae causes reduction in photosynthetic activity and defoliation of leaves. Disease easily recognized by rusty red spots mainly on leaves and sometimes on petioles and bark of young twigs; it's epiphytic in nature. Spots are greenish grey and velvety in texture. Later, they turn reddish brown. Circular and slightly elevated spots sometimes coalesce to form larger and irregular spots.

Disease is common in closed plantations. High humidity favors development of fruiting bodies. Pathogens reproduce and survive in spots on leaves or stems and in fallen plant host debris. Frequent rains and warm weather are favorable conditions. For hosts, poor plant nutrition, poor soil drainage, and stagnant air are predisposing factors to algal infection.

Discrete and discolored areas all over fruit. These areas turn dark brown to black at maturity. Black fruit bodies appear on spots. Disease is caused by Phomopsis mangiferae and is soil-borne, with conidia transmitted by wind and rain water.

Integrated disease management combines cultural practices (pruning, sanitation, balanced fertilization, proper spacing), use of disease-free planting material, selection of resistant varieties where available, mechanical removal of infected parts, biological control agents where appropriate, and need-based application of CIB&RC approved fungicides or bactericides. The strategy emphasizes prevention through good cultural practices, with chemical intervention only when necessary based on disease pressure and economic thresholds.

Orchard sanitation removes inoculum sources for both pests and diseases. This includes: removing fallen fruits (reduces fruit fly, weevil populations), destroying infected plant debris (reduces fungal and bacterial inoculum), cleaning branch junctions before flowering (disturbs resting weevils), removing malformed panicles and galls (reduces pathogen spread), burning affected branches (eliminates disease sources), and ploughing to expose pupae and resting stages to predators and heat. Sanitation is fundamental to reducing pest and disease pressure.

Copper fungicides are most popular, often combined with mancozeb for effectiveness. Monthly applications of copper oxychloride with mancozeb work well. Preventive treatments with copper-based or triazole fungicides are common. Contact fungicide chlorothalonil is effective but phytotoxic to fruit larger than a golf ball, so use only after early fruit set. Systemic options include prochloraz (pre-harvest), imazalil (post-harvest), and strobilurins (limit to 3 applications per season). Alternate fungicides with different modes of action to prevent resistance.

Start spraying at panicle emergence and continue through harvest. In humid environments, up to 25 sprays may be needed seasonally. Typical schedules: Australia and Philippines use 6-13 sprays from panicle emergence; Malaysia sprays every 10 days from flower bud stage; Honduras uses 7 sprays alternating contact and systemic fungicides from blossom start. Apply pre-flowering treatments to reduce inoculum on foliage and branch terminals. In areas with regular rainfall, use calendar-based schedules; in seasonally dry areas, forecasting models can reduce applications.

Use hot water treatment (45°C for 5 minutes) combined with fungicide dips. Prochloraz at 250-300 ppm by overhead spray or dip effectively controls anthracnose. In Australia, hot water with benomyl followed by prochloraz spray controls anthracnose, stem-end rot, and alternaria during storage. In Israel, use chlorine sanitation, hot-water brushing (15-20s), then spray with 50mM hydrochloric acid alone or with prochloraz. Hot-water brushing at 50-60°C for 20 seconds induces fruit resistance. Gamma irradiation requires hot fungicide dip for complete control.

Establish orchards in areas with well-defined dry seasons for fruit development under low humidity. Modify flowering time using potassium nitrate sprays to mature foliage to advance flowering by several weeks, moving fruit development to drier periods. Practice orchard sanitation by removing dry panicles and mummified fruits. Choose less susceptible varieties like 'Tommy Atkins' and 'Keitt' over 'Irwin', 'Kent', 'Haden', and 'Edward'. Fruit bagging reduces severity but may reduce red color. Store fruits at 10-12°C immediately after harvest in well-ventilated areas.

Anthracnose is caused by Colletotrichum species. The most important is C. asianum, a mango biotype reported in Australia, Brazil, Florida, Ghana, Mexico, Panama, Philippines, South Africa, and Thailand. Other species in the C. gloeosporioides complex (22 species total) include C. fructicola, C. gloeosporioides, C. queenslandicum, C. theobromicola, and C. tropicale. Secondary roles are played by C. acutatum complex (C. fioriniae, C. simmondsii), C. boninense complex (C. cliviae, C. karstii), and C. siamense complex species.

Lasiodiplodia theobromae is the most common and widespread pathogen. Other important pathogens include L. pseudotheobromae, Neofusicoccum parvum, N. mangiferae, Botryosphaeria dothidea, Neoscytalidium hyalinum, Dothiorella dominicana, D. mangiferae, Phomopsis mangiferae, and Pestalotiopsis mangiferae. Infection occurs before harvest through endophytic colonization of pedicel tissues from previous growth flushes. The disease produces heavy losses during fruit storage.

Postharvest control includes dipping, spraying, or ultra-low-volume application of prochloraz or sodium hypochlorite. Combined treatment of wax and hot water (55°C) provides very effective control. For high-value export fruit, use 20 minutes in 53°C water for 48-61% reduction. Low-dose UV-C irradiation (<3 kJ/m²) or 0.45 kGy gamma irradiation help manage the disease. Pre-harvest: implement pruning programs to reduce endophytic inoculum, prevent water stress during fruit development, avoid placing fruits on ground, and cool to 13°C immediately after harvest.

Alternaria rot or black spot is caused by Alternaria alternata. It appears as black spots on fruits, alternaria leaf spots, and lesions on inflorescences. The disease is most prevalent in arid environments. In Israel, it's more important on fruit than leaves. The fungus is cosmopolitan with many host plants but effects on mango are strongest in dry conditions. It has been reported in Australia, Egypt, India, Israel, and South Africa.

Pre-harvest: three sprays with maneb starting 2 weeks after initial fruit set are most effective. Post-harvest is simpler and more efficient: spray fruits with prochloraz on packing line. Best results come from combining physical and chemical treatments: hot water brushing (HWB) at 50-55°C for 15-20 seconds followed by prochloraz spray. For low infection levels, use milder treatment with chlorine. For enhanced control, use HWB followed by 50mM hydrochloric acid spray, which modulates pH to inhibit pathogen. Prochloraz at 45µg/ml in 50mM HCl works better than HCl alone.

Three genetically distinct groups cause bacterial black spot: Group I (Africa, Europe, Asia) is Xanthomonas citri pv. mangiferaeindicae; Group II (Brazil) is X. axonopodis pv. anacardii; Group III (French West Indies) is X. axonopodis pv. spondiae. The disease is widespread in Asia (Japan, India, Malaysia, Thailand, Philippines), Australia, UAE, Indian Ocean islands, and East/Southern Africa. It's also known as bacterial canker in India and can be the most important disease where other fungal diseases are well managed.

Chemical control: Apply copper-based bactericides during rainy weather, focusing on fruit protection. Timing varies by wet exposure duration. Agricultural antibiotics like streptomycin sulphate or nitrate are effective but resistance develops with continued use. Cultural practices: Use pathogen-free planting material for new orchards. Install windbreaks to reduce wounding. Remove infected twigs from canopy. Varietal resistance: Use resistant cultivars in high-pressure areas. The pathogen spreads short distances in wind-blown aerosols within orchards; long-distance spread occurs mainly via infected propagation material.

Sooty moulds are diverse saprophytic fungi that develop on honeydew secreted by insects like aphids, mealybugs, and scales. Black mildews are caused by tropical obligate plant pathogens, especially Meliola mangiferae. Sooty blotch refers to diseases not associated with honeydew, caused by several dothidiomycete groups. All produce dark, superficial growths on stems, leaves, and fruits. While sooty mould itself doesn't directly damage plants, heavy coating reduces photosynthesis and fruit quality.

Malformation is one of the most destructive mango diseases, first described in India in 1891. Trees usually aren't killed, but the vegetative phase affects canopy development and flower infection dramatically reduces fruit yield. It's widely distributed worldwide and continues spreading to disease-free areas. The disease has been reported in Australia, Brazil, Myanmar, China, Egypt, El Salvador, India, Israel, Malaysia, Mexico, Nicaragua, Oman, Pakistan, Senegal, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Sudan, Spain, Swaziland, Uganda, and the United States.

Fusarium mangiferae is the primary agent, reported from Australia, China, Egypt, Florida, Israel, Malaysia, Oman, South Africa, Spain, and Sri Lanka. Additional causal species include F. mexicanum and F. pseudocircinatum in Mexico; F. sterilihyphosum in Brazil and South Africa; F. tupiense in Brazil, Senegal, and Spain; F. proliferatum in Australia, China, and Malaysia; and other described and undescribed Fusarium species in various countries. The pathogen's internal location in affected trees makes chemical control difficult.

Chemical control is difficult due to the pathogen's internal location. In India, carbendazim spray every 15 days is recommended. In Pakistan, clipping malformed branches 45cm away followed by benomyl spray showed 70% reduction. Prochloraz applications with sanitation measures provide significant reductions but aren't approved in some countries. Fosetyl-Al injections reduced malformation from 96% to 48% without yield increase. In South Africa, intensive phosphonate applications show effectiveness, but efficacy needs demonstration elsewhere and must address residue limits. In Egypt, nano-chitosan foliar application improved growth, quality, yield, and decreased malformation.

Establish new plantings with pathogen-free nursery stock - never take scion material from affected orchards. Remove and burn any affected nursery plants immediately. In established orchards, remove all affected terminals plus the subtending three nodes and burn them. Continuous removal of infected inflorescences over four years significantly declines disease incidence, though difficult on large trees. Select resistant varieties: consistently resistant include 'Bhadauran' (Brazil, India), 'Primor' (Brazil), and 'Zebda' (Egypt). Susceptibility varies by variety and location.

Several biocontrol agents show promise in India. Trichoderma species (T. viride, T. virens, T. harzianum) effectively decrease Fusarium growth, varying in efficacy. Plant leaf extracts show antifungal activity against Fusarium, with Azadirachta indica, Achyrenthes roseus, and Calotropis gigantea most effective. Dhatura stramonium, Calotropis gigantean, and Azadirachta indica also show activity. In South Africa, bacterial isolates (Alcaligenes faecalis) significantly inhibit pathogen growth through competition for space and production of volatiles, phenolic compounds, and siderophores.

Powdery mildew is caused by the host-specific fungus Oidium mangiferae. It was first described in Brazil in 1914 and is now reported in most mango-producing regions worldwide. The disease appears as white powdery fungal growth on leaves, flowers, and young fruits, causing leaf curl, distortion, premature drop, flower browning, and failure to set fruit. It's most severe during dry weather with high humidity at night.

Multiple fungicide groups are effective: copper-based, sulfur, chlorothalonil, systemic benzimidazoles, imidazoles, morpholines, organophosphorus, oxathiins, piperazine, pyrimidines, strobilurins, and triazoles. Sulfur fungicides (dusts or sprays) provide reasonable protection but can burn flowers and young fruits in warm, sunny conditions. Systemic fungicides are very effective. Apply at 15-20 day intervals after dormant sprays. Some fungicides (dinocap, fenbuconazole, hexaconazole) reduce pollen germination, so limit use during flowering. Phosphate solutions (K2HPO4, KH2PO4) alternated with systemics are effective and safer.

Yes, several biocontrol agents are effective. Ampelomyces quisqualis parasitizes powdery mildew and is tolerant to many fungicides. Bio-fungicide AQ10 (A. quisqualis) at 0.005% shows good disease reduction. Verticillium lecanii, Bacillus subtilis, and Tilletiopsis minor applied at 15-day intervals effectively control the disease on blossom clusters. B. subtilis and A. quisqualis show high disease control with three sprays at 15-day intervals starting two weeks after panicle emergence. Mixing kaolin and monopotassium phosphate with biocontrol agents increases efficacy. Control mechanisms include mycoparasitism, antibiosis, competition, and induced resistance.

Regular orchard inspection and removal/pruning of infected leaves and malformed panicles reduce primary inoculum and improve fungicide effectiveness. Select resistant or less susceptible varieties: 'Sensation', 'Tommy Atkins', and 'Kensington' are slightly susceptible; 'Haden', 'Glenn', 'Carrie', 'Zebda', 'Hindi be Sennara', 'Ewaise', and 'Keitt' are moderately susceptible. Very susceptible varieties include 'Zill', 'Kent', 'Alphonso', 'Seddek', and 'Nam Doc Mai'. In India, 'Baigan Phalli', 'Barbalia', 'Dabari', 'Dilpasand', 'Khirama', 'Nagarideeh', 'Oloor', and 'Totapari' are highly resistant.

Seca was first reported in 1938 in Pernambuco, Brazil, and sudden decline in 1998 in Oman, Pakistan, and UAE - they're considered the same disease. It's a lethal fungal disease. In Brazil, Ceratocystis fimbriata is the primary cause. In Oman and Pakistan, C. manginecans is the primary agent; C. omanensis is a minor pathogen. The pathogen spreads via infected propagation materials, pruning equipment, and beetle vectors. Trees killed by the disease are significant reservoirs of vectors and pathogens.

Prevention is critical: use pathogen-free propagation material for new plantings. Use clean pruning tools in affected areas, frequently disinfested with bleach, formalin, or other disinfectants. Remove and destroy killed trees to eliminate vector and pathogen reservoirs. In resistant cultivar areas, remove and burn affected branches, treat exposed stubs with copper fungicides. Use resistant/tolerant genotypes: in Brazil, 'Manga Dagua', 'Pico', 'IAC 101', 'IAC 102', 'Edwards', 'Van Dyke', 'Carabao' resist two pathotypes; 'Rosa', 'Sabina', 'Tommy Atkins', 'Irwin' are tolerant. In Oman, 'Hindi Besennara', 'Mulgoa', 'Rose' develop less disease.

Diverse biotic and abiotic factors cause decline. Main fungal pathogens are endophytes with Botryosphaeria or Botryosphaeria-like teleomorphs, especially Lasiodiplodia theobromae and Neofusicoccum parvum. Stress and wound predisposition are usually associated with symptom development. Other causes include Dothiorella dominicana, Diplodia recifiensis, Ceratocystis fimbriata, Neoscytalidium dimidiatum, Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, Phomopsis spp., and Botryosphaeria ribis. Predisposing factors include injury, insects, drought, hardpan soil, high temperatures, sun scorch, high humidity, water stress, nutritional deficiencies, frost, and physical damage.

Phytophthora palmivora causes multiple diseases: wilt, crown rot, root rot, and death of nursery stock in Arizona, Philippines, and Thailand; trunk damage in mature trees in Ivory Coast; fruit damage in Australia, Malaysia, and West Africa. In Spain, a Phytophthora species was isolated from wilted, chlorotic trees with sparse canopies and cracked bark. These are oomycete diseases that can cause significant damage to seedlings, nursery stocks, and mature trees, though relatively less important than foliar and floral diseases.

Pythium vexans (oomycete) causes root rot and wilt of seedlings. Symptoms include wilting foliage that initially becomes pale green but later develops necrotic patches. Roots develop wet, blackened necrosis beginning in finer roots and progressing to larger roots and root collar. Rhizoctonia solani (basidiomycete) also causes root rot and damping off of seedlings in India. Both pathogens can cause significant damage to young mango plants.

Sclerotium rot is caused by the fungus Sclerotium rolfsii (teleomorph: Athelia rolfsii). This disease has been reported in Brazil, India, and the Philippines. It's a soil-borne fungal disease that can affect mango trees. Like other soil-borne diseases, it's relatively less important than foliar and floral diseases but can cause significant damage when conditions favor its development.

Pink disease is caused by the basidiomycete Erythricium salmonicolor (anamorph: Necator decretus). Also known as cobweb, rubellosis, and thread blight, it affects many woody plants in humid tropics and is one of the most destructive mango diseases. It significantly reduces tree vigor and yield, especially in young trees. The disease has been mainly studied on rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) in Southeast Asia. It thrives in humid tropical conditions.

Scab is caused by Elsinoë mangiferae (anamorph: Sphaceloma mangiferae). First described in Cuba and Florida in the 1940s, it's now widespread in the western hemisphere. Scab is important in nurseries since young tissues are most susceptible. High humidity promotes infection. The disease affects young, developing tissues more severely than mature plant parts, making it a particular concern for nursery operations and young tree establishment.

Apical necrosis is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae. Reported in Spain, Israel, Portugal, and possibly Egypt, it affects apical buds, leaves, and panicles but not fruit. Dark brown to blackish necrosis develops on vegetative floral buds and can extend from affected buds to leaf petioles. In high damage conditions, it can kill large portions of the canopy and much of the tree's bloom, significantly impacting productivity.

Leaf blight is caused by the fungus Macrophoma mangiferae (Ascomycota). It has been reported in India and Nigeria and detected in shipments to the USA from Mexico, though it doesn't seem to be a serious problem. The disease affects mango foliage but is not considered a major threat to mango production. It represents one of several minor foliar diseases that can occur on mango under certain conditions.

Grey leafspot is caused by Pestalotiopsis mangiferae (synonym: Pestalolia mangiferae), which also causes stem-end rot. It's a weak pathogen that usually requires wounding to infect mango. The disease is usually unimportant and occurs mainly on unhealthy or poorly maintained trees. The fungus produces abundant conidia in acervuli that develop in grey leafspot lesions and necrotic areas on fruit. Other Pestalotiopsis species affecting mango include P. mangifolia and P. versicolor.

Algal leaf spot, also known as red rust, is caused by the alga Cephaleuros virescens and less frequently by C. parasiticus (family Trentepohliaceae, division Chlorophyta). This is an algal infection rather than a fungal disease. It appears as rust-colored spots on leaves. While not typically devastating, it can affect tree appearance and in severe cases may impact photosynthesis. It's more common in humid environments where algae can thrive on leaf surfaces.

Phoma blight is caused by Phoma glomerata and is widespread in India. It occurs only on old leaves. Initially, lesions are minute and yellow-brown. As they expand, they darken to brown or cinnamon, become irregular, and may develop dark margins and dull-grey centers. In severe cases, necrotic patches as large as 13 cm in diameter may develop, causing defoliation. This disease specifically targets older foliage rather than young, developing tissues.

Phoma leafspot is caused by Phoma sorghina and is present in India. On young leaves, it causes irregular to roughly circular, water-soaked spots up to 2.5mm in diameter. Lesions are brown with yellow to brown margins. Lesions on midribs are elongated and more conspicuous and may coalesce to up to 14cm in diameter. The symptoms can be confused with those caused by anthracnose. Unlike phoma blight which affects old leaves, this disease targets young foliage.

Gall and scaly bark disorders are caused by Fusarium decemcellulare (synonym: F. rigidiuscula). These are usually minor problems but can cause general loss of vigor. The disease has been reported in Florida (USA), Mexico, and Venezuela. While not typically devastating, these disorders can affect tree health over time, particularly when trees are under other stresses or in suboptimal growing conditions.

Black-banded disease is a relatively unimportant disease affecting mango leaves and branches. The causal fungus is Rhinocladium corticola (teleomorph: Peziotrichum corticolum), described on the bark of trees in Poona, India. While not a major threat to mango production, it can occur under certain conditions and may contribute to overall tree stress when combined with other factors.

Verticillium wilt is caused by Verticillium dahliae (originally attributed to V. albo-atrum). The disease was first reported in Florida. It's a soil-borne fungal disease that can affect mango trees, causing wilting symptoms due to vascular infection. Like other soil-borne diseases of mango, it's relatively less important than foliar and floral diseases but can cause problems in affected trees.

White root disease is caused by Rigidoporus lignosus, a basidiomycete common in soils of humid tropics of Africa and Asia. More recently, Rosellinia necatrix was reported as the causal agent of white root rot in mango trees in Spain. These are soil-borne fungal pathogens that attack the root system, potentially causing significant damage to affected trees in areas where they occur.

Traditional sanitizer is chlorine at 100-150ppm with water pH 6.5-7.5 (sodium hypochlorite, calcium hypochlorite, or chlorine gas). Alternatives include ozone (O3) and ozonated water (FDA-approved 1997), which control postharvest rots and increase antioxidant activity. Electrolyzed water produced by adding sodium chloride to tap water and passing electrical current creates oxidizing (acidic) and reducing (alkaline) water that works against bacteria and fungi. Hydrogen peroxide is effective against several fungi. Sulfur dioxide has been used as fungal disinfectant. These sanitizers wash and kill microorganisms on fruit surfaces.

Heat treatment reduces postharvest diseases through multiple methods: hot-water dipping and rinsing, hot water vapor, and dry-air treatments. Benefits include postharvest decay reduction, pest killing, color and flavor preservation, and shelf-life improvement. Hot-water brushing at 50-60°C for 20 seconds reduces decay via surface cleansing and inducing fruit resistance against pathogens. Hot-water dipping for 3-7 minutes is moderately efficient at delaying rot and controls anthracnose and alternaria better than stem-end rot. Growing demand for residue-free fruits encourages these alternative technologies.

Yes, both UV-C and gamma irradiation help control diseases. Low-dose UV-C irradiation (<3 kJ/m²) manages postharvest diseases caused by Botryosphaeria dothidea, Lasiodiplodia theobromae, Alternaria alternata, and Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, even without direct pathogen impact. Gamma irradiation at 0.45 kGy reduces disease caused by L. theobromae. For anthracnose control, gamma irradiation requires incorporation of hot fungicide dip for complete effectiveness. Shortwave infrared radiation treatments also reduce anthracnose damage and can be considered for organic markets.

Cold storage at 10-12°C is one of the best ways to delay fruit ripening and decrease postharvest decay. Fruits should be cooled to 13°C immediately after harvest and stored in well-ventilated places. Prevention of water stress during fruit development and maturation, and avoiding placing fruits on the ground also suppress disease development. Cold temperature storage is encouraged by growing public demand for chemical residue-free fruits as an alternative technology to chemical treatments.

Yes, Bacillus licheniformis isolated from leaf and fruit surfaces effectively controls anthracnose and soft rot caused by Botryosphaeria. Applied at 3-week intervals from flowering until harvest, it controls moderate disease levels. Use alone or alternated with copper oxychloride (organic-approved), or combined with hot water treatments (45°C, 5 minutes) and low-dose prochloraz or sodium hypochlorite - though only alone qualifies for organic agriculture. Bacillus coagulans from mango phylloplane is effective against bacterial black spot strains. In Thailand, Bacillus sp. MB61 and LB72 reduce lesion size from Colletotrichum.

Several yeasts show potential but haven't been widely applied commercially. Rhodotorula minuta has been suggested as a potential biocontrol agent for anthracnose. Debaryomyces nepalensis decreases anthracnose decay incidence while maintaining storage quality of mango fruits. A non-pathogenic strain of Colletotrichum magna colonizes fruit endophytically and prevents infection by C. gloeosporioides. Expression of an antifungal peptide in Saccharomyces yeast controlled postharvest diseases caused by C. coccodes. While promising in research, commercial application remains limited.

Integrated management combines multiple strategies: use tolerant cultivars, practice orchard hygiene (remove dry panicles, mummified fruits, infected terminals), manipulate flowering timing with potassium nitrate to avoid rainy seasons, implement chemical control (fungicides, bactericides) at proper timing based on disease forecasting or calendar, use biological controls (Bacillus, Trichoderma, beneficial yeasts), apply physical treatments (heat, cold storage, irradiation), employ fruit sanitizers, establish proper sanitation and pruning programs, use pathogen-free planting material, and maintain tree vigor through proper nutrition and water management. Success requires combining appropriate tactics for local conditions.

Since anthracnose development depends on high humidity, modifying flowering time to a less sensitive (drier) period is appropriate. Flowering can be advanced by several weeks by applying potassium nitrate sprays to mature foliage. The growth retardant paclobutrazol, alone or followed by potassium nitrate sprays, can also advance flowering, though its use isn't allowed in some countries. In tropics where mango flowers during dry seasons, anthracnose incidence can be near zero in fruits developing completely in dry season without additional control. In rainy season, >90% incidence is common.

Anthracnose forecasting models have been developed to schedule and reduce fungicide applications. However, differences exist between models' time predictions, so use caution when applying a model in areas other than where it was developed. Forecasting is most useful in seasonally dry situations where infection occurs only after significant rainfall. Calendar-based application schedules are needed wherever regular rainfall occurs. Models help optimize spray timing and reduce unnecessary applications, saving costs and reducing environmental impact while maintaining disease control.

Anthracnose appears as dark brown to black lesions on leaves, stems, flowers, and fruits. On fruits, it causes dark, sunken spots that can merge and lead to fruit rot. On leaves, you'll see irregular brown spots with dark margins. The disease is most severe during warm, humid conditions and can cause significant yield loss if not managed properly.

Bacterial canker manifests as dark, sunken lesions on branches and trunks, often with gum exudation. On leaves, you'll see water-soaked spots that turn brown or black. Infected branches may show dieback, and the disease can spread rapidly during wet, warm weather. The cankers can girdle branches, leading to wilting and death of affected parts.

Die back disease shows as progressive wilting and drying of shoots from tip downwards. You'll see browning of young twigs and branches, starting at the tips and moving toward the main stem. Leaves turn brown, dry up, and remain attached to dead branches. The disease often occurs during flowering and fruiting stages, causing significant yield reduction.

Powdery mildew appears as white, powdery fungal growth on leaves, flowers, and young fruits. You'll see a dusty white coating on the upper and lower leaf surfaces, panicles, and young shoots. Infected leaves may curl, become distorted, and drop prematurely. On flowers, the disease causes browning and failure to set fruit. The disease is most severe during dry weather with high humidity at night.

Sooty mould appears as black, velvety fungal growth on leaves, branches, and fruits. The black coating covers the leaf surface, reducing photosynthesis and making the tree look dirty. This mould grows on honeydew secreted by sucking insects like scales, mealybugs, and aphids. While the mould itself doesn't directly damage the plant, heavy coating can reduce fruit quality and tree vigor.

Sooty mould results from interaction between sap-feeding insects (like aphids and scale) and non-parasitic fungi (Meliola mangiferae). The insects produce honeydew which acts as food for fungi, causing black growth on plant surfaces.

Sooty mould reduces gas exchange and photosynthesis by forming a black layer on leaf surfaces. It develops as a result of honeydew secretion from sap-feeding insects, which fungi use as food substrate.

Control the sucking insects (aphids, scale) and ants that protect them to cut off honeydew supply. Use traps, moderate fertilizers, crop rotation, sanitation, and products like Jambo Clean to clear existing mould.
White superficial fungal growth appears on leaves, fruits, panicle stalks and flowers. The fungus Oidium mangiferae thrives in high humidity and moderate temperatures.
Use sulphur- and copper-based fungicides containing: Probineb + cymoxanil; Metalaxyl + Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole; Metaxyl-M + Chlorothalonil; or Bacillus subtilis + sulphur.
Caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides and Glomerella cingulata (sexual stage). The fungus survives saprophytically on dead branches and plant debris.
Use copper-based fungicides with active ingredients like Azoxystrobin, Propineb, Difenoconazole, or Hexaconazole. Apply after first appearance on panicles.
Caused by Elsinoe mangiferae or Denticularia mangiferae fungi. Lesions can be confused with anthracnose but have distinct corky, cracked appearance.
Prune diseased parts, maintain proper spacing, and use copper-based fungicides like copper hydroxide or copper sulphate.

Irregular brown to black necrotic patches on leaves, twigs, stems, branches and fruits. Fruits show water-soaked spots that erupt producing exudates. Cankerous lesions release gummy ooze containing bacteria.
Spray copper-based fungicides like Streptocycline or products containing streptomycin sulphate. Use resistant varieties (e.g., Bombay Green) and maintain orchard hygiene.
Caused by Lasiodiplodia theobromae or Colletotrichum species. Characterized by elongated black necrotic areas on twigs with death progressing from tip downwards.
Prune infected parts using disinfected tools, destroy pruned material, and spray copper-based fungicides to prevent spread.
Interveinal chlorosis and marginal necrosis, dieback of young stems, eventual tree death. Gummosis appears on necrotic tissue over time.
Apply iron, manganese, and zinc micronutrients. Avoid tree wounding, use disinfected tools, prune infected parts, and apply fungicides. Use Trichoderma spp. for biological control.
Water-soaked lesions on leaves that become sunken. Caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. Mangiferaeindicae.
Cracks on stems and branches leading to bark rupture followed by resin exudation. Different from bacterial canker which has distinct bacterial ooze.
Ensure adequate spacing, air circulation, and sunlight exposure to reduce humidity. Regulate watering and remove infected plants that act as inoculum sources.
Use disease-free certified germplasm, avoid poor orchard aeration, keep plants healthy to avoid stress, practice sanitation, and use resistant varieties like Tommy Atkins.
Use disease-free certified germplasm, maintain orchard hygiene, use resistant varieties like Bombay Green, and prune infected parts promptly.

Refer to registered products from pesticide boards (like PCPB in Kenya). Products like Jambo Clean or other effective available market products can clear existing mould once insect sources are controlled.

Powdery mildew appears as whitish grey mycelial wefts initially on inflorescence (flowers and flower buds). The fungus spreads to tender fruits, leaves and shoots, covering the entire surface with a powdery substance consisting of millions of spores (conidia) borne in chains. On young fruits, the entire surface becomes covered by mildew, and as fruit grows, the epidermis cracks and corky tissues form with purplish brown blotchy areas. On young leaves, small irregular greyish patches appear mostly on the underside, which coalesce and turn purplish brown under favorable conditions.

Several fungicides are effective: Sulphur dust, wettable sulphur, dinocap, tridemorph, and carbendazim (Bavistin 0.1%) are quite effective. Newer fungicides include triadimefon, thiophanate-methyl, bitertanol, hexaconazole, flusilazole, fenarimol, cyproconazole, and penconazole. Spraying of Bavistin (0.1%) at 20 day intervals or three sprays of either Microsul (0.2%) or Bavistin (0.1%) at emergence of panicles, opening of flowers, and fruit set stages are most effective. Spray during flowering stage is essential as blossom infection causes the main loss.

Yes, effective eradication of inoculum contributes greatly in lowering infection levels and improves fungicide control effectiveness. The loss can be reduced by 50-75% if branches are shaken after each shower to remove infected flowers and reduce inoculum load. This mechanical method combined with chemical sprays provides integrated disease management.

On leaves, anthracnose appears as oval or irregular vinaceous brown to deep brown spots of variable size scattered over the leaf surface. Under damp conditions, elongated brown necrotic areas measuring 20-25 mm in diameter form, which later get blighted and rupture, showing a 'shot hole' appearance. On fruits, small water-soaked lesions develop that turn dark brown to black. Initially spots are round but after coalescence form large irregular blotches or cover the entire fruit. The spots have large deep cracks that penetrate deep into the fruit causing extensive rotting. Under moist conditions, blackened areas become covered with minute pinkish reproductive bodies.

Blossom blight is the most destructive phase of anthracnose as it affects fruit set and yield. Blackish brown specks appear on peduncles and flowers which gradually enlarge and coalesce to cause death of flowers. The infected flowers fall off, leaving persistent spikes on the peduncles. Continuous wet weather during flowering causes serious blossom blight.

The disease can be controlled effectively by sprays of zineb (0.2%) or Bordeaux mixture (4:4:50) sprayed twice at flowering and then at 15 days interval until harvest. Bavistin (0.1%) at 15 day intervals, Captan, Blitox, and Difolatan are also effective. Spraying copper oxychloride (0.2%) + zineb (0.2%) after heavy showers followed by carbendazim (0.3%) at pea stage and zineb (0.2%) before stone hardening reduces anthracnose incidence. In South Africa, fortnightly sprays of flusilazole or pyrazophos at 20% flowering controlled blossom spot along with powdery mildew.

Major postharvest control strategies include: (1) Regular scheduled fungicide sprays in field to reduce latent infection, (2) Hot water treatment at 50-55°C for 15 min or 46°C for 90-115 min, (3) Fruit dip at 55°C for 5 min in benomyl + TBZ solution, (4) Heated benomyl treatment at 55°C for 5 min or 52-53°C for 10 min, (5) Instantaneous dip in benomyl (0.05% a.i.) or TBZ (0.09% a.i.), (6) 30 sec dip in flusilazole (0.01%), (7) Forced air treatment at 48°C for 150 min or 51.5°C for stored fruits, (8) Prochloraz dip (0.025%) for 30 sec combined with storage in 6% O2.

Diseased leaves, twigs and fruits lying in the orchard should be collected and all infected twigs from the tree should be pruned and burnt. This sanitation practice reduces the initial inoculum source as the pathogen survives on fallen leaves, blighted peduncles, dead persistent stems and diseased twigs attached to trees, which produce spores under favorable conditions serving as infection source for succeeding bloom.

Small water-soaked lesions appear in groups on the leaf surface, which increase in size, turn brown to black and get surrounded by a yellowish halo. Several lesions may coalesce to form large necrotic patches which are often rough and raised. On young fruits, water-soaked lesions develop that turn dark brown to black. Infected fruits may show cracks in the skin and badly affected ones drop prematurely. Under natural conditions, the pathogen causes water-soaked spots which turn into cankers on fruits, leaves, petioles, twigs and branches.

Agrimycin-100 (250ppm) proved effective when used as fruit dip. Monthly sprayings of Bavistin (1000 ppm) reduce the disease. Two sprays of streptocycline (200-300ppm) at 20 days interval, streptomycin sulphate (250 ppm) followed by Aureofungin, and 3 sprays of streptocycline (200ppm) at 10 days interval are effective. In further studies, streptocycline (300 ppm) + copper oxychloride (0.3%) was found more effective. Stem injection of Bavistin (1000ppm) in 3 to 5 years old seedlings has also been effective.

Regular inspection of orchards, sanitation and seedling certification are recommended as preventive measures. Selection of stones from healthy fruits for root stock is advised. The bacterium survives in infected plant parts on trees and in resident form on weed hosts and mango leaves and fruits. Twig cankers initiate infection on fruits. Removing infected weeds and maintaining disease-free planting material are crucial preventive steps.

The disease is characterized by dying back of twigs from top downwards with drying of leaves, particularly in older trees, followed by complete defoliation giving a fire scorch appearance. Discoloration and darkening of bark on young twigs at a certain distance from the tip is external evidence. Upper leaves lose green color and gradually turn brown with upward folding of margins. Such leaves shrivel and fall off in a month, leaving shrivelled twigs bare. Internal browning in wood tissue is observed on splitting open the twigs along the long axis. The disease is most conspicuous during October and November.

Pruning of dead wood and pasting of cut ends and healthy bud wood with protective fungicides are the main alternatives. It should be ascertained that scion wood selected for propagation is free from infection. The orchard should be inspected regularly for fresh infection to ensure disease-free orchard by judicious pruning followed by spraying/pasting of Bordeaux mixture/Bordeaux paste. Pruning 3 inches below the infection site followed by spraying Bordeaux mixture (2:2:250) is the most effective treatment. Sprays of 1% Bordeaux mixture followed by 0.8% Bordeaux mixture and carbendazim are also effective.

The disease is characterized by presence of a black velvety thin membranous covering on the leaf surface. In severe cases, the tree appears black due to heavy infestation of moulds on entire surface of leaves and twigs. Affected leaves curl and shrivel under dry conditions. The foliage appears black, ugly with masses of black spores that adhere to leaf surface due to sticky 'honey dew', hence the name 'sooty mould'. Severity depends upon sugary secretion by insects like mango hopper, scales, coccids and mealy bugs. During flowering, if fungus infects blossoms, fruit setting is affected and small fruits may fall.

The remedy appears in removing the cause by destroying the insects. Mould dies for want of suitable growth medium if honey dew secreting insects are killed by suitable insecticides. Application of pesticides should cover both surfaces of leaves. Spraying of Elosal (900 g/450 water) at 10-15 days intervals proved effective. Spraying of Wettasul (wettable sulphur) + Metacid (methyl parathion) + Gum acacia (0.2 + 0.1 + 0.3%) and Indian oil formulation (tree spray oil) 1% at 15 days interval controls sooty mould effectively. Disease is severe in old and dense orchards where light intensity is low.

Bunchy top phase appears on young plants in nursery beds when they are 4-5 months old. The characteristic symptom is formation of a bunch or occasionally several bunches at the top or a little lower down the main shoot. The bunch is formed of numerous thickened small shootlets, clustered together and arising from a leaf axil, on which are borne many small rudimentary leaves. These shootlets are much thicker than the main axis from which they arise. Growth of the plant is stopped, giving a 'Bunchy top' appearance.

The most characteristic symptom is reduction in length of the primary axis and secondary branches of the panicle which makes flowers appear in clusters. Frequently, flower buds are transformed into vegetative buds and large numbers of small leaves and stems with appreciably reduced internodes are compacted together, giving a witches broom-like appearance. In other cases, flower buds seldom open and remain as dull, green unopened buds. The main axis is shortened but flowers are changed into small leaves. Malformed panicles normally do not bear fruits. Even fruits set in the season do not grow more than pea size. The malformed heads dry up in black masses and persist on the tree for a long time, even until next flowering season.

Foliar spray with 200 ppm Bavistin (carbendazim) gave maximum disease reduction (95% in cv. Dashehari and 91.31% in cv. S.B. Chausa). Potassium metabisulphite and NAA caused 92.5% and 94% reduction respectively in cv. Dashehari. Spraying of 200 ppm NAA in the first week of October followed by de-blossoming at bud burst stage is advocated. Some recovery in plants treated with Phorate and Captan after pruning has been reported. Spraying of Benlate in combination with thorough pruning could reduce disease from 69% to less than 1%. Early flowers should be de-blossomed.

It is advisable to avoid scion stock from trees bearing malformed inflorescence for propagation. Indexing of healthy mango trees should be done to serve as material for propagation. Only certified saplings should be used. As soon as disease symptom is noticed, affected terminals should be pruned along with the basal 15-20 cm apparently healthy portion and burnt. Healthy orchards located in disease prone pockets should be sprayed with fungicides/insecticides as prophylactic measure to avoid further recurrence. Using disease-free plant material and prophylactic spray with fungicides keep plants healthy and check further spread.

Dry weather favors the development of disease. Predominance of susceptible cultivar 'Dashehri', high wind velocity for 3-4 days with maximum temperature around 30°C, minimum temperature around 15°C, and minimum and maximum relative humidity of 23.4-25.5% and 73.3-83.9% respectively are conducive for rapid spread of mildew pathogen in Kakori and Malihabad mango belt. Conidia are mainly liberated from 12:00 to 16:00h. Full bloom and fruit set to pea size stages are most susceptible. July-August is critical period in South Africa.

The optimum temperature for infection is around 25°C. Damage caused by anthracnose is mainly dependent on humidity, rain, misty conditions or heavy dews at the time of blossoming. Continuous wet weather during flowering causes serious blossom blight. A relative humidity of more than 95% for 12h is considered essential for infection and development on mango fruits. Infection progresses faster in wounded tissues and ripe fruits. Rainfall, high RH and high temperature favor anthracnose development. Continuous rainfall is the most important factor contributing to anthracnose development on fruits.

Development in field is favored by high relative humidity (above 90%) and temperatures between 25-30°C. The pathogen is more active under field conditions from July to September. Though temperature from April onwards remains favorable (28-30°C), in trees having infected twigs, infection on fruit starts early in the last week of April and continues during May while weather is dry. Maximum and minimum temperatures between 30-40°C and 17.3°C, RH between 68-100%, and high wind velocity during May are favorable for build up and spread. Generally, disease spread is rapid during rains.

The disease is characterized by presence of profuse gumming on the surface of affected wood and bark of trunk and larger branches, more common at branch cracks. In severe cases, droplets of gum trickle down on stem, and bark turns dark brown with longitudinal cracks. Bark rots and the tree dries up because of girdling effects. Recent surveys show 30-40% of young mango trees are affected especially in sandy soil. The disease occurs on stems and branches of seedling as well as grafted trees and is noticed after rainy season towards winter.

The disease can be kept under control if proper curative treatments are given at initial stages. The diseased bark/portion should be removed, cleaned and treated with Bordeaux paste. Application of copper sulphate at 250-500 g (depending upon the age of tree) in soil around the tree trunk is normally advocated. Gummosis is very less in orchards receiving copper oxychloride sprays for control of leaf spot diseases. Studies show only Botryodiplodia theobromae has been encountered along with other fungi in diseased samples.

The disease is readily recognized by presence of rusty red fructifications of the alga on surface of leaves, veins, petioles and young twigs. Initially spots are greenish grey in color and velvety in texture, finally turning reddish brown. Spots are circular to irregular in shape, erumpent, measuring 2 mm in diameter but when coalesce may reach up to 1 cm. After shedding of spores, the algal matrix remains attached to leaf surface, leaving a creamy white mark at the original rust spot. The disease can cause reduction in photosynthetic activity and defoliation which results in lowering the vitality of plants.

Bordeaux mixture (2:2:250) followed by copper oxychloride is recommended for control of this algal disease. Sprays with fungicides such as Difolatan, Bordeaux mixture and copper fungicides have been reported effective in checking algal infection. Maximum temperature of 30°C, minimum temperature around 25°C with high RH and frequent moderate rains with high wind velocity are conducive for growth and spread of this algal pathogen. Rain water has been found to be a source for spread of the alga and infection increases during rainy season. Avoidance of close planting may be helpful. Pruning and manuring of host trees may also be beneficial.

Grey blight is characterized by presence of brown spots on leaf lamina. These spots may develop from margins or tip. Initially, spots are brown and minute which gradually increase in size and become dark brown. Some spots form large lesions, with greyish white center and tan colored margins. At this stage, black spots of acervuli may become visible to naked eye in the central region, more on upper surface of leaf and never extend beyond midrib. Small brown spots also appear on green mature fruits which gradually increase in size, become dark brown with greyish white center and black dots of acervuli appear. Fruits drop off when disease advances to stalk end. Moist atmosphere helps in increasing and hastening infection.

First spray of wettable sulphur (0.2%) + zineb (0.2%) after completion of heavy showers, second spray of wettable sulphur (0.2%) before flowering, third spray of carbendazim (0.3%) at pea stage and final spray of zineb (0.2%) before maturation of stone is recommended. This spray schedule reduces the incidence of grey blight significantly. The disease is a weak parasite capable of infecting injured tissues, and healthy fruits in contact with diseased ones.

The disease is noticed as pinkish powdery coating on twigs and branches. Later, the fungus invades bark to get established in internal tissues and interferes with transport of nutrients. Often fungal growth spreads to girdle the stem. Severely infected bark gets shredded and wood is exposed. Leaves turn yellow and dry. Roots are not infected. The pink color on tissues represents profuse conidial production by the fungus, hence the name 'pink disease'. Also known as 'thread blight', rubellosis or cobweb. The disease is widespread in many tropical and subtropical regions.

The disease can be kept under control by cutting and removing affected branches, thus eliminating entire infected ends. Such ends should be protected with Bordeaux paste. The disease can also be controlled by lime sulphur and oil-based coppers. The disease is seen after rainy season and persists from one season to another through dormant mycelium inside the bark. The cankerous tissues serve as a potential source of infection in wet season.

The disease is characterized by presence of mycelial weft on base of stem at ground level. Beneath mycelial growth, a dark brown spot may develop which gradually encircles the base of stem. At this stage, the succulent top droops and bends towards ground, tissues lose turgidity and seedling dies within a week. When disease is at peak, fungus may be seen encircling the stem up to 2 inches or more above ground level. The disease also causes severe rotting of seeds during or before germination. Sclerotia are pin head size, initially white, but at maturity chocolate brown in color measuring 1.0-2.6 mm in diameter.

Infected soil should be thoroughly surface-burnt before seed beds are prepared. Diseased mango seedlings and weeds should be removed and burnt. Excessive use of water and close planting should be avoided as organism is moisture-loving. Seed beds should be prepared with sufficient drainage arrangement. Planting of susceptible hosts should be avoided. Two minutes dipping of stones in Agallol/Brassicol/Captan/Thiram and subsequent soil drenching at 10-15 days interval reduces disease incidence. Soil treatment with Ceresan is recommended - first application ten days before sowing and second two days later, after turning over soil to 20 cm depth.

The disease is characterized by sudden drooping of leaves after emergence of seedlings from soil. During prolonged rainy and humid weather, infection occurs at/or below ground level with circular to irregular water-soaked patches. These patches enlarge and ultimately girdle entire base of stem. On account of rotting, diseased tissues become soft, dark brown or black and entire seedling collapses and dies. Fungal mycelia and sclerotia are densely present on severely infected parts. Rotting may spread both above and below the stem, down to roots, and infected roots are disintegrated.

Soil treatment with Ceresan is recommended. First application can be given ten days before sowing and second two days later, after turning over the soil up to a depth of 20 cm. During growing season, Bordeaux mixture (1.5%) may be sprayed on plants and soil at weekly intervals. Root rot and damping off is a serious problem in nurseries caused by the common fungal pathogen Rhizoctonia solani in the nursery stage.

The disease is characterized by presence of yellowish pinhead spots on leaves, twigs and rarely on stems. Soon after, spots enlarge and become light to dark brown in color. Later, these spots become oval to irregular in shape, raised and dark purplish. Tissues become ash colored due to appearance of pycnidia on surface of lamina. Due to complete drying of leaf, infection travels downwards towards petiole. The bark of infected stem/twig turns grey because of appearance of elliptical lesions. The disease has been found present throughout the year in Delhi and other parts of India with heavy incidence during rainy season (July-September).

Removal and destruction of infected parts is helpful in reducing initial disease inoculum. Effect of Burgundy mixture, Perenox, Lime sulphur and Dithane M-45 on spore germination indicated that these fungicides may be profitably utilized for control of disease in field. Although disease is considered of little economic importance, for the last 4-5 years it has assumed significance. The pathogen also weakly infects Eriobotrya japonica, Eugenia jambolana, Ficus sp., Carica papaya and Vitis vinifera.

The disease is very common in Bijnore (U.P.) and Malda (West Bengal) on old trees. Younger trees less than 5-6 years are not affected. Unlike gummosis, bark cracking is characterized by development of deep longitudinal cracks in main branches of tree trunk, but without much exudation, measuring 15-40 cm in length. Rotting is not associated with cracks but underlying wood is severely pitted. Gum pockets are also noticed along with cracks. Later, bark gets dried and pulled off resulting in girdling effects such as yellowing and shedding of leaves and die back of branches. These symptoms have been noticed in cvs. Fazli, Himsagar, Lakhan Bhog, Ashina, Kuwan Pahar, Dashehari and Bombay Green.

Spraying of copper fungicides on trees is recommended. Soil application of copper at 250-500 g/tree may reduce incidence of cracking. Removal of dead bark and pasting with Bordeaux paste is advocated in orchards where disorder is more common. Bark cracking disorder has been reported in 36.6% of indigenous selection and 61.2% of imported varieties. In some orchards, 93% of trees are affected by this disorder. The cause of disease is unknown.
