In India, incidence of powdery mildew has assumed such a devastating proportion that the disease has become the single limiting factor in expansion of mango crop cultivation. Dropping of unfertilized infected flowers and immature fruits leads to serious losses. In Australia, incidence of mildew up to 23% on unsprayed trees has been reported. In an estimate, the loss varied from 22.35-90.41% in certain orchards in India. The disease causes heavy loss every year and is present in almost all states of the country.

Losses due to fruit infection have been estimated from 2-39%. Young plantation of cv. Bombay green was completely wiped out in Tarai region of Uttar Pradesh (India) due to severe wither tip. The blossom blight is the most destructive phase as it affects fruit set and ultimately the yield. Lesions on leaves are important sources for blossom and fruit infection. It is a widespread fungal disease on mangoes and avocados reported from numerous countries worldwide including India, USA, Cuba, Philippines, Australia, Bangladesh, Thailand, Costa Rica, Barbados, Malaysia and South Africa.

Bacterial canker causes 10 to 100% loss to mango crop in field as well as in storage. Earlier the disease was known to attack southern Indian cultivars but now its occurrence has been reported in northern Indian cultivars also. Although not common on Dashehri variety, it was observed in Barebanki area of U.P. and caused severe damage to crop during 1979. Apart from India, the disease is present in Australia, Congo, Cuba, Brazil, Egypt, France, Gold Coast, Japan, Kenya, Morocco, Mozambique, Malaysia, New Mexico, Pakistan, Philippines, Paraguay, Reunion Island, and South Africa.

About 30-40% plantations are found affected with the disease in the Moradabad region of Uttar Pradesh. The disease is known to be present in India and other mango growing countries of the world including Barbados, Puerto Rico, Egypt, Dutch East Indies (Indonesia), El-Salvador, Brazil, Nigeria, California (U.S.A.), Hawaii and South Africa. The disease is steadily gaining ground each year, spreading into new orchards and damaging by way of declining many such mango grooves mainly at latitude of 28.5°N and longitude of 78.49°E in tropical and sub-tropical world.

Malformation, also known as bunchy top, is a serious threat to mango growing areas of the world. In recent years, the extent of this malady has taken such magnitude that the mango industry is being threatened of its extinction in India, particularly in northern parts. The disease was first recognized in 1891 from Darbhanga, Bihar. It is mainly restricted to northern India, where over 50% of trees are affected. It has also been reported from Egypt, South Africa, Israel, Central America, Mexico, Florida (U.S.A.), Sudan, Cuba, Brazil, Australia, Bangladesh, Pakistan and United Arab Emirates.

Since the description of the perfect stage of the pathogen has not been given, the conidial stage is known as Oidium mangiferae Berthet. The pathogen is not reported on hosts other than mango. Mildew pathogen persists on infected leaves of previous year's flush which are retained on plant in succeeding year. Abundant conidia are produced and blown over to new flushes and provide sufficient spore load for initiating disease. Fresh infection on young leaves in first week of December (when flowers are not present) confirms the fungus perpetuates in asexual form on leaves of mango.

The disease is caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides Penz. (=Glomerella cingulata (Stons.) Spauld & Schrenk). Seven species of Colletotrichum are known to cause fruit rot in Queensland. It was found desirable to designate a new form as Glomerella cingulata var. minor. The conidial state causes anthracnose on mango, papaya, avocado, apple and other hosts in Queensland. Colletotrichum acutatum has been reported from New South Wales and India, isolated from leaves, panicles and fruits. Twig blight phase is caused by Gloeosporium mangiferae P. Henn but it is identical to C. gloeosporioides. Six new species of Colletotrichum including C. mangiferae on mango were also reported.

The disease is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. mangiferaeindicae (Patel et al.) Robbs et al. It is a gram negative rod, motile by monotrichous flagella and 3 to 4 pathotypes have been identified. The bacterium survives in infected plant parts on the tree and in resident form on weed hosts and mango leaves and fruits. It survives up to 8 months in diseased leaves. The pathogen was found pathogenic on several hosts. The bacterium enters into mango leaves through stomata, through stomata and lenticels in fruits, and through lenticels in twigs. It is an exclusively intercellular parenchymatous pathogen.

In India, die back of mango is caused by Botryodiplodia theobromae Pat. In U.S.A. (California) twig blight of mango was associated with Botryosphaeria ribis. In Florida, tip die-back has been reported and they isolated the conidial stage of Botryosphaeria ribis. Other causal agents include Physalospora rhodina and Ceratocystis fimbriata associated with same type of die-back. Botryodiplodia theobromae is an aggressive and vigorous pathogen able to infect exceptionally large number of host plants, causing root rot, fruit rot, dry rot, wood stain, die-back, stem end rot, seedling rot, graft union blight, twig blight and brown rot of panicle.

Recent findings demonstrate that disease may be of fungal origin. Fusarium moniliforme Sheld. was reported for first time, associated with bodies similar to chlamydospores, particularly in cortex when inoculated with spore suspension. Cross inoculation studies with strains of F. moniliforme confirmed host specificity and mango strains only caused typical disease symptoms. Fusarium oxysporum was shown to be involved in causing malformation and fungus was isolated from all parts of plants. It is just possible that disease is caused by more than one species of Fusarium. The fungus was further identified as F. moniliforme var. subglutinans. Although fungus does not sporulate in situ, it does so on drying malformed panicles.

Sooty mould is caused by several fungi including Meliola mangiferae Earle, Capnodium mangiferae Cke. and Brown, Capnodium ramosum (Cke.) Tripospermum acerinum (Syd.) Speg. The disease is also caused by Microxyphium columnatum, Leptoxyphium fumago and Tripospermum myrti. The mycelium of fungi is superficial and does not penetrate the host tissue. The fungi involved, in true sense, are non-pathogenic, because these do not either enter host tissue or absorb nutrients. They draw their nutrition not from host, but from sweet 'honey dew' secreted by insects. Damage by fungi is not direct but indirect, as they interfere with normal functioning of plant by cutting off effective leaf area for photosynthesis.

The disease is caused by the alga Cephaleuros virescens Kunze (Syn. C. parasiticus Karst, C. mycoidea Karst). The thallus is a pseudo-parenchymatous tissue, one to several cells in thickness, in which cells are arranged radially. Rain water has been found to be a source for spread of alga and infection increases during rainy season. Maximum temperature of 30°C, minimum temperature around 25°C with high RH and frequent moderate rains with high wind velocity are conducive for growth and spread of this algal pathogen.

The bacterium survives in infected plant parts on trees and in resident form on weed hosts and mango leaves and fruits. Twig cankers initiate infection on fruits. Removing infected weeds and maintaining disease-free planting material are crucial preventive steps.

The disease is characterized by dying back of twigs from top downwards with drying of leaves, particularly in older trees, followed by complete defoliation giving a fire scorch appearance. Discoloration and darkening of bark on young twigs at a certain distance from the tip is external evidence. Upper leaves lose green color and gradually turn brown with upward folding of margins. Such leaves shrivel and fall off in a month, leaving shrivelled twigs bare. Internal browning in wood tissue is observed on splitting open the twigs along the long axis. The disease is most conspicuous during October and November.

Pruning of dead wood and pasting of cut ends and healthy bud wood with protective fungicides are the main alternatives. It should be ascertained that scion wood selected for propagation is free from infection. The orchard should be inspected regularly for fresh infection to ensure disease-free orchard by judicious pruning followed by spraying/pasting of Bordeaux mixture/Bordeaux paste. Pruning 3 inches below the infection site followed by spraying Bordeaux mixture (2:2:250) is the most effective treatment. Sprays of 1% Bordeaux mixture followed by 0.8% Bordeaux mixture and carbendazim are also effective.

The disease is characterized by presence of a black velvety thin membranous covering on the leaf surface. In severe cases, the tree appears black due to heavy infestation of moulds on entire surface of leaves and twigs. Affected leaves curl and shrivel under dry conditions. The foliage appears black, ugly with masses of black spores that adhere to leaf surface due to sticky 'honey dew', hence the name 'sooty mould'. Severity depends upon sugary secretion by insects like mango hopper, scales, coccids and mealy bugs. During flowering, if fungus infects blossoms, fruit setting is affected and small fruits may fall.

The remedy appears in removing the cause by destroying the insects. Mould dies for want of suitable growth medium if honey dew secreting insects are killed by suitable insecticides. Application of pesticides should cover both surfaces of leaves. Spraying of Elosal (900 g/450 water) at 10-15 days intervals proved effective. Spraying of Wettasul (wettable sulphur) + Metacid (methyl parathion) + Gum acacia (0.2 + 0.1 + 0.3%) and Indian oil formulation (tree spray oil) 1% at 15 days interval controls sooty mould effectively. Disease is severe in old and dense orchards where light intensity is low.

Bunchy top phase appears on young plants in nursery beds when they are 4-5 months old. The characteristic symptom is formation of a bunch or occasionally several bunches at the top or a little lower down the main shoot. The bunch is formed of numerous thickened small shootlets, clustered together and arising from a leaf axil, on which are borne many small rudimentary leaves. These shootlets are much thicker than the main axis from which they arise. Growth of the plant is stopped, giving a 'Bunchy top' appearance.

The most characteristic symptom is reduction in length of the primary axis and secondary branches of the panicle which makes flowers appear in clusters. Frequently, flower buds are transformed into vegetative buds and large numbers of small leaves and stems with appreciably reduced internodes are compacted together, giving a witches broom-like appearance. In other cases, flower buds seldom open and remain as dull, green unopened buds. The main axis is shortened but flowers are changed into small leaves. Malformed panicles normally do not bear fruits. Even fruits set in the season do not grow more than pea size. The malformed heads dry up in black masses and persist on the tree for a long time, even until next flowering season.

Foliar spray with 200 ppm Bavistin (carbendazim) gave maximum disease reduction (95% in cv. Dashehari and 91.31% in cv. S.B. Chausa). Potassium metabisulphite and NAA caused 92.5% and 94% reduction respectively in cv. Dashehari. Spraying of 200 ppm NAA in the first week of October followed by de-blossoming at bud burst stage is advocated. Some recovery in plants treated with Phorate and Captan after pruning has been reported. Spraying of Benlate in combination with thorough pruning could reduce disease from 69% to less than 1%. Early flowers should be de-blossomed.

It is advisable to avoid scion stock from trees bearing malformed inflorescence for propagation. Indexing of healthy mango trees should be done to serve as material for propagation. Only certified saplings should be used. As soon as disease symptom is noticed, affected terminals should be pruned along with the basal 15-20 cm apparently healthy portion and burnt. Healthy orchards located in disease prone pockets should be sprayed with fungicides/insecticides as prophylactic measure to avoid further recurrence. Using disease-free plant material and prophylactic spray with fungicides keep plants healthy and check further spread.

Dry weather favors the development of disease. Predominance of susceptible cultivar 'Dashehri', high wind velocity for 3-4 days with maximum temperature around 30°C, minimum temperature around 15°C, and minimum and maximum relative humidity of 23.4-25.5% and 73.3-83.9% respectively are conducive for rapid spread of mildew pathogen in Kakori and Malihabad mango belt. Conidia are mainly liberated from 12:00 to 16:00h. Full bloom and fruit set to pea size stages are most susceptible. July-August is critical period in South Africa.

The optimum temperature for infection is around 25°C. Damage caused by anthracnose is mainly dependent on humidity, rain, misty conditions or heavy dews at the time of blossoming. Continuous wet weather during flowering causes serious blossom blight. A relative humidity of more than 95% for 12h is considered essential for infection and development on mango fruits. Infection progresses faster in wounded tissues and ripe fruits. Rainfall, high RH and high temperature favor anthracnose development. Continuous rainfall is the most important factor contributing to anthracnose development on fruits.

Development in field is favored by high relative humidity (above 90%) and temperatures between 25-30°C. The pathogen is more active under field conditions from July to September. Though temperature from April onwards remains favorable (28-30°C), in trees having infected twigs, infection on fruit starts early in the last week of April and continues during May while weather is dry. Maximum and minimum temperatures between 30-40°C and 17.3°C, RH between 68-100%, and high wind velocity during May are favorable for build up and spread. Generally, disease spread is rapid during rains.

The disease is characterized by presence of profuse gumming on the surface of affected wood and bark of trunk and larger branches, more common at branch cracks. In severe cases, droplets of gum trickle down on stem, and bark turns dark brown with longitudinal cracks. Bark rots and the tree dries up because of girdling effects. Recent surveys show 30-40% of young mango trees are affected especially in sandy soil. The disease occurs on stems and branches of seedling as well as grafted trees and is noticed after rainy season towards winter.

The disease can be kept under control if proper curative treatments are given at initial stages. The diseased bark/portion should be removed, cleaned and treated with Bordeaux paste. Application of copper sulphate at 250-500 g (depending upon the age of tree) in soil around the tree trunk is normally advocated. Gummosis is very less in orchards receiving copper oxychloride sprays for control of leaf spot diseases. Studies show only Botryodiplodia theobromae has been encountered along with other fungi in diseased samples.

The disease is readily recognized by presence of rusty red fructifications of the alga on surface of leaves, veins, petioles and young twigs. Initially spots are greenish grey in color and velvety in texture, finally turning reddish brown. Spots are circular to irregular in shape, erumpent, measuring 2 mm in diameter but when coalesce may reach up to 1 cm. After shedding of spores, the algal matrix remains attached to leaf surface, leaving a creamy white mark at the original rust spot. The disease can cause reduction in photosynthetic activity and defoliation which results in lowering the vitality of plants.

Bordeaux mixture (2:2:250) followed by copper oxychloride is recommended for control of this algal disease. Sprays with fungicides such as Difolatan, Bordeaux mixture and copper fungicides have been reported effective in checking algal infection. Maximum temperature of 30°C, minimum temperature around 25°C with high RH and frequent moderate rains with high wind velocity are conducive for growth and spread of this algal pathogen. Rain water has been found to be a source for spread of the alga and infection increases during rainy season. Avoidance of close planting may be helpful. Pruning and manuring of host trees may also be beneficial.

Grey blight is characterized by presence of brown spots on leaf lamina. These spots may develop from margins or tip. Initially, spots are brown and minute which gradually increase in size and become dark brown. Some spots form large lesions, with greyish white center and tan colored margins. At this stage, black spots of acervuli may become visible to naked eye in the central region, more on upper surface of leaf and never extend beyond midrib. Small brown spots also appear on green mature fruits which gradually increase in size, become dark brown with greyish white center and black dots of acervuli appear. Fruits drop off when disease advances to stalk end. Moist atmosphere helps in increasing and hastening infection.

First spray of wettable sulphur (0.2%) + zineb (0.2%) after completion of heavy showers, second spray of wettable sulphur (0.2%) before flowering, third spray of carbendazim (0.3%) at pea stage and final spray of zineb (0.2%) before maturation of stone is recommended. This spray schedule reduces the incidence of grey blight significantly. The disease is a weak parasite capable of infecting injured tissues, and healthy fruits in contact with diseased ones.

The disease is noticed as pinkish powdery coating on twigs and branches. Later, the fungus invades bark to get established in internal tissues and interferes with transport of nutrients. Often fungal growth spreads to girdle the stem. Severely infected bark gets shredded and wood is exposed. Leaves turn yellow and dry. Roots are not infected. The pink color on tissues represents profuse conidial production by the fungus, hence the name 'pink disease'. Also known as 'thread blight', rubellosis or cobweb. The disease is widespread in many tropical and subtropical regions.

The disease can be kept under control by cutting and removing affected branches, thus eliminating entire infected ends. Such ends should be protected with Bordeaux paste. The disease can also be controlled by lime sulphur and oil-based coppers. The disease is seen after rainy season and persists from one season to another through dormant mycelium inside the bark. The cankerous tissues serve as a potential source of infection in wet season.

The disease is characterized by presence of mycelial weft on base of stem at ground level. Beneath mycelial growth, a dark brown spot may develop which gradually encircles the base of stem. At this stage, the succulent top droops and bends towards ground, tissues lose turgidity and seedling dies within a week. When disease is at peak, fungus may be seen encircling the stem up to 2 inches or more above ground level. The disease also causes severe rotting of seeds during or before germination. Sclerotia are pin head size, initially white, but at maturity chocolate brown in color measuring 1.0-2.6 mm in diameter.

Infected soil should be thoroughly surface-burnt before seed beds are prepared. Diseased mango seedlings and weeds should be removed and burnt. Excessive use of water and close planting should be avoided as organism is moisture-loving. Seed beds should be prepared with sufficient drainage arrangement. Planting of susceptible hosts should be avoided. Two minutes dipping of stones in Agallol/Brassicol/Captan/Thiram and subsequent soil drenching at 10-15 days interval reduces disease incidence. Soil treatment with Ceresan is recommended - first application ten days before sowing and second two days later, after turning over soil to 20 cm depth.

The disease is characterized by sudden drooping of leaves after emergence of seedlings from soil. During prolonged rainy and humid weather, infection occurs at/or below ground level with circular to irregular water-soaked patches. These patches enlarge and ultimately girdle entire base of stem. On account of rotting, diseased tissues become soft, dark brown or black and entire seedling collapses and dies. Fungal mycelia and sclerotia are densely present on severely infected parts. Rotting may spread both above and below the stem, down to roots, and infected roots are disintegrated.

Soil treatment with Ceresan is recommended. First application can be given ten days before sowing and second two days later, after turning over the soil up to a depth of 20 cm. During growing season, Bordeaux mixture (1.5%) may be sprayed on plants and soil at weekly intervals. Root rot and damping off is a serious problem in nurseries caused by the common fungal pathogen Rhizoctonia solani in the nursery stage.

The disease is characterized by presence of yellowish pinhead spots on leaves, twigs and rarely on stems. Soon after, spots enlarge and become light to dark brown in color. Later, these spots become oval to irregular in shape, raised and dark purplish. Tissues become ash colored due to appearance of pycnidia on surface of lamina. Due to complete drying of leaf, infection travels downwards towards petiole. The bark of infected stem/twig turns grey because of appearance of elliptical lesions. The disease has been found present throughout the year in Delhi and other parts of India with heavy incidence during rainy season (July-September).

Removal and destruction of infected parts is helpful in reducing initial disease inoculum. Effect of Burgundy mixture, Perenox, Lime sulphur and Dithane M-45 on spore germination indicated that these fungicides may be profitably utilized for control of disease in field. Although disease is considered of little economic importance, for the last 4-5 years it has assumed significance. The pathogen also weakly infects Eriobotrya japonica, Eugenia jambolana, Ficus sp., Carica papaya and Vitis vinifera.

The disease is very common in Bijnore (U.P.) and Malda (West Bengal) on old trees. Younger trees less than 5-6 years are not affected. Unlike gummosis, bark cracking is characterized by development of deep longitudinal cracks in main branches of tree trunk, but without much exudation, measuring 15-40 cm in length. Rotting is not associated with cracks but underlying wood is severely pitted. Gum pockets are also noticed along with cracks. Later, bark gets dried and pulled off resulting in girdling effects such as yellowing and shedding of leaves and die back of branches. These symptoms have been noticed in cvs. Fazli, Himsagar, Lakhan Bhog, Ashina, Kuwan Pahar, Dashehari and Bombay Green.

Spraying of copper fungicides on trees is recommended. Soil application of copper at 250-500 g/tree may reduce incidence of cracking. Removal of dead bark and pasting with Bordeaux paste is advocated in orchards where disorder is more common. Bark cracking disorder has been reported in 36.6% of indigenous selection and 61.2% of imported varieties. In some orchards, 93% of trees are affected by this disorder. The cause of disease is unknown.

In India, incidence of powdery mildew has assumed such a devastating proportion that the disease has become the single limiting factor in expansion of mango crop cultivation. Dropping of unfertilized infected flowers and immature fruits leads to serious losses. In Australia, incidence of mildew up to 23% on unsprayed trees has been reported. In an estimate, the loss varied from 22.35-90.41% in certain orchards in India. The disease causes heavy loss every year and is present in almost all states of the country.

Losses due to fruit infection have been estimated from 2-39%. Young plantation of cv. Bombay green was completely wiped out in Tarai region of Uttar Pradesh (India) due to severe wither tip. The blossom blight is the most destructive phase as it affects fruit set and ultimately the yield. Lesions on leaves are important sources for blossom and fruit infection. It is a widespread fungal disease on mangoes and avocados reported from numerous countries worldwide including India, USA, Cuba, Philippines, Australia, Bangladesh, Thailand, Costa Rica, Barbados, Malaysia and South Africa.

Bacterial canker causes 10 to 100% loss to mango crop in field as well as in storage. Earlier the disease was known to attack southern Indian cultivars but now its occurrence has been reported in northern Indian cultivars also. Although not common on Dashehri variety, it was observed in Barebanki area of U.P. and caused severe damage to crop during 1979. Apart from India, the disease is present in Australia, Congo, Cuba, Brazil, Egypt, France, Gold Coast, Japan, Kenya, Morocco, Mozambique, Malaysia, New Mexico, Pakistan, Philippines, Paraguay, Reunion Island, and South Africa.

About 30-40% plantations are found affected with the disease in the Moradabad region of Uttar Pradesh. The disease is known to be present in India and other mango growing countries of the world including Barbados, Puerto Rico, Egypt, Dutch East Indies (Indonesia), El-Salvador, Brazil, Nigeria, California (U.S.A.), Hawaii and South Africa. The disease is steadily gaining ground each year, spreading into new orchards and damaging by way of declining many such mango grooves mainly at latitude of 28.5°N and longitude of 78.49°E in tropical and sub-tropical world.

Malformation, also known as bunchy top, is a serious threat to mango growing areas of the world. In recent years, the extent of this malady has taken such magnitude that the mango industry is being threatened of its extinction in India, particularly in northern parts. The disease was first recognized in 1891 from Darbhanga, Bihar. It is mainly restricted to northern India, where over 50% of trees are affected. It has also been reported from Egypt, South Africa, Israel, Central America, Mexico, Florida (U.S.A.), Sudan, Cuba, Brazil, Australia, Bangladesh, Pakistan and United Arab Emirates.

Since the description of the perfect stage of the pathogen has not been given, the conidial stage is known as Oidium mangiferae Berthet. The pathogen is not reported on hosts other than mango. Mildew pathogen persists on infected leaves of previous year's flush which are retained on plant in succeeding year. Abundant conidia are produced and blown over to new flushes and provide sufficient spore load for initiating disease. Fresh infection on young leaves in first week of December (when flowers are not present) confirms the fungus perpetuates in asexual form on leaves of mango.

The disease is caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides Penz. (=Glomerella cingulata (Stons.) Spauld & Schrenk). Seven species of Colletotrichum are known to cause fruit rot in Queensland. It was found desirable to designate a new form as Glomerella cingulata var. minor. The conidial state causes anthracnose on mango, papaya, avocado, apple and other hosts in Queensland. Colletotrichum acutatum has been reported from New South Wales and India, isolated from leaves, panicles and fruits. Twig blight phase is caused by Gloeosporium mangiferae P. Henn but it is identical to C. gloeosporioides. Six new species of Colletotrichum including C. mangiferae on mango were also reported.

The disease is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. mangiferaeindicae (Patel et al.) Robbs et al. It is a gram negative rod, motile by monotrichous flagella and 3 to 4 pathotypes have been identified. The bacterium survives in infected plant parts on the tree and in resident form on weed hosts and mango leaves and fruits. It survives up to 8 months in diseased leaves. The pathogen was found pathogenic on several hosts. The bacterium enters into mango leaves through stomata, through stomata and lenticels in fruits, and through lenticels in twigs. It is an exclusively intercellular parenchymatous pathogen.

In India, die back of mango is caused by Botryodiplodia theobromae Pat. In U.S.A. (California) twig blight of mango was associated with Botryosphaeria ribis. In Florida, tip die-back has been reported and they isolated the conidial stage of Botryosphaeria ribis. Other causal agents include Physalospora rhodina and Ceratocystis fimbriata associated with same type of die-back. Botryodiplodia theobromae is an aggressive and vigorous pathogen able to infect exceptionally large number of host plants, causing root rot, fruit rot, dry rot, wood stain, die-back, stem end rot, seedling rot, graft union blight, twig blight and brown rot of panicle.

Recent findings demonstrate that disease may be of fungal origin. Fusarium moniliforme Sheld. was reported for first time, associated with bodies similar to chlamydospores, particularly in cortex when inoculated with spore suspension. Cross inoculation studies with strains of F. moniliforme confirmed host specificity and mango strains only caused typical disease symptoms. Fusarium oxysporum was shown to be involved in causing malformation and fungus was isolated from all parts of plants. It is just possible that disease is caused by more than one species of Fusarium. The fungus was further identified as F. moniliforme var. subglutinans. Although fungus does not sporulate in situ, it does so on drying malformed panicles.

Sooty mould is caused by several fungi including Meliola mangiferae Earle, Capnodium mangiferae Cke. and Brown, Capnodium ramosum (Cke.) Tripospermum acerinum (Syd.) Speg. The disease is also caused by Microxyphium columnatum, Leptoxyphium fumago and Tripospermum myrti. The mycelium of fungi is superficial and does not penetrate the host tissue. The fungi involved, in true sense, are non-pathogenic, because these do not either enter host tissue or absorb nutrients. They draw their nutrition not from host, but from sweet 'honey dew' secreted by insects. Damage by fungi is not direct but indirect, as they interfere with normal functioning of plant by cutting off effective leaf area for photosynthesis.

The disease is caused by the alga Cephaleuros virescens Kunze (Syn. C. parasiticus Karst, C. mycoidea Karst). The thallus is a pseudo-parenchymatous tissue, one to several cells in thickness, in which cells are arranged radially. Rain water has been found to be a source for spread of alga and infection increases during rainy season. Maximum temperature of 30°C, minimum temperature around 25°C with high RH and frequent moderate rains with high wind velocity are conducive for growth and spread of this algal pathogen.
White powdery patches appear on leaf undersides. Upper leaf surfaces turn chlorotic (yellowish) and leathery. Severe during rainy and cool periods.
Remove and destroy diseased leaves immediately. Maintain adequate soil moisture and organic matter. Ensure good air circulation through proper spacing.
Spray 0.1% Carbendazim or 0.2% Sulphur when symptoms appear. Avoid overhead irrigation immediately after spraying to prevent wash-off.
Brownish, irregular spots appear on leaves that may coalesce into larger patches. Leaves yellow and shed prematurely. Favored by humid conditions.
Spray Carbendazim/Bavistin at recommended concentration. Practice sanitation by removing and burning infected leaves to reduce disease spread.
Small brown or black pustules form on leaf undersides, with corresponding yellowing on upper surfaces. Severe infections cause defoliation.
Spray Copper oxychloride or Blitox per label instructions. Strong sanitation practices help reduce inoculum - remove fallen infected leaves.
Sudden wilting and yellowing of plants. Roots decay and turn black. Plants become easily uprooted due to root system destruction.
Use disease-free planting material. Apply neem cake to soil to boost soil health and suppress pathogens. Ensure proper drainage to avoid waterlogging.
Prune and burn severely affected plants. Apply integrated biopesticide formulations near root zones of mildly affected plants.
Mulberry diseases are mostly fungal (powdery mildew, leaf spot, rust, root rot), though some bacterial and viral diseases can occur. Fungal diseases thrive in humid conditions.
Grasserie is caused by Bombyx mori Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus (BmNPV). It's a viral disease that affects silkworms throughout the year, with peak severity during summer and rainy seasons.
Silkworms get infected by eating contaminated mulberry leaves. The milky white fluid from infected larvae, contaminated rearing houses, and appliances also spread the virus.
Infected larvae have shiny skin before moult but fail to moult. They develop inter-segmental swelling, turn yellowish, move restlessly, and eventually rupture with turbid white haemolymph oozing out.

Practice thorough disinfection of rearing houses and appliances. Maintain optimum temperature/humidity, feed quality leaves, avoid overcrowding, apply bed disinfectants, and feed Amruth as per schedule.

Flacherie is caused by Bombyx mori Infectious flacherie virus, Densonucleosis virus, or bacteria like Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Bacillus thuringiensis, Serratia marscesence - individually or in combination.

Larvae become soft/flaccid with retarded growth, vomit gut juice, produce soft/moist faeces (sometimes chain-type), and show rectal protrusion. Infected larvae may turn black (Bacillus) or red (Serratia).
Disinfect rearing areas, remove diseased larvae, feed sun-exposed quality leaves, avoid starvation/overcrowding, maintain optimal conditions, prevent injuries, and apply bed disinfectants regularly.
White Muscardine is caused by Beauveria bassiana fungus. It's common during rainy and winter seasons when low temperature combines with high humidity.
Infected larvae lose appetite, become inactive, develop moist skin specks, vomit, turn flaccid, then harden and mummify. White aerial mycelia cover the body, turning it chalky white.
Control mulberry pests, remove larvae before mummification, avoid low temperature/high humidity, use heaters if needed, dust slaked lime during moult, and apply recommended bed disinfectants.
Pebrine is caused by microsporidia Nosema bombycis and other strains. It's non-seasonal and spreads through transovarian transmission (infected eggs) or contaminated leaves.
Irregular hatching, uneven larval size, appetite loss, wrinkled skin, black pepper-like spots on body, and white pustules on silkglands containing shiny oval spores under microscope.
Conduct strict mother moth examination, surface disinfect eggs, maintain hygiene, control mulberry pests, apply bed disinfectants (Vijetha/Ankush), and constantly monitor seed crops.
In tasar silkworms, pebrine (Nosema mylittansis) causes poor egg adherence, irregular hatching, appetite loss, uneven growth, black pepper spots from 3rd instar, and heavy mortality after 2nd moult.
Virosis in tasar silkworms is caused by cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus (AmCPV), a Reovirus. It accounts for 25-30% crop loss and is intensive during 1st and 2nd crop rearings.

Infected larvae lose appetite, become sluggish with disproportionate heads, lose natural shape, distend lengthwise, turn brownish, lose proleg grip, hang head down, and ooze dark brown fluid with foul smell.
Use 0.01% Sodium hypochlorite, slaked lime, chlorinated lime, formalin, TKO, Jeevan Dhara, Jeevan Suraksha, or LSM. Practice preventive measures as early symptoms are atypical.
Three distinct symptoms: 1) Sealing of anal lips with soil-colored sticky fluid, 2) Chain-type excreta in jelly substance, 3) Rectal protrusion as transparent bag filled with haemolymph.
Provide quality leaves to prevent nutritional stress, use TKO, Jeevan Suraksha, Jeevan Dhara, and LSM. Healthy silkworms with balanced nutrition resist bacterial infections better.
Tasar muscardine is caused by Penicillium citrinum and Paecilomyces varioti fungi. Incidence peaks September-November, favored by high humidity and low temperature.
Infected larvae become inactive/pale → harden → hang obliquely → die → become spongy → develop white encrustations → turn greenish with spores → become dry/brittle mummies.
Apply Jeevan Suraksha or TKO as scheduled. Dust 1-2% Dithane M45 in slaked lime or captaf in Kaolin on silkworm body. Control alternate hosts and manage humidity.
Feed Amruth as per recommended schedule to control grasserie and flacherie diseases. Follow dosage instructions carefully for effective disease prevention in silkworms.
Leaf spot appears as brown, irregular necrotic spots on leaves. Spots enlarge and merge to form 'shot holes'. In severe cases, leaves turn yellow and fall.
Leaf spot spreads through air-borne spores carried by rain droplets. Temperature of 24–26°C and 70–80% humidity favor disease development.
Spray 0.2% Bavistin (Carbendazim 50% WP) on leaves. Maintain a safe waiting period of 5 days before leaf harvest.
Powdery mildew shows white powdery patches on the lower leaf surface and yellow chlorotic patches on the upper surface. Severe infection turns patches brown-black.
Powdery mildew spreads by air-borne spores carried by wind. Temperature of 24–28°C with high humidity (75–80%) favors infection.
Spray 0.2% Karathane (Dinocap) or Bavistin on the lower leaf surface. Alternatively, spray Sulfex 0.2%. Follow safe period before harvest.
Wider spacing (90×90 cm) or paired row planting improves air circulation and reduces humidity around leaves, lowering powdery mildew incidence.
Leaf rust shows small circular brown eruptive spots on leaves that later cause yellowing and drying of mature leaves.
Spray 0.2% Kavach (Chlorothalonil 75% WP) on leaves. Maintain safe period of 5 days before harvest.
Follow wider spacing, avoid delayed leaf harvest, and remove infected leaves to reduce humidity and disease spread.
Sooty mould forms a thick black coating on the upper surface of mulberry leaves, reducing photosynthesis and leaf quality.
Sooty mould grows on honeydew secreted by whiteflies. Presence of whiteflies in the garden leads to fungal growth on leaves.
Spray 0.2% Indofil M-45 to control fungal growth and control whiteflies using recommended insecticides. Maintain safe period of 15 days.
Controlling whiteflies reduces honeydew secretion on leaves, which prevents growth of sooty mould fungi.
Affected plants show stunted growth, yellowing of leaf margins, low moisture in leaves, and knots or galls on roots. Roots have spherical swellings of different sizes.
The disease spreads through contaminated soil, farm tools, irrigation run-off, infected saplings, and susceptible weeds around the garden.
Temperature of 27–30°C, soil moisture below 40%, and soil pH between 5–7 favor root knot nematode development.
Apply neem oil cake @ 800 kg per acre per year in 4 split doses near the root zone after pruning or leaf harvest. Cover with soil and irrigate.
Use healthy saplings, avoid planting in infected fields, remove susceptible weeds, clean tools, and improve soil organic matter.
Sudden withering of plants, yellowing and dropping of leaves from bottom to top, and weak regrowth after pruning are common symptoms.
Roots show rotting of cortex, blackening due to fungal growth, poor anchorage in soil, and severe plants can be easily uprooted.
Root rot spreads through contaminated soil, tools, irrigation water, diseased saplings, and cultivation practices.
High temperature (28–34°C), low soil moisture (below 40%), and low organic matter favor root rot development.
Prune dried shoots 15–30 cm above ground. Apply Navinya solution (10 g per litre of water) around stump @ 1 litre per plant. Cover with soil after drenching.
Prepare solution by mixing 1 kg Navinya in 100 litres of water. Apply 1 litre per plant around pruned stump and cover with soil to avoid sunlight exposure.
Plants show stunted growth and yellowing of leaf margins. Roots develop spherical galls or knots of different sizes.
Use nematode-free saplings, deep digging and soil solarization, apply neem/pongamia oil cake, intercrop with marigold or sunhemp, and apply biocontrols like Bionema or Nemahari.

Leaf spot appears as small brown or dark spots on leaves. Later, spots enlarge and join together, forming shot holes. Severely affected leaves turn yellow and fall early. The disease spreads more during rainy and winter seasons.

Spray Carbendazim 0.2% (2 g per liter of water) thoroughly on both sides of leaves. Repeat after 10 days if infection is severe. Harvest leaves only after 8 days of spraying for safe silkworm feeding.
Powdery mildew shows white powdery patches on the lower surface of leaves. Later, the whole leaf surface gets covered and turns blackish-brown. Leaves may dry and drop in severe cases.
Spray Dinocap 0.2% (2 ml per liter of water) ensuring the lower surface of leaves is fully wet. Repeat after 10–12 days if needed. Leaves can be harvested after 10 days of spraying.
Leaf rust appears as small brown or black pin-head sized pustules on the lower surface of leaves. Leaves later turn yellow and dry prematurely, reducing leaf yield.
Spray Carbendazim or Dinocap 0.2% during winter months. Harvest leaves early without delaying to reduce disease severity. Maintain proper spacing between plants to reduce humidity.
Infected plants show weak growth, yellowing, leaf wilting, and sudden drying. White or violet fungal growth may appear on roots and stem base. Plants may die suddenly.
Uproot and burn infected plants. Remove old roots from soil. Improve drainage and avoid waterlogging. Apply soil sterilization and avoid replanting in infected soil without treatment.
Water-soaked patches appear on leaves which later turn brown or black. Leaves curl and rot in severe cases. Black streaks may appear on young shoots.
Spray Streptocycline or Streptomycin 0.1% along with Mancozeb 0.2%. Remove infected plants and expose soil to sunlight to reduce bacteria load.
Leaves show curling at margins and tips with yellow mosaic patches. Growth becomes weak and uneven. The disease spreads through insect vectors and infected planting material.
Uproot and destroy infected plants. Control insect vectors using neem-based or recommended insecticides. Use only healthy planting material from disease-free nurseries.
Leaf margins turn black and burn-like symptoms appear. Twigs show black longitudinal cracks and may dry completely. Buds may rot in severe infection.
Spray Mancozeb or Captafol 0.2% on leaves and drench soil with 0.5% solution. Remove and destroy severely infected twigs to reduce spread.
Plants show stunted growth and yellow leaves. Roots develop knot-like galls which block water and nutrient flow, causing weak plants.
Apply neem cake 1 ton/ha/year in split doses. Deep ploughing during summer exposes nematodes to sunlight. Use Carbofuran or approved nematicides if infestation is severe.
Avoid overhead irrigation, maintain spacing for airflow, remove infected leaves, and apply preventive Mancozeb spray during rainy season.
Maintain proper pruning for air circulation, avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, and apply sulfur or Dinocap spray during early disease appearance.
Use disease-free cuttings, avoid injuries during pruning, ensure good drainage, and apply copper-based sprays during rainy season.

Maintain wider spacing, avoid overhead irrigation, remove infected leaves from the field, and apply preventive Mancozeb spray before heavy rains start.
White powder-like patches appear first on the lower leaf surface, later covering the entire leaf. Leaves become dull, dry, and may drop early if infection is severe.
Prune dense branches for airflow, avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, spray Dinocap or sulfur when disease starts, and remove heavily infected leaves.
Small brown to black rust pustules appear on the lower surface of leaves. Leaves slowly turn yellow, dry, and fall, leading to reduced leaf availability for silkworms.
Spray Carbendazim or Dinocap 0.2% during winter and early infection stages. Harvest leaves on time and avoid overcrowded planting.
Plants show sudden wilting, yellowing of leaves, poor growth, and white or violet fungal growth near the root collar region. Plants may collapse suddenly.
Improve drainage, uproot infected plants, avoid water stagnation, disinfect soil before replanting, and use healthy planting material.
Water-soaked lesions appear on leaves and later turn dark brown or black. Leaves curl and rot in severe infection. Young shoots may show black streaks.

Remove infected plants immediately, control insect vectors with neem oil or recommended sprays, and use certified healthy cuttings for planting.
Leaf margins show burning, twigs develop black cracks, and branches dry from tips. Buds may rot and fail to sprout properly.
Spray Mancozeb or Captafol 0.2% and drench soil around infected plants with recommended fungicide solution. Prune and destroy infected twigs.
Plants grow slowly with yellow leaves. When roots are checked, swollen galls or knots are visible, which block water and nutrient flow.
Apply neem cake annually, deep plough soil in summer, and use approved nematicides only in severe infestation. Maintain proper soil moisture and drainage.
Spray Carbendazim or Mancozeb 0.2% at first appearance of spots. Repeat after 10 days if disease pressure is high.
White powdery growth appears on lower leaf surface and later spreads over the leaf. Leaves lose freshness and dry early if infection spreads.
Spray Dinocap 0.2% or wettable sulfur 0.3% covering the lower leaf surface. Maintain a 10-day waiting period before leaf harvest.
Avoid injuring plants during pruning, ensure good drainage, use disease-free planting material, and apply copper sprays before monsoon.
Control aphids and leafhoppers using neem oil or recommended insecticides. Remove infected plants immediately to prevent virus spread.

Prune infected twigs, maintain field hygiene, avoid water stagnation, and ensure good aeration between plants.
Plant on raised beds, improve drainage, avoid over-irrigation, and remove old infected roots before replanting.
Remove infected leaves, improve air circulation, avoid overhead irrigation, and apply Carbendazim or Mancozeb during early infection.
Early leaf spot appears as tiny brown specks on leaves that gradually enlarge and merge. Later, holes form and affected leaves turn yellow and fall, reducing leaf yield.
Spray Carbendazim or Mancozeb 0.2% thoroughly on both sides of leaves. Repeat after 10 days if disease pressure remains high.
White powdery coating appears on lower leaf surface, later spreading to the entire leaf. Leaves lose freshness, become dull, and dry early in severe cases.
Ensure good air circulation by pruning, avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, remove heavily infected leaves, and spray Dinocap or sulfur at early infection.
Small brown to black rust pustules appear mainly on the lower leaf surface. Leaves turn yellow and dry early, reducing the number of healthy leaves for silkworms.
Spray Carbendazim or Dinocap 0.2% at early disease stage, especially during winter. Maintain proper spacing to reduce humidity.

Ensure good drainage, avoid water stagnation, plant on raised beds, and remove old infected roots before replanting.

Spray Dinocap 0.2% or wettable sulfur 0.3% ensuring good coverage of lower leaf surface. Repeat after 10 days if required.

Spray Carbendazim or Dinocap 0.2% at early infection stage, especially during winter. Maintain proper plant spacing to reduce humidity.

Leaves show yellow mosaic patches and curl at the margins. Growth becomes uneven, and leaf yield reduces gradually.

Apply protective fungicides like Propineb (150-200 gm/200L water) or Mancozeb (200-250 gm/200L water) at first appearance. For curative action, use Tebuconazole + Trifloxystrobin combination. Spray at 15-day intervals, ensuring coverage on both leaf surfaces.
Use Chlorothalonil (250-300 gm/200L) or Carbendazim (100-150 gm/200L) at initial symptom appearance. Repeat after 15 days if needed. Remove severely infected leaves to prevent spread.
Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (250 gm/200L) or Fosetyl-Al (200-250 gm/200L) when first signs appear. Apply in early morning for best absorption. Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce humidity.

1. Use resistant varieties like Punjab-7, Punjab-8
2. Control whitefly vectors with Imidacloprid or Thiamethoxam
3. Remove infected plants immediately
4. Avoid continuous okra cropping
5. Use yellow sticky traps for whitefly monitoring
Spray Sulfur dust (300-400 gm/acre) or Wettable Sulfur (200-250 gm/200L). For systemic control, use Hexaconazole (50-60 ml/200L) or Penconazole (40-50 ml/200L). Apply at 10-15 day intervals.
Treat seeds with Thiram or Captan @ 2-3 gm/kg seed. Drench nursery with Copper oxychloride (3 gm/L). Avoid overwatering. Ensure good drainage and proper spacing.
Apply Carbendazim drenching @ 1 gm/L soil. Use Trichoderma viride treated FYM @ 2.5 kg/acre. Solarize soil before planting. Practice crop rotation with non-host crops.

Spray Copper oxychloride (300 gm/200L) or Mancozeb (250 gm/200L) at first symptom. Remove affected leaves. Avoid overhead irrigation. Maintain proper plant spacing for air circulation.
Drench with Carbendazim (1 gm/L) + Mancozeb (2 gm/L). Apply Trichoderma mixed FYM around base. Avoid waterlogging. Remove infected plants with surrounding soil.

Alternaria leaf spot appears as small brown to dark circular spots on older leaves with yellow halos around them. As disease increases, spots enlarge and merge, causing leaf drying and premature leaf fall. Severe infection reduces plant vigor and yield.

Remove and destroy infected leaves, avoid overhead irrigation, maintain proper plant spacing for good air circulation, follow crop rotation, and avoid continuous okra cropping. Keep the field weed-free to reduce humidity and disease spread.

Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 600–800 g/acre or Chlorothalonil @ 500 ml/acre in 200–300 L water. For severe infection, apply Tebuconazole or Difenoconazole as per label recommendation at 10–15 day intervals.
Cercospora leaf spot appears as small, grey to light brown spots with dark borders on leaves. In severe cases, leaves turn yellow, dry up and fall, reducing photosynthesis and pod yield.
Collect and destroy infected leaves, avoid overcrowding, ensure proper spacing, avoid overhead irrigation, and maintain field sanitation. Crop rotation with non-host crops reduces disease carryover.
Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 600–800 g/acre or Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP @ 500 g/acre in 200–300 L water at 10–15 day intervals if disease appears.
Downy mildew causes yellow patches on the upper surface of leaves and greyish fungal growth on the lower surface. Leaves may curl, dry and fall, reducing plant strength.
Maintain proper spacing, avoid water stagnation, use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering, and remove infected leaves. Grow the crop in sunny, well-ventilated fields.
Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb @ 500 g/acre or Copper oxychloride @ 600 g/acre in 200–300 L water. Repeat after 10 days if disease persists.
Leaves become curled, thickened and distorted with stunted plant growth. Infected plants show reduced flowering and small malformed pods.
Control whitefly population using yellow sticky traps (2 per acre), neem oil spray, and imidacloprid or thiamethoxam as per label. Rogue and destroy infected plants early.
Use healthy seeds, remove infected plants, plant border crops like maize to reduce whitefly entry, avoid overlapping okra crops, and maintain field sanitation.
Small round brown spots with yellow margins appear on leaves. Black tiny dots (fungal fruiting bodies) may be seen inside spots. Leaves dry prematurely under heavy infection.
Remove infected leaves, avoid overhead irrigation, maintain spacing, follow crop rotation, and ensure good drainage to reduce leaf wetness duration.
Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 600–800 g/acre or Copper oxychloride @ 600 g/acre in 200–300 L water at 10–15 day intervals.

Alternaria leaf spot develops rapidly under warm and humid conditions with frequent rainfall or overhead irrigation. High leaf wetness and poor air circulation increase disease spread in dense crop canopy.

Start preventive fungicide sprays when the crop canopy starts closing or when humid weather begins. Apply protectant fungicides like Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil at 10–15 day intervals to prevent initial infection.
Cercospora spreads through infected crop residues, wind-borne spores and rain splash. Continuous okra cropping and high humidity accelerate disease spread within the field.
Collecting and destroying infected crop residues after harvest reduces fungal survival in the field and lowers disease pressure in the next season.
Downy mildew increases under cool to warm temperatures with high humidity, cloudy weather, frequent dew, and poor field drainage that keeps leaves wet for long periods.
Use proper spacing, avoid overhead irrigation, remove infected leaves, improve drainage, and apply fungicides like Metalaxyl + Mancozeb when weather favors disease development.
Leaf curl virus spreads mainly through whiteflies. The virus moves from infected plants to healthy plants when whiteflies feed on plant sap.
Removing infected plants at early stage prevents the virus source from spreading to healthy plants through whiteflies, reducing field-level disease outbreak.
Planting barrier crops like maize, sorghum or pearl millet around okra fields reduces whitefly entry and slows virus spread into the crop.
Phyllosticta leaf spot increases under warm and humid conditions, prolonged leaf wetness, dense canopy and poor air circulation.
Follow crop rotation, avoid overcrowding, maintain field sanitation, and apply protective fungicides before disease becomes severe.

Cercospora leaf spot appears as brown, irregular spots on leaves caused by C. malayensis, or sooty black, angular spots on the lower surface of leaves caused by C. abelmoschi. Both types cause severe defoliation and are common during humid season. The spots are distinctive and can lead to significant leaf loss if not managed.

Remove and properly dispose of infected leaves by burning them. This prevents the spread of the disease. The fungi survive through conidia and stromata on crop refuse in soil, so field sanitation is crucial. Wind-dispersed conidia spread the disease secondarily.

The characteristic symptom is yellowing of the entire network of veins in the leaf blade (vein clearing). In severe infections, younger leaves turn yellow, become reduced in size, and the plant is highly stunted. Infection restricts flowering and fruits are not formed or turn smaller, harder, and rough. Loss in fruit yield ranges from 50-100% based on disease incidence.

The virus is transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Control whitefly by planting tall border crops like maize, sorghum or pearl millet (4 rows) to reduce infestations. Install yellow sticky traps at 2 per acre for monitoring. Use peppermint plants as repellent. Spray oxydemeton-methyl 25% EC at 400 ml in 200-400 l of water per acre or other recommended insecticides. Grow tolerant varieties like Pusa Sawani, Pusa A 4, Arka Abhay.

Yellow vein mosaic virus resistant/tolerant varieties include: Pusa Sawani, Pusa A 4, Arka Abhay, Arka Anamika, Varsha Uphar, Hisar Unnat, Hisar Naveen, HBH-142 (F1 hybrid), Gujarat Anand Okra-5, CO 1, CO 3, COBhH 1, Azad Bhindi-1, and Azad Bhindi-3. Contact your nearest KVK or SAU for updated information.

Powdery mildew appears as grayish powdery growth on both the under and upper surface of leaves. Affected leaves turn yellow and drop off, leading to severe yield loss. The disease is caused by Erysiphe cichoracearum.

Monitor adjacent fields for infection and maintain proper plant spacing to reduce relative humidity. The fungus survives through dormant mycelium and cleistothecia in crop residue, and spreads through wind-dispersed conidia.

Spray sulphur 80% WP at 1252g in 300-400 liters of water per acre or dinocap 48% EC at 90 ml in 300 liters of water per acre. You can also spray azadirachtin 0.03% (300 ppm) neem oil based EC at 800-1000 ml in 200 liters of water per acre as a biological control option.

Damping off occurs in two stages: Pre-emergence phase where seedlings are killed just before reaching soil surface with complete rotting of radical and plumule. Post-emergence phase shows infection of young collar tissues at ground level. Infected tissues become soft and water-soaked, causing seedlings to topple over or collapse.

Use Trichoderma and Pseudomonas fluorescens as seed and nursery treatment. Apply well-decomposed FYM at 8-10 t/acre or vermicompost at 5 t/acre treated with Trichoderma spp. and/or Pseudomonas sp at 2 kg/acre. Practice soil solarization by covering beds with 45 gauge polythene sheet for three weeks before sowing. Deep ploughing during summer also helps reduce soil-borne pests.

Spray protectant fungicides like Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil at 10–15 day intervals during humid weather. Reduce interval to 7–10 days under severe disease pressure and stop sprays close to harvest as per label PHI.
Good spray coverage ensures fungicide reaches both upper and lower leaf surfaces where fungal spores develop. Poor coverage leads to incomplete control and repeated infections.
Begin spraying when initial spots appear on lower leaves or when weather remains humid for several days. Early intervention prevents rapid spread to upper canopy.
Rotating fungicides with different modes of action prevents resistance development in the fungus and maintains long-term effectiveness of sprays.
Early warning signs include prolonged cloudy weather with high humidity, dew formation on leaves in mornings, and appearance of pale yellow patches on upper leaf surface.
Spray fungicides in the early morning or late afternoon when wind is low and temperature is moderate. This improves leaf coverage and reduces spray drift.
Raise seedlings away from infected fields, cover nursery with insect-proof net, apply neem oil sprays, and monitor for whiteflies. Remove any infected seedlings immediately.
Using certified healthy seed reduces the chance of introducing virus-infected plants into the field. Avoid seeds collected from infected crops.
Field sanitation removes infected plant debris that carries fungal spores. This reduces the initial inoculum and lowers disease recurrence in the next crop cycle.
Start with protectant fungicides at first appearance of spots and repeat every 10–15 days during humid periods. Ensure good leaf coverage and rotate fungicide groups.
Interwoven network of yellow veins with islands of green tissue on leaves. Later, entire leaves turn yellow. Spread by whitefly; economically most important disease.
Rogue out YVMV affected plants from time to time. Remove and destroy borer-affected shoots and fruits periodically.

Alternaria spots are typically brown to dark with concentric rings (target-like) and yellow halos, often starting on older leaves. Cercospora spots are greyish with dark borders, while Phyllosticta spots show tiny black dots inside lesions.
Cercospora spots are small to medium, greyish centers with dark margins. Alternaria shows target-like concentric rings, while Phyllosticta lesions have tiny black fruiting bodies inside the spots.
Yellow patches appear on the upper leaf surface, while grey to purplish fungal growth is visible on the underside in humid conditions, confirming downy mildew.
Look for severe leaf curling, thickened veins, stunted growth, and reduced flowering. Presence of whiteflies in the field supports virus suspicion. Remove infected plants immediately.
Lesions are small round brown spots with yellow margins and tiny black dots (pycnidia) inside the lesions. Severe infection leads to premature leaf drying.

Cercospora leaf spot shows two types of symptoms: Brown irregular spots caused by Cercospora malayensis or sooty black spots caused by C. abelmoschi. In wet conditions, the disease significantly reduces leaf area, affecting plant photosynthesis and overall vigor.

For effective control of Cercospora leaf spot, spray Mancozeb 0.25% (2.5 grams per liter of water) or Carbendazim 0.1% (1 gram per liter of water). Apply these fungicides when you first notice symptoms and repeat as needed based on disease severity and weather conditions.

To prevent Cercospora leaf spot, avoid overhead irrigation which keeps foliage wet. Remove and destroy infected plant debris from the field. These practices reduce humidity around plants and eliminate sources of infection.
Cercospora leaf spot thrives in high humidity, wet foliage conditions, and warm temperatures. The disease is most severe during rainy seasons when leaves remain wet for extended periods.
Cercospora leaf spot spreads through rain splash, wind, and infected plant debris. The fungus survives on crop debris in the soil and can infect new plants when favorable conditions return.

Yes, apply Trichoderma harzianum to the soil as a biological control agent. This beneficial fungus helps suppress Cercospora and other soil-borne pathogens, providing an eco-friendly disease management option.

Yellow Vein Mosaic Disease (YVMV) shows a characteristic yellow network pattern on leaf veins with green islands between them. As the disease progresses, entire leaves turn yellow, plants become stunted, and fruits are small and deformed, making them unmarketable.
Yellow Vein Mosaic Disease is caused by Bhendi Yellow Vein Virus, a Begomovirus from the Geminiviridae family. It is a single-stranded DNA virus that is transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci.
Grow resistant varieties like Punjab Kesari and Arka Anamika. These varieties have built-in resistance to YVMV and can significantly reduce disease incidence in your field.

Since YVMV is transmitted by whiteflies, control the vector by spraying Acephate 0.15% (1.5 ml per liter) combined with Imidacloprid 0.033% (0.33 ml per liter). This combination controls whitefly populations and reduces virus transmission.

Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to eliminate virus sources. Remove weeds that serve as alternate hosts for the virus and whiteflies. Plant border crops like maize or sorghum to act as physical barriers against whitefly migration into your okra field.

Yes, apply neem seed kernel extract (NSKE) at 2% concentration (20 ml per liter of water). NSKE has antifeedant and repellent properties against whiteflies, reducing virus transmission. Spray every 7-10 days during high whitefly pressure.
YVMV is most severe during warm, dry weather when whitefly populations are high. The disease intensifies when weed hosts are present near the field, as they harbor both the virus and its vector.

YVMV spreads through the whitefly vector Bemisia tabaci. Whiteflies acquire the virus when feeding on infected plants and transmit it to healthy plants during subsequent feeding. The virus also survives on weed hosts and infected plants between cropping seasons.

Enation Leaf Curl Disease (OELCV) shows distinctive pin-head sized enations (outgrowths) on the underside of leaves, giving them a warty, rough texture. Leaves curl severely, stems become twisted, and fruits are small and deformed. This disease is different from YVMV due to the characteristic enations.
Enation Leaf Curl Disease is caused by Okra Enation Leaf Curl Virus (OELCV), a Begomovirus with single-stranded DNA. Like YVMV, it is also transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci.
Remove and burn infected plants immediately. This eliminates virus sources and prevents further spread by whiteflies. Also remove weeds and crop debris where the virus can survive between seasons.

Control the whitefly vector by spraying Acephate 0.15% (1.5 ml/L), Imidacloprid 0.03% (0.3 ml/L), or Monocrotophos 0.05% (0.5 ml/L). These insecticides reduce whitefly populations and limit virus transmission to healthy plants.
Use NSKE (Neem Seed Kernel Extract) at 2% concentration as an organic solution. It repels whiteflies and reduces their feeding activity, thereby lowering virus transmission rates.

Yellow sticky traps attract and trap adult whiteflies, helping you monitor whitefly populations and reduce their numbers. Place traps at canopy height throughout the field. When you see high numbers of whiteflies on traps, it's time to spray insecticides.

OELCV is most severe during summer season with warm temperatures, low humidity, and high whitefly populations. These conditions favor rapid multiplication of whiteflies and efficient virus transmission.

Fusarium wilt causes wilting of seedlings and older plants. Leaves turn yellow (chlorosis), vascular tissues show brown discoloration when stems are cut, plants become stunted, and eventually die. The disease can occur at any growth stage.

Fusarium wilt is caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum. This pathogen has a wide host range and can survive in soil for many years, making it difficult to manage once established in a field.

Use certified disease-free seed for planting. Rotate okra with non-host crops like cereals or grasses for at least 2-3 years. Improve soil drainage as the fungus thrives in waterlogged conditions. These practices reduce disease pressure significantly.

If your field has a history of Fusarium wilt, consider soil fumigation before planting. However, this is costly and mainly recommended for high-value crops or severe disease situations. Consult agricultural experts for appropriate fumigants and application methods.

Yes, plant resistant varieties if available in your region. Resistant varieties have genetic tolerance to Fusarium wilt and can grow normally even in infested soil. Check with local agricultural universities or seed companies for suitable varieties.
Fusarium wilt is favored by warm soil temperatures, infected seed or soil, and poor drainage. The fungus enters through roots and spreads through the vascular system, causing wilting and death.

Fusarium spreads through soil movement on tools, machinery, and water. Infected seeds can introduce the pathogen to new fields. Once in soil, the fungus can survive for many years, spreading slowly through the field.

Look for round, water-soaked, sunken spots on ripening fruit. The spots turn chocolate-colored and depressed. You may see black dots arranged in rings with pinkish-orange powder (spores). These spots appear especially during humid weather.

Spray Chlorothalonil (0.2%) or Thiophanate methyl (0.2%) or Bavistin (0.2%) every two weeks. For better control, use Prochloraz (0.1%) or Tricyclazole (0.1%). Mix 2 ml or 2 gm per liter of water depending on the product. Remove and destroy infected leaves before spraying.

Dip harvested fruits in hot water. First dip for 30 minutes at 42°C, then dip for 20 minutes at 49°C. This kills the fungus on fruit surface and prevents spots from developing during storage and transport.

Anthracnose spreads rapidly in high humidity and warm temperatures typical of tropical and subtropical regions. The disease is worst during rainy season. Spores spread through wind and rain splash from infected plant debris.

Bacterial spot appears as small, water-soaked spots on leaves that later turn brown or black. The spots may have a yellow halo around them. On fruits, you'll see raised, dark spots that may ooze bacterial liquid in humid conditions.

Leaves become curled, twisted, and deformed. You'll notice mosaic patterns (light and dark green patches) on leaves. Plants become stunted and don't grow properly. Fruit yield reduces significantly. This is caused by a virus spread by tiny insects called aphids.

Start with healthy seedlings raised in insect-proof nets. Plant border crops like maize, sorghum, sesbania, or castor around your papaya field before planting papaya. Keep the field clean by removing weeds regularly. Destroy any infected plants immediately to prevent virus spread.

Spray Dimethoate (1.5 ml per liter) or Acephate (1.25 gm per liter) to kill aphids. You can also use organic option: Neem or Pongamia soap (10 gm per liter). Spray every 2-3 weeks for 8 months after planting. This controls aphids that spread the virus.

Spray foliar nutrients to strengthen plants: mix 2% urea + 2% Zinc Sulphate + 0.1% boron in water. This means 20 gm urea + 20 gm ZnSO₄ + 1 gm boron per liter. Spray every 15 days for 6 months. This improves plant health even if virus is present.

Mosaic shows as irregular light and dark green patches on leaves, creating a mosaic pattern. Leaves may also curl and become distorted. Young leaves are more severely affected. The disease is caused by virus and spreads through aphids and infected tools.

On fruits, you'll see circular rings or spots that are slightly raised. These rings may have different colors from the normal fruit skin. On leaves, circular spots with ring patterns appear. The disease is viral and severely reduces fruit quality and marketability.

The base of the stem (crown area) becomes soft, water-soaked, and dark brown or black. Roots rot and plant wilts even with adequate soil moisture. Leaves turn yellow and drop. Young plants may die quickly. The disease spreads in waterlogged soils.

Mix 1 kg Trichoderma powder with 100 kg well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM). Let it sit for 7-10 days in shade. Apply this enriched FYM in planting pits before planting papaya. Trichoderma fights the foot rot fungus in soil and protects roots.

In severe cases, drench soil around plant base with Ridomil (Metalaxyl) at 1.5 gm per liter of water. Use 2-3 liters of solution per plant. Ensure proper drainage to prevent waterlogging. Avoid over-irrigation which makes the disease worse.

Plant papaya on raised beds or mounds to ensure good drainage. Avoid waterlogged areas. Don't plant too deep - crown should be slightly above soil level. Improve drainage by digging channels. Never over-irrigate. Use disease-free seedlings and avoid injury to stem base.

Fruits develop circular to oval depressed lesions that turn black. The spots may grow and cover the whole fruit. On leaves, you'll see light to dark brown spots with concentric rings (zonate pattern). Crown area may also get infected showing dark lesions.

Spray Chlorothalonil (0.2%) or Zineb (0.2%) or Iprodion (0.2%) or Propineb (0.2%) every two weeks. This means 2 gm per liter of water. Start spraying from flowering stage. Regular spraying prevents black spots on fruits and leaves.

Dip harvested fruits in hot water at 48°C for 20 minutes. This kills the fungus on fruit surface and prevents black spot development during storage and transport. Handle fruits carefully to avoid wounds which allow fungus entry.

Remove and burn all infected leaves, fruits, and plant debris. Don't leave fallen fruits in the field. Avoid overhead irrigation which splashes spores. Maintain proper spacing for air circulation. Harvest fruits at right maturity - not over-ripe. Handle fruits gently to avoid wounds.

Tiny aphids (Acerophagus papaya) suck sap from infected plants and carry virus to healthy plants. The virus also spreads through infected planting material, contaminated tools, and nearby weeds. Wind can blow aphids to new plants. Virus does NOT spread through soil or water.

Anthracnose attacks fruits, leaves, petioles (leaf stalks), and flowers. On fruits it causes most damage - creating sunken rotten spots. On leaves, brown spots appear. Flowers may rot and drop. The fungus survives on infected plant debris and attacks new growth.

Some papaya varieties show better tolerance to PRSV but complete resistance is rare. Ask your local agriculture office for locally adapted tolerant varieties. Hybrid varieties often show better field tolerance. Even with tolerant varieties, follow vector control and border crop practices.

Foot rot spreads fast in waterlogged or poorly drained soils. Heavy clay soils with poor drainage are high risk. Over-irrigation and continuous flooding create ideal conditions. The pathogens survive in soil and infected plant material. Disease is worst during rainy season.

Spray fungicide every 2 weeks (14 days) starting from flowering until harvest. In rainy season or high humidity, spray every 10 days. After rain, spray within 1-2 days. Always spray before expected rain if possible. Mix a sticker to help fungicide stick on leaves and fruits.

Yes, immediately uproot and destroy severely infected plants, especially young ones. This prevents virus spread to healthy plants. Burn or bury infected plants away from field. Don't use them for composting. Replant with healthy seedlings from insect-proof nursery.

Combine multiple practices: Remove infected leaves promptly. Spray Chlorothalonil or Propineb every 2 weeks from flowering. Use hot water treatment (48°C for 20 min) for harvested fruits. Maintain field sanitation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Ensure good air circulation through proper spacing.

Use sterile potting mix - don't use field soil. Mix Trichoderma in growing medium. Water carefully - don't overwater. Ensure good drainage in nursery pots. Treat seeds with Trichoderma before sowing. Use raised benches to keep pots off ground. Select only healthy seedlings for transplanting.

Plant maize, sorghum, napier grass, sesbania, or castor as border crops 2-3 weeks before planting papaya. These tall crops act as barriers catching virus-carrying aphids. Maintain 3-4 rows of border crops around papaya field. Don't allow these crops to flower and dry - maintain green barrier.

Harvest fruits at proper maturity with slight yellow color break. Don't harvest over-ripe fruits. Use clean, sharp tools. Avoid injuries and bruises. Harvest early morning when it's cool. Don't harvest wet fruits after rain or dew. Leave short stem attached. Handle gently - don't drop fruits.

Add well-decomposed organic matter to improve drainage. For heavy soils, add sand and compost. Incorporate Trichoderma-enriched FYM. Create raised beds 15-20 cm high. Ensure slope for water drainage. Avoid low-lying areas. Deep plowing before monsoon helps. Apply lime if soil is too acidic.

Raise nursery in aphid-proof net house (40-50 mesh). Site nursery away from old papaya fields. Remove all papaya and cucurbit plants within 500 meters. Use virus-free seeds. Don't allow workers to move between old field and nursery. Spray neem oil weekly. Inspect seedlings daily and remove any showing symptoms.

Yes, rotate fungicides to prevent resistance. Alternate between Chlorothalonil (contact fungicide) and systemic fungicides like Bavistin or Prochloraz. Example: Spray Chlorothalonil twice, then Bavistin twice, then back to Chlorothalonil. This rotation improves control and delays resistance development.

First small spots appear, then they become depressed and turn dark brown to black. Spots enlarge in circles and may merge. Severe cases: spots cover entire fruit making it unmarketable. The fungus sporulates on surface creating black powder. Flesh remains firm - unlike anthracnose which causes soft rot.

Check stem base near soil - if soft, water-soaked, dark brown with foul smell, it's likely foot rot. Plant wilts despite wet soil. Roots are brown and rotten when pulled. Cut stem shows brown discoloration inside. Disease starts at ground level and moves up, unlike other diseases that affect leaves first.

Start aphid control sprays immediately after transplanting seedlings. First 3-4 months are most critical - young plants are most susceptible. Weekly monitoring in first 2 months. Spray at first sign of aphids. Don't wait for symptoms - by then virus has already infected. Prevention is better than cure.

Fungus survives on infected plant debris, fallen leaves, rotting fruits in field. It survives on alternative host plants nearby. Survives in soil attached to organic matter. Can remain dormant in field for several months. This is why removing all debris and deep plowing are important.

Use drip irrigation instead of flood irrigation. Water early morning so excess evaporates during day. Don't water near stem base - keep 15-20 cm radius dry around trunk. Allow soil to dry between irrigations. Reduce watering in rainy season. Never irrigate if soil is already moist.

Virus can survive in cucurbits (cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon), tomato, pepper, and various weeds. Remove these from field vicinity. Don't grow papaya near cucurbit fields. Clean up weed hosts especially Parthenium, Euphorbia. This reduces virus reservoir around your papaya crop.

After hot water treatment, dry fruits completely. Store at 10-13°C with 85-90% humidity. Don't store damaged or wounded fruits. Maintain good air circulation. Check stored fruits daily and remove any showing spots. Don't pack too tightly. Use single layer packing. Market fruits quickly.

Remove and burn infected leaves weekly. Collect and destroy fallen fruits. Clean field borders of weeds and plant debris. Don't leave pruned material in field. Plow under crop residue after harvest. Maintain 2-3 meters space between rows for air movement and quick drying.

Make raised mounds 30-45 cm high. Plant seedling so crown is slightly above soil level. Don't plant too deep. Press soil gently - don't compact. Water around the plant, not on stem. Apply Trichoderma-enriched compost in pit. Handle roots carefully to avoid injury. Transplant in evening.

Zinc strengthens plant immune system and helps recovery. Zinc sulphate spray improves chlorophyll production reducing mosaic symptoms. Combined with urea and boron, it helps plants maintain growth even with virus. Spray 20 gm ZnSO₄ per liter water every 15 days.

Spray Bordeaux mixture (1%) or copper oxychloride (0.3%) for organic control. Use baking soda 0.5% with oil. Apply neem oil 1% mixed with garlic extract. Spray compost tea. These have moderate effectiveness - combine with good cultural practices and sanitation for better results.

Some varieties show better tolerance to root diseases. Red Lady and Taiwan varieties show moderate tolerance. Pusa varieties developed in India have some field tolerance. However, no variety is completely resistant. Even with tolerant varieties, ensure good drainage and proper management practices.

Yes, intercrop with non-host crops like turmeric, ginger, or vegetables from cabbage family. These don't harbor the virus. Avoid growing tomato, pepper, cucurbits near papaya - these can carry the virus. Good intercrop also reduces aphid movement between plants.

Increase spray frequency to 7-10 days during monsoon. Spray immediately after rain stops. Use sticker with fungicide for rain-fastness. Improve field drainage to avoid water stagnation. Prune lower branches to improve air flow. Support fruits to prevent soil contact. Harvest frequently.

Black spot: lesions remain firm, turn black, don't penetrate deep, fruit flesh stays hard. Anthracnose: lesions become soft, sunken, rot develops, shows pink spore masses, flesh becomes watery. Both need different management - correct identification is important for effective control.

If caught early: Stop irrigation immediately. Expose crown to air by removing soil around base. Drench with Ridomil. Apply Trichoderma around roots. Improve drainage. If more than 50% stem is rotten or plant is wilting badly, better to remove and destroy - focus on protecting other plants.

If infection occurs in first 3 months: 80-100% yield loss - plants may not fruit at all. If infection after 6 months: 30-50% loss - some fruits form but are small and poor quality. Early protection is critical. Virus-infected plants never fully recover - prevention is the only solution.

Use high-pressure sprayer reaching 3-4 meters height. Spray from multiple angles - side and upward. Cover both fruit and foliage. Use sufficient water volume - 600-800 liters per hectare. For very tall plants, consider pruning to manageable height or use motorized sprayer. Add spreader for better coverage.
