The centers of these spots turn tan or grey and eventually white - this white center distinguishes it from leaf scorch. Late in the season, tan or bluish areas form on leaf undersurfaces. In warm weather, one or two black spots (black seed disease) may form on fruit. The organism can infect leaves, fruits, petioles, runners, fruit stalks and berry calyxes.

The key to good control is sanitation. Minimize disease spread by: 1) Maintaining good air flow through proper plant spacing and renovation. 2) Removing old leaves after harvest. 3) Minimizing free water - leaf spot needs at least 12 hours of continuous free moisture for infection. 4) Ensuring good control in nursery/plant-production fields, as these are important sources of infection for fruiting fields. 5) Using resistant varieties. Fungicides can be used but cultural control is more important for long-term management.

Leaf blight, caused by Phomopsis obscurans, is most common after harvest. It's distinct from leaf spot and leaf scorch - the infected area becomes V-shaped with the widest part at the leaf margin. Spots are initially reddish-purple and develop a darker brown or reddish-brown center surrounded by light brown area with purple border. Leaves can eventually become blighted and die. The fungus also infects fruit caps with similar symptoms and can cause a soft, pale pink rot at fruit ends.

First symptoms are curling of leaf edges, followed by dry purplish to brownish patches on leaf undersurfaces. As disease progresses, patches of white, powdery fungus mycelium develop on undersides of leaves and reddish discoloration appears on upper surfaces. Infected fruit become hard and fail to ripen normally. The disease is facilitated by temperatures of 15-27°C and moderate to high humidity.

Yes, biological control agents have been identified with potential to control powdery mildew in strawberries. Research has shown promising results with specific biocontrol organisms. Additionally, resistant varieties exist for powdery mildew. Combining biological controls with cultural practices like proper spacing for air circulation and avoiding overhead irrigation provides the best results.

Leather rot, caused by Phytophthora cactorum, can infect fruit at any development stage. In green fruit, diseased areas are dark brown or natural green outlined with brown margin, and the whole berry eventually becomes brown with rough texture and leathery appearance. Infected ripe fruit show less dramatic symptoms but can be identified by duller color, bitter taste and marked darkening of xylem connections to seeds. Eventually mature fruits become tough and leathery, sometimes with white moldy growth. The disease is usually serious only during excessive rain in temperate regions.

Straw mulch is very important in controlling leather rot by directly protecting fruit from inoculum and limiting splash dispersal of the pathogen. The fungus overwinters as oospores in mummified fruit on soil. In spring, these germinate in free water and produce zoospores that swim to fruit surfaces. Good drainage is critical. Remove and destroy mummified fruit. During growing season, both sporangia and zoospores spread by splashing or wind-blown water, so minimizing water splash is essential.

Red stele (red core), caused by Phytophthora fragariae, causes stunted plants that produce few runners and lose normal shiny green luster. Younger leaves have metallic bluish-green color, while older leaves turn yellow or red. During hot, dry periods, diseased plants rapidly wilt and die. They produce few roots and the stele (core) of roots is pink to brick red - this is the diagnostic symptom. The disease is particularly troublesome in heavy clay soils saturated with water during cool seasons, with optimal development at 13-15°C.

Initial infection occurs mainly through distribution of infected plants or infested soil. The fungus produces oospores that generate large quantities of mobile zoospores that swim when soil moisture is high. These attack developing root tips and move to vascular system. Once established, fungus can survive in soil for more than a decade. Prevention requires: 1) Starting with clean, certified disease-free plants. 2) Ensuring excellent drainage - avoid heavy clay soils or improve drainage. 3) Avoiding fields with history of red stele. 4) Using resistant varieties. 5) Avoiding waterlogged conditions especially during cool seasons.

Verticillium wilt causes leaves to wilt rapidly, dry and become reddish-yellow or dark brown. Few leaves and runners are formed. New roots are dwarfed with blackened tips. In new plantings, symptoms begin to appear as runners form, whereas in established plantings symptoms are most prevalent just before picking. The disease is caused by Verticillium albo-atrum and V. dahliae, which can remain alive in field for up to 25 years.

Management is challenging since the fungus survives 25 years in soil as dormant mycelium or microsclerotia. Under favorable conditions, these germinate and produce hyphae that penetrate root hairs and destroy the vascular system. Control strategies: 1) Avoid planting in fields with Verticillium history. 2) Use long rotations with non-host crops. 3) Plant resistant varieties. 4) Start with certified disease-free plants. 5) Soil fumigation before planting can help. 6) Maintain plant health to reduce stress. 7) Some biological controls using rhizobacteria strains show promise.

Black root rot is caused by a complex of organisms including Pythium and Rhizoctonia species. Affected roots show: 1) Much smaller root systems than normal. 2) Main roots spotted with dark patches or zones. 3) Most feeder roots lacking. 4) All or part of main root dead and blackened throughout. Plants are less vigorous and produce few runners. Often associated with nematodes, winter injury, fertilizer burn, soil compaction, herbicide damage, drought, excess salt, waterlogging or improper soil pH. Can affect scattered plants or localized regions within fields.

Factors most highly correlated with severe black root rot: 1) Lack of crop rotation. 2) Compacted or fine-textured soils. 3) High rates of herbicide terbacil. 4) Flat versus raised bed culture. Management: 1) Use raised beds. 2) Rotate crops every 2-4 years with non-host crops. 3) Avoid soil compaction - subsoil between rows if needed. 4) Maintain proper soil pH (5.5-6.5). 5) Ensure good drainage. 6) Avoid fertilizer burn and herbicide damage. 7) Post-planting drenches or foliar sprays of azoxystrobin and azoxystrobin + potassium phosphite have shown effectiveness.

Charcoal rot, caused by Macrophomina phaseolina, has become widespread problem in California and Florida since methyl bromide fumigation was phased out. Symptoms usually appear after plants are well established and have started producing fruit. Older leaves begin to wilt and turn grey-green, then dry up. As disease progresses, all foliage eventually collapses and dries up except central, youngest leaves. Vascular and cortical tissues of crowns turn dark brown to orange-brown, along with main roots. Severe outbreaks reported in Argentina, Italy, Spain, Turkey, Greece and Israel.

Fusarium wilt, caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. fragariae, emerged as problem in California after methyl bromide fumigation stopped. Symptoms can appear as early as 30 days after transplanting when plants stop growing and appear stunted. As disease progresses, virtually all foliage collapses and dries except central, youngest leaves. Vascular and cortical tissues turn dark brown to orange-brown, similar to charcoal wilt. There are no field symptoms to separate Fusarium from charcoal wilt - affected plants must be tested by plant pathology laboratory for definitive diagnosis.

Yes, several biological strategies exist: 1) Previous inoculation with non-pathogenic strains of Fusarium oxysporum can protect plants. 2) Soil amendments with chitin-degrading yeast Streptomyces anulatus. 3) Trichoderma species have been used successfully to control Fusarium wilt. 4) Root colonization by mycorrhizal fungi may help. 5) Strains of rhizobacteria have been used against soil fungi. These work best when combined with good cultural practices and use of resistant varieties.

Crown rot (vascular collapse) is caused by a distinct pathotype of Phytophthora cactorum - the same organism that causes leather rot on fruit. Young leaves wilt suddenly, turn brown and whole plant dies within a few days. Crowns break easily at their tops, leaving most of crown behind. Crowns are brown with disintegrated vascular tissue. Infection occurs primarily in runnering bed or after transplanting. Most susceptible when temperatures are high in early to mid-summer, soil drainage is poor and plants are stressed. Cultivars vary greatly in susceptibility.

Prevention strategies: 1) Source of inoculum is oospores in soil or infected plants, so start with certified clean plants. 2) Zoospores infect through wounds - minimize plant injury during handling and transplanting. 3) Ensure excellent drainage, especially during summer. 4) Avoid planting when temperatures are high and conditions stressful. 5) Plant resistant cultivars. 6) Some biological controls like Trichoderma species show effectiveness against Phytophthora cactorum. 7) Avoid stressed conditions - maintain adequate but not excessive moisture.

Key cultural controls for fruit rots: 1) Excessive nitrogen in spring increases Botrytis fruit rot - use moderate rates. 2) Foliar calcium applications delay post-harvest grey mould development. 3) Straw mulch is very important for controlling leather rot, grey mould and anthracnose by protecting fruit and limiting splash dispersal. Note: plastic mulches actually increase anthracnose incidence. 4) Good drainage is essential. 5) Remove and destroy foliar residues. 6) Proper plant spacing for air circulation. 7) Remove overripe and damaged fruit promptly.

After methyl bromide phase-out, most widely used alternatives are: 1) Chloropicrin alone or combined with 3-dichloropropene, followed by metam sodium application. 2) Methyl iodide was considered but abandoned due to human toxicity concerns. Future approaches likely require integrated management: disease-resistant cultivars, soil amendments that suppress pathogen activity, maintaining good airflow, minimizing standing water, clean planting stock, and composts that encourage growth of beneficial bacteria and fungi. Solarization works in areas with long periods of high temperatures.

Several biological strategies: 1) Trichoderma species control Fusarium wilt, charcoal rot and Phytophthora cactorum. 2) Mycorrhizal fungus colonization confers resistance to Phytophthora fragariae (red stele). 3) Rhizobacteria strains work against crown rot, red stele and Verticillium wilt. 4) Composts encouraging beneficial bacteria and fungi suppress pathogens. 5) For Fusarium, non-pathogenic strains or chitin-degrading yeast Streptomyces anulatus help. These work best combined with resistant varieties and good cultural practices. Future will likely rely more on integrated approaches than fumigation alone.

Main virus groups: 1) Aphid-transmitted: Strawberry mild yellow-edge (SMYEV), vein banding (SVBV), crinkle (SCV), mottle (SMoV), and others. SCV causes chlorotic spotting and crinkled leaves. SMoV causes small chlorotic spots and mild mottling. SMYEV shows marginal chlorosis and leaf cupping. 2) Whitefly-transmitted criniviruses. 3) Pollen-borne ilarviruses including strawberry necrotic shock virus. 4) Nematode-transmitted nepoviruses like tomato ringspot and strawberry latent ringspot viruses. Multiple virus infections act synergistically causing severe reductions in vigor, runner production and yield.

Prevention strategies: 1) Plant only virus-free, certified stock - this is most critical. 2) Eliminate insect and nematode vectors through pest control. 3) Annual replanting prevents virus build-up over time. 4) Use varieties with resistance to common aphid vectors. 5) Control aphids, whiteflies and nematodes promptly. 6) Remove infected plants immediately to prevent spread. 7) Avoid planting near infected fields. There are NO effective treatments once plants are infected, so prevention is essential. Thermal treatment of meristems is used to eliminate viruses from propagation stock.

Phytoplasma diseases transmitted by leaf hoppers: 1) Aster yellows - older leaves turn red, lie flat on ground, plant usually dead within 2 months. Common in North America, Europe, Australasia, Japan and Russia. 2) Green petal disease (clover phyllody) - most obvious symptom is production of virescent and adherent green petals that later turn red, and fruits become 'buttoned'. Found in north-eastern North America, Europe and Australia. Both caused by phytoplasma in aster yellows taxonomic groups.

Control measures: 1) Plant virus-free stock (phytoplasma control is similar to virus control). 2) Eliminate leafhopper vectors through insecticide application when populations are high. 3) Remove infected plants immediately as they cannot be cured. 4) Control weeds that serve as alternate hosts for leafhoppers. 5) No effective treatments exist once plants are infected, so prevention through vector control and clean plants is essential. 6) Monitor for leafhopper populations and control before they can transmit disease.

Site selection is critical: 1) Choose land with well-drained soil - many diseases favor wet conditions. 2) If planting on site previously in sod/grass, evaluate white grub presence and density. 3) Avoid siting near woods or fencerows to avoid clipper and root weevils. 4) Avoid siting near old plantings to prevent migration of aphids, clipper, crown borers, fungal diseases, miners, moths and root weevils. 5) During site preparation, plant cover crop(s) year prior. 6) Adjust soil pH to 5.5-6.5. 7) Cultivate deeply to break up hard pan or subsoil problems. 8) Use raised bed system for sites with excessive water or poor drainage.

Variety selection is crucial: 1) Select clean plant material from reputable nursery to avoid angular leaf spot, crown rot, cyclamen mite, leaf fungal diseases and viruses. 2) Plant varieties resistant to insect pests when available. 3) Plant varieties resistant to leaf diseases - resistant varieties exist for most leaf pathogens. 4) Plant varieties resistant to root rots and crown rot. 5) Some varieties have resistance to aphid vectors. 6) Genotypes with some resistance to anthracnose and Botrytis fruit rots have been identified, though resistance not strong enough to preclude other controls. Resistant varieties are foundation of integrated disease management.

Water management is critical for disease control: 1) Avoid standing water and saturated soils to minimize spread of fungal and bacterial diseases. 2) Minimize free water on leaves - leaf spot needs at least 12 hours continuous free moisture for infection. 3) Many pathogens spread by splashing water (anthracnose, leaf scorch, leather rot, leaf blight). 4) Red stele develops best when soils are saturated during cool seasons. 5) Phytophthora diseases favor wet conditions. 6) Use drip irrigation instead of overhead when possible. 7) Irrigate in morning so foliage dries quickly. 8) Ensure good drainage throughout field. Water management affects nearly every strawberry disease.

Crop rotation is essential: 1) Rotate every 2-4 years for 2-3 years with non-host crops to minimize various pests especially root pathogens and weeds. 2) Rotations incorporating other crops and fallow helps reduce populations of shorter-lived pathogens. 3) Lack of crop rotation is most highly correlated factor with severe black root rot. 4) Verticillium can survive 25 years in soil, so very long rotations needed if present. 5) Red stele fungus survives more than decade in soil. 6) Avoid planting strawberries after potatoes, tomatoes, peppers (Verticillium hosts). 7) Small grains or legumes make good rotation crops. Rotation breaks disease and pest cycles.

Planting system choices affect disease: 1) Use raised bed planting system for sites with excessive soil water or poor drainage to minimize fungal diseases of roots and fruit. 2) Establish plant rows with adequate spacing to minimize fungal diseases of leaves and fruit. 3) Flat culture associated with worse black root rot compared to raised beds. 4) Raised beds improve drainage critical for controlling red stele, crown rot, black root rot, leather rot. 5) Proper spacing improves air circulation reducing leaf diseases and grey mould. 6) In annual production, plastic mulches increase anthracnose but straw mulch reduces it. Consider disease pressure when choosing system.

Mulch choice critically affects diseases: 1) STRAW MULCH: Very important for controlling leather rot, grey mould and anthracnose by directly protecting fruit from inoculum and limiting splash dispersal. Recommended for disease management. 2) PLASTIC MULCH: Actually INCREASES incidence of anthracnose and splash dispersal compared to straw. Used in annual systems but has disease trade-offs. 3) After harvest, maintain mulch between rows to suppress weeds and control fruit rots. 4) However, moist thick straw mulches favor slug development - balance needed. 5) Remove or thin mulch after harvest if slug problems exist. Straw superior for disease control despite slug concern.

Nitrogen management affects disease: 1) Excessive nitrogen use in spring has been associated with INCREASED levels of Botrytis fruit rot - use moderate rates. 2) High nitrogen produces lush, dense foliage that stays wet longer, favoring leaf diseases. 3) Excessive nitrogen reduces air circulation within canopy. 4) However, nitrogen deficiency stresses plants making them more susceptible to other problems. 5) Use moderate, balanced fertilization. 6) Avoid heavy nitrogen applications just before bloom. 7) Consider split applications rather than single heavy dose. Proper nitrogen rates support plant health without promoting disease.

Moisture requirements vary by disease: 1) LEAF SPOT: Needs at least 12 hours of continuous free moisture for infection to occur - this is critical threshold. 2) LEAF SCORCH: Conidia produced throughout season when moisture levels adequate; spread mostly by splashing water. 3) LEAF BLIGHT: Conidia spread primarily by water. 4) POWDERY MILDEW: Spread facilitated by moderate to high humidity (doesn't require free water like others). 5) Most leaf diseases spread by splashing water. This is why minimizing leaf wetness duration and avoiding overhead irrigation are so important. Morning irrigation allows leaves to dry quickly.

Temperature requirements vary: 1) RED STELE: Optimal disease development at 13-15°C - cool season disease. 2) POWDERY MILDEW: Spread facilitated by temperatures of 15-27°C and moderate to high humidity. 3) GREY MOULD: Disease development favored by wet conditions and WARM temperatures. 4) CROWN ROT: Plants most susceptible when temperatures are HIGH in early to mid-summer. 5) CHARCOAL ROT and FUSARIUM: Appear after plants established, generally in warmer conditions. 6) Cool, wet conditions favor most Phytophthora diseases. Understanding temperature relationships helps predict disease risk and time preventive measures.

Soil characteristics affect diseases: 1) RED STELE: Particularly troublesome in HEAVY CLAY SOILS saturated with water during cool seasons. 2) BLACK ROOT ROT: Compacted or fine-textured soils most highly correlated with severe infestations. 3) Root diseases generally worse in poorly drained, heavy soils. 4) Sandy loams with good drainage reduce many root disease problems. 5) Raised beds help overcome poor drainage in heavy soils. 6) Clay soils hold more water, favoring water-mold diseases like Phytophthora. 7) Soil amendments to improve drainage and structure help disease management. Proper soil management is foundation of disease control.

Alternaria black leaf spot, caused by Alternaria alternata f. fragariae, occurs in Europe, New Zealand, Korea and Japan. It causes localized economic problems in these regions. Lesions appear on upper leaves as circular or irregular patches (2-5 mm) that are brown with dark purplish margins. This disease is distinct from the common leaf spot and leaf scorch found in North America. Controlled through same general cultural practices as other leaf diseases - sanitation, air circulation, and resistant varieties where available.

Rhizoctonia fruit rot (hard rot), caused by Rhizoctonia solani, is important pathogen of many worldwide crops. In strawberries, it's most severe where fruit are allowed to touch soil. Symptoms include light brown fruit that soften and collapse, with their juices leaking out. The same organism also causes Rhizoctonia root rot where plants suddenly collapse during early fruiting. Undersides of leaves become purplish and numerous side crowns formed around dead ones. Control by using mulch to prevent fruit-soil contact and maintaining good drainage.

Rhizopus rot (leak), caused by Rhizopus species, can occur worldwide and has caused severe problems in UK preserve industry. Symptoms include slightly discolored fruits that gradually turn light brown. Fruit eventually collapse, become covered with dense, fluffy mycelium and their juices leak out - hence name 'leak'. The importance of Rhizopus rot is GREATLY DIMINISHED BY RAPID COOLING AFTER HARVEST. This is key control measure. Proper post-harvest handling - immediate cooling and refrigeration - is more important than field control for this disease.

Sclerotina crown rot, caused by Sclerotina sclerotiorum, is primarily crown rotting organism in southern USA but can also affect fruit (Sclerotina rot). Both crowns and fruit become covered with dense white mycelium containing sclerotia - hard, black survival structures. This distinguishes it from grey mould which has grey, dusty spores rather than sclerotia. The sclerotia can survive in soil for years, making crop rotation important. Most problematic in areas with mild winters where sclerotia survive well.

Phomopsis (Dendrophoma) soft rot, caused by Phomopsis obscurans, is very important fruit rot in Florida. The same organism also causes leaf blight. On fruit, it's commonly associated with stem-end rot and appears initially as light pink, water-soaked lesions that eventually turn brown with crusty centers. This pink appearance distinguishes it from other fruit rots. Can be serious in warm, humid conditions. Control through fungicides, sanitation, and avoiding conditions that favor the disease.

Fungicide timing is critical: 1) Most efficient control strategies incorporate fungicide sprays PRIMARILY AT BLOOM for fruit rots. 2) Grey mould fungus initially colonizes senescing flowers during bloom period, so bloom sprays are most effective. 3) Predictive models have been developed to target fungicide sprays based on disease cycles and environmental conditions rather than calendar-based applications. 4) For leaf diseases, regular preventive sprays may be needed, but good sanitation is more important. 5) Although fungicides are frequently used as prophylactics, targeted sprays at critical times (especially bloom) are most efficient and economical.

Sanitation is KEY to good disease control: 1) For leaf diseases, good sanitation is key - more important than fungicides. 2) Remove old leaves after harvest - they serve as inoculum source. 3) Remove and destroy foliar residues to control fruit rots. 4) For fruit rots, promptly remove all ripe fruit and cull berries from field. 5) Destroy mummified fruit that overwinter and produce spores in spring. 6) Remove litter in and around fields. 7) Nursery fields are important source of some leaf diseases in fruiting fields, making good control in plant-production fields critical. 8) Many pathogens overwinter on plant debris, so removal eliminates inoculum source. Sanitation prevents disease before it starts.

Stress greatly increases disease susceptibility: 1) Root weevils cause worst damage when plants under periods of stress. 2) Drought-stressed plants most subject to spider mite attack. 3) Crown rot infection most severe when plants are stressed and temperatures high. 4) Black root rot often associated with winter injury, fertilizer burn, soil compaction, herbicide damage, drought, excess salt, waterlogging or improper pH. 5) Many root diseases more severe in stressed plants. Maintaining plant health through proper nutrition, irrigation, pH management, and avoiding injury reduces disease and pest problems. Healthy plants better resist all problems.

Organic amendments show promise for disease control: 1) Use of composts that encourage growth of bacteria and fungi that suppress plant pathogens will prove important in future. 2) Sustaining high yields likely requires integrated approach employing disease-resistant cultivars AND soil amendments that suppress pathogen activity. 3) Composts work by supporting beneficial microorganism communities that compete with or antagonize pathogens. 4) This approach becoming more important with fumigation phase-out. 5) Cover crops during year prior to planting can also help. 6) Biological strategies work best when combined with other management practices. Future of strawberry disease management likely involves more biological and organic approaches.

Future disease management will be integrated: 1) With methyl bromide phase-out, sustaining high yields requires INTEGRATED approach. 2) Key components: disease-resistant cultivars, soil amendments suppressing pathogen activity, maintaining good air flow, minimizing standing water, starting with clean planting stock. 3) Use of composts encouraging beneficial bacteria and fungi. 4) Biological controls for soil-borne and foliar diseases. 5) Solarization in high-temperature areas. 6) Strategic use of alternative fumigants where needed. 7) Emphasis on prevention through cultural practices rather than just chemical control. 8) Combination of multiple tactics will replace reliance on single fumigation approach. Future is about building healthy soil and plant systems.

Look for angular dark brown or black spots on leaves with a yellow border. On stems and fruit, you'll see longer, sunken lesions. It often looks like dark, sunken sores.
Rotate your watermelon crop with a non-cucurbit crop (like corn or beans) for 1-2 years. After harvest, plow any leftover vines or fruit deeply into the soil to break down the fungus.

Yes. Downy mildew first causes yellow mottling on leaves, which then develop dark brown, angular lesions. Infected leaves often curl inwards. You might see a fuzzy, purplish-gray growth on the leaf underside in humid conditions.

Avoid overcrowding plants for better air flow. Always water at the base of the plant (drip irrigation is best), never overhead, to keep leaves dry. Remove and destroy severely infected leaves if the outbreak is small.
These are classic symptoms of Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV). Plants are often severely stunted, leaves show a yellow mosaic pattern, curl downwards, and fruit becomes small and distorted.

The main strategy is controlling aphids, which spread the virus. Use reflective mulches early in the season to deter them. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control weeds that host aphids.
This is Powdery Mildew. It starts as white powdery spots on older leaves, which can spread to cover the leaf surface. Leaves may turn reddish or bronze underneath the powder.

Plant in full sun with good air movement. Avoid too much nitrogen fertilizer which makes plants succulent and susceptible. Some resistant varieties are available. Spraying with a baking soda solution (1 tbsp per gallon of water) can help as a preventative.

This could be Fusarium Wilt. A key symptom is wilting that starts on one or a few vines. The leaves look dull gray-green before yellowing. If you cut the stem near the base, you may see reddish-brown streaks inside.

The most effective strategy is long crop rotation (at least 4-5 years) away from watermelon, cucumber, and other cucurbits. Plant certified, disease-free seed. Choose resistant varieties if available for your region.
This describes Gummy Stem Blight. Look for round brown lesions on leaves that may have faint rings. On stems and fruit, you'll see circular brown spots that may ooze an amber-colored, sticky gum.

Start with disease-free seed. Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-cucurbits. After harvest, plow debris deep. Fungicide sprays (like chlorothalonil) may be needed preventatively, especially in warm, wet weather.
Alternaria causes small, irregular or circular dark brown to black spots on older leaves. The spots often have a target-like pattern of concentric circles. They can merge to form large dead patches.

Protective fungicides like Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or copper-based products can be applied when conditions favor disease. Apply at first sign of disease and repeat as per label, ensuring thorough leaf coverage.
This is a warning sign for Bacterial Fruit Blotch (BFB). The small, dark green, water-soaked spots on the fruit surface can quickly enlarge, turn brown or crack, ruining the fruit.

This is critical: Always use certified, pathogen-free seed and transplants. Inspect seedlings carefully. Avoid overhead irrigation. Do not work in the field when plants are wet, as the bacteria spread easily in water.
Yes, Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV) also causes mosaic symptoms. Leaves show a green mosaic pattern, vein banding, or yellow rings. It is also spread by aphids and symptoms can be very similar to CMV.
This describes Angular Leaf Spot, a bacterial disease. The spots are confined by leaf veins, giving them an angular shape. In high humidity, you might see a milky ooze that dries to a white crust.
This could be Cercospora Leaf Spot. It starts as small, light brown spots with a darker border on older leaves. The spots can enlarge and the centers may become brittle and crack.

These are bizarre symptoms of Aster Yellows, caused by a phytoplasma. Plants are stunted, produce many secondary shoots (witches'-broom), leaves turn yellow and may be thickened. It is spread by leafhoppers.

This could be Verticillium Wilt. Unlike Fusarium, it often appears later (after fruit set) and symptoms may be one-sided. Cutting the stem may show brown discoloration in the vascular tissue. It favors cooler spring weather.

For downy mildew, use fungicides specifically labeled for it, such as those containing fosetyl-Al, metalaxyl, or fungicides from the strobilurin group (e.g., azoxystrobin). Always rotate different chemical groups to prevent resistance. Start sprays when weather is cool and humid.

Yes, but you must use fungicides that are safe and labeled for use on watermelons during the fruiting stage. Products containing chlorothalonil or mancozeb are often used as protectants. Always follow the pre-harvest interval (PHI) on the label—the number of days you must wait between spraying and harvest.

Practice strict sanitation. Disinfect tools (pruners, knives, stakes) and hands frequently. Use a solution of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water, or a commercial disinfectant like Virkon. Especially important after handling an infected plant.

Yes. Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV) causes some of the most severe symptoms: extreme stunting, leaves become severely deformed, blistered, and show a yellow mosaic. Fruits are also badly distorted.

Anthracnose appears as dark brown to black sunken spots on leaves, stems, and fruits. Leaf spots may develop holes in the center. Fruits develop round, sunken lesions that later turn black. The disease spreads fast during rainy and humid weather.

Spray protective fungicides like Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb at 7–10 day intervals. For better control, rotate systemic fungicides such as Azoxystrobin or Pyraclostrobin + Boscalid. Always rotate fungicide groups to avoid resistance.
Use disease-free seed, follow 2–3 year crop rotation with non-cucurbit crops, remove infected plant debris after harvest, and avoid overhead irrigation. Good air circulation reduces disease spread.
Downy mildew starts as yellow angular spots on the upper side of leaves. On the lower surface, grey to purple fuzzy growth appears. Leaves dry up quickly in cool and humid weather.
Use fungicides like Cymoxanil + Mancozeb, Cyazofamid, or Propamocarb in rotation with Chlorothalonil. Spray at 7-day intervals during cool and wet weather for best control.
Avoid overhead irrigation, maintain proper plant spacing for airflow, remove infected leaves, and avoid working in wet fields. Early detection and timely spray help prevent crop loss.
Mosaic virus causes light and dark green patchy patterns on leaves, leaf curling, stunted growth, and deformed fruits. Plants remain weak and yield reduces heavily.
Control aphids using neem oil or recommended insecticides, remove and destroy infected plants, and avoid planting near old cucurbit crops. There is no cure once plants are infected.
Use virus-free seedlings, control aphids in nursery, remove weeds around the field, and avoid planting near infected cucurbit crops. Reflective mulching also reduces aphid landing.
Water-soaked spots appear on fruits which later turn dark and crack. Leaves may show small brown lesions. Fruits rot quickly in humid weather and become unmarketable.
Spray copper-based bactericides at early flowering stage. Use disease-free seed and avoid overhead irrigation. Chemical sprays give only partial suppression.
Damping off causes seedlings to rot at soil level and collapse. It occurs due to fungal infection in wet and poorly drained nursery beds.
Use sterilized soil media, avoid overwatering, ensure good drainage, and treat seeds with fungicide or Trichoderma before sowing.
Plants wilt during daytime and recover at night initially. Later, one side of the vine yellows and the whole plant collapses. Cutting the stem shows brown discoloration.
Follow long crop rotation (5–6 years), use resistant varieties, avoid planting in infected fields, and improve soil health using organic matter.
Dark brown lesions appear on stems and leaves with gummy ooze. Leaves dry up and vines may crack near the base.
Spray Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Pyraclostrobin + Boscalid in rotation at 7–10 day intervals. Avoid using same fungicide repeatedly.
Fruits develop water-soaked lesions that quickly become soft and rotten. White fungal growth may appear on fruit surface in wet fields.
Select well-drained fields, avoid waterlogging, use raised beds, and rotate with non-host crops. Fungicides provide only partial suppression.
Use certified seed, maintain field sanitation, rotate crops, ensure proper spacing, monitor pests regularly, and apply sprays only when needed.
Combine resistant varieties, crop rotation, field sanitation, regular scouting, and need-based fungicide spraying. Avoid repeated use of same chemicals.

Water-soaked lesions appear on leaves which later become yellowish irregular spots. These foliage spots are irregular and turn dark brown or black. Stem lesions can girdle the stem and cause vines to wilt.

The most striking diagnostic symptoms are circular, black, sunken cankers on the fruit. The spots may measure 1/4 to 1/2 inch (6 to 13 mm) in diameter and up to 1/4 inch (6 mm) deep. When moisture is present, the black center of the lesion is covered with a gelatinous mass of salmon-colored spores.

Use trellising or provide support system for watermelon plants. Control alternate weed hosts like wild cucumber, golden creeper and volunteer cucumbers in neighboring fence rows and field edges. The bower system of cropping reduces disease incidence. Seed production should be preferably carried out in summer season because summer crop is often free from diseases.
The fungus survives in diseased plant debris and overwinters on diseased residue from the previous vine crop in the form of resting spores. Secondary infection occurs by means of wind-borne conidia.
Temperature of 24-30°C and high relative humidity up to 100% for 24 hours is optimum for fungal growth and infection. A thin film of water on the leaf surface is required for infection.
Watermelon-F1 midnight, watermelon F1 bengal tiger, watermelon-F1 sweet dragon, and watermelon-F1 wonder hybrid are resistant/tolerant to both anthracnose and wilt.

Yellow, angular spots restricted by veins resembling mosaic mottling appear on upper surface of leaves. The corresponding lower surface of these spots shows a purplish downy growth in moist weather. The spots turn necrotic with age and diseased leaves become yellow and fall down.
Relative humidity greater than 85%, high soil moisture, and frequent rains favor downy mildew development. The disease is most severe during rainy seasons.

Use trellising or provide support system for watermelon plants to improve air circulation. Control alternate weed hosts such as wild cucumber, golden creeper and volunteer cucumbers in neighboring areas. The bower system of cropping reduces disease incidence. Avoid water stress and water stagnation conditions.

The pathogen survives in diseased plant debris. Primary spread occurs by means of oospores in soil and sporangia from perennial collateral weed hosts in the vicinity. Secondary spread occurs by wind and rain splashes.

Symptoms of mosaic appear on the youngest leaves when infection occurs at 6-8 leaves stage. Leaves curl downwards and become mottled, distorted, wrinkled and reduced in size. Veins appear bunchy because of shortening of internodes. Fruits are often misshapen, mottled, warty and reduced in size.

Raise 4 rows of barrier crops such as maize/sorghum/bajra around the field. Avoid planting tomatoes next to cucurbits, spinach, or other vegetables and flowers susceptible to these diseases. Control aphid vectors effectively and remove weed hosts from the vicinity.

The virus particles are transmitted by aphids (Aphis craccivora, Myzus persicae) and spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Primary infection comes from virus particles on collateral and other weeds, ornamentals or crops.

Avoid high levels of nitrogen fertilizer as it favors aphid reproduction. Release 1st instar larvae of green lacewing (Chrysoperla zastrowi sillemi) @ 4,000 numbers per acre. Use yellow sticky traps @ 4-5 traps per acre. Spray tobacco decoction (1 Kg tobacco boiled in 10 liters of water for 30 minutes and making up to 30 liters + 100 g soap).

Whitish powdery growth appears on upper foliage, stems and young growing parts. The superficial growth ultimately covers the entire leaf area. The diseased areas turn brown and dry leading to premature defoliation and death. Fruits remain underdeveloped and are deformed.
Morning relative humidity greater than 50% combined with cool and dry weather favors powdery mildew development.
The bower system of cropping with proper gapping reduces the disease incidence by improving air circulation. Ensure adequate plant spacing and good ventilation in the field.
Arka Manik variety shows resistance/tolerance to powdery mildew.
The symptoms are first observed at the top portion of the plant. Round to irregular target board spots appear on older leaves.
The disease is favored by continuous wet conditions with frequent rainfall and high humidity.
Sugar baby, Fairfax, and Calhoun gray varieties show resistance/tolerance to Alternaria leaf spot.
The first symptom appears as chlorosis (yellowing) of the leaves. Wilting of leaves from bottom to top occurs. Brown vascular discolouration inside infected stem or root leads to the death of plants.
Relatively high soil moisture and high soil temperature are favorable for Fusarium wilt infection.
Immediately uproot and burn the infected plants to prevent further spread of the disease in the field.

Watermelon-F1 sweet sensation, watermelon-F1 big guy are resistant to wilt. Additionally, Watermelon-F1 midnight, bengal tiger, sweet dragon, and wonder hybrid are resistant to both anthracnose and wilt.

Chlorotic rings, mottling, and crinkling appear on leaves of stunted plants. These spots turn brownish black, and leaves become brown and distorted. The surface of fruits develop ring spots which later turn to tan, necrotic or scab-like lesions.
Thrips are the main vector for transmitting the bud necrosis virus. Dry and hot periods when thrips population increases rapidly favor the spread of the disease.

Maintain a clean buffer zone free of weeds of at least 25 meters between a virus source and a susceptible crop to considerably reduce virus levels. Control thrips population through appropriate management practices.
Start fungicide sprays when vines begin to run or as soon as the first disease spots appear. During rainy and humid weather, spray at 7-day intervals. Early protection prevents severe yield loss.
Rotate fungicides with different modes of action, avoid repeated use of the same product, and always mix systemic fungicides with protectant fungicides like Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil.
Monitor local disease alerts and weather forecasts. Downy mildew spreads rapidly in cool and humid conditions. Begin preventive sprays when the disease is reported in nearby areas.
During favorable disease conditions (cool, humid weather), spray every 7 days. In dry weather, extend spray interval to 10–14 days while continuing field scouting.
Yes, removing infected leaves, avoiding movement in wet fields, and destroying crop residues after harvest help reduce disease spread and carryover.
Regularly check the underside of young leaves for aphids. Use yellow sticky traps to monitor aphid movement. Early aphid control reduces virus spread.
Yes, immediately remove and destroy infected plants to reduce virus sources for aphids. Do not compost infected plants inside the field.
Weeds can host aphids and virus. Keeping field borders and bunds weed-free reduces aphid buildup and lowers virus transmission to watermelon plants.
Use pathogen-free seed, avoid overhead watering in nursery, disinfect tools and trays, and avoid transplanting wet seedlings.
Avoid working in wet fields, provide good air circulation, rotate crops for at least 2 years, and remove infected plant residues.
Yes, seed treatment with fungicides or biologicals like Trichoderma helps prevent damping off. Avoid excessive watering to reduce fungal growth.
Fusarium survives in soil for many years. Planting in previously infected fields increases disease risk. Choose clean fields with long crop rotation history.
Yes, growing fusarium-resistant varieties reduces plant loss and improves yield, especially in fields with past disease history.
The pathogen survives in plant debris. Removing and destroying crop residues after harvest reduces carryover of disease to the next season.
Yes, preventive fungicide sprays at vine running stage reduce early infection and limit disease spread during humid weather.
Phytophthora spreads rapidly in standing water. Raised beds, proper drainage, and avoiding flood irrigation reduce disease outbreaks.
No, fungicides only suppress phytophthora blight. Best control comes from field drainage, raised beds, and crop rotation combined with sprays.
Yes, contaminated tools can spread pathogens between fields. Clean and disinfect tools regularly, especially after working in infected fields.

Anthracnose appears as small brown spots that are circular to angular in shape on leaves. These leaf spots enlarge, coalesce and crack. On stems and petioles, elongated tan-colored lesions develop. On fruit, circular spots ranging from ¼ to ½ inch in diameter appear, which crack and become sunken with decay extending into the flesh.

Anthracnose can be managed with fungicide spray programs consisting of preventive sprays on 7- to 14-day intervals beginning at bloom and early fruit set. Use resistant varieties classified as resistant to anthracnose race 1, though note that race 2 (common in watermelon) may still cause disease. Combine fungicide applications with crop rotation for best results.

Anthracnose is favored by extended periods of warm and rainy weather. The disease spreads through splashing rain, sprinkler irrigation, or surface runoff. Spores produced on infected debris and volunteers spread to plants through these water-mediated means, and disease increases through repeated cycles of infection.

Practice crop rotation with non-cucurbit crops for at least 3 years. The fungus overwinters on infected debris and volunteers, so plow under crop residue completely and control volunteer plants from diseased melons left in the field. Avoid overhead irrigation when possible, as splashing water spreads the disease. Use disease-free seed from reputable sources.

Downy mildew first appears as pale green to yellow blotches on older leaves that develop into circular to irregular spots that are dark brown to black. Affected leaves curl inward, quickly die and remain attached to upright petioles, giving a scorched appearance. Unlike anthracnose, petioles and stems remain intact for some time after defoliation.

Preventive fungicide spray programs are essential for downy mildew control. Protectant fungicides like chlorothalonil and mancozeb are effective when applied on a preventive schedule. Numerous other fungicides with specific activity on downy mildews are available. Important: some fungicides effective for anthracnose and gummy stem blight may not control downy mildew, so proper selection is crucial.

Late-season crops are at highest risk from downy mildew, though it can occur as early as July in Oklahoma. The disease is favored by high humidity, leaf wetness, and warm temperatures up to 80°F. The pathogen doesn't overwinter locally but spreads northward as airborne spores from southern production areas as the season progresses. The spores can tolerate hot days and remain infective.

Yes, downy mildew forecasts are available at https://cdm.ipmpipe.org/. These forecasts are based on reported occurrences of the disease during the season that serve as sources of spores to infect new fields. The forecast provides an assessment of the risk of losing a watermelon field to downy mildew, helping growers time their fungicide applications.

Virus symptoms are most striking on new growth of young plants. Leaves become dwarfed, misshapen, puckered, pale green and exhibit mosaic patterns of light and dark green color. Infected plants remain stunted throughout the season and may fail to set fruit or produce small, poor-quality fruit. Sometimes vine terminals become erect and hover over the canopy. Plants infected early are most severely affected.

Viruses are primarily spread by aphids, but can also spread mechanically or by cucumber beetles. Aphids acquire virus by feeding on infected crops or weeds that serve as virus reservoirs. They then migrate to watermelon crops and rapidly infect plants during probing and feeding. Initial infection comes from aphids moving field to field, while melon aphids within fields cause secondary spread. Aphid numbers increase as the season progresses, making late plantings particularly vulnerable.

Plant early to avoid late-season aphid buildup. Use reflective plastic mulches to repel aphids. Control weeds in and around fields as they harbor aphids and viruses. Don't plant late-season watermelons near or downwind of infected fields. Consider planting alternating strips of grain sorghum or short-statured summer grass with watermelons to act as a 'virus sieve' - aphids intercepted by grass may lose infectivity. Note: insecticide control of aphids is not effective as they infect plants before being killed.

Follow integrated pest management: 1) Rotate with non-cucurbit crops for 3-4 years, 2) Select well-drained sandy loam sites with pH 6.0-6.8, 3) Use disease-free seed and healthy transplants, 4) Remove or incorporate crop debris after harvest, 5) Use drip irrigation instead of sprinkler when possible, 6) Scout fields weekly for early pest detection, 7) Plant resistant varieties where available, 8) Apply preventive fungicide sprays when needed. Avoid planting late crops adjacent to early plantings.

Symptoms typically appear from vine running through fruit set. Foliage takes on a dull, greyish-green appearance. Vines wilt, become dry, turn brown and die. Wilt is often one-sided - individual vines wilt before the entire plant dies. Elongated brown lesions may appear on stems near the crown with pink spore masses in wet weather. The key diagnostic sign is a distinct reddish-brown discoloration of the central vascular core (xylem) when stems are cut near the soil line.

Yes, resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 is widely available in varieties and hybrids. Race 1 is predominant in Oklahoma with only a few cases of race 2 identified. However, seedless (triploid) watermelons are generally susceptible. For susceptible varieties, grafting onto resistant rootstocks is an effective alternative. Bottle gourd and interspecific winter squash hybrid rootstocks provide resistance to Fusarium wilt.

Two main rootstock types: 1) Bottle gourd (Lagenaria siceraria) varieties include Coloso, Emphasis, Macis, Skopje, FR Gold, Jingxinzhen No. 1, WMXP 3938, and WMXP 3945 - these provide Fusarium wilt resistance, chilling tolerance, and promote earlier maturity. 2) Interspecific hybrids (Cucurbita maxima x C. moschata) include P360, Marathon, RS 841, Shintosa, Shintosa Camel, Strong Tosa, Carnivor, and Qingyanzhen No.1 - these increase root vigor but may delay maturity. Test combinations before large-scale production.

A minimum 6-year crop rotation is recommended to reduce levels of Fusarium wilt fungus. Shorter rotations (3-4 years) can help limit fungus increase and prevent development of races that attack resistant varieties. Avoid fields with known Fusarium wilt history. Cover crops like hairy vetch and crimson clover have reduced Fusarium wilt in some environments. Clean equipment to avoid introducing infested soil into clean fields.

Fruit infections first appear as small, water-soaked areas on the upper surface of melons. As melons mature, the water-soaked area rapidly expands to cover a large portion of the fruit surface. Initially, blotches don't extend into the rind, but affected rinds eventually crack and become invaded by secondary pathogens. On foliage, small water-soaked areas (few millimeters) appear on cotyledons or leaves but are easily overlooked and later turn brown.

Control centers on planting pathogen-free seed and transplants. The seed industry has adopted testing protocols including seed testing, seedling grow-outs, and inspection of seed production fields to limit sale of contaminated seed lots. Only use high-quality seed tested for bacterial fruit blotch. Ensure transplants appear healthy before planting. The bacterium is primarily seedborne, making seed quality critical for disease prevention.

The disease is favored by warm humid conditions, splashing water, and overhead irrigation. Transplant production greenhouses with crowded plants, sprinkler irrigation, and warm temperatures favor transplant infection and disease spread. The disease has been more severe where crops are initiated with transplants compared to direct seeding. Yield losses up to 50% have been reported when conditions are favorable.

On watermelon, gummy stem blight is mainly confined to foliage. Leaf spots are circular to irregular, large (up to ¾ inch diameter), and dark brown to black. Spots often develop at leaf margins, which is unusual for most foliar diseases. Heavily spotted leaves are killed. Fruiting bodies of the fungus appear as tiny black specks on affected petioles. Unlike downy mildew, affected foliage does not remain erect.

The gummy stem blight fungus has developed resistance to several classes of fungicides. It's critical to alternate applications of fungicides with different modes of action in preventive spray programs. Control is achieved primarily with fungicides combined with crop rotation. Apply fungicides preventively rather than waiting for symptoms to appear. Consult the OSU Extension Agent's Handbook for current fungicide recommendations.

Practice a minimum 2-year crop rotation for complete decomposition of infested crop debris. Separate new fields from old infested fields by at least 1,000 feet to reduce exposure to spores. The fungus survives on infested crop residue and contaminated seed. Disease is favored by cool to warm rainy weather, high humidity, and wet soils. Both asexual spores (spread by splashing rain) and sexual spores (airborne, long-distance spread) are produced.

Cercospora leaf spot appears on younger leaves as circular dark brown to purple spots about ¼ inch in diameter. As spots enlarge, the centers become tan to grey but retain their dark margins. The disease is mostly confined to leaves, though stems and petioles may be affected. Leaves are killed when enlarging spots coalesce. The disease generally is of minor importance but can cause defoliation in eastern Oklahoma where humidity is highest.

Yes, fungicide spray programs are very effective on Cercospora leaf spot. Combine with crop rotation, incorporation of old crop residue, and rotation with non-cucurbit crops for 3 years to limit pathogen carryover. The fungus overwinters on crop debris where it produces airborne spores. Infection is favored by warm temperatures (80-90°F) and extended periods of leaf wetness.

Powdery mildew first appears on oldest leaves as yellow areas on the upper leaf surface. White mildew on the leaf underside may only be visible with a hand lens initially. As disease progresses, whitish powdery growth becomes apparent and can cover both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Affected leaves eventually wither and die, causing extensive defoliation. Fruit may also develop mildew symptoms. The disease has increased in importance on watermelon, particularly late plantings.

All watermelon varieties and hybrids are susceptible to powdery mildew, making fungicide sprays essential. Preventive spray programs with fungicides are effective, but the fungus readily develops fungicide resistance, often within a single season. Therefore, utilize fungicides with different modes of action in rotation. Sulfur is effective on powdery mildew and is permitted in organic production. Apply fungicides before disease becomes established for best results.

Aboveground symptoms include yellowed, stunted, or generally unthrifty plants, often appearing in patchy areas. Diagnosis requires uprooting plants to examine roots. Affected roots are disfigured, swollen, and stubby with characteristic galls ranging from ¼ to over ½ inch in diameter. Gall size depends on nematode species and infestation degree. Southern root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita) is most common in small farms and gardens in Oklahoma.

Prevention is key - avoid carrying infested soil on tools, equipment, or transplants. Practice crop rotation with non-host crops, though southern root-knot has a wide host range including most vegetables and corn. Soil solarization (capturing solar radiation to heat soil) reduces nematodes. Add organic matter as nematodes thrive in coarse, sandy soils low in organic matter. Test soil for nematode levels before planting. Grafting onto citron melon 'Ojakkyo' rootstock provides nematode resistance but not Fusarium wilt resistance.

Yellow vine is caused by the interaction of squash bugs (Anasa tristis) and the bacterium Serratia marcescens. Affected plants, often in patches near field edges, turn yellow and die back. Numerous squash bugs or evidence of feeding will be present. When basal stems are cross-sectioned, a ring of light brown discoloration appears around the outer part (phloem) of the vascular core. The dysfunctional phloem causes yellowing. While less susceptible than pumpkins and squash, it's significant in Oklahoma watermelons.

Management focuses on squash bug control, which is critical for successful watermelon production. Methods include: 1) Mechanical removal of bugs and bronze-colored egg masses from leaf undersides, 2) Insecticide applications, 3) Physical exclusion using row covers, 4) Novel trap crop approach - plant nearby strips of summer squash (highly attractive to squash bugs), then spray the trap crop to kill bugs, avoiding treatment of the main watermelon crop.

Anthracnose spots are dark, round to irregular, and often develop sunken centers that later form holes. On fruits, lesions are circular and sunken. Other leaf spots usually lack deep sunken fruit lesions.
Yes, during frequent rains and high humidity, shorten spray intervals to 5–7 days. In dry weather, extend to 10–14 days while continuing scouting.
Check older leaves first for yellow angular patches on the upper surface and grey-purple growth on the lower surface, especially in low-lying and humid parts of the field.
Rotate fungicides with different FRAC groups, avoid repeated use of the same active ingredient, and always tank-mix systemic fungicides with protectants like Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb.
Downy mildew infects the lower leaf surface. Good spray coverage ensures fungicides reach the underside of leaves, improving disease control.
Young plants show light green mottling, slight leaf curling, and slow growth. Symptoms become clearer as the plant grows.
Yes, non-host border crops can reduce aphid movement into watermelon fields. Reflective mulch and border crops together lower virus spread.
Keep nursery insect-proof with nets, control aphids early, remove symptomatic seedlings, and avoid raising seedlings near cucurbit crops.
Inspect young fruits for small water-soaked spots that enlarge quickly. Early morning inspection helps because lesions look fresh and shiny when wet.
Warm temperatures combined with high humidity and frequent rain favor bacterial fruit blotch. Avoid overhead irrigation during such conditions.
Disinfect trays, use sterile growing media, ensure good drainage, and avoid overcrowding seedlings to reduce fungal spread.
Healthy soils with good organic matter and microbial diversity suppress fusarium. Adding compost and practicing crop rotation improves soil health.
Yes, avoid moving contaminated soil on tools and footwear between fields. Clean equipment before entering clean fields.
Small brown leaf spots with yellow halos and dark streaks on stems are early signs. Gummy ooze may appear later.
Warm and humid weather with frequent rains favors gummy stem blight. Dense canopy and poor airflow increase risk.
Fields with poor drainage, low-lying areas, and water stagnation show higher risk. Sudden wilting after heavy rain is a warning sign.
Prepare raised beds, improve drainage, avoid fields with disease history, and plan long rotations with non-host crops.
Monitoring rainfall, humidity, and temperature helps predict disease outbreaks and plan timely preventive sprays.
Spraying based on disease risk, weather conditions, and scouting reduces costs, slows resistance, and improves overall disease control.
The anthracnose pathogen survives on crop residues and infected fruits. Removing and destroying vines and leftover fruits after harvest reduces carryover infection for the next crop.
Downy mildew develops resistance quickly. Rotating fungicides with different modes of action slows resistance and keeps sprays effective throughout the season.
Scout at least twice a week during cool and humid weather. Early detection allows timely spraying and prevents rapid spread.
Yes, reflective mulch repels aphids that transmit mosaic virus, reducing virus spread especially in early crop stages.
Older cucurbit crops can harbor virus and aphids. Planting watermelon away from them reduces early virus infection.
Yes, remove any seedlings with leaf spots or water-soaked lesions. Transplanting infected seedlings spreads the disease into clean fields.
The pathogen can survive on seed. Using certified, tested seed greatly reduces the chance of introducing the disease into the field.
Maintaining good ventilation, moderate temperature, and proper spacing reduces humidity and fungal growth, preventing seedling death.
Yes, covering moist soil with transparent plastic during hot months raises soil temperature and reduces fusarium populations in the upper soil layer.
Yes, adding compost and organic matter improves beneficial microbes in soil that suppress fusarium and improve root health.
Better airflow lowers humidity within the canopy, making conditions less favorable for fungal growth and disease spread.
Yes, treating seed with recommended fungicides or biocontrol agents reduces early seedborne infection and improves seedling health.
Fields with previous phytophthora outbreaks remain risky for several years. Avoid planting watermelon in such fields or improve drainage and rotation.
Drip irrigation is safer than flood or overhead irrigation because it reduces leaf wetness and standing water that favor disease.
Weed-free borders reduce pest and disease reservoirs, lowering the chance of disease and insect movement into the crop.
